fn.0: We have herein translated the words אֹל עוֹלָם in the sense which Maimonides himself ascribes to them in several places, and notably in chapter 29 of the third part of the Guide, albeit in the biblical passage (Genesis, 21, 33) these words signify the eternal God.
fn.1: The verb כנת (كُنتَ) which commenceth the sentence relateth to the words עטֹּם שׁאנך, which it serveth to render in the pluperfect.
fn.2: Vid. my aforementioned Notice upon Joseph ben Yehuda. We shall return to this disciple of Maimonides in the general introduction of this work.—The letters עֹּצ, which follow the name of Joseph, are the abbreviation of עֲמָרָהּ צוּר, the Hebrew preterite being employed, after the Arabic manner, in the sense of the optative.
fn.3: Literally: from the extremities of the lands. Joseph had come from Sabta or Ceuta, situated in the north-west of Africa, which the Arabs called Al-Maghreb al-Akṣa or the extreme West. Vid. the aforesaid Notice, pages 6 and 14.
fn.4: The Makâmât among the Arabs are tales or narratives written in rhymed prose mingled with verse; one is acquainted with the celebrated Makâmât or Sessions of Harizi. This species of composition was imitated in Hebrew by the Jews as early as the first half of the XIIth century, and they were given the name of מחברות; it is indeed this word which R. Yehuda al-Harizi employeth here in his translation, and which rendereth the sense of the Arabic word far better than the word חרוזיך used by Ibn Tibbon. Al-Harizi, in his collection of Makâmât known under the title of Taḥkemoni (תחכמוני), himself citeth from our Joseph a Makâma which had become celebrated. Vid. my aforementioned Notice, p. 48 et seq.
fn.5: Several manuscripts bear במאלך, others במה לך, and others yet כמאלך; it is this latter reading which the translation of Al-Harizi, bearing שכלך השלם, appeareth to express. One must doubtless read במאלך (from מָאל), which Ibn Tibbon hath well rendered by אחריתך. I know not whence Hyde hath derived the reading עקלך, which he pretendeth to change into עקבך. (Vid. the Syntagma dissertationum of Hyde, published by Sharpe, vol. I, p. 436.) This reading is found in none of the Oxford manuscripts, nor in the two mss. of Leyden.
fn.6: This name designateth the religious philosophers or the scholastics of the Arabs. Touching its origin, vid. my Notice upon Rabbi Saadia Gaon, p. 16 et seq. (Bible of M. Cahen, vol. IX, p. 88 et seq.). The author himself giveth numerous details upon the Motekallemin in several places of this work, and notably in the Ist part, ch. 71, 73 et seq. I have given a succinct overview of their doctrines in the Dictionnaire des sciences philosophiques, art. Arabes.
fn.7: All the manuscripts, even those possessing diacritical points, bear בדתך; I deem that it must be pronounced بِذَلِكَ, from the verb بَنّ filaments, prævertit, vicit, so that the words אלדהשֹׁה ברח signify: the trouble or the confusion had taken possession of thee. Ibn Tibbon hath well rendered the word בלחך by דפקתך.
fn.8: These latter words, which the author hath written in Hebrew, are derived from Ecclesiastes, ch. 12, <small>V</small>. 10.
fn.9: By names the author understandeth here not only substantives and adjectives, but also verbs in the infinitive or names of action.
fn.10: The common or appellative noun is called by the Arabs الاسم المتواطئ , or else الاسم المقول بتواطؤ , that is to say, conventional name or stated by convention. The Rabbins have translated these terms by השם המוסכם and השם הנאמר בהסכמה; one may see the definition thereof in the Compendium of Logic (באור מלות ההגיון) of Maimonides, ch. 13. The Arabic term بتواطؤ correspondeth to the Greek words κατὰ συνθήκην, and is borrowed from the Arabic translation of Aristotle’s Organon; vide the treatise On Interpretation, at the commencement of ch. II, where the words: Ὄνομα μὲν οὖν ἐστι φωνὴ σημαντικὴ κατὰ συνθήκην are thus rendered in Arabic: فالاسم هو لفظة دالة بتواطؤ (Ar. Ms. of the Bibl. Nat., no. 882 A).
fn.11: The word man, for example, may be applied to a living man, as well as to a dead man, or to a statue, or to a portrait. If one regardeth only the outward form, the word man, taken in these various senses, may be considered as a true appellative, or common name, designating all that presenteth outwardly the human form; but if one regardeth that which constituteth the true essence of man, the word man, taken in the various senses indicated, will be an homonym, since it designateth at once things of a diverse nature. From this point of view, the word man is called اسم مشكك , ambiguous name or amphibological. Vide Maimonides, loco citato, and the present work, Part Ist, ch. 56 (fol. 68 b of our Arabic text).
fn.12: By פקח فقه the Arabs understand that which we call canon law, and in general all the legislation that relateth to the Koran and the traditions, including therein also all religious ceremonies and ordinances. The Arabic Jews, as well Karaites as Rabbanites, likewise use this word to designate the body of doctrines and practices based upon tradition, and the Arabic Rabbins apply this word to the Oral Law or to the Talmud. Wherefore the translators generally render the Arabic word פקח by תלמוד, and it is this word which Ibn-Tibbon hath here employed.
fn.13: The author meaneth to speak of the other works which he had himself composed upon this matter, such as certain parts of his commentary upon the Mishna and the first treatises of his Mishneh Torah or Abridgment of the Talmud.
fn.14: That is to say, that which he hath understood in a superficial manner, by adhering solely to the literal sense, which will lead him to corporify the Divinity and to admit other absurdities.
fn.15: Literally: for him with whom he should converse.
fn.17: The Talmud speaketh of profound mysteries contained in the 1st chapter of Genesis, beginning with the word beréshîth, in the 1st chapter of Ezekiel and in certain passages of Isaiah and Zechariah. The visions of these prophets, and notably those of Ezekiel, are designated by the name of Ma’asé mercabâ, or account of the chariot (celestial). The mysteries of Beréshîth and of the Mercabâ play a great part in the writings of the Kabbalists, who are little agreed upon what must be understood by these mysteries, for the Talmud hath not pronounced in this regard. Maimonides, who was no partisan of the Kabbalah, speaketh nevertheless, as a Talmudist, of the Ma’asé beréshîth and of the Ma’asé mercabâ, and, being imbued with the philosophical doctrines of the Arabian schools, he explaineth both in such wise as to find therein the principal parts of the Peripatetic philosophy, seeing in the one the physics and in the other the metaphysics of Aristotle. It is in this sense that he speaketh thereof already in his Talmudic works. Vide Commentary on the Mishnah, IInd part, treatise ’Haghîghâ, ch. II, § 1; Abridgment of the Talmud, book I, 1st treatise (or Yesodé ha-Torah), ch. 1 to 4.
fn.18: Vide Mishnah and Babylonian Talmud, treatise ’Haghîghâ, ch. 2, fol. 12 and 13. In enumerating therein diverse Biblical subjects which must not be interpreted in public, the Talmud forbiddeth the interpreting of the mercabâ, even unto a single pupil in private, unless he be a subject of a superior intelligence.
fn.19: Instead of אלתצריח, one of the Leyden manuscripts hath: תצריחהא כל אלתצריח, a reading which Ibn-Tibbon appeareth to have rendered by לגלותם · · · · · בביאור.
fn.20: Vide Mishnah and Babylonian Talmud, loco citato.
fn.21: Literally: unto their extremity and their end.
fn.22: Literally: the matters and the habits, that is to say, things pertaining to matter and to daily life. Ibn-Tibbon hath rendered the word אלמואדّ (matters) by הטבעים, and Al-’Harizi by כחות הטבע, which seemeth unto me inaccurate.
fn.23: Ibn-Tibbon addeth here, in his Hebrew version, the explanatory words במעט הפרש ביניהם with small intervals.
fn.24: The Hebrew version of Ibn-Tibbon addeth here the following passage: .ויש מי שיהיה לו בין ברק וברק הפרש רב היא מדרגת רוב הנביאים This passage is found in none of the Arabic manuscripts; neither is it met with in the Hebrew version of Al-’Harizi, nor in the excerpts of R. Shem-Tob ibn-Falaquera. See his Moré ha-Moré, printed at Pressburg (1837, octavo), p. 9. Nevertheless, this passage existeth likewise in the manuscripts of the version of Ibn-Tibbon, and is reproduced by the commentators of that version, as also by Samuel Zarza in his Mekor ’hayyîm or commentary upon the Pentateuch at the Book of Numbers, ch. 11, v. 25. This passage, moreover, is superfluous; for that which followeth the words ויתנבאו ולא יספו saith well-nigh the same thing.
fn.25: All the Arabic manuscripts bear עלינא. The word עליו in the editions of Ibn-Tibbon’s version is an error; one must read עלינא, as indeed the manuscripts of that version have it.
fn.26: The word רבאני hath not here the sense of rabbinical or rabbanite, but that of theologian or metaphysician, much like the word אלאהי which precedeth it; it is derived from رَبّ, in the sense of master par excellence, or of God. It is thus that Ibn-Tofail styleth the intellectual faculty of man امر ربانی الاهی (Epistola de Hai Ebn-Yokdhan, ed. Pococke, p. 137). See also the observations of R. Shem-Tob Ibn-Falaquera upon the version of Ibn-Tibbon, Moré ha-Moré, p. 148.
fn.27: All the Oxford MSS. bear למעניין מתפקארבה̈ which is incorrect. In one of the two Leyden MSS. we read למעאני instead of למעניין; in the other is read למעניין מתקפארבין and it is this latter reading which we have adopted as being the most correct.
fn.28: מתאכׄם is a participle of the IIIrd form of the verb תכׄם تخم This reading is found in six manuscripts of the Bodleian Library at Oxford, and it is that which is expressed by the version of Ibn-Tibbon, which beareth מצרנית bordering. The version of Al-’Harizi beareth: כי המרע הטבעי הוא אחרון למדע האלהי. This translator read מתאבׄר (متأخر) a reading which is indeed found in the two manuscripts of the Leyden Library, but which offereth no plausible sense and accordeth ill with the words found immediately thereafter. The author meaneth to say that there is no intermediate science between physics and metaphysics, and that in the order of studies the former must precede the latter. The whole course of philosophical studies was divided, among the Arabian Peripatetics, notably since Avicenna, into three parts: 1st, logic; 2nd, physics (therein including mathematics and astronomy); 3rd, metaphysics. Compare Maimonides, in the present work, Ist part, ch. 34 (at the 3rd cause), fol. 39 a of our Arabic text. See also my article Ibn-Sina in the Dict. des sciences philos., vol. III, p. 175.
fn.29: The reading which we have adopted is that of the greater part of the MSS.; that which was expressed in the two Hebrew versions is found only in one of the Leyden MSS., which beareth: עטׄם אמור עלי מא הי עליה.
fn.30: See the introduction to the Xth (XIth) chapter of the treatise Synhedrin, at the seventh article of faith; Porta Mosis, by Pococke, p. 170.
fn.31: That is to say, the allegorical interpretations and the legends contained in the Midrashim and in the Haggadoth of the Talmud.
fn.32: All the MSS. bear אלאממא אלמשכלה̈ ואלאמתאל; instead of והמושאלים, which is read in most editions of Ibn-Tibbon's version, one must read והמשלים, as it is found in the MSS. and the editio princeps of 1480. It is singular that the same error should have crept into the unique MS. remaining to us of Al-Harizi's version, wherein one likewise reads והמושאלים. It would appear that it is the preceding word הממופקים which gave rise to the error, the copyists having believed that this word designated amphibological names; but the Arabic word אלמשכלה̈ designateth, in general, the obscure names of the various categories mentioned at the commencement of this introduction.
fn.33: That is to say, in other words, that, on the one hand, one doth not consider as an allegory that which is one, and that, on the other hand, one considereth as an allegory that which ought to be taken in its literal sense. The commentary of Ephodi citeth for example, on the one hand, the image of the adulterous woman (Prov., ch. VII), which, according to our author, designateth matter, and which many commentators take in the literal sense, and, on the other hand, the narrative relating to Bathsheba (II. Sam., ch. XI, v. 2 et seq.), which evidently must be taken in its literal sense, and wherein certain commentators have seen an allegory.
fn.34: This passage and the following are found, with some variants, in the Midrash of the Song of Songs (שיל השירים רבה, fol. 1 d).
fn.35: The verb is understood, and the word ורד which is found in some modern editions of Ibn-Tibbon's version must be deleted. This word is found neither in the ancient editions, nor in the Arabic and Hebrew manuscripts of the Guide. In the passage of the Midrash indicated in the preceding note, there is read more regularly: כך מדבר לדבר יממשל למשל עמד שלמה על סודה של תורה.
fn.36: Religious doctrine, saith the author, consisteth not essentially in ceremonial laws, such as the prescriptions relating to the feast of Tabernacles and other like things, nor in civil laws, as, for instance, the provisions relating to the four kinds of depositaries (Vid. Mishna, part II, treatise Shebuoth or of Oaths, ch. VIII); but it consisteth in the fundamental principles of the faith and in the profound subjects wherewith Theology is concerned.
fn.37: We translate this verse according to the explanation which the author himself is about to give thereof.
fn.38: The root of this Chaldaic word, according to the author, is the same as that of the Hebrew word Maskiyyoth.
fn.39: The form ארי (instead of ז or הנר) is incorrect; nevertheless, as the author employeth it very often and as it is found in all the manuscripts which we have consulted, we have deemed it necessary to preserve it.
fn.40: By proximate or immediate matter the author understandeth all that constituteth the animal organism, as, for instance, the members of the body, the flesh, the blood, the humours, etc.; for, in this respect, man perfectly resembleth the animals, and formeth with them one and the same species. The elements form a more remote and more general matter, embracing all sublunary bodies. The most remote and most general matter is the prime matter or the hyle ג which embraceth the whole of creation.
fn.41: The version of Ibn-Tibbon addeth here the words: למצוא כל עניני המשל בנמשל, the equivalent whereof is found in none of the MSS. of the Arabic original.
fn.43: The words ולא יתהאפת ללרדّ are thus rendered by Ibn-Tibbon: ולא יהרוס ויקפוץ עצמו להשיב על דברי. It was Maimonides himself who had counselled him to translate thus, as is seen in the supplement of the letter beginning with the words: לפי שכלו יהולל איש וכו׳. This supplement hath been preserved in a manuscript of the Bodleian Library (Cod. Poc., no. 74).
fn.44: Literally: and if it (this treatise) quencheth his thirst. Ibn-Tibbon hath translated somewhat freely: ואם ירפא לו מדוה לבבו, and if it healeth the sickness of his heart; nevertheless Maimonides himself had counselled the translator to render these words by ואם רוה צמאו, as is seen in the supplement whereof we have just spoken in the preceding note. Instead of מדוה, a manuscript of the Hebrew version beareth מחום, and in the margin is read the variant ואם ירוה לו צמאו. One may compare hereafter, Part Ir, at the end of Chapter 45, where the words מא ישפי גלילך are rendered by מה שירוה צמאך. — Instead of שפת (شَفَتْ), as we have written in our text, one readeth שפאת in all the manuscripts which we have consulted (to the number of eight), as well as in the supplement of the letter of Maimonides whereof we have just spoken.
fn.45: The author meaneth to say that they will flee from true doctrines because these will reveal unto them all the falsity of the hypotheses and theories which they have imagined to silence their doubts and appease the trouble of their soul, and which are, as it were, their sole treasure, prepared beforehand to save them from distress. There is question here, doubtless, of those who followed the doctrines of the Motécalemîn. See above p. 5, note 1.
fn.46: The words אלתי ענדנא מא אלף פיהא, which are found in all the Arabic MSS., have been omitted by the two Hebrew translators.
fn.47: It is known that the Rabbis ascribe to the 126th verse of Psalm 119 the following sense: When it is the time to act for God, it is even permitted to transgress the Law, that is to say, one may allow oneself to violate some secondary precepts when it is a matter of consolidating the religious edifice in general.
fn.48: That is to say, when the two statements, or one of the two, must not be understood in an absolute manner, but under a certain reservation or implied condition. Thus, for example, whilst it is said, on the one hand, that God punisheth the sins of the fathers upon the children (Exod. xx. 5; xxxiv. 7), and on the other hand, that the fathers shall not be put to death for the children, nor the children for the fathers (Deut. xxiv. 16), the Rabbis, perceiving a contradiction in these passages, say that the punishment of children for the sins of the fathers taketh place under the condition that the children persist in the evil way of their fathers. — To cite another example, whilst we read, on the one hand, that Moses entered into the midst of the cloud (Exod. xxiv. 18), and on the other hand, that Moses could not enter into the tabernacle of the congregation when the cloud abode thereon (Ib., xl. 35), the Rabbis say that he could enter into the cloud under the condition that he were expressly called thither by the Deity.
fn.49: According to some commentators, the author intendeth to speak here of two propositions containing homonymous subjects, and where, by taking the homonyms in the same sense, one might find an apparent contradiction. But the words of the author seem to have a more general sense. If, for example, it be said, on the one hand, that God revealeth Himself to certain prophets in a dream (Numb. xii. 6), and, on the other hand, that dreams speak only falsehoods (Zechariah x. 2), the doctors, in order to remove the contradiction, say that it concerneth dreams of a different nature, the one true, the others false. See Babylonian Talmud, treatise Berakhôth, fol. 55 verso, Albo, ’Ikkarîm, book III, ch. 10.
fn.50: Moses of Narbonne, in his commentary, citeth as an example the notions of species and of genus concerning which Aristotle had need to say a few words, when desiring to explain the category of substance (Categories, ch. iii), although the exact explanation of these notions cometh only later (in the Topics). The double nature, logical and ontological, of the categories and of divers other notions treated of in the Organon, often necessitateth the provisional and summary explanation of certain notions which are truly fathomed only in the Metaphysics.
fn.51: The author stateth further on that, in his work itself, certain contradictions are found resulting from the fifth cause. Let us cite an example thereof: in chapter lxx of the Ist part the author presenteth God as the immediate mover of the upper sphere, whilst at the end of chapter iv of the IInd part he saith that the first among the intelligences of the spheres, produced by God, setteth the first sphere in motion. It is because, in the first passage, the author hath no other aim than to present God as the mover of the universe in general, without entering into the details of the motion of the different spheres and of their intelligences, as he doth in the second passage. Thence results a contradiction which is only apparent.
fn.52: By the author's own admission his work also containeth contradictions resulting from this seventh cause. One of the most serious appeareth to us to be this: the author, who combateth the eternity of prime matter, admitted by the Peripatetics, nevertheless admitteth it as a premise in demonstrations relating to the most important metaphysical questions, as he himself declareth in ch. lxxi of the Ist part and at the beginning of the IInd part.
fn.53: That is to say, Rabbi Judah the Holy, the redactor of the Mishnah.
fn.54: It is well known that the word אמוראי designateth the doctors who appear in the Gemara, and who discuss the opinions of the Tannaim or doctors of the Mishnah.
fn.55: The MSS. of the Arabic original generally have both examples; the Hebrew version hath only that of Raba.
fn.56: It is known that Rabbi Ashi is one of the principal redactors of the Babylonian Talmud.
fn.57: Vide Babylonian Talmud, treatise Shabbath, fol. 30. Divers passages are therein cited wherein Solomon is at variance with David or with himself, and the difficulty is sought to be resolved by establishing that in the contradictory passages different subjects are treated of. Thus, for example, we read in Proverbs (ch. XXVI, v. 4): Answer not a fool according to his folly, and immediately thereafter (v. 5): Answer a fool according to his folly. In order to remove the contradiction, the Talmud saith that, in one of the two passages sacred matters are intended, and in the other, profane matters.

fn.59: See above, page 28, note 1, and page 29, note 1.
fn.60: One would scarce believe that Jewish doctors could have fallen into such aberrations, were we not in possession of the positive testimony of Maimonides, as well as that of his son Abraham and of several of his contemporaries, who were constrained to defend Maimonides against the attacks of divers Talmudists, and notably against a portion of the rabbis of France, who deemed it necessary to take the anthropomorphisms of the Bible in a literal sense. We content ourselves with recalling in this regard the unimpeachable testimony of a stern adversary of Maimonides, R. Abraham ben David of Posquières, in his critical notes upon the Mishneh Torah or Compendium of the Talmud (Book I, treatise Teshubah or of Repentance, ch. 3, § 7). Maimonides having numbered among the heretics (מינים) him who admitteth the corporeality of God, R. Abraham asketh: “Wherefore doth he call such a one a heretic, seeing that men greater and better than he (Maimonides) have followed this opinion, according to what they had seen in the texts of Scripture, and still more in the Haggadoth which confuse the mind?”
fn.61: In place of בדפע (with daleth) several MSS. bear ברפע (with resh), which altereth naught of the sense.
fn.62: The author intendeth to say that he doth not here employ the word form in its philosophical sense, but in that of the vulgar tongue.
fn.63: That is to say, the form peculiar to the human species, or that which characterizeth man and distinguisheth him from the other animals.
fn.64: Literally: Their sense (their idea) which one imagined to oneself, that is to say, the false notion which one formed of them, or the virtue attributed to them in error.
fn.65: It is generally believed that the malady of the Philistines, designated by the word te’horīm (טחרים) or, according to the reading of the khetīb, ’apholīm (עפלים), consisted in a species of tumours or pustules in the secret parts; the Rabbins perceive therein hemorrhoidal varices, and it is likely in this sense that Maimonides himself understandeth this word. Jewish physicians of the Middle Ages commonly employ the word טחורים to signify hemorrhoids.
fn.67: The words שׂגארחה̈ and שׂגאנחה̈ designate here particularly those members which serve to grasp aught or to perform a task. שׂגארחה̈, derived from שׂגרח (جرح) to wound, is employed to signify the hand; שׂגאנחה̈ is used to signify the ribs, and seemeth also to be used for שׂגנאח جناح wing, and, like the latter, in the sense of arm. The version of Ibn-Tibbon hath: ולא מעשה גוף ילא יד ולא רגל, which is not entirely exact; yet this translation is to be preferred to that of Al-Harizi, which hath: לא אבר ולא נתח.
fn.68: The author alludeth here to that which the Arabian philosophers call الاتصال, the conjunction, or the union of the active intellect (proceeding from God through the medium of the Intelligences of the spheres) with the passive intellect. This subject shall be explained in several places of this work. Vid. infra ch. LXVIII; Part IInd, ch. IV; Part IIIrd, ch. LI, and other places.
fn.69: Allusion is here likely made to some Oriental fable; I suppose reference is intended to Nimrod, who, according to Oriental traditions, rebelled against God and caused the Tower of Babel to be built, and who is said to have been placed in the heavens by identifying him with the constellation of the Giant (الجبّار) or Orion. Vid. the Chronicon Paschale, p. 36; concerning the Djebbâr or Orion vid. the commentary on the treatise of Ulug-Beigh, by Hyde, in the Syntagma dissertationum, vol. I, pages 42 et seq., and p. 57.
fn.70: Literally: with the beginnings of his thoughts and his ideas, that is to say, according to what presenteth itself at first to his mind.
fn.71: The distinction which the author here establisheth between matters of the intellect and those which fall within the domain of probable opinions is borrowed from Aristotle (Topics, Book I, ch. 1). The Stagyrite recogniseth four species of syllogisms, the first two whereof are: the demonstrative, which is based upon principles of absolute truth and self-evident, being founded in the intellect; and the dialectical, which proceedeth from probable opinions (ἐξ ἐνδόξων), and which hath for its basis the suffrages of the whole or the majority of men, or only those of the whole or the majority of the wise, or of the most illustrious amongst them. Good and evil, virtues and vices, belong to the domain of probable opinions, and have no relation with God nor with the pure intellect (Vid. Nicomachean Ethics, Book VII, ch. 1). The Arabic word אלמשהוראת, which signifieth things generally known or celebrated things, designateth here evidently matters admitted by opinion and correspondeth to the Greek term τὰ ἔνδοξα; the Hebrew versions render this word as המפורסמות. The Greek word ἔνδοξος having at once both meanings which we have just indicated, the Arabians have rendered it by a word signifying generally known or celebrated, although this word doth not exactly render the idea of Aristotle. Thus, for example, these words: Διαλεϰτιϰὸς δὲ συλλογισμὸς ὁ ἐξ ἐνδόξων συλλογιζόμενος (Top., I, 1), “the dialectical syllogism is that which resulteth from probable opinions,” were thus rendered in the Arabic version: والقياس الجدلى هو الذى ينتج من مقدمات ذائعة. For the word ذايعة a marginal variant, in the Arab. MS. No. 882 A, giveth the synonym مشهورة, which is the term generally employed by the Arabian philosophers. Thus expresseth himself Ibn-Roschd, in his Epitome of the Organon, at the beginning of the كتاب الجدل (Book of Dialectics), corresponding to the Topics of Aristotle.
fn.72: That is to say: he manifested his disobedience by an act. The words פלמא עצא pertain to the change which was wrought within him; the second, עצא, unto the material disobedience.
fn.73: That is to say, in that which appertaineth to the domain of the intellect and is necessarily true in itself; the author intendeth to say that the pure intellect hath to occupy itself only with the true and the false. Good and evil appertain to the domain of probable opinion.

But they have not reflected that the primitive sense of the verb קום is to rise, whilst the author's explanations relate to another signification of the same verb, namely, that of to stand upright; it is this latter sense which he giveth to the verb קום in the biblical passages which he is about to cite. One shall therefore no longer marvel, with the commentator Shem-Tob, that the author, instead of citing passages from the Pentateuch, should have sought an example of the proper sense in the book of Esther; in the examples proposed by Shem-Tob, to wit: ויקם אברהם (Genesis, 23, 3), ויקם פרעה (Exodus, 12, 30), the verb קום signifieth to rise up, whereas in the passage from Esther it may be translated to stand. Al-Harizi hath committed a misconstruction in translating וענינו לקום היושב ממקומו; by bringing out the sense of to rise up, he did not perceive the author's intention, and hath even altered his words. Ibn-Tibbon hath translated literally ואחד מעניניו הקימה, taking הקימה in the sense of the Arabic word קיאם, to stand. Instead of מעניני, which the editions of Ibn-Tibbon's version bear, one must read מעניניו, as it is found in the MSS.

fn.278: The commentators thus explain these latter questions: If the soul of man be separable from the body and if it existeth after death as a separate substance, then 1st, how is this existence, that is to say, doth the soul of each man exist individually, or do all souls form but a single substance? 2ndly, by what means doth it attain unto immortality? is it by philosophical speculation, or by the practice of religious precepts? and finally 3rdly, to what end, that is to say, whither doth the permanence of the soul lead? is it unto union with the active intellect, or unto union with God? Indeed, these are the questions which have principally occupied the Arabian Peripatetics, and which have given rise to interminable discussions both among the Arabian philosophers and among the Scholastics.
fn.279: Ibn-Falaquera citeth as an example, in numbers, unity, and in geometrical figures, the circle. All powers and roots of the number one are one, and this number giveth the idea of that which can be neither multiplied nor divided without ceasing to be what it is. It is the same with the circle; for the circumference, the image of unity, could not be increased or diminished without ceasing to be a circumference, whilst the straight line can be increased and diminished while yet remaining a straight line. Thus the number one and the circumference give us the idea of absolute unity, excluding the ideas of the multiple and the divisible, which we must remove from the Divinity. If the author insisteth particularly upon that which we must remove from the Divinity, it must be remembered that, according to him, the attributes of God must be expressed by negations, and that he insisteth upon negative attributes (אלסואלב), in order to establish, in its greatest purity, the principle of the unity of God. He next citeth, without adopting it, the opinion of an author of Andalusia, who thought that in this narrative it was a case of apparent death. Several commentators, such as Ibn-Caspi, Moses of Narbonne, Ephodi, insinuate that Maimonides wished to veil his thought, and that he himself adopteth the opinion of the Andalusian author. They rely upon another analogous narrative (II Kings, iv. 19 and 20), where it is expressed: and he died (וימת), which would destroy the reasoning of Maimonides; but Abravanel, in his commentary on the Moreh (fol. 66), observeth that there also mention is first made of the sickness and afterwards of the death, which indicateth that a real death is meant, according to the reasoning of Maimonides on the passage relating to the son of the widow of Sarepta. Howsoever it may be, one cannot admit that Maimonides, for the purpose of veiling an heresy, should have made an argument void of logic and contradicted himself. One cannot admit the opinion of Abravanel, who, to justify Maimonides, pretendeth that the words of the Andalusian author refer to Nabal; it seemeth to me quite evident, from the whole, that it is here a question of the son of the woman of Sarepta; but, as we have said, Maimonides citeth this opinion without adopting it himself. It is certain, moreover, that this passage is one of those of which the adversaries of Maimonides took possession to render his orthodoxy suspect. Vid. the reply of R. Judah ibn-al-Fakhar to R. According to the system of the author, the individuals of the human race alone are guided by Providence; whilst as regards other animals, Divine Providence extendeth only unto the species, abandoning the individuals to chance. See the IIIrd part of this work, chap. XVII.
