fn.431: See at the end of section 21.
fn.432: That is to say, the word להט, flame, brilliance, designateth the angels, elsewhere called אש לוהט, a flaming fire.
fn.433: The author shall himself cite a passage wherein the angels are designated by the name of נשים, women; the name of אנשים, men, is found, e.g., Genesis, 18, 2; that of רוח, wind or spirit, Ps. 104, 4, and I Kings, 22, 21.
fn.434: That is to say, that the corporeal figures under which they appear exist only in the mind of him who beholdeth them, and possess no real existence. One frequently encountereth the expression כֿארג׳ אלדֿהן, outside the mind, to indicate objective reality, even as it is said that a thing is פי אלדֿהן, in the mind, to indicate the subjective conception, whether it correspondeth or no to aught real. The word דֿהן (ذهن) embraseth the whole of all spiritual faculties and dispositions, even the imagination, whilst עקל (عقل) designateth the intellect or the intelligence; one may therefore say that a thing is פי אלדֿהן in the mind, even when it is only in the imagination. Vide, e.g., supra, chap. III (pp. 43 and 44), where the perception of the senses, independently or outside the mind (כֿארג׳ אלדֿהן), is opposed at once to the imagination and to the perception of the intelligence (עקל). The Hebrew translators, having found no word to render the Arabic word דֿהן, have almost always rendered it, as well as עקל (intellect), by the word שׂכל, which may cause confusion. It is necessary to be thoroughly imbued with what we have just stated in order to understand aright, in the Hebrew versions, the expressions בשׂכל and חוץ לשׂכל. See the excellent observations made upon this subject by M. Scheyer, in his work entitled: Das Psychologische System des Maimonides, pp. 60 et seq.
fn.435: Literally: and that which falleth not into the net of the imagination.
fn.436: The author here alludeth to the system of the motecallemîm; see hereafter in chap. LXXIII, 10th proposition.
fn.437: Literally: if one had stopped, for them, at this imagination, that is to say, at this manner of presenting them to the imagination.
fn.439: One MS. readeth מן שכל; likewise Al-’Harizi: מתבנית (with the prefix מ). After the word חיואן one of the Leyden MSS. addeth גיר נאטק, and this reading hath been followed by Ibn-Tibbon, who hath שאינם מדברים.
fn.440: That is to say, in the wings and the feet which serve as the substratum for these two faculties.
fn.441: That is to say, the subject in the verb ויעף, and he flew, is in no wise God, but the cherub; so that the translation should run: he was mounted upon a cherub that flew.
fn.442: The author meaneth that, in these passages, Ezekiel seemeth to attribute unto the angels, out of the bodies of animals, parts other than wings, contrary to that which was aforementioned.
fn.443: Vide Part IIIrd, chap. Ist, wherein the author saith that here are meant human faces resembling the faces of certain animals.
fn.444: That is to say, the celestial animals of Ezekiel, which, according to the author, signify the spheres themselves, and not the angels nor the Intelligences of the spheres.
fn.445: Vide the first chapters of Part III<sup>rd</sup>.
fn.446: Maimonides, as the commentators observe, here maketh particular allusion to the movement of the celestial spheres, represented, according to him, by the ’hayyôth or celestial animals in the vision of Ezekiel; the ’hayyôth have four wings, and even so the causes of the movement of the spheres are four in number, to wit: their sphericity, their soul, their intelligence, and the supreme separate intelligence or God, the object of their desire. Vide Part IInd of this work, chap. IV and X.
fn.447: This chapter serveth as an introduction unto that which the author shall deliver, in the ten subsequent chapters (LI to LX), concerning the attributes. Before entering upon his purely spiritualist theory of the attributes of God, a theory so far removed from vulgar beliefs, he deemeth it necessary to give a definition of belief, that is to say, of that which verily meriteth such a name, and which is not a mere profession of faith, but an inward thought, an idea which, albeit it were not objectively true, is at least so in the mind of him who hath conceived it, and containeth nothing absolutely inadmissible.
fn.448: The question of attributes is one of those which most occupied the Muslim and Jewish doctors of the Middle Ages. Certain doctors, whilst professing the absolute unity of God, yet believed they might admit a certain number of eternal and essential attributes, that is to say, inherent in the divine essence, such as life, science, power, etc.; the sect of the Mo’tazales, in general, denied the attributes as incompatible with absolute unity; there were however, amongst them, some who implicitly admitted essential attributes by saying that God is living by His essence, and not by the attribute of life, that He knows by His essence, and not by the attribute of science, and so forth. (Cf. Pococke, Spec. hist. Arab., pag. 214 et seq., and ibidem, the text of Abu’l-Faraj, pag. 19). These latter, according to our author, are no more in the truth than those who openly profess the attributes of God. Faithful to the principles of the philosophers, he rejecteth essential attributes in an absolute manner. See the details further on, in chap. LIII.
fn.449: Those, saith the author, who bestow upon God numerous attributes whilst proclaiming His unity, His incorporeality, and His absolute simplicity, are in contradiction with themselves, and it would seem that, according to them, it is rather a matter of expressing themselves in a certain manner than of penetrating the true sense of beliefs. The Mo’tazales, in arguing against the partisans of eternal and essential attributes, reproach them, like our author, with falling into an error similar to that of the Christians, who admit three persons in God. Vid. Pococke, loco citato, pag. 216: Infidelitatis arguuntur christiani quod tria statuunt æterna; quid ergo de iis pronuntiandum qui septem aut plura statuunt ?
fn.450: That is to say, upon the necessity of setting aside from God all affirmative attributes.
fn.452: ומא hath here the same sense as כמא, which is found, in effect, in some MSS. The author meaneth that these things are so clear that even the simple man, whose mind hath not been cultivated, admitteth them at first sight, without there being any need to demonstrate them unto him.
fn.453: Vid. supra, pag. 59, note 5, and pag. 98, note 2.
fn.454: Literally: to establish these evident things and to annul (or to set aside) the existence of these supposed things.
fn.455: Vid. the Physics of Aristotle and notably the refutation of the proofs alleged by Zeno against the existence of motion, bk. VI, chap. 2, and bk. VIII, chap. 8.
fn.457: That is to say, by considering the attribute as the mere explanation of the name which is the subject thereof.
fn.458: Vide the following chapter, wherein the author showeth that God cannot be defined.
fn.459: The author addresseth himself here to those who, whilst ascribing attributes to God and saying that these attributes are something which is added unto His essence, nevertheless pretend to admit that God hath no accidents: it sufficeth not, saith he, to eschew the word accident in order to efface also the idea thereof, and as soon as one admitteth that God hath attributes distinct from His essence, one necessarily admitteth that He hath accidents; for that which is added to the essence and is distinct therefrom can be naught but an accessory thereto, and could not form an essential complement thereof.
fn.460: That is to say, which in itself hath no multiplicity and which cannot even appear multiple to the mind. Vide supra, page 175, note 5.
fn.461: By אהל אלנטׄר, literally: men of speculation, the author meaneth not here the philosophers properly so called, but the theologians who apply philosophical speculation to religious dogma; the several propositions which he is about to cite belong to the Motécallemîn or Muslim schoolmen (cf. supra, p. 5, note 1), whom the Karaite Aaron ben-Elijah, in his עץ חיים, often designateth under the name of חכמי המחקר, similar to that which our author employeth here.
fn.462: An Arab theologian, quoted by Reland, expresseth himself thus upon the attributes of God: “All these eternal attributes are contained within His essence and subsist in Him from eternity to eternity, without division or variation, yet so that one cannot say that these attributes be Himself, nor can one say that they be essentially different from Him, each of the said attributes being conjoined with another, as life with knowledge, or knowledge with power, etc.” Vide The Religion of the Mohammedans, taken from the Latin of Reland (The Hague, MDCCXXI), IInd lesson; Cf. Brucker, Hist. crit. philos., vol. III, p. 160.
fn.463: The words אלמעאני אלמעאני אלכליה signify the universals, or general ideas, expressing genera, species, etc.; cf. Maimonides, Compendium of Logic, chap. X. It is seen, by this passage, that the question which was agitated between the nominalists and the realists occupied also the Arabian thinkers, and that there were, amongst them, those who sought to reconcile the two opinions and to remove what was too absolute in each of them, much as the conceptualists have done. It is natural that this question, which hath its true origin in the theories of Plato and Aristotle and which Porphyry touched upon at the beginning of his Isagoge, should have been agitated by the Arabian philosophers; but it had not, with them, the same importance as with the Christian philosophers of the Middle Ages. As for Maimonides himself, a faithful disciple of Aristotle, he declareth that universals have no existence outside of the mind. Vide the IIIrd part of this work, at the commencement of chap. XVIII.
fn.464.sub_0: This proposition pertaineth unto the atomistic Motécallemîn, whose doctrine shall be expounded hereafter (chap. LXXIII). By מכאן (سكان), they seem to understand space in relation to its extension or its dimensions; by חיז (حيّز), space circumscribed within limits. Albeit the atom, they say, hath no extension, it is nevertheless circumscribed and separated, by limits, from that which is adjacent to it; it is, as it were, the body without dimensions, the point considered as the first element of extension, yet which possesseth none itself. Lo, thus doth Al-Djordjâni, in his Kitâb al-Ta’rifât or Book of Definitions, explain the words مكان and حيز, as they are employed by the Motécallemîn: المكان عند المتكلمين هو الفراغ المتوهم الذي يشغله الجسم وينفذ فيه ابعاده «Macân, among the Motécallemîn, is the ideal void which the body occupieth and into which it causeth its dimensions to penetrate.» الحيز عند المتكلمين هو الفراغ المتوهم الذي يشغله شيء ممتد كالجسم أو غير ممتد كالجوهر الفرد «’Hayyiz, among the Motécallemîn, is the ideal void which is occupied by a thing whether extended like the body, or non-extended like the simple substance (or the atome).» It is perceived that macân is attributed only to the body having dimensions, whilst ’hayyiz is attributed simultaneously to the extended body and to the atom. The words الجوهر الفرد signify, according to M. Silv. de Sacy, substance isolated from form (see Notices et extraits des mss., vol. X, p. 65); but this explanation is incorrect. These words, which, in truth, signify literally isolated substance, were employed by the Motécallemîn to designate the atome which they also call الجزء الذي لا يتجزأ or simply الجزء, as might have been seen somewhat further back.
fn.464.sub_1: Thus expresseth himself Ibn-Roschd, in his Epitome of the Metaphysics, Book I, when speaking of the substance الجوهر; we cite the Hebrew version: וכן מי שראה כי העצמות הרמוז אליו יתחבר מחלקים אשד לא יתחלקו קרא אותם עצמים כמו שנשמע המדברים מאנשי זמננו יקראו החלק אשר לא יתחלק העצם הפדדי «In like manner, those who think that the indicated substance is composed of atoms give to these latter the name of substances, even as we hear the Motécallemîn of our day call the atom the isolated or simple substance (الجوهر الفرد).» The term الجوهر الفرد resembleth that of the monad, used by Leibnitz, albeit it doth not designate exactly the same thing; the proposition of the Motécallemîn, quoted here by Maïmonides, offereth a striking analogy with what Leibnitz saith, when speaking of monads: Substantia nempe simplex, etsi non habeat in se extensionem, habet tamen positionem, quæ est fundamentum extensionis. See the Works of Leibnitz, Dutens edition, vol. II, part I (Epistolæ ad P. des Bosses), p. 280.
fn.465: Several doctors of the sect of the Asharites (who profess an absolute fatalism), whilst admitting that the actions of men emanate only from the will and the omnipotence of God (see Part III of this work, chap. XVII, 3rd opinion), sought nevertheless to attribute unto man, in the causality of actions, a small part whereby he acquireth merit or demerit; this concurrence of man in the action created by God, an ungraspable hypothesis and void of sense, is designated by the word acquisition اكتساب كسب. See Pococke, Specimen hist. Arab., pp. 239, 240, 248 et seq.), and mine article Arabes in the Dictionnaire des sciences philosophiques, vol. I, p. 176. Cf. hereafter, chap. LXXIII, towards the end of the 6th proposition, and Aaron ben-Elijah, עץ חיים, chaps. IV and LXXXVI (pages 17 and 115 of the Leipzig edition), where acquisition is designated, in Hebrew, by the word ריוח.
fn.466: That is to say, the mind can attach no idea to these assertions, which, for a still greater reason, correspond to nothing real and objective outside the mind.
fn.467: The author alludeth to the verbose style and the pompous images which the Motécallemîn employed in their books, as well as to the vehemence they displayed in discussion, supplying the place of arguments with invectives and sophisms. Cf. hereafter, at the beginning of chap. LXXIV. The version of Ibn Tibbon doth not entirely accord with the text; the words במאמרים שמשתדל אומרם לשמרם ברוב דברים must be erased therefrom, as they seem to be but an explanatory gloss which the copyists have introduced into the text. The words ובהוצאת דִּבּוות והרחקות are a double translation of the Arabic word ואלתשניעאת, and we believe that the word והרחקות should be suppressed; the Arabic words באלציאח ואלתشניעאת signify literally: clamoribus et infamationibus. The version of Al-Harizi is here preferable to that of Ibn Tibbon; it runneth: כי יעשו להם חיוק ברוב הטלות והדמיונים המזויפים ויחזקו אותם בקולות ובגערות.
fn.468: Literally: and by numerous modes (of argumentation) composed of dialectic and sophistic.
fn.469: The version of Ibn Tibbon hath באלו הדברים, which appeareth to be an ancient error of the copyist; one must read באלו הדרכים, as indeed Al-Harizi hath it.
fn.470: That is to say, if one thereafter interrogateth his inward conviction.
fn.471: Literally: between (this alternative) that of two things one is the other or is something else. The author alludeth to those who maintained that the attributes of God are neither identical with His essence, nor aught besides His essence.
fn.472: The word עצמיים which the editions of Ibn-Tibbon's version have in this place must be changed to עצמו, as indeed the manuscripts and the editio princeps have it.
fn.473: The word דרך (دَرُك) signifieth bottom, depth, lowest degree; we read, for instance, in the Korân (IV, 144): إنّ المنافقين في الدرك الاسفل من النار Verily, the hypocrites shall be in the lowest bottom of the fire (of Hell). The two Hebrew translators, as Ibn-Falaquera hath already observed, have ill rendered the word דרך: Ibn-Tibbon, who seemeth to have taken it for a Hebrew word, hath translated: ואנשים סרו מזה ה ד ר ך; Al-’Harizi, taking דרך in the sense of אדראך (إدراك , perception), hath yet more poorly rendered this passage, translating: ואנשים לא רצו זאת ה ה ש ג ה ורחקו מעליה. The same error was committed by both translators in chap. VIII of the IIIrd part of the Guide, wherein the words לא ללאנحטאט ללדרך אלאספל (not to descend to the lowest degree) are rendered, in both versions, by: לא לרדת ל ה ש י ג השפל.
fn.475: The words תוג̇ב לה צפה̈ signify: unto whom an attribute is affirmatively given. In this chapter the author commenceth his researches concerning the attributes which are or are not suitable unto God, and he passeth through the divers classes of affirmative attributes; it will be seen in the sequel that he admitteth, in respect of God, none but negative attributes.—The word صفة , employed in the sense of attribute, signifieth literally description, from the verb وصف , to describe, which, in philosophical language, signifieth also: to designate by an attribute. We translate this verb, according as the context of the sentence requireth, sometimes by to give or to have an attribute, sometimes by to designate, and lastly by to qualify, taking this latter word in a general sense, and not in the special sense of ascribing a quality, that is to say, of giving an attribute of the CATEGORY of QUALITY. In this latter sense the verb كيف is employed, as will be seen further on, in the IIIrd class of attributes.
fn.476: Literally: the quiddity of a thing and its reality, that is to say, what a thing is in reality.
fn.478: It must be remembered that, according to Aristotle, the best definition, to wit, that which maketh known the essence of a thing, is that which at the same time maketh known its cause (Posterior Analytics, book II, chap. 10). Definition is effected by means of the genus and the difference, and it must proceed from things prior and better known; to weak intelligences the prior is sometimes shown by the posterior, but these are not true definitions (See Metaph., book VII, chap. 12; Topics, book VI, chap. 4). It followeth that that which is primitive and simple cannot be defined, for definition supposeth something general encompassing the particular object which is to be defined, whereas the primitive being hath nothing general preceding it which might be its cause. See Metaph., book VIII, chap. 6: ὅσα δὲ μὴ ἔχει ὕλην, μήτε νοητὴν μήτε αἰσθητήν, εὐθὺς ὅπερ ἕν τι εἶναί ἐστιν ἕκαστον, ὥσπερ καὶ ὅπερ ὄν τι, τὸ τόδε, τὸ ποιόν, τὸ ποσόν. διὸ καὶ οὐκ ἔνεστιν ἐν τοῖς ὁρισμοῖς οὔτε τὸ ὄν οὔτε τὸ ἕν · καὶ τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι εὐθὺς ἕν τί ἐστιν ὥσπερ καὶ ὄν τι. διὸ καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν ἕτερόν τι αἴτιον τοῦ ἓν εἶναι οὐθενὶ τούτων, οὐδὲ τοῦ ὄν τι εἶναι. Cf. ibid., chap. 3: ὥστ’ οὐσίας ἔστι μὲν ἧς ἐνδέχεται εἶναι ὅρον καὶ λόγον, κ. τ. λ. God, therefore, cannot be defined; for He hath no prior cause, He entereth not into a genus and is not distinguished by a difference, and, in general, He is not within the conditions of true definition.
fn.479: The words אלמחצלין למא יקולונה signify: who reduce that which they say unto its true sense, to wit, who employ terms in their precise signification and express themselves with clarity and exactness. The word אלמחצלין (المحصّلين) is the participle of the IInd form of the verb حصل, taken in the sense of: ad summam ac sensum suum redegit (sermonem). Certain manuscripts bear אלמכׄלצין (المخلصين), that is to say: who explain or set forth with lucidity. Ibn Tibbon's version (mss. and editio princeps) beareth המבררים; in several editions, this word hath been corrupted into המדברים. Al-’Harizi translateth: המשכילים למה שהם אומרים, that is to say, who reflect well upon that which they say, and render a faithful account thereof unto themselves.—By the words in question, the author meaneth to suggest that they who do not render unto themselves an exact account of what a definition truly is, imagine that God may be defined; for, by employing a defective definition and shewing that which is prior by that which is posterior, one may say, for example: God is the Being who moveth the universe, or: God is the form of the universe. It is this example which Ibn Rushd citeth when speaking of definitions wherein the thing, having naught prior to it, is defined by that which is posterior to it (and which are not true definitions): مثال ذلك من حدّ البارى تعالى بانه المحرّك للعالم او انه صورة الكل. See Compendium of the Organon (book of Demonstration, chap. on definitions); cf. Ibn Falaquera, Moré ha-Moré, p. 25. Elsewhere Ibn Rushd observeth that, if the philosophers have said that the First Being could not enter into the same genus with another being, nor be distinct therefrom by a difference, this is only true when the words genus and difference are taken in their proper sense, relating to things which possess at once a general form and a particular form, and of which a true definition may be given; but if, by homonymy, one should take the word genus in an improper sense, that is to say, by taking the posterior for the prior, one might also include God within a genus, by saying, for example, that He is Being or Substance, etc., and then one could give a definition thereof, albeit an insufficient one. See The Destruction of the Destruction, at the commencement of the VIIth question; cf. the Commentary of Moses of Narbonne upon our passage.
fn.480: That is to say, wherein the thing is qualified by the genus alone or by the difference alone.
fn.481.sub_0: The word אלתלאזם (التلازم) betokeneth the close and necessary connection between two things. In the Kitâb al-Ta’rifât, at the word ملازمة, we read: that this word expresseth the impossibility of separating two things from one another, and that the words لزوم and تلازم are employed in the same sense. Cf. Freytag's Dictionary, at the root لزوم. The enunciation of this connection or inherence formeth a necessary proposition or judgment, such as, for example, the proposition cited here by our author: every man is rational. — The author appeareth to have in view that which Aristotle saith regarding demonstration, in explaining the three terms whereby he designeth the different degrees of the necessary. See Posterior Analytics, book I, chap. 4. He seemeth to allude especially to the terms ϰατά παντός and ϰαθ’ αὑτό. The ϰατά παντός designeth an attribution which pertaineth unto every individual, and not merely to such or such an one, and which is at all times and not merely at such or such a time. Thus, animal being predicated of every man (ϰατά παντός άνθρώπου), it will suffice that it be true that such an individual be a man for it to be true to say of him that he is an animal. The term ϰαθ’ αὑτό, in itself (which hath four principal senses), designeth first the attribution which expresseth that a thing is essential or inherent unto another, and wherein the attribute entereth into the essential definition of its subject; e.g., the line in the triangle, the point in the line. Secondly, the ϰαθ’ αὑτό designeth the attribution wherein the subject entereth into the essential definition of the attribute, or, in other words, wherein the attribute is so essential to the subject that the latter containeth the definition thereof (ὅσοις τῶν ἐνυπαρχόντων αὐτοῖς αὐτὰ ἐν τῷ λόγῳ ένυπάρχουσι τῷ, τί ἐστι, δηλοῦντι). Thus, e.g., the line necessarily entereth into the definition of the straight and of the curved, and number into that of the even and of the odd. Ibn Rushd observeth that, in the first case, that is to say, when the attribute entereth into the definition of the subject, it concerneth either the complete definition or a part of the definition, as, per-
fn.481.sub_1: adventure, when one defineth the triangle by saying that it is a figure bounded by three straight lines; in the second case, that is to say, when the subject entereth into the definition of the attribute, it concerneth the partial definition, as, for example, when one taketh the line as the definition of the straight and of the curved, which exist in the line, or else number as the definition of the even and of the odd, which exist in number. That which, saith he, entereth especially into the propositions subserving demonstration, are these first two kinds of ϰαθ’ αὑτό (אשר בעצם), wherein there is a necessary and essential attribution; for, he addeth, the partial definition findeth itself in a necessary relation with the thing defined (כי יחם חלק הגדר אל הנגדר יהיה הכרחי). See the Middle Commentary on the Posterior Analytics, Hebrew version, at the passage in question. One will now understand what our author had in view in saying that there is here the idea of inherence etc.
fn.482: Literally: of that whereby the essence is completed and subsisteth.
fn.483: By superior genus, the author meaneth the category of quality in all its generality; for it will be seen further on that this category compriseath four diverse species. It is in the same sense that the words superior genus are employed by Al-Farabi, who, in his Logic, when speaking of the category of quality, expresseth himself thus (according to the Hebrew version): ותתחלק האיכות אשר הוא הסוג העליון אל ארבעה סוגים אמצעים “Quality, which is the superior genus, divideth into four intermediate genera.” See Hebrew ms. of the Imperial Library, Oratory collection, No. 107. Maimonides, in his Treatise on Logic (chap. X), designateth the categories, in general, under the denomination of superior genera. Aristotle himself often giveth unto the categories the name of genera (γένο), because they represent the most general notions designated by words. See, e.g., the treatise On the Soul, book I, chap. I (§ 3), wherein the words ἐν τίνι τῶν γενῶν signify evidently: in which of the categories; see also Categories, at the end of chap. 8: έν ἀμφότεροις τοῖς γένεσι, in the two categories (of quality and of relation); likewise, in several passages of the Metaphysics.—The author meaneth that quality, considered first in its generality, as one of the ten categories, formeth part of the nine accidents, and cannot be attributed unto God. He will thereafter provide the special demonstration for each of the four genera of quality.
fn.484: Literally: and this would suffice to be far from His reality and His essence, I mean (to admit) that He possesseth a quality. The sense is: God becoming, by means of qualifying attributes, a substratum of accidents, it is a sufficient reason to exclude this kind of attributes.
fn.485: Albeit it be evident, saith the author, that one cannot give unto God qualifying attributes, one must marvel that the partisans of attributes have excluded qualification from God; for, from their point of view and to be consistent, they must needs admit qualifying attributes, since every attribute, unless it be the essence itself and, consequently, a tautology (as hath been said above, chap. LI), is necessarily qualifying.
fn.486: See above, and chap. L, p. 180, note 1.
fn.487: These four genera, enumerated by Aristotle, are the following: 1st, capacity (or talent) and disposition (ἕξις καὶ διάθεσις); 2nd, that which is said in relation to natural power or impotence (ὅσα κατὰ δύναμιν φυσικὴν ἢ ἀדυναμίαν λέגεται); 3rd, affective qualities and affections, or passions (παθητικαὶ ποιότητες καὶ πάθη); 4th, the figure and the external form which every thing possesseth (σχῆμά τε καὶ ἡ περὶ ἕκαστον ὑπάρχουσα μορφή). See the details in the Categories of Aristotle, chap. 8; the examples which Maimonides is about to cite relate to the words of Aristotle.
fn.488: מלכה̈ مكة is here the translation of the Greek word ἕξις, which, according to the explanation of Aristotle himself (Categories, loc. cit.), signifieth something more durable and more stable (χρονιώτερον καὶ μονιμώτερον) than disposition; cf. supra, p. 121, note 2, and 129, note 3.
fn.489: The words ἕξις καὶ διάθεσις which the Arabic version of Aristotle rendereth by الملكة والحمال (Hebr. הקנין והענין) are thus explained by Al-Farâbi (loc. cit.): כל תכונה הيئة בנפש וכל תכונה בבעל נפש במה שהוא בעל נפש ‘Every disposition in the soul, and every disposition in the animate being in so far as it is an animate being.’ The dispositions in the soul, or ἕξεις, are acquired capacities, such as the sciences, the arts, and the virtues, or natural capacities, such as the knowledge of axioms or the arts possessed by certain animals; the dispositions possessed by the animate being as such, or διαθέσεις, are, e.g., heat, coldness, health, sickness, etc. Ibn-Roschd, in his Compendium of the Organon, distinguisheth in the same terms these two species of dispositions, calling the former الهيآت التي في النفس , and the latter الهيآت الحاصلة في المتنفس بها هو متنفس .
fn.490: Both Hebrew versions bear הרופא, but we do not believe that the author hath employed here the word حكيم in the sense of physician, which it sometimes hath in the vulgar tongue; the author meaneth that the words learned and wise designate dispositions in the soul (see the preceding note), as well as carpenter, and that none of these dispositions, any more than the others, can be attributed unto God. Immediately thereafter, he maketh the same observation for moral dispositions, intending to say that one can no more attribute unto God the quality of merciful than that of chaste.
fn.491: Literally: powerful or having taken possession (of man). Cf. infra, note 3.
fn.492: The author meaneth that one can no more give unto God the attribute of strong than that of hard; for strong and weak designate, as do hard and soft, a natural aptitude or inaptitude to do or to suffer certain things. Cf. Aristotle, Categories, loc. cit. (under the second species of quality).
fn.493: Literally: when the moral quality hath not become powerful, or hath not consolidated itself (in man), that is to say, when it is but the effect of a transient impression; for, in this case, it is not a quality properly so called, but a simple affection. Cf. Arist., ibid.: ὅσα δὲ ἀπὸ ῥᾳδίως διαλυομένων καὶ ταχὺ ἀποκαθισταμένων γίνεται πάθη λέגεται, ποιότητες δὲ οὔ. κ. τ. λ.
fn.494: Colours are termed affective qualities, insofar as they proceed from an affection (ἀπὸ πάθους), as, for example, the redness which cometh from shame, or the paleness which cometh from fear. See Aristot., ibid.
fn.495: Literally: by that which reacheth it or toucheth it on the side of quantity insofar as it is quantity. Our author designateth the fourth genus of quality by terms which differ entirely from those employed by Aristotle, albeit the Arabic translation of the Categories is here wholly conformable to the Greek text; the words σχῆμά τε καὶ ἡ περὶ ἕκαστον ὑπάρχουσα μορφή are thus rendered in Arabic: الشكل والخلقة الموجودة في واحد واحد . The terms whereof Maimonides maketh use are the same which were employed by Al-Farabi and, in general, by all the Arabian philosophers. Behold how Al-Farabi expresseth himself in his Logic (Hebrew version): והסוג הרביעי האיכויות אשר ימצאו במיני הכמות במה שהוא כמות “The fourth genus (compriseth) the qualities which are found in the divers species of quantity, insofar as it is quantity.” Al-Farabi giveth as an example the straightness and curvature of lines, the convexity and concavity of surfaces, the geometrical figure (σχῆμα), such as the circle, the triangle, the square, etc., and the form (μορφη), which, saith he, is a species of figure in the surface of an animated body, and lastly the even and the odd in number. Ibn-Roschd, in his Abridgment of the Organon, expresseth himself thus: والضرب الرابع من اجناس الكيف هو مثل الاستقامة والانحناء والشكل وبالجملة الكيفيات التى فى الكمية بها هى كيفية . “The fourth of the genera of quality (compriseth), e.g., straightness, curvature and (geometrical) figure, and, in general, the qualities which are in quantity insofar as it is quantity.” One perceiveth that the words σχῆμα and μορφὴ, whereof Aristotle maketh use, have been generally interpreted by the Arabian philosophers in the sense of a quantitative quality, or, as they themselves express it, of a quality situated in quantity insofar as it is quantity, that is to say, which qualifieth the thing from the point of view of abstract quantity or of geometrical or arithmetical form in general, without designating the more and the less.
fn.496: Both Hebrew versions have הכח, in the singular; likewise, some Arabic MSS. bear: אלקווה.
fn.498: That is to say, which belongeth to the category of quality in general. See above, p. 193, note 2.
fn.500: See the II<sup>nd</sup> part of this work, chap. I.
fn.501: Some MSS. add: ולד⁠לדך קיל אנה תעאלי ואחד באטלאק “Wherefore it hath been said that God is absolutely one;” likewise the version of Ibn-Tibbon: ולזה נאמר שהוא אחד גמור. The version of Al-Harizi hath not rendered these words.
fn.502: Time, saith Aristotle, is not itself motion; for change and motion are in the thing alone which changeth and which moveth, whilst time is everywhere and in every thing. Every change is more or less rapid or slow; time is neither the one nor the other, for it is by time that rapidity and slowness are indicated (Vide Physics, book IV, at the end of chap. 10). Being not itself motion, it must necessarily be somewhat of motion (ἀνάγϰη τῆς ϰινήσεώς τι εἶναι αὐτόν), or, as our author saith, an accident appertaining to motion. We recognize time, in determining motion by the determination of the anterior and of the posterior (ὅταν ὁρίσωμεν τῆν ϰίνησιν τὺ πρότερον ϰαὶ ὕστερον ὁρίζοντες), that is to say, by that which is before and after an intermediate point, which is the present (το νὺν). Time is therefore the number of motion, according to the before and the after (ἀ ρ ι θ μ ὸ ς ϰινήσεως ϰατὰ τὸ πρότερον ϰαὶ ὕστερον. Ibid., chap. 11). Time being the measure or the number of motion, it followeth that that which is always (τὰ ἀεὶ ὄντα) is not in time; for it is not contained in time, and its being is not measured by time (Ibid., chap. 12). Cf. the IInd part of this work, chap. XIII.
fn.503: For space is not something which is contained, but something which containeth (Vide Aristotle, ibid., chap. 2); it cannot therefore be placed in relation with God.
fn.504: The word נסב̈ה (نسبة) designateth a relation or a connection of any kind, notably a proportional relation, whilst the word אצׄאפה̈ (إضافة) is employed particularly to designate the Category of Relation (τὰ προό τι), or the relation between two things so termed in respect of each other, as, for example, greater and smaller, father and son, master and slave (Vide Arist., Categories, chap. 7). It is this relation which the author here saith to be absolutely inapplicable to God.
fn.505: Literally: inversion with mutual equality. Relatives, or the words which enter into the category of relation, have this property, that they are said of reciprocal things (πάντα δὲ τὰ πρός τι πρὸς ἀ ν τ ι σ τ ρ έ φ ο ν τ α λέγεται, Arist., loc. cit.). Thus, the slave is the slave of the master, as the master is the master of the slave; both the one and the other, they are what they are only by their reciprocal condition, and they could not be one without the other. — The word אנעכאס (انعكاس, inversion), whereof our author here maketh use, cometh from the verb عكس, which, in the Arabic versions, correspondeth to the Greek verb ἀντιστρέφειν. Ibn-Roschd, in the Epitome of the Organon, speaking of the two relatives, expresseth himself likewise: ومن خواصها ايضا ... ان يرجع كل واحد منهما على صاحبه منعكساً "Which is also one of their properties..., that each of them relateth to its fellow reciprocally."
fn.506: Vide the II<sup>nd</sup> part of this work, introduction (Props. XIX et seq.) and chap. I.
fn.507: That is to say, although the existence of the intellect and that of colour be of the same nature. The author here maketh allusion to that which he will set forth further on, to wit, that with the exception of the existence of God, all existence is an accident of the thing existing. This thesis, maintained by Avicenna and contested by others, is adopted without reserve by our author; wherefore he addeth here the words: according to our opinion. Vide infra, at the commencement of chap. LVII.
fn.508: More literally: between him who hath absolutely naught in common with that which is outside of him. We see that the author hath expressed himself in an incomplete manner, and that one must understand the words: and another being. The sense is: How could one conceive a relation between two beings which have absolutely naught in common, not even the kind of existence? for in the one, existence is His substance, and in the other, it is an accident.
fn.509: The proximate or immediate species is that which followeth immediately upon individuality, and which, in no respect, can be considered as a genus; it is the species specialissima (τὸ εἰδιϰώτατον εἶδος). Cf. the Isagoge of Porphyry, chap. 2: ϰαὶ πᾶν τὸ πρὸ τῶν ατόμων π ρ ο σ ε χ ῶ ς ϰατηγορούμενον εἶδος ἄν εἴη μόνον, οὐϰέτι δὲ ϰαὶ γένος.
fn.510: Even as Moses of Narbonne remarketh, the author here referreth to that which was set forth by Aristotle at the end of the VIIth book of the Physics (chap. 4). Aristotle there treateth of the divers species of motion and of the relations which they may have among themselves; it is a question of knowing which are the motions between which a comparison may be established and which differ from each other by quantity alone. For two motions to be compared together, it is necessary that they be capable of being equally swift, that is to say, they must differ only in quantity, and there must exist between them no difference of quality. In general, for two things to be compared with one another, it sufficeth not that they be not mere homonyms, but it is necessary that the two things be distinguished by no essential difference, neither in themselves nor in their substratum; that is to say, that they be not only comprised within the same genus, but also characterised by the same difference, in a word, that they be of the same species: A’λλο’ ἀρὰ οὐ μόνον δεῖ τὰ σνμβλητὰ μὴ ὁμώνυμα εἶναι ἀλλὰ ϰαὶ μὴ ἔχειν δ ι α φ ο ρ ά ν, μήτε ὅ μήτ’ ἐν ᾧ. Thus, for example, saith Aristotle, colour hath a division (into divers colours). Colours as such are therefore not comparable among themselves; one cannot say that a certain black is stronger than a certain white. Comparison can only be established for the same colour, e.g., between two white or two black objects. Cf. supra, page 131, note 2.
fn.511: The MSS. bear כאנת; but it is peradventure necessary to read כאנא or better כאנתא.
fn.512: The version of Ibn-Tibbon beareth תחת שני סוגים עליונים (under two superior genera); the word עליונים must be deleted, although it be found also in the MSS. of this version. One must likewise delete the words …אין ספק ש, and a little further on, the words שאין ספק לשום אדם, which are found neither in the MSS. of the version of Ibn-Tibbon, nor in the Arabic text.
fn.513: The word genus is here employed in the sense of category. Vide supra, page 193, note 2.
fn.514: After having given an example of two things belonging to two superior genera or to two different categories, the author here giveth an example of two intermediate genera belonging to the same category.
fn.515: The feminine suffix in בינהא referreth to God and to the creatures (מכ֗לוּקאתה).
fn.516: The word תבלע, which I pronounce تخص, as the infinitive of the Vth form, signifieth deliverance, means of salvation; the sense is: there be no means of extrication in desiring to give God any attribute whatsoever, and in whatever manner one proceedeth, one encountereth difficulties. This is what Al-’Harizi hath expressed by the words ואי אפשר להמלט מחטוא. Ibn-Tibbon, who translateth: הנה לא תנצל, hath pronounced تَخَلَّصَ, as the 2nd person of the fut. passive of the IInd form.
fn.517: Literally: even from the side of the relation, that is to say, should this attribute be taken in the relation which existeth between God and His creatures.
fn.518: More literally: but they (the attributes of relation) are, among the attributes, those which most merit indulgence in their employment as qualifications of God.
fn.519: The editions of the version of Ibn-Tibbon generally bear שלא יתחייב רבוי הקדמות; one must read, with the MSS.: הקדמון שלא יחייב רבוי.
fn.520: The editions of the version of Ibn-Tibbon add הצייר (the painter), a word which is not found in the MSS. of this version.
fn.521: See above (p. 194) the first example of the IIIrd class of attributes.
fn.522: Literally: of the essence of him to whom they relate or to whom they are attributed. One of the Leyden MSS. bears אלמוצוף, a word which designateth the subject of the attribute; it is this latter reading which hath been adopted by Al-’Harizi, who translateth: המתואר. The meaning is that actions, whilst emanating from the divine essence alone, as shall be stated, are nevertheless not aught permanent in the essence, such as would be an artistic capacity, and thought separateth them from the essence by limiting them to a past, present, or future moment. Cf. the Commentary of Ibn-Caspi: וזה לפי שלא נתארהו בתאר מיושב נח בו כמו שמות הבינוני והפעול ויתר שמות התארים אבל זה פעל אם עבר ואם עתיד וכו׳.
fn.523: Literally: that it must not be that these diverse actions be performed by things (or ideas) diverse in the essence of the agent.
fn.524: See the following chapter, wherein the author enlargeth upon the attributes of action. It will be seen that the author shareth in this regard the opinion of other Arabian philosophers.
fn.525: A MS. bears זאיד עלי ד̇אתה; likewise Ibn-Tibbon מוסף על עצמו.
fn.526: Literally: wherefore, the succinct exposition of that which is (contained) within this chapter is etc.
fn.527: Literally: … which are found in the books (sacred) and whereby God is signified, are (employed) in respect of the multiplicity of His actions, and not by reason of a multiplicity in His essence.
fn.528: Vide supra, chaps. XXVI, XLVI (p. 160) and XLVII.
fn.529: Literally: that which hath induced the belief in the existence of attributes of the Creator, among those who believe therein, is well-nigh that which hath induced the belief in corporeity, among those who believe therein.
fn.530: Literally: and the books of revelation; the word אלתנזיל (التنزيل) is here particularly applied to the books of Moses and employed in the sense of תורה. Cf. supra, chap. XLVI, p. 158: “In all the books of the prophets and likewise in the Pentateuch”, where the text hath (fol. 50 a): פי גׄמיע כתב אלאנביא ופי אלתורה. At other times, the word אלתנזיל is applied to the whole of Holy Writ in general; vide, e.g., at the end of chap. LI: כתב אלתנזיל.
fn.531: Vide that which the author saith, in the preceding chapter, concerning the III<sup>rd</sup> class of attributes.
fn.532: In the verbs יצרחוא and עהדוה, one must understand, as the subject, the prophets, and not those who believe in the attributes, as some commentators have supposed; for, in the latter case, the verbs ought to be in the singular, like the word מעתקד. Instead of the words יבארהו בו, which are found in the editions of the version of Ibn-Tibbon, one must read יבארוהו, as the MSS. of that version have it. The sense of this passage is this: the attributes which the prophets give to God, and wherein some have claimed to see essential attributes, that is to say, forming part of the divine essence (Vide supra, p. 180, note 1), are at bottom naught else but qualities; and the prophets, without declaring themselves clearly in this respect, and by metaphorically assimilating God to animate beings, have given Him attributes similar to the conditions of those beings, which are familiar to all.
fn.533: Literally: by the diversity of actions the ideas existing in the agent are not made diverse. Here the author entereth upon the discussion of the attributes of action to which he preluded at the close of the last chapter, and he maketh understood, by examples, the distinction that must be established between this kind of attributes, applicable to God, and those which have been called essential attributes. The question of attributes, as we have said above (p. 180), had already occupied the Muslim theologians and philosophers, and we find likewise among them the distinction between essential attributes and attributes of action. Vide Pococke, Specimen hist. Ar., p. 223; Shahrastani, History of the religious and philosophical sects, Arabic text (published by Mr. Cureton), p. 64; German translation by Mr. Haarbrücker, vol. I, p. 95. Cf. Bahya, Duties of the Hearts, book I (Of the Unity of God), chap. 10.
fn.534: Literally: and that the idea of no action among them be the idea of the other.
fn.535: That is to say, when our perception causeth us to behold in God things unto which we attach diverse ideas, because, within ourselves, they are perfectly distinct one from another.
fn.536: As shall be seen hereafter, knowledge, power and will are, beside life, the principal attributes which the ancient Muslim theologians, and, after them, certain Jewish theologians (notably the Karaites), acknowledged in God as attributes essential and eternal. Vide Schahrestâni, Germ. transl., vol. I, pp. 42, 95 and passim; Pococke, Specimen hist. Ar., p. 223; Schmölders, Essai sur les écoles philosophiques chez les Arabes, pp. 187 and 196. These same attributes are cited by Al-Gazâli, in his Destruction of the Philosophers (at the commencement of the sixth Question), whilst speaking of the opinion of the philosophers and of the Mo’tazales; we cite the Hebrew version: הסכימו הפלוסופים על שקרות קיום המדע והיכולת והרצון בהתחלה הראשונה כמו שהסכימו עליו המעתזלה וכו׳ «The philosophers are agreed that it is false to affirm knowledge, power and will in the first principle (or in God), and the Mo’tazales also are agreed thereupon, etc.» Cf. Saadia, Book of Beliefs and Opinions, II, 1 to 4; Ahron ben-Elie, Tree of Life, chap. LXVII.
fn.537: The author alludeth, on the one hand, to the cifâtiyya or partisans of attributes, who, without any evasion, acknowledge in God eternal attributes, and, on the other hand, to a portion of the Mo’tazales, who thought to satisfy the principle of absolute unity by saying that God is powerful, not by power, but by His essence, that He is living, not by life, but by His essence, and so forth. Vide Pococke, l. c., p. 214, and the text of Abu’l-Faraj, p. 19; Schahrestâni, l. c., p. 42; Schmölders, l. c., pp. 196, 197. The discussion touching the attributes was renewed among the Jewish theologians; there were some (notably in the sect of the Karaites) who, following the example of certain Mo’tazales, admitted essential attributes (ספורים עצמיים, vide Ahron ben-Elie, Tree of Life, at the end of chap. LXVII). Among the Rabbanite doctors, Maimonides himself nameth the Spaniard R. Joseph ibn-Zaddik as having followed the opinion of the בעלי התארים or partisans of attributes; vide the collection of the Letters of Maimonides (letter to R. Samuel ibn-Tibbon), Amsterdam edition, fol. 14 b. — As for the expression لذاته, by His essence, the Muslim theologians themselves were not altogether agreed upon its precise meaning (Vide Pococke, ibid., p. 215 et seq.); for which reason Maimonides saith that they do not express themselves in intelligible words. According to Ibn-Falaquera (Moré-ha-Moré, p. 151), the Mutakallimûn understood by this expression that power, knowledge, etc., attributed to God, are somewhat which belongeth to His essence alone, and that He hath therein nothing in common with any being.
fn.538: It is well to recall here what the author saith elsewhere of the rational part of the soul in accordance with the Peripatetic theories. In the first of the Eight Chapters serving as an introduction to the treatise Aboth, after having spoken of nutrition, sensibility, imagination and appetite, behold how he expresseth himself upon the fifth part of the soul or the rational faculty (Vide Pococke’s Porta Mosis, pp. 188 and 189): «The rational part is that faculty existing in man whereby he is intelligent, whereby reflection is accomplished, whereby he acquireth knowledge, and whereby he distinguisheth between that which is base and that which is beautiful in the matter of actions. The actions (of the rational faculty) are some practical, others speculative. The practical belongeth to the domain of art or reflection; the speculative is that whereby man knoweth invariant beings as they are, and this is what is termed knowledge in an absolute sense. The artistic faculty is that whereby man acquireth the arts, as, for example, carpentry, agriculture, medicine and navigation. Reflection is that whereby one examineth in a thing one wisheth to do, and at the moment one wisheth to do it, whether it be possible or not to do it, and, supposing it be possible, how it must be done.» We see that what the author calleth the rational part or reasonable of the soul is the whole of all those faculties of the soul which belong to man alone; all other faculties, forming the irrational part of the soul, belong equally to animals. This division of the faculties of the soul into two parts, the one reasonable (τὸ λογιστιϰὸν or τὸ λόγον ἔχον), the other irrational (τὸ ἄλογον), belongeth rather to Plato than to Aristotle; the latter seemeth even to disapprove of it openly, by criticizing those who say that the soul hath parts (Vide Treatise on the Soul, book III, chap. 9, and the Commentary of Trendelenburg on the same chapter, §§ 2 and 3, p. 528). Nevertheless Aristotle himself maketh use of this division in his classification of the virtues. See Eth. Nicom., book I, chap. 13; book VI, chap. 2: Πρότερον μέν οὖν ἐλέχθη δύ’ εἶναι μέρη τῆς ψυχῆς, τό τε λόγον ἔχον ϰαὶ τὸ ἄλογον · νῦν δὲ περὶ τοῦ λόγον ἔχοντος τὸν αὐτόν τρόπον διαιρετέον. ϰαὶ ὑποχείσθω δύο τὰ λόγον ἔχοντα, ἕν μὲν ᾧ θεωροῦμεν τὰ τοιαῦτα τῶν ὄντων ὅσων αἱ ἀρχαὶ μὴ ἐνδέχονται ἄλλως ἔχειν, ἕν δὲ ᾧ τὰ ἐνδεχόμενα · ϰ. τ. λ. It is this classification which hath served as the basis for that which Maimonides saith of the rational part of the soul in the passage which we have just cited.
fn.539: Literally: and their number hath well-nigh no end, I mean the number of the arts which the rational faculty produceth. Instead of מספר הפעולות which is read in all the editions of Ibn Tibbon's version, one must read מספר המלאכות, as found in the MSS. and the version of Al-Harizi.
fn.540: The author is not in agreement with that which he elsewhere saith to be the opinion of Aristotle and of all the Peripatetic philosophers, to wit, that the first cause, which is absolute unity, can have for its effect naught but unity, and that from the absolute one the multiple cannot emanate. We shall have occasion to return thereto in the Second Part of this work, chap. XXII, where this question is particularly treated.
fn.541: Literally: be an attribute (proceeding) from His action, and not an attribute of His essence.
fn.542: Literally: for because they (the partisans of attributes) abandon not the word COMPOSITION, the idea thereof is not for that reason removed from the essence endowed with attributes; that is to say: as soon as one admitteth an essence having essential attributes, one admitteth implicitly composition, whilst in admitting only attributes of action, it followeth not that the essence whence the actions emanate be aught composed. — The words יבטל מענאה are rendered in the version of Ibn-Tibbon by יבטל ענינה, the feminine suffix in ענינה referring to מלת ההרכבה; it is by a typographical error that the editions bear, some ענינם, others ענינים.
fn.543: Literally: but there is here a ground of doubt which hath led them to this, that is to say, which hath led certain theologians to admit essential attributes.
fn.544: The author hath here expressed himself in a truncated and obscure manner, and his words have been diversely interpreted. He meaneth probably that, according to the partisans of attributes, a distinction must be made between transitive attributes, which indicate an action produced upon an object, and those which may be called neuter; these latter alone are what they call essential attributes, which proceed not from His actions, whilst transitive attributes, on the contrary, as, for example, that of Creator, could not be essential, as they relate necessarily to something outside of God, for it would be absurd to say that God is the Creator of Himself. Here is how Moses of Narbonne explaineth these last words: ירצה אבל היותו בורא הוא בורא לזולתו לא לעצמו ולכן לא יהיה תאר עצמי לו יתעלה לפי שהוא מכלל פעולותיו. “He meaneth: but to be Creator signifieth that He createth that which is outside of Him, and not Himself; wherefore this is not an essential attribute of God, for it appertaineth to His actions.” Joseph Caspi saith that the author speaketh here of the arguments of little worth imagined by the most subtle among the Motécallemîn to defend their opinion concerning attributes: they have, saith he, divided attributes into transitive and neuter (והוא שיעשו חלוקה בין תארים יוצאים ובין מה שהם בודדים), which the author indicateth by citing as an example the attribute derived from the verb to create, for which (addeth Caspi) any other transitive verb might be substituted, such as to build, to write, etc.
fn.545: The numerous attributes admitted by the Cifâtiyya, according to the texts of the Koran, were subsequently reduced to seven, which are: life, knowledge, will, power, speech, hearing, and sight. See Schahrestâni, Germ. transl., vol. I, p. 95; Schmœlders, loc. cit., p. 187; cf. Pococke, Sp. hist. Ar., p. 216. Ibn-Roschd observeth that these seven attributes apply as well to the soul, and that the essence of God determined by these attributes would be of the same genus as the soul, with this difference, that it is not found in a body. See the observations added by Moses of Narbonne, at the end of his Commentary, upon this chapter.— The word כתאב, Scripture, signifieth not here the Bible, but, in general, a book considered as divine, and notably the Koran; for it is here a question especially of the doctrines professed by the Muslim theologians, and which certain Jewish doctors had borrowed from them.
fn.546: These are, as we have said above, neuter attributes, indicating in no wise an action produced upon an object.
fn.547: The author wisheth now to show that it is wrongly believed that these four attributes could be separated from the other attributes indicating actions and made into essential attributes. Here is in substance his reasoning, which he hath not presented with all desirable clarity: Firstly, if by knowledge be understood to perceive oneself, then life and knowledge are absolutely identical in God, both indicating a perception of oneself, and there is no ground to make of them two distinct attributes. If, however, one admitteth the sense which the partisans of attributes attach here to the word knowledge, by which they understand the knowledge that God hath of created things, there is no reason to make of knowledge an essential attribute, and the same holdeth for power and will; for all these attributes indicate necessarily, according to them, relations existing between God and created things, and are found in the same conditions as the attributes of action, as, for example, that of Creator. Thus, the essential attributes, reduced to their true value, are but a vain hypothesis.
fn.548: Life, saith Aristotle, consisteth principally in sensibility and in intelligence (ἔοιϰε δὴ τὸ ζἠν εἶναι ϰυρίως τὸ αἰσθάνεσθαι ἤ νοεῖν, Eth. Nic., Bk. IX, ch. 9). To say of a being that it liveth, it sufficeth that there be in it intelligence, or sensibility, or motion (See Treatise on the Soul, Bk. II, ch. 2). In God there can be no question but of an intelligible perception, of the perception of Himself; His life is intelligence, and for Him knowledge and life are absolutely identical. See Metaph., XII, 7: ϰαὶ ζωὴ δέ γε ὑπάρχει · ἡ γὰρ νοῦ ἐνέργεια ζωή, ϰ. τ. λ.
fn.549: This is what the author will explain more fully in Ch. LXVIII. — The first אלמדרכה̈ is the active participle (المُذَكِّرَة) ; the second, the passive participle (الْمُدْرَكَة) .
fn.550: The inanimate body hath no perception, and all perceptions, both sensible and intelligible, belong unto the various faculties of the soul.
fn.551: That is to say, the attributes called essential.
fn.552: Instead of והוא, which several editions of Ibn-Tibbon's version bear, one must read, according to the Arabic: העצם ההוא, as do indeed the MSS. and the princeps edition.
fn.553: That is to say, one cannot establish a difference between the attributes of action and the attributes of relation; these latter can no more be called essential attributes than the former.
fn.554: Literally: and with that which we have also set forth concerning the reality of relation and (saith he) that it is erroneously admitted. The author meaneth to say: Besides that the attributes of relation cannot be considered as essential attributes, we have shown above, in setting forth the true meaning of relation, that it is but by error that men have believed it possible to admit any relation whatsoever between God and created things. Vid., in the preceding chap., the IVth class of attributes.—By the words ואנהא מטֿנונה̈, the author alludeth to what he hath said at the place indicated (fol. 60 b of our text): אמא אן חכון בינהמא נסבה̈ מא פהו אמר יָסֶךְ בה אנה יעח ולים כדֿלך But that there should be between them any relation whatsoever, is a thing which hath been judged admissible, although it be not so (p. 200).
fn.555: That is to say, that they are attributes relating unto actions.
fn.556: The author here entereth upon the interpretation of certain important passages of the Pentateuch, wherein mention is made, in an allegorical manner, of the perception of the Divine Essence and of the attributes of God. The commentators observe that Moses is here called prince of the learned, and not, as elsewhere, prince of the prophets, because the matter here concerneth the highest metaphysical questions, whereof Moses sought the solution, and which were to be for him the object of philosophical speculation.
fn.557: It is doubtless by design that the author hath here inverted the order of the two prayers of Moses, in order to mention first the most important, that which had for its object the very essence of God. As for Moses, saith Abravanel, he followed the usual order of studies, beginning with that which is easiest, to pass thenceforth unto that which is more difficult.
fn.558: The author, as shall be seen, doth not here take the word נאמן in the sense of faithful, but in that of true and stable or solid, and he beholdeth therein an allusion to thoughts true and solid.
fn.559: The Arabic text expresseth itself here in an irregular manner, saying literally: thus therefore the perception of these actions are his attributes etc. One might be tempted to believe that there is here some error of the copyist, and, in sooth, the MSS. offer here divers variants which show that this passage hath been corrupted by copyists. One of the MSS. of Leyden beareth: לא׳ן אלארא אלגיר צחיחה̈ אדׄא לא תתׄבת תלך אלאפעאל ותלך אלאפעאל הי צפאתה תעאלי; in another manuscript, we read: לא׳ן אלארא אלגיר צחיחה̈ לא תתׄבת אדראך תלך אלאפעאל אלתי הי צפאתה תעאלי. It is seen that the reading which we have adopted is yet the least incorrect; the version of Ibn-Tibbon is in perfect accord with our reading, and reproduceth the same incorrectness. The unique MS. of the version of Al-’Harizi beareth: כי הדעות שאינם אמתיות לא תתקיים השגתם והפעלים ההם הם מדותיו; in the edition of the first part of this version which was made at London (p. 53), this passage hath been arbitrarily changed; therein we read: כי הדעות שאינם אמתיות לא תתקיים השגתם אם כן השגת הפעלים ההם הם מדותיו.
fn.560: The word מדה, which signifieth measure, is employed, in Rabbinic language, in the sense of property, quality, or character.
fn.561: Vid. Mishnah, IVth part, treatise Aboth, chap. V, §§ 13 and 14.
fn.562: Literally: by actions whereby I must imitate thy actions (employed) in their governance.
fn.563: All the MSS. bear אגׄנה̈ (أجنة, pl. of جنين), the embryos, although all the suffixes referring thereto, in the words following, are in the singular.
fn.564: It must be remembered that we employ here, as elsewhere, the word passion in the sense of the Greek word πάθος, rendered in Arabic by انفعال, and which signifieth passivity in general, or the affection by an impression coming from without.
fn.565: Passion, or passivity, implieth a change in him who is the object of the impression, and, consequently, no passivity or affective quality could be attributed to God. See towards the end of chap. XXXV (p. 133), and hereafter, at the beginning of chap. LV (p. 225).
fn.566: That is to say, grant unto us the women whom we have carried away; אותם relateth to the women, and the masculine suffix is irregular, as in אבותם and אחיהם. In several editions of Ibn-Tibbon's version, another example hath been substituted, taken from Job (19, 21); but the editio princeps is conformable to our text.
fn.567: Literally: or a general thing which causeth to perish, or which destroyeth.
fn.568: Literally: the children, and the children of the children.
fn.569: Literally: which emanate from none of us against another.
fn.570: That is to say, if he desireth, like Moses, to know the ways of God, and to conform his actions unto those which emanate from God.
fn.571: The author departeth here from the interpretation of Onkelos and the Talmud (Yômâ, fol. 86 a) and from that of all the commentators, who agree in giving to the verb נַקֵּה the sense of declaring pure or innocent, to absolve. In the passage of Isaiah, the word וְנִקָּתָה signifieth literally: she shall be made empty, which is to say: she shall be despoiled of her inhabitants, devastated; wherefore it is unseasonably that the author citeth this passage in support of the sense of uprooting, destroying, which he giveth here to the verb נַקֵּה.
fn.572: Literally: and none is called שונא (hating, enemy) save the idolater. Ibn-Tibbon addeth the word alone (לבד), which is not found in our Arabic text, nor doth it express the words כאשר אמר, which are found in the two Hebrew versions. We have deemed it necessary to add the words: who is also presented as the object of God's hatred; for, in the passage cited, hatred is not attributed to the idolater, but to God, and this passage doth not well accord with that which precedeth.
fn.574: That is to say, in the enumeration of the thirteen middôth and in the Decalogue, brought into relation with the passage of Deuteronomy concerning the idolatrous city.
fn.575: The reading varieth somewhat in the MSS.: the greater part bear גמאר (غبار), some few גמר (خُمُرُ or دور), and one of the MSS. of Leyden, אגמאר (أغمار); all these words, some being singulars, others plurals, signify a mixed troop, a crowd (miscella hominum turba). The unique MS. of Al-’Harizi's version beareth בחיי, during the life; the London editor hath, for what reason we know not, substituted בחטא, following the faulty reading of the editions of Ibn-Tibbon's version.
fn.576: That is to say, to those designated by the thirteen middôth.
fn.577: The author seemeth here to have committed an error of memory in stating that these words of the Rabbins serve as a commentary upon this passage of Leviticus: Ye shall be holy; for I, the Lord your God, am holy. fn.578: It goeth without saying that the word privation is taken here in the Aristotelian sense of the word στέρησις. Cf. above, chap. XVII, p. 69.
fn.579: One of the manuscripts of Leyden beareth: ,מת״ל אן יכון לה שי באל קוח̈ as, for example, (to admit) that He hath a thing IN POTENTIALITY. Al-’Harizi translateth: כדי שלא יהיה לו שום דבר בכח. It is seen that Al-’Harizi preferred to read באלקוה̈, but he hath fallen into an error of sense by retaining the negation שלא; the word כדי is doubtless a copyist's error for כמו.
fn.581: This followeth from the whole body of the Aristotelian doctrines concerning motion. Vid., among others, Physics, Book III, ch. 2: Ἡ τε ϰίνησις ἐνέργεια μέν τις εἶναι δοϰεῖ, ἀτελὴς δέ · αἴτιον δ’οτι ἀτελὲς τὸ δυνατόν, οὗ ἐστίν ἡ ἐνέργεια ϰίνησις.
fn.582: Cf. above, chap. LII, pp. 200 and 201.
fn.583: The sphere of the fixed stars, which encompasseth the spheres of the planets and which formeth in a manner the limit of the universe, is (after the superior or encompassing sphere) the most extensive body that can be imagined. See, concerning the celestial spheres and their number, the second part of this work, chap. IV; cf. IIIrd part, chap. XIV.
fn.584: The editions of the version of Ibn Tibbon bear ויודע וחכם; the word ויודע must be erased, for it is not to be found in the manuscripts.
fn.585: Literally: (in such wise) that the difference between these attributes and our attributes would consist (only) in the greater, etc.
fn.586: That is to say, that the attributes of God and our own would fall under the same genus, and the same definition would apply unto both; for their quiddity would be the same, and they would be distinguished only by the more and the less. Cf. above, chap. XXXV, p. 131.
fn.587: Literally: for one expresseth oneself by the form AF’ALU (أَفْعَلُ) only between things of which that which is in question (the adjective) is spoken CONVENTIONALLY, that is to say, unto which the adjective whereof it is a question is applied in a manner like unto a common or appellative noun; thus, for example, living is a common noun for everything that hath life; powerful, for everything that hath power. Upon the meaning of the word בתואטא (بتواطؤ), vide supra, page 6, note 2.
fn.588: Behold, in summary, the sense of this entire passage: The partisans of the essential attributes, saith the author, ought to understand that the difference between the attributes of God and our own could not consist solely in the more and the less; for, in such a case, there would be between them a proportional relation and, consequently, a similitude, which they could no more admit than the similitude between the divine essence and our own. But where there is no similitude, there is likewise no common definition; consequently, the partisans of attributes, who, whilst rejecting similitude, nevertheless admit that the same definition embraceth the attributes of God and our own, are in contradiction with themselves.
fn.593: In the preceding chapters, the author hath refuted those who believe themselves able to admit as essential attributes of God, life, knowledge, power, and will. Here he goeth on to show that one cannot even admit as attributes of God existence, unity, and eternity, which are more generally considered as attributes inherent in the divine essence. Cf. Bahya, Duties of the Hearts, book I, chap. 10.
fn.594.sub_0: From the manner in which the author here expresseth himself, one might believe that it concerneth a well-known proposition belonging to Aristotle; but, as several commentators observe, this subtle distinction between the quiddity of a thing and its existence belongeth to Ibn-Sînâ, and it hath been impugned by other Arabian philosophers, and notably by Ibn-Roschd, who informeth us that those who have seen in existence an accident have based their view, among other things, upon the fact that the Arabic word موجود, which the philosophers employ in the sense of existent or that which is (τὸ ὄν), is primarily a passive participle signifying found, and indicateth, by its etymology, something accidental. At the commencement of the 1st book of his Epitome of Metaphysics, Ibn-Roschd, after having set forth the divers meanings of the philosophical term درو جود (that which is, τὸ ὄν), thus summarizeth (Hebr. vers.): ולכן היה שם הנמצא שב אל שני אלו הענינים לבד ר״ל אל הצודק ואל מה שהוא נמצא חוץ לשכל, that is to say, that in summary, the said term is used either for that which the mind judgeth to be true (ἔτι τὸ εἶναι σημαίνει ϰαί τὸ ἔστιν ὅτι ἀληθές, ϰ. τ. λ. Arist., Metaph., book V, chap. 7), or of being in itself, of that which hath an objective reality outside the mind, and, in this sense, it applieth to all the categories (ϰαθ’ αὑτὸ δέ εἶναι λέγεται ὅσαπερ σημαίνει τὰ σχήματα τῆς ϰατη-γορίας, ϰ. τ. λ. Ibidem). Accidental existence, addeth Ibn-Roschd, cannot be conceived in the isolated being or in being in itself (ϰαθ’ αὑτό), for the substance of the thing and its quiddity cannot be accidental; it can only be conceived in the mutual relation of beings, that is to say, when the ὄν expresseth an accidental relation of one thing to another, or when it is said, as Aristotle expresseth it, ϰατὰ συαβεβηϰός: אולם הנמצא במקרה הוא לא יצויר במציאות הנפרד כי עצמות הדבר ומהותו אי אפשר ש׳היה במקרה ואמנם יצויר מיחם הנמצאות קצתם لا קצת.
fn.594.sub_1: He then refuteth the opinion of Ibn-Sînâ, according to whom existence is an accident supervening upon the essence or the quiddity of the thing which existeth, and, after having shown all that is false in this way of viewing the matter, he addeth: אבל זה דרך האיש הזה ברוב מה שיביאהו מצד עצמו «But such is the manner of this man in almost all that he allegeth of his own accord.» Ibn-Roschd looked with disfavour upon a proposition which appeared to him to be in opposition to the Aristotelian doctrines. In truth, this ideal separation between what the thing is (τὸ τί ἦν εἶνο ι) and its existence is contrary to the spirit of Aristotle’s doctrine; it would be at most in artificial objects that one might separate the what from the existence, the idea of the thing being in the mind of the artist before existing (cf. Aristotle, Metaph., book VII, chap. 7: ἀπὸ τέχνης δὲ γίγνεται ὅσων τὸ εἶδος ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ, εἶδος δὲ λέγω τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι ἑϰάסטου ϰαί τὴν πρώτην οὐσίαν’). According to the partisans of Ibn-Sînâ, the same would hold true of all that is produced by nature; for, say they, all things being in the first cause, or in God, who knoweth them beforehand, the quiddity of things is prior to their existence, which, consequently, is an accident of the quiddity (vide the commentary of Shem-Tob, on our passage). But this reasoning leadeth to the admission, with Plato, of pre-existing ideas or forms, and is little in accordance with the Peripatetic doctrines. —Vide also note 1 of the following page.
fn.595: That is to say, something that hath newly occurred to its quiddity and which is posterior thereto. The manuscripts generally bear טריא (طاريا) and עארצ̇א (عارضاً), and these two words must be considered as the enunciative (خبر) of the negation لا, which hath here the force of a verb, whilst وجودة or هو is to be understood; it is as though one had said: ليس وجوده طارئاً.
fn.596: It is erroneously that Pococke (Specimen hist. Ar., pag. 214) compareth these words of Maimonides with what certain Mo’tazales said, namely, that God is powerful by His essence, knowing by His essence, etc.; we have seen above (chap. LIII, pag. 209) that Maimonides himself blameth these words of the Mo’tazales, which he findeth little intelligible and wherein he seeth a covert admission of essential attributes. The author, by saying: existent, not by existence, living, not by life, etc., evidently avoideth expressing himself, like the Mo’tazales, in affirmative terms. Cf. the last of the Eight Chapters with which our author precedeth his commentary on the treatise Aboth; concerning the same question, he likewise expresseth himself by negative terms, saying: אן אללה תעאלי לים הו עאלמא בעלם ולא חיא בחייא̈ (Vide Pococke, Porta Mosis, pag. 254).
fn.597.sub_0: As the commentator Shem-Tob observeth, that which the author saith here is nowhere to be found in the Metaphysics of Aristotle, but rather the contrary. Indeed, the one (τὸ ὄν) per se, unto which Aristotle assigneth four principal significations, which are: the continuous, the whole, the individual, and the universal (according as one considereth therein the indivisibility of motion or that of the idea), is inseparable from the very nature and quiddity of the thing which is one, and cannot be considered as an accident of the quiddity. The one is not in itself an essence, and it can exist only in a subject. Its proper character is to be indivisible and the first measure in every genus, and notably the measure of quantity; but, even as being (τὸ ὄν), with which it is confounded and identified, it applyeth to all the categories, and is not found particularly in one alone. The manifold is opposed to the one, as the divisible to the indivisible, and not as non-being to being; for the manifold is in being, as well as the one, and is attributed, like the latter, to all the categories. The one and the manifold in number, designating quantity alone, are abstractions and entirely distinct from being. See the details in the Metaphysics of Aristotle, book V, chap. 6, and book X, chap. 1 et seq. — Maimonides, who seeth in the one and the manifold naught but accidents distinct from being, hath further followed the opinion of Ibn-Sīnā, who, as Ibn-Roschd observeth, hath confounded the one of number with the absolute one: “A difficulty which may be found here,” saith Ibn-Roschd (loc. cit., book III), “is this: how, whilst admitting that the one of number belongeth to the category of quantity, can we subsequently admit that it is found in all the categories, and moreover that it is in the categories themselves, and not something which is accessory thereto? Wherefore Ibn-Sīnā hath thought that its substratum must be an accident which is found in all the categories.”
fn.597.sub_1: “But it is not so; for the one in number is of another nature than other unities. Indeed, the numerical one is individuality, abstracted from that which is quantity and quality—I mean from that whereby the individual is an individual; for it is an individual only in the sense of the indivisible, and the mind abstracteth it from material things, limiteth it, and taketh it for something separate. The one in number, the numerical unity, is but a thing which the soul effecteth in individual beings, and without the soul there would be neither numerical unity nor number in general, contrary to that which obtaineth for the line and the surface, and, in general, for continuous quantity; wherefore number is, more than any other thing, pure from matter. Ibn-Sīnā hath confounded the nature of the one, the principle of number, with the absolute one, which embraceth all the categories, and since the one, the principle of number, is an accident, he hath admitted that the absolute one, which is the same thing as being, is also an accident.” Cf. R. Levi ben-Gerson, Mil’hamôth, book V, 3, chap. 12.
fn.598: Quantity, saith Aristotle (Categories, chap. 6), is either discrete (διωριτμένον, منفصل), or continuous (συνε χές, متصل); discrete quantity, he addeth, consisteth of number and speech, whereof the parts have between them no common term where they unite. It is evident that the author, in saying here that the one belongeth, like number, to the genus or category of discrete quantity, hath confounded, as did Ibn-Sīnā, numerical unity with absolute unity. See the preceding note.
fn.599: The verb تسامح (the VIth form of جسم), which signifieth to act with gentleness, to show oneself easy or indulgent, is also employed, as a technical term, in the sense of to permit oneself an improper expression, that is to say, to be lax regarding the words one employeth and not to adhere to their rigorous sense, when one desireth to express an idea for which the proper terms are not found (cf. supra, p. 203, note 5). According to the definition of the Kitâb al Ta’rîfât (reported also in the Dictionary of Freytag), this term signifieth that the idea which one aimeth to express doth not emerge from the words employed, and that it is necessary, in order to divine it, to understand another expression as implied.
fn.600: The word חאדתֹ (حادث) signifieth that which hath newly occurred, that which is produced or created, and is opposed to קדים قديم, ancient, eternal.
fn.601: Literally: for ETERNAL is said only of that which time affecteth, which etc. See supra, chap. LII, p. 199, and ibid., note 1. It must not be forgotten that the author here reasoneth upon the Arabic word (قديم), employed in the sense of eternal, but which signifieth primarily that which precedeth, anterior, ancient, and which evidently designateth something that hath a relation unto time.
fn.602: Literally: And it is also of the class of the relative; that is to say, the word قديم (anterior, eternal) belongeth to the category of relation, which embraceth, according to the expression of Aristotle (Categ., chap. 7), all that which is said to be what it is because of things other than itself, or, in other words, all that which relateth to a thing other than itself (cf. Maimonides, Compendium of Logic, chap. 11). Indeed, the anterior is said in relation to that which is posterior; the ancient, in relation to that which is new; the eternal, in relation to that which hath not always been and which is originate from something. The author meaneth probably that the word eternal, being a relative, cannot be applied unto God, who cannot be brought into relation with any thing. Cf. supra, p. 200, and ibid., note 1.
fn.603: That is to say: even as long and short are relatives which apply to the line, so eternal and created, ancient and new, are relatives which apply unto time. The words פי ערץֹ אלזמאן signify here: in the extent or in the region of time, and likewise, פי ערץֹ אלכֹט: in the extent of the line. One must here pronounce عرض, and not عرض‍‍, as did the two Hebrew translators, who render the words in question by במקרה הזמן (in the accident of time) and במקרה הקו (in the accident of the line), which yieldeth scarcely any sense. Ibn-Falaquera hath already observed that the word ערץֹ must here be rendered in Hebrew by רוחב (breadth), taken here in the sense of מדה, measure, extent. See Moré ha-Moré, p. 28, and the appendix, p. 151. Cf. infra, chap. LXXII (fol. 101 b, line 6, of our text): בקדר ערץֹ דֹלך אלנוע, according to the EXTENT of this species.
fn.604: More literally: and who examines them, the intellect grasping and abstracting them, and not with the total idea indicated by the words, that is to say, who examines them with a profound intelligence, capable of grasping these things in themselves, in all their abstraction, and is not guided by the general sense which certain words possess. Thus, for example, he who comprehendeth these metaphysical subjects shall know that, when it is said of God that He exists, that He is one and eternal, these words have here an abstract sense, entirely independent of that which they have in their general application. — Instead of באלתגֹמל, several manuscripts bear באלתגֹמים (with corporification or the corporeal idea); but our reading is confirmed by the two Hebrew versions, which bear, the one בכללות, the other בחבור. The word תגֹמל (تجمل) is a noun of action (of the Vth form), derived from the substantive جهالة , totality, and signifies here generality, ensemble.
fn.606: That is to say: the words first and last, applied unto God, must be taken figuratively, even as the eye and the ear, which are attributed unto Him.
