fn.607.sub_0: Literally: know that to describe (or designate) God — may He be glorified and exalted! — by means of negations, is the true description (or manner of assigning attributes unto Him), which is affected by no improper expression (on تسامح , vide supra, page 235, note 1), and in which there is in no wise, nor in any manner whatsoever, a defect in respect of God; that is to say: the attributes expressed by negations are alone true, containing, within their terms, nothing which one need regard as an improper expression, and saying naught, in respect of God, which implieth an imperfection. — Already before Maimonides, the Jewish theologians, and notably those of Spain, had insisted upon this point and had established that one cannot express what God is, but only what He is not, and that the attributes which are commonly ascribed unto Him, far from having an affirmative sense, indicate nothing else than the exclusion of their contrary; by one, it is meant only that God is not manifold; by eternal, that He is not created, and so forth. Vide Bahya, Duties of the Hearts, bk. I, chap. 10; Judah ha-Levi, Khozari, bk. II, § 2; Abraham ben David, Emunah Ramah (The Sublime Faith), bk. II, 3rd foundation (p. 51 of the text, and p. 65 of the German translation by M. Simon Weil, Frankfort, 1852). The Arabian philosophers pronounce themselves in the same sense, and certain Muslim sects had made of negative attributes an essential point of their doctrine, as, e.g., the Dhirâriyya (vide Shahrastâni, Germ. transl., vol. I, p. 94). The Karaite Ahron ben Elijah, in his עץ חיים or Tree of Life (chap. LXXI), refutes the partisans of negative attributes. These latter believed they could support themselves by the opinion of Aristotle, whom Bahya cites expressly in this regard.
fn.607.sub_1: Here follow the terms of the Arabic original of the treatise on the Duties of the Hearts: ולהדֹא קאל ארמטוטאלים אלמואלב מן צפאת אלכֹאלק תעאלי אצדק מן אלמוגֹכאת לאן כל מא יוגֹב לה מן אלצפאת לא תכֹלו פן צפאת אלגֹוהר או אלערץֹ וכֹאלק אלגֹוהר ואלערץֹ לא ילחקה פי דֹאתה וצף מן אוצאפהמא וכל מא ינפי ענה מן אלצפאת פהי צאדקה̈ לא מהאלה̈ “Wherefore Aristotle saith: The negative attributes of the Creator are more true than the affirmative; for all the attributes that one might assign Him affirmatively could only be attributes of substance or of accident, and the Creator of substance and of accident cannot have in His essence any of their attributes. But the attributes which are removed from Him (that is to say, the attributes expressed negatively) are indubitably true.” — This passage, which is cited also by Ibn-Falaquera (Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 29), is evidently apocryphal. It is true that Aristotle, in speaking of the first mover, very often expresseth himself by negative terms, such as: being immutable, separate from all that is sensible, which can have no extension, which is indivisible, etc. (Metaph., XII, 7 and passim); but he in no wise excludeth affirmative terms, and that which the doctrine of the Arabian philosophers possesseth of the absolute in this regard appeareth to be drawn from the Neoplatonic commentators and to be connected with the doctrines of Plotinus (cf. Ritter, Geschichte der Philosophie, vol. IV, p. 573 et seq.). St. Thomas in his turn, in saying that we cannot express ourselves concerning God save by the negative way, followed the Arabian philosophers, from whom he doubtless borrowed the term via remotionis (طريق النفي) . Vide Summa C. Gent., bk. I, chap. 14.
fn.608: Literally: as for His description by means of affirmations, there is therein, in the matter of association and imperfection, that which we have already set forth; that is to say: by assigning to God affirmative attributes, one implicitly acknowledgeth that there are in Him divers ideas associated together, and one also ascribeth unto Him imperfection. By the word שרך (شُرَك) , association, the author appeareth to make allusion to the comparison which he established above (chap. L, p. 181) between the belief in essential attributes and the Christian dogma of the Trinity. For the Mo'tazals also, to give God an attribute is to give Him an associate (مشريك) . Their chief said expressly: He who admitteth with the (divine) idea an eternal attribute, admitteth two gods. Cf. Pococke, Specimen hist. Ar., p. 216.
fn.609: Literally: although there be in them no other particularization than (that) of removing that which is denied from among all that we believed ought not to be denied, that is to say, to divest the subject of certain qualities which one might attribute unto it, and to confine it by negations within a narrower circle, so as to determine it in a certain manner.
fn.610: Literally: make us to know absolutely nothing of the essence of which one desireth to know what it is.
fn.611: Literally: we apprehend but His THAT only, not His WHAT (for God, being incapable of definition, we cannot say what He is; vide supra, p. 190). The word אני̈ (أنيّة) is derived, doubtless, from the conjunction أن or أنَّ, that (quod), and, to render this Arabic term exactly, one should have to form the word quoddity (analogous to quiddity). It is the ὅτ’, which Aristotle placeth at the head of those objects which the intelligence hath in view in every science, and which designateth the pure existence of the thing (vid. Posterior Analytics, bk. II, chap. 1). It is only after having recognised that the thing is, that one enquireth what it is (μετὰ ταῦτα γνόντες, ὅ τ ι ἐστί τι, τ ί οὖν τοῦτ’ ἐστί, ζד τοῦμεν. Ibid., chap. 2). In the Kitâb al-Ta’rifât, we read the following definition: الانية تحقق الوجود العينى من حيث رتبة الذاتية “The anniyya establisheth the existence in itself, considered at the degree of pure essence.” The sense of this definition is thus: the ὅτι (the that or the quoddity) is limited to establishing pure and abstract existence, from the point of view of being, or of essence (to render الذاتية exactly, one would need to form the word essentiality); it is being considered in itself and whilst making abstraction of all that might serve to determine it, such as quiddity (τί ἐστιι), quality (πσ̃ς ἐστι) and cause (τὸ διότι). Cf. my Extracts from the Source of Life of Ibn Gabirol, or Avicebron, bk. V, § 30. M. Silv. de Sacy hath given of the said definition a translation entirely different from mine own; yet he himself confesseth that he doth not warrant the accuracy of his translation, and he offereth upon the etymology of the word الإنية a conjecture of little plausibility. Vid. Notices et extraits des manuscrits, t. X, p. 85.
fn.612: Even as the author hath said at the commencement of the preceding chapter, existence and quiddity in God are one and the same thing, and could not be separated the one from the other; wherefore one could not make of one of the two the attribute of the other, and, as was said above, one cannot even give unto God as an attribute being or existence. It hath been established, moreover, that God cannot be defined, and that, consequently, one could not give Him any attribute indicating His quiddity (vid. chap. LII, p. 190).—The editions of Ibn Tibbon's version bear: מפני שאין לו מהות חוץ לישותו; one must read, according to the Arabic, ישות חוץ למהותו, as several manuscripts indeed have it, and likewise Ibn Falaquera, Moré ha-Moré, p. 29.
fn.613: Beings which have a prior cause enter into a genus and are distinguished by a difference, and their quiddity, consequently, is composed of two things; man, for example, is animal and rational, and his quiddity is contained within these two attributes, whereof one indicateth the genus, and the other the difference. God hath no prior cause and entereth into no genus, and His quiddity can be naught but of an absolute simplicity. Cf. supra, p. 190, and ibid., note 3. — The editions of Ibn Tibbon's version generally bear על שני חלקים; one must read: על שני חלקיה, as found in the manuscripts and the editio princeps. Al-Harizi and Ibn Falaquera (loc. cit.) have, the one על הלקים, the other על החלקים, which is inaccurate.
fn.614: That is to say: which is the very essence of this being and hath no cause outside of it (cf. supra, at the commencement of chap. LVII). — There is some obscurity in this sentence, of which the literal translation is this: thenceforth we understand that (as for) this being, its existence, which is its essence, sufficeth it not, that it should exist only, but that, on the contrary, there THENCE emanateth, etc. One discerneth not clearly whether the word ענה, which we have rendered by thence, signifieth from him (referring to this being), or else from it (referring to the existence). In the editions of Ibn Tibbon's version, there are here some inaccuracies; thus must one read, according to the manuscripts: ואחרי כן השגנו שזה הנמצא אין מציאותו אשר הוא עצמו ממפיק לו שיהיה נמצא בלבד אבל שופעות מאתו מציאויות רבות. It is by design that the translator hath here given to the word מציאות the masculine gender, in order, as he himself saith, to allow the ambiguity which we have remarked in the Arabic text to remain; thus doth he express himself in a note, upon the words אשר הוא עצמו (MS. of the Sorbonne collection, No. 108): שמתי הנה מלת מציאות על לשון זכר בהכרח כנוי וכנוי מאתו אפשר שהוא שב אל הנמצא או אל המציאות וראי וה לא כראי זה ואילו הייתי עושה שם מציאות לשון נקבה הייתי מכריע הדרך האחד וברחתי מזה והעתקתי מלה במלה.
fn.615: Literally: but it is an overflow which constantly prolongeth for them their duration and order, by a well-established governance; that is to say, that God, in producing these existences, acteth with liberty and with full consciousness, and not without will, as nature. The word פיץֹ (فيض overflow, emanation) designateth the overflow of divine grace, the inspiration whereby God manifesteth Himself in the prophets, and, in general, the divine action manifesting itself upon created beings. The author himself explaineth, in another place, why the divine action is called فيض, by comparison with water gushing from a fountain and spreading on all sides. Vid. the IInd part of this work, chap. XII.
fn.617: Literally: that they are not neglected and existing as it happeneth (by chance), but (that they are) as is everything which he who willeth, leadeth with intention and will. One must read ככון (with caph), and not בכון (with beth), as some manuscripts have it; likewise one must read, in Ibn Tibbon's version, כהיות, as the editio princeps hath it, and not בהיות, as the other editions have.
fn.618: In several manuscripts, we read פקלנא אנה ואחד ואלמעני… (we say therefore that He is unique, which signifieth...), which is more conformable to the manner in which the author hath expressed himself in the preceding passages.
fn.619: Literally: the negation of plurality. The Arabic word וחד signifieth at once one (that is to say not multiple) and unique; it hath here necessarily the latter sense, since the concern is to deny that there be another being similar unto God, and, for the same reason, the word כתרה̈ must here be translated by plurality, and not by multiplicity. To set forth more fully the idea which attacheth to the Hebrew word אחד and to the Arabic word واحد, the author ought to have said: «Finally we understand that this being hath no likes, and that there is naught in Him that is composite.» Behold how the author, in his Thirteen Articles of Faith, expresseth himself upon the unity of God: «It is that He who is the (first) cause of all things is one, not as the one of the genus, nor as the one of the species, nor as the composite individual, which divideth into several units, nor even as the simple body, one in number, but which is susceptible of being parted and divided unto infinity; but God is of a unity whereunto no unity resembleth in any manner.» See commentary on the Mishnah, IVth part, treatise Sanhedrin, chap. X (Pococke, Porta Mosis, p. 165).
fn.620: Literally: or else its meaning is the negation of its privation; that is to say: the affirmative attribute which one ascribeth unto God, if it designate not an action proceeding from God, must be considered as the negation of a privative adjective. Thus, for example, powerful must be taken in the sense of not powerless; living, in the sense of not inanimate; He is ONE signifieth He is not NOT ONE (or multiple), and so forth. Al-Gazâli, in his Makâcid al-Falâsifa (Metaphysical section, Book III), speaking in the name of the Peripatetics, thus expresseth himself upon the attributes of action (which he also calleth relative) and the negative attributes — (we cite the Hebrew version)—. ויולדו מתארי הצירוף והשלילה לראשון שמות לא יחייבו רבוי בעצמותו כי כאשר נאמר אחד הנה ענינו שלילת השתוף והדמיון ושלילת החלוק וכאשר נאמר קדמון הנה ענינו שלילת ההתחלה ממציאותו וכאשר נאמר טוב ונכבד ורחמן הנה ענינו צירופו אל פעולות םודרו ממנו. «From relative and negative attributes, there result for the first being (God) names which imply no multiplicity in His essence; for, when we say one, we mean to deny association and assimilation (of other beings unto God), as well as divisibility; when we say eternal, we mean to deny that His existence had a beginning; when we say good, glorious, merciful, this expresseth a relation to the actions proceeding from Him.»
fn.621: The author meaneth that the negative attributes of God must always have the sense of universal and absolute negations, and not that of particular negations; the negation contained in the negative attribute must resemble, saith the author, this proposition: the wall seeth not, which signifieth: no wall ever seeth, because it is not in its nature to see, whilst this other proposition: man seeth not, signifieth that such a man seeth not, because he is blind or sleepeth, or by some other accident whatsoever, although it be in his nature to see (cf. Aristotle, Categories, chap. 11; treatise De Interpretatione, chap. 7; and the Logic Abridgment of our author, ch. 2 and 11). It is evident that the negative attributes, wherewith one seeketh to remove from God all imperfection, could not be negations of the latter kind, that is to say particular negations; for imperfection must be denied here in an absolute sense, as a thing which can never exist in God.
fn.622: That is to say, which is moved by another thing, and which, consequently, hath not its cause within itself.
fn.623: The suffix הא, in חרכאתהא, which we have referred to the words הדׄה אלםמא this heaven, might also refer to אגׄזא parts (a word which here designeth the different spheres), so that one should translate: and the greater part of THEIR movements. Indeed, the editions of Ibn-Tibbon's version bear תנועותיהם, with the plural suffix, referring to חלקים; but in the manuscripts we read תנועותיו, wherein the suffix referreth to רקיע.
fn.624: The word צׄרורה̈ (necessarily) is wanting in several manuscripts; it is likewise omitted in Al-Harizi's version.
fn.625: On the meaning of the participle מחצלת̈ (محلة), cf. supra, page 190, note 4.
fn.626: It is in much the same negative terms that Aristotle expresseth himself concerning the ether, which, according to him, formeth the substance of the celestial spheres; see the treatise On the Heavens, Book I, chap. 3: τὸ δὲ ϰύϰλῳ σῶμα, φερόμενον ἀδύνατον ἔχειν βάρος ἢ ϰουφὸτητα, ϰ. τ. λ., and further: ὥστ’ εἴπερ τὸ ϰύϰλῳ σῶμα μήτ’ αὔξησιν ἔχειν ἐνδέχεται μήτέ φθίσιν, εὔλογον ϰαί ἀναλ-λοίωτον εἶναι. Διὸτι μἐν οὖν αἴδιον ϰαί οὔτ’ αὔξησιν ἔχον οὔτε φθίσιν, ἀλλ’ ἀγή-ρατον ϰαί ἀναλλοίωτον ϰαί ἀπαθές ἐστι τὸ πρῶτον τῶν σωμάτων, ϰ. τ. λ. Cf. the IInd part of this work, chap. XIX.
fn.628: Literally: if demonstration leadeth (this conviction) that the thing perceived is only THAT HE EXISTETH.
fn.629: See above, chap. XVII, p. 68, note 3.
fn.630: Literally: that the gradual superiority in this is manifold.
fn.631: Literally: and he who attributeth (that is to say, he who maketh the attributes), draweth nigh unto perception, unto reality.
fn.632: Literally: in order to possess it certain or with certainty.
fn.633: Literally: whereof it is known, by demonstration, that it is false that this thing can be attributed unto him. The verb תעלם is the preterite of the Vth form, and it must be pronounced تَعَلَّمَ; instead of והודיע, which the editions of the version of Ibn-Tibbon contain, one readeth, in the manuscripts, ונודיע or ונודע, and it is this latter reading which must be adopted. Al-’Harizi hath likewise שנודע.
fn.634: The word הכונה, which is read here in all the editions of the version of Ibn-Tibbon, is an error; the manuscripts bear האמונה.— Wrongly doth Ibn-Falaquera pretend here to rectify the version of Ibn-Tibbon, by rendering the Arabic verb וילקי by וישליך, so that one should translate: and he casteth God into this belief, which, saith he, is a figurative expression; Ibn-Falaquera hath been led into error by a faulty reading, for he read פי הדה אלעקידח̈, whilst the true reading is בהדה אלעקידה̈. See the Appendix to the Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 151.
fn.635: The word באלהבת̇ is not expressed in the editions of the version of Ibn-Tibbon; the manuscripts of this version bear בדרישה ובחקירה.
fn.636: Concerning the meaning of the word מלכה̈ (مَلَكَة), which we render by capacity, and which correspondeth to the Greek word ἕξ·ς, cf. supra, p. 195, notes 1 and 2.
fn.637.sub_0: This somewhat obscure passage hath been diversely interpreted, and the commentators appear greatly perplexed to indicate its precise meaning, as may be recognized in the varied explanations given by Shem-Tob and by Profiat Duran or Ephodi. The simplest sense, it seemeth to me, is this: One could not attribute to God that which, from our point of view, would be a perfection; for perfections, being ever certain capacities (ἕξεις), belong to one of the genera of the category of quality, and could not, consequently, be attributed to God, as resulteth from what the author hath said in chap. LII (p. 195), touching qualities. For a more ample explanation, the author addeth: and every capacity existeth not in everything (being) endowed with capacity; that is to say, that in created beings, capacities are somewhat accidental, being found not equally in all, and not being always in act where they are found. Capacities (ἕξεις), albeit more durable and more solid than dispositions (διαθέσεις), are nevertheless naught else than consolidated dispositions, and designate somewhat which hath been acquired and which hath not always existed in the being endowed therewith (cf. p. 195, note 2). As Aristotle himself saith, capacities are also dispositions; for those who are endowed with capacities are in some wise only disposed for these selfsame capacities (οί μὲν γὰρ ἕξεις ἔχοντες ϰαί διάϰεινταί γέ πως ϰατ’ αὐτά. Categ., chap. 8). Let us add thereto that capacities are often opposed the one to the other, and cannot exist together in the same subject. It resulteth from all this that, if one attributed to God all that which, in relation to us, is a perfection, one would attribute unto Him acquired capacities and even opposing capacities, two things equally inadmissible. — Moses of Narbonne, the most profound commentator of Maimonides, confessing the embarrassment which he had long experienced in explaining the words of the author, supposeth that this entire passage, beginning from these words: Thus it is clear unto thee, etc., relateth to a passage of the Metaphysics (book
fn.637.sub_1: XII, chap. 9), where Aristotle saith that the intelligence perceiveth naught else than itself, being unable to be affected by anything outside of itself. Maimonides, in speaking here of all that must be denied of the supreme intelligence, or of God, would allude to this absolute negation, in God, of every perception which should not have for its object the divine intelligence itself. The latter hath its perfection in itself, and cannot be affected by anything. In denying that it perceiveth aught else than itself, one doth not attribute unto it any imperfection; for all perfections are capacities, but these capacities do not constitute perfection for every being endowed therewith. There be many privations which are preferable to capacities; for, as Aristotle saith in the passage indicated, to not see certain things is better than to see them (ϰαί γὰρ μὴ ὁρᾶν ἔνια ϰρεῖττον ἢ ὁρᾶν). Such is, in substance, the interpretation given to our passage by Moses of Narbonne; but we greatly doubt whether it be the true one and whether there be a real relation between the words of Maimonides and the said passage of Aristotle.
fn.638: Literally: of the thing whereof one denieth that which one denieth.
fn.639: That is to say, that our entire perception, when it hath God for its object, consisteth in recognizing that we are powerless to perceive His true being.
fn.640: The author alludeth perhaps to a passage of Ba’hya (Duties of the Hearts, book I, chap. 10), wherein the same subject hath been at length developed. In establishing that it is impossible for the intelligence to perceive directly the divine essence, which manifesteth itself to us only through its works, Ba’hya likewise employeth the comparison taken from the light of the sun, which the sight could not perceive directly.
fn.641: Literally: a charge, a burden, or an attack (from حَبَلَ, impetum fecit); the author meaneth: in believing that one praiseth God, one chargeth Him with somewhat which is not worthy of His true being, and one offendeth Him. Ibn-Tibbon rendereth the word חמל by מעמם (charge). Ibn-Falaquera preferreth to render it by טורח or by משא, which is well-nigh the same thing; vide the Appendix to the Moreh ha-Moreh, where one readeth at our passage: והנכון להעתיק נמצא בו משא מה או טורח מה. This passage, drawn from the Hebrew MS. No. 352 of the ancient collection, is wanting in the edition of the Moreh ha-Moreh and in the greater part of the manuscripts.
fn.642: One should read, in the version of Ibn-Tibbon, וההמתפקות, and not וההשתקפות, as is found in several editions.
fn.643: Vide Babylonian Talmud, treatise Berakhôth, fol. 33 b. This passage, as it is cited in our text, is not entirely conformable to our editions of the Talmud, and the various Arabic and Hebrew manuscripts of the Guide likewise offer numerous variants. It is the same with almost all the Talmudic citations, and sometimes the Biblical citations, which the authors were wont to make from memory, and which have often been corrected by copyists. Ba’hya, in his treatise on the Duties of the Hearts (book I, chap. 10), cites the same passage with other variants. We have followed several manuscripts which are nearly conformable, and our reading differs but little from that of Al-’Harizi.
fn.645: Concerning the assembly called the Great Synod or the Great Synagogue, and to which is attributed the composition of the daily prayers, vide my History of Palestine, pp. 479 and 480.
fn.646: Some manuscripts bear אלאיג̇אב, with the article, and likewise the two Hebrew versions, החיוב.
fn.647: That is to say: if the matter were abandoned to our own judgment, and if certain attributes had not been consecrated by Holy Scripture and by the ritual of the prayers. The verb תרכנא is in the passive, and one must pronounce تُرِكْنَا; Ibn-Tibbon hath very accurately rendered it by הונחנו (mss. and edit. princeps), and it is erroneously that, in most editions, this word hath been changed into הונחו.
fn.648: Instead of קלנאהא, one of the Leyden manuscripts bears עקלנאהא; this reading, expressed by Al-’Harizi (לא השכלנו אותם), offereth no suitable sense.
fn.649: The words אן יוצף depend upon the verb אלג̇את, of which the words צ̇רורה̈ אלכ̇טאב form the subject; the literal translation would be this: since the necessity of speaking to men… hath forced to describe God, etc.
fn.650: See above, at the commencement of chap. XXVI.
fn.651: That is to say: we ought to limit ourselves, in the matter of attributes, to the words great, mighty and terrible.
fn.652: Literally: our limit (ought to be) to say them (them) only; that is to say: we ought, in prayer, to confine ourselves to pronouncing these three attributes alone.
fn.654: Literally: who have extended and prolonged (the attributes) and have bestowed efforts (in this regard), in prayers which they have composed and in orisons which they have fashioned, whereby, in their opinion, they drew nigh unto God, and wherein they described God by such attributes, that, if one thus described an individual among men, it would be (to express) an imperfection in his regard. The verb אטנבוא, which signifieth they have extended themselves or they have insisted, hath been rendered, in the version of Ibn-Tibbon, by המריצו בשבחים (they have insisted upon the praises); the word בשבחים is an addition of the translator, and likewise he hath rendered further on ויטנבון by וימריצו לשבח. In place of ואג̇תהדוא (and they have bestowed efforts), certain manuscripts bear ואמתועבוא (Xth form of وعب ), and they have accumulated; 'tis this latter reading which Ibn-Tibbon appeareth to have followed, who translateth: והרבו דברים, and they have accumulated words, whilst Al-’Harizi hath וישתדלו, which accordeth with our reading.
fn.655: Literally: they took God the Most High for the footstool of their tongues, and described Him and spake unto Him by everything which they believed permitted. מדרמה̈ مَدْرَسَة signifieth here the place which one treadeth upon; this word is wanting in the dictionaries.
fn.656: Literally: Upon the place of transgression or of sin. Certain manuscripts have מואצ̇ע, the places, and likewise Al-’Harizi, מקומות.
fn.657: The author here intentionally employeth the Hebrew words לשון הרע (the evil tongue or slander), and הוצאת שם רע (spreading an evil report), which are in the mouths of all the Hebrew moralists; 'tis thus that a little further on he inserteth in the Arabic phrase the Hebrew words חרוף וגדופ בשגגה, and yet others.
fn.658: We depart somewhat from the true sense of this passage, and we translate it as required by the application thereof made here by Maimonides.
fn.659: These words contain an allusion to a passage of the Mishnah; vide supra, chap. XXXII, p. 113, note 2.
fn.660: The author alludeth to the words of R. Eleazar reported in the Babylonian Talmud, Succah, fol. 53 a, and Ta’anith, fol. 25 a.
fn.661: Vide the preceding chapter, p. 245, note 3.
fn.662: The word אחכאם, as hath been remarked by Ibn Falaquera (Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 151), must be pronounced إحكام (verbal noun of the IVth form), and signifieth arrangement, good order; the author meaneth to speak of the wise manner in which R. Hanina had disposed his words, so as to bring forth several important teachings. Ibn Tibbon translateth ואחכאמה by וחכמותיו; it is evident that he pronounced it أَحْكَامُ (pl. of حُكْمٌ , principle of wisdom). According to Ibn Falaquera, the word אחכאם ought to be rendered, in Hebrew, by תקון, even as Ibn Tibbon himself hath rendered it in the IIIrd part of this work, chap. XIX, where mention is made of the wise disposition of the organs of sight, and where the words אלתי הי מן אלאחכאם עלי מא קר עלם are translated by אשר בהם מן התקון מה שנודע.— Al-Harizi hath entirely neglected, in his translation, the word ואחכאמה.
fn.663: Instead of כמאלא, several manuscripts have כמאל (or אנהא) אנה, or אנהא כמאלאת; the reading which we have adopted, and which is more correct, accordeth with the version of Ibn Tibbon.
fn.664: By these latter words, the author designateth various species of bodies with circular bases, such as the cylinder, the ellipsoid, etc., and all bodies having plane surfaces, like the cube and all prisms in general.
fn.665: Literally: … that thou addest the negation of a thing by means of demonstration, and that thou dost not deny only by word of mouth.
fn.666: Ibn Tibbon translateth: לא שיש לשם מקום, which is not altogether exact; Ibn Falaquera translateth more accurately: לא ששם קרבת מקום (Moré ha-Moré, p. 33). Likewise Al-’Harizi: לא שיש למעלה קרבת מקום.
fn.667: Literally: walk thou therein, then, if thou wilt.
fn.669: Literally: and in like manner, it must needs exist, not in the sense of the existence (which is) within us.
fn.670: In the version of Ibn Tibbon, one must read הענין בחיוב התארים, and not העיון בהיות התארים, as found in the editions.
fn.671: The word محمول, which the author employeth here, signifieth the logical attribute (prædicatum), whilst صفة signifieth the metaphysical attribute, or the real quality of a subject; it concerneth here the subject and the attribute, taken in their most general sense. Instead of these words: לא דׄלך אלמוצׄוע מתׄל הדׄה אלמחמולאת, we read in most of the manuscripts: לא דׄלך אלמוצׄוע מתׄל הדׄה אלמוצׄועאת ולא תלך אלמחמולאת מתׄל הדׄה אלמחמולאת, and that this subject is not as those other subjects, nor those attributes (are) as those other attributes, that is to say, it concerneth a subject and attributes which could not be compared unto anything familiar to us in the matter of subjects and attributes. The version of Ibn Tibbon confirmeth this latter reading; but that which we have thought proper to adopt is warranted by the better of the two Leyden manuscripts, as well as by the version of Al-’Harizi, which beareth: ואין המוםד ההוא כאלו הנשואים. It is wrongfully that the editor of this version thought he ought to complete the passage in the sense of Ibn Tibbon's version. Vide also the following note.
fn.672: That is to say: the belief which admitteth affirmative attributes would result, in the final instance, in admitting within God diverse ideas associated together. Concerning the word شُرْك, cf. supra, chap. LVIII, p. 239, note 1. This word, rendered in Hebrew by שתוף, hath generally been taken by the commentators of Ibn Tibbon's version in the sense of homonymy (استراك); that which seemeth to have given rise to this error is the variant of which we spake in the preceding note, and which was reproduced by Ibn Tibbon. The sense which the commentators attribute to the words of Maimonides is this: with affirmative attributes, one arriveth only at the conclusion that God is a subject having attributes, and that subject and attribute, when God is concerned, must not be taken in the same sense as elsewhere, so that we should have, as the sole result, naught but words employed by homonymy, the true sense whereof would be unknown. This interpretation is very little plausible, and the word شرك, taken in the sense of association, seemeth to us fully to confirm the reading we have adopted.
fn.673: That is to say: as soon as a thing is designated as a subject, it hath necessarily one or several attributes, and, although the subject and the attribute form together but one single being, they are nevertheless two distinct things, each of which hath its own definition. If I say, for example: this man is learned, I speak of a single being who is at once man and learned; but unto the words man and learned are attached two distinct ideas, each of which hath its own definition apart.
fn.674: The author signifieth that he will not confine himself to reproaching the adherents of affirmative attributes with possessing an imperfect conception of the Deity, or with implicitly associating other beings with God and admitting, in some wise, a plurality within the divine idea, or finally, with forming an idea of God contrary to the truth. On the one hand, these reproaches might, from their own point of view, appear insufficiently grounded; on the other hand, particularly as regards the third reproach, it would be to acknowledge in them a certain notion concerning the existence of God which, in reality, they possess not. The grievous reproach which may justly be addressed to them is that they render God an imaginary being and fall into atheism.
fn.675: The partisans of attributes, saith the author, might repel the reproach of association by refining upon the significance of this word and by demonstrating that they associate no other being with God, inasmuch as they ascribe to no being an essence semblable to the divine essence, and that the attributes which they assign unto Him, whilst forming part of the divine essence, are not that selfsame essence. If, somewhat earlier, the author hesitated not to declare that affirmative attributes result in association, he intended to speak of the multiplicity in the divine idea or of the association of diverse ideas forming together the essence of God, whereas in this place it concerneth plurality, or the opinion which would admit other essences similar to the essence of God. This distinction is essential. Cf. supra, chap. LVIII, p. 245, note 2.
fn.676: He, for instance, who should declare bitter that which is sweet, would yet agree that it is a thing which affecteth the taste, and that it concerneth a quality; he would thus possess an exact notion of taste, whereas he who should say that taste is a quantity would manifest a complete ignorance of the nature of taste.
fn.677: The words ענקא מגרב (عَنْقَاءُ مُغْرِبِ) designate, among the Arabs, a fabulous bird, like unto our griffon. The word مغرب is an epithet concerning the meaning of which the Arabs themselves are not in accord; but it is most generally believed that this epithet was bestowed upon the bird ’ankâ because, it is said, it beareth far away all the prey which it seizeth. Vid. Les oiseaux et les fleurs, by M. Garcin de Tassy, p. 218 et seq., and the Séances de Hariri, edit. of MM. Reinaud and Derenbourg, p. 678, and the French notes, ibid., p. 202. — The two Hebrew translators have put העזניה הנפלאה, taking the word مغرب in the sense of marvellous, and seeing in the bird ’ankâ one of the species of eagle, that which, in the Pentateuch (Levit., XI, 13, and Deut., XIV, 12), is called עזניה. Verily, Saadia, in his Arabic version of the Pentateuch, rendereth this word by عنقاء; but he hath been censured by Ibn Ezra, who rightly observeth that the bird ’ankâ, being a fabulous creature, could not appear among the animals whose flesh was forbidden unto the Hebrews. It seemeth nonetheless to result from the whole of our passage that Maimonides also believed that the word عنقاء designated originally a real being; indeed, according to Damiri, cited by Bochart, this word would denote a species of eagle, and would be synonymous with عُقَاب. Vid. Bochart, Hierozoïcon, t. II, p. 812 (edit. of Rosenmüller, t. III, p. 803).
fn.678: The author, in concluding here his discussion concerning the attributes, summariseth once more, in this final sentence, his theory relative to the attributes encountered in Holy Writ. Cf. supra, at the end of chap. LIII. — Concerning כתאב אלתנזיל, vid. supra, p. 206, note 1.
fn.679: The author, after having shown that every species of attribute must be removed from God, addeth, in this chapter and in the three following, some considerations upon various names of God found in Holy Writ, and which might be regarded as attributes. He showeth that all names are derived from the actions of God, with the exception of one alone, which designateth the divine essence itself. Cf. the Khozari, book II, §2. Already, in a writing attributed unto Aristotle, and which peradventure formed part of his exoteric books, we find a similar essay at explaining the names of the Greek deities by applying them all to a single being, in conformity with philosophical doctrines. Vid. the treatise of the World, chap. 7: Eῖς δἐ ὢ ν πολυὤνομὸς ἐστι, ϰατονομαζόμενος τοῖς πάθεσιν ἅπ’ρ αὐτὸς νςοχοῖ, ϰ. τ. λ.).
fn.680: The Arabs call improvised name (اسم مرتجل) that which hath been, from its origin, the proper name of an individual, and which is not derived from an appellative noun or from a verb. Vid. Silv. de Sacy, Grammaire arabe, t. I, p. 268 (2nd edition).
fn.681: The words שם המפורש (Mishnâ, IInd part, treatise Yômâ, chap. VI, § 2) signify, without doubt: the name of God distinctly pronounced, that is to say, the tetragrammaton, written and read by the four letters yod, hé, wâw, hé, and which is also called השם המיוחד, or the particular name (Bab. Talm., Synhedrîn, fol. 56 a; Schebou’ôth, fol. 36 a). The words ונקב שם י״י (Lev., XXIV, 16) are rendered, in the Chaldaic version of Onkelos, by ודי פרש שמא די״י, and he who PRONOUNCETH the name of the Eternal; cf. the commentary of Ibn Ezra: והנה הטעם בעת שיקלל אם יפרש השם יומת «The sense is: if, whilst blaspheming, he pronounceth the name of God, he shall be put to death.» Our author understandeth the word מפורש in this sense, that this name designateth expressly the divine essence, and is by no means an homonym, that is to say, that it is not applied at once to God and to other beings. This interpretation of the word מפורש, generally adopted by the theologians who followed Maimonides (cf. Albo, Ikkarîm, II, 28), was assuredly not in the thought of the ancient Rabbis.
fn.682: Vide above, chap. LIV, p. 219 et seq.
fn.683: It is known that, from the most ancient times, the Jews, out of a pious reverence for the proper name of God, dared not pronounce this name, and alway read אדני in the place of יהוה; wherefore already the Septuagint render for the latter name ὁ ϰύρις, the Lord. The Masoretes have, for the same reason, given unto it the vowels of the word אֲדֹנָי, so that one readeth Jehovah, the which is not the true pronunciation of the name of יהוה. It is by reason of the same scruple that the author, instead of writing this name in its true form, spelleth out the letters thereof, and alway writeth: yod, he, waw, he.
fn.684: Literally: for there is in this emphasis and generality; that is to say, names such as Adonai and Sarai are emphatic words, or, as the grammarians say, plurals of majesty, and their very form indicateth that they were not originally proper names belonging to a single individual, but common names applying to a generality of individuals. Thus, the name Adonai, which signifieth my lords, necessarily cometh from an appellative name belonging to several individuals.
fn.685: Concerning this latter name, vide supra, chap. II, p. 37.
fn.686: The author, following the example of other theologians (cf. Khozari, book IV, § 3), deemeth it necessary to set apart the Tetragrammaton from all other names of God, and to behold therein a proper name, without any known etymology, albeit it be evident that the name יהוה containeth the sense of being (from the verb הוה or היה), like that of אהיה, which the author himself deriveth from the verb היה, as shall be seen in chap. LXIII.
fn.687: Literally: And He (God) hath it not in common with another.
fn.688: These words, which the author setteth down in Hebrew, seem to refer to a passage in the 2<sup>nd</sup> book of Chronicles, chap. XXVI, <small>v</small>. 18.
fn.689: In the sanctuary at Jerusalem, the priests, when delivering unto the people the benediction prescribed by the Law (Numbers, chap. 6, v. 24-26), pronounced the Tetragrammaton even as it is written, whilst, without the sanctuary, they substituted the name of Adonai. Vide Mishnah, IIIrd part, treatise Sotah, chap. VII, § 6.
fn.690: That is to say: on the Day of Atonement, wherein the High-Priest, in the confession of sins, did likewise pronounce the name of יהוה by its own consonants. Vide Mishnah, treatise Yoma, loc. cit.; Babylonian Talmud, same treatise, fol. 39 b.
fn.691: The manuscripts bear ליםת ענדנא, which is incorrect; it is necessary to write לים.
fn.692: The manuscripts generally bear לא ישארך אחד; it is peradventure necessary to read אחר֞א, in the accusative, so that the literal translation would be: inasmuch as He (God) hath no community, with any of the creatures, in this indication. In one manuscript, we read ישארכה with the suffix. According to this reading, it would be necessary to translate: …that none of the creatures hath community with Him, &c.
fn.693: The author will cite further on the Talmudic passage which he hath here in view. Vide p. 272.
fn.694: In the place of ד֞את צפאת, certain manuscripts bear דאת להא צפאת, which is peradventure preferable.
fn.695: Thus, for example, the words merciful, just, almighty, indicate the ideas of mercy, justice, and power, and a subject whereunto these ideas are attached, and which is understood; consequently, these words, employed as names of God, would make of God a composite being.
fn.696: Vide supra, chap. LIX, pp. 254 and 255.
fn.698: That is to say: amulets, containing magical formulae and imaginary names of the Divinity, and which were worn as preventatives against maladies. Vide Mishnah, IInd part, treatise Shabbath, chap. VI, § 2, and Babylonian Talmud, the same treatise, fol. 61 a. b.
fn.699: Literally: which they sew together. Instead of ילפקונהא, certain manuscripts bear אלפוהא, which they have composed.
fn.700: Instead of אבׄבאר (اخبار), which signifieth here stories invented at pleasure, or fables, one of the manuscripts beareth כׄראפאת (خرافات), which hath the same sense; this word hath not been rendered in either of the two Hebrew versions.
fn.701: That is to say: the word thus (כה) signifieth that the priests must recite the blessing in the prescribed terms, without changing aught therein, and pronouncing the Tetragrammaton name as it is written.
fn.702: That is to say: in the sanctuary of Jerusalem, the priests, whilst reciting the prescribed blessing, pronounce the true Tetragrammaton name; but, outside the central sanctuary, they substitute the name of Adonai.
fn.704: Literally: if it be a letter receiving the TESHDID. In the name of יהוה, there are only the letters י and ו which may receive the teshdid or dagesh; for the ה never receiveth it.
fn.705: These latter words, written in Hebrew, refer to the Talmudic passage which the author is about to cite.
fn.707: Vide the preceding chapter, p. 267, note 2.
fn.708: The Talmud, as shall be seen hereafter, speaketh of a divine name composed of twelve letters and of another of forty-two letters, without explaining either the meaning of these names or the letters of which they were composed.
fn.709: The words ולא מצינא בה, which signify literally and they were not sparing of it (cf. supra, at the commencement of chap. XVII), have been omitted in the version of Ibn-Tibbon, which beareth: ולא היה נמנע מעולם מԃאחד וכו׳; the word מעולם is the translation of the Arabic word קט, which we find indeed in one of the Leyden manuscripts, wherein we read: ומא כאן קט ממנועא·
fn.710: Literally: lost or corrupted beliefs; the sense is, that these men, not having well apprehended the profound metaphysical mysteries hidden within this name, were troubled in their faith and arrived at false beliefs.
fn.711: The author relateth this fact, in well-nigh the same terms, in his Compendium of the Talmud, book II, treatise Tephillah, chap. XIV, § 10; I doubt, however, that the citation be literal. The fact is recorded in the Babylonian Talmud, Yoma, fol. 39 b, and Menahoth, fol. 109 b, and it is these two passages that the author seemeth to have had in view, and wherein he had perhaps a reading differing from that of our editions.
fn.713: Instead of אבי אמא, the father of the mother, our editions of the Talmud bear: אחי אדמי, the brother of my mother.
fn.714: That is to say, by denying of God every species of imperfection; for therein lies, according to the author, the sole manner of conceiving approximately the divine essence. One perceiveth, moreover, from the manner in which the author here expresseth himself, that he was unaware of, or did not believe authentic, the name of forty-two letters which figureth in the books of the Cabbalists, and which commenceth with the letters אבגיתץ, albeit this name was known already, two centuries before Maimonides, to R. Hai Gaon, who speaketh thereof in one of his Consultations, concerning the divine names and addressed to the school of Kairwan. R. Hai, speaking expressly of the name of אבגיתץ, saith that, although its letters be known, there is no agreement as to the manner of pronouncing it, which is known only by tradition: וזה בן מ״ב אותיות אע״פ שאותיותיו ידועות אין מםור בהגיונו וקריאתו אלא בקבלה וכוי. Vide the collection of unpublished pieces recently published under the title of טעם זקנים, by M. Eliezer Ashkenazi (Frankfort on the Main, 1854, in-8vo), fol. 57 a. — Certain Cabbalists have seen in the forty-two letters, beginning with אבגיתץ, the initials of as many attributes of God; the enumeration thereof is to be found in the commentary of Moses of Narbonne upon this passage.
fn.715: The adjective אלערי, being in the masculine singular, relateth to אלעטק (the pronunciation), and it is erroneously that the two Hebrew translators have rendered it in the plural, as though it referred to אלאחרף (the letters).
fn.716: In all the manuscripts, both Arabic and Hebrew, the name of twelve letters precedeth that of forty-two, and it is erroneously that, in all the editions of the version of Ibn Tibbon, the order hath been inverted.
fn.718: Cf. supra, chap. XXXV, p. 132. Instead of אוצׄחנא, some manuscripts bear בוא.
fn.719: In some manuscripts, one readeth אלמוצׄועה̈, instead of אלמדונה.
fn.720: The doctrine of Aristotle concerning the intelligence, which he divideth into active and passive (vide Treatise on the Soul, book III, chap. 5), hath received great developments among the Arabs; there hath been discussion upon the nature of the material or passive intellect and upon the manner in which this intellect passeth from potentiality to act; and that which hath especially occupied the Arabian philosophers is the question whether and how the intellect in act may unite with the universal active intellect, emanated from God, and which, in the system of the Arabian philosophers, is one of the separate intelligences, that which presideth over the sphere of the moon. See the places indicated above, p. 146, note 2. The words אדראך אלעקל אלפעאל (the perception of the active intellect) admit of a twofold meaning: one might understand thereby the perception of which the human intellect is capable, having become intellect in act, or else the perception which hath for its object the universal active intellect, and which consisteth in comprehending it and becoming identified therewith. It is evidently this latter sense which must be admitted, and it is also in this sense that our passage hath been explained by Moses of Narbonne: השגת השכל הפועל ירצה בו שישוב הוא הוא ושישיג הנמצאות באופן שישיגם הוא “The perception of the active intellect is to become it, and to perceive beings in the manner in which it perceiveth them, it.” This sublime perception, the result of metaphysical speculation, and wherein the intelligent and the intelligible are completely identified, is in no wise subject to oblivion, forasmuch as the lower faculties of the soul, such as imagination and memory, have no part therein. Abu-Becr ibn-al-Sayigh, or Ibn Bajja, treating the same subject in his Letter of Farewell, saith likewise (Heb. version): אולם החכמה האחרונה אשר הוא הציור השכלי והוא מציאות השכל הנאצל אי אפשר בו השכחה אלא אם יהיה זה יוצא מהטבע וכו׳ “The ultimate science, which is the pure intelligible conception and the very existence of the emanated intellect, cannot be forgotten, unless it be by an exception of nature, etc.” Vide the commentary of Moses of Narbonne on this passage, and the Appendix to the Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 142 (where, instead of וכתב אבדנצר, one must read וכתב אבובכר), and cf. the IIIrd part of this work, chap. LI. Concerning the whole of the theory of the intellect, some details will be found hereafter, in chap. LXVIII.
fn.721: Literally: It expandeth for them (the faculty) to lie and to say, etc.
fn.722: Instead of אבתדעהא, certain manuscripts bear אכׄתרעהא, which maketh no difference as to the sense.
fn.723: The word מיןאן (ميزان) , which signifieth balance, is employed figuratively in the sense of intelligence or of judgment. Ibn-Falaquera hath read מיאז, or rather מין (تميز , discernement); vide Moré ha-Moré, at the end of page 151. It is this selfsame reading that is expressed by the version of Al-Harizi, which beareth הכרה, whilst that of Ibn-Tibbon hath מאזנים, which accordeth with the reading we have adopted according to eight manuscripts; one alone, one of the Leyden manuscripts, beareth מיאזן, a word which signifieth naught and is but a copyist’s error for מיזאן.
fn.724: The preceding sentence must be considered as a parenthesis, wherein the author, the better to bring into relief the obscurity of the words of Moses cited at the commencement of the chapter, opposeth to them the clarity of other words recounted in the same Biblical narrative. Here he resumeth the difficulties presented by the words first cited.
fn.725: By the word צאבה̈ (صابة) , Sabians or Sabaeans, our author, after the example of other Arabian writers, designateth the worshippers of the stars, and in general the idolaters; details concerning the Sabians will be found in the IIIrd part of this work, chap. XXIX, where the author saith that the religion of the Sabians embraced the whole earth.
fn.726: By روحانية , is meant the spirit which presideth over a star or a constellation, as well as the manifestation of this spirit; the faculty of causing the spirits of the stars to descend into idols or talismans is called استنزال الروحانيات or simply استنزال . Talismans (τε έσματα) are figures engraved upon a stone or a tablet, and representing certain constellations under whose influence one desireth to place oneself.
fn.727: In the version of Ibn-Tibbon one must read דבר, and not כבר, as most editions have it; one must also read בזמנים כלם and delete the pronoun ההם.
fn.728: That is to say: to call men unto them and make them partakers of their own conviction, they employed the means of study and instruction. Instead of ידעון, Ibn-Tibbon hath perhaps read ירשדון, for his translation beareth היו מישרים, they directed. Al-Harizi translateth: היו מיהרים, which offereth no suitable sense; it may be presumed that there is here a copyist’s error in the unique manuscript of the version of Al-Harizi.
fn.729: The author understandeth by these words the persons whom Abraham and Sarah had instructed and converted to their belief. The Chaldaic version of Onkelos likewise saith: וית נפשתא דשעבדו לאוריתא בחרן, and the persons whom they had brought into subjection to the religious Law in Haran. It is in the same sense that this passage hath been explained by the ancient Rabbis; vide Babylonian Talmud, Synhedrin, fol. 99 b: כל המלמד את בן חברו הורה מעלה עליו הכתוב כאילו עשאו שנאמר ואת הנפש אשר עשא בחרן Cf. Bereshith Rabba, section 39, towards the end.
fn.730: In the system of the Arabian grammarians, the relative pronoun is a kind of conjunction or conjunctive adjective (اسم موصول), which necessarily requireth after it, as a complement, a conjunctive proposition, termed in Arabic صِلَةُ, adjunction; vid. Silv. de Sacy, Grammaire arabe, vol. I, pp. 443 and 444 (2nd edition). In the words אהיה אשר אהיה, the second אהיה formeth the adjunction of the conjunctive adjective אשר.
fn.732: Literally: and it is that whereunto the demonstration necessarily leadeth.
fn.733: The Arabic text saith: מא אלקיתה אליך, that which I have taught thee, and likewise the version of Ibn Tibbon: מה שהורעתיו לך; concerning this irregular construction, wherein the conjunction أنّ serveth to introduce a direct discourse, and wherein it replaceth the verb in saying, vid. Silv. de Sacy, Grammaire arabe (2nd edition), vol. I, p. 568, and vol. II, p. 468 (no. 843). The same construction is found a little further on: כאנה יקול אן דׄאתך וחקיקתך לא יגׄהלהא אחד. The Greek conjunction ὅτι is sometimes employed in the same manner, especially in the New Testament, and likewise the Syriac conjunction די or ד.
fn.734: This is the miracle of the transformation of the rod, whereunto the author hath alluded above.
fn.735: Literally: to exalt and glorify (God) in speaking unto Him.
fn.736: All the manuscripts bear םאלת; but, this verb being evidently in the passive, we have more correctly written סילת (سُئِلَتْ).
fn.737: The author, who doth not explain himself clearly, appeareth to indicate here that the name YAH (יה) is, like EHYÉ (אהיה), derived from the verb היה, to be; elsewhere, however, he declareth that יה is a portion of the Tetragrammaton name (מקצת שם המפורש, vid. Abridgment of the Talmud, treatise Yesôdé ha-Tôrâ, chap. VI, § 4). Howsoever that may be, this name, saith the author, indicateth eternal existence and expresseth the idea of the necessary being which the author findeth in the name EHYÉ; it is this same meaning which the author, at the end of this chapter, expressly ascribeth to the shem ha-mephorash, albeit above (chap. LXI) he only expressed himself in this regard in a dubitative manner (vid. supra, pp. 269 and 270). Upon these various names, cf. Khozari, book IV, § 3.
fn.738: Instead of אמתמראה several manuscripts bear אמתמראה (with resch), which is well-nigh the same thing; cf. infra, at the end of chap. LXIX.
fn.739: That is to say: the word צור, which signifieth rock, and which is sometimes employed to designate God. Vide supra, chap. XVI.
fn.740: In the version of Ibn-Tibbon, we read צור ואמת; but the word אמת, truth, is never employed as a name of God. It is true that some Arabic manuscripts likewise have צור ואמת; but ואמת seemeth to be naught but an abbreviation of the Arabic word ואמת׳אלה, which is read in several Arabic manuscripts. Al-’Harizi hath not rendered this word.
fn.742: Vide, concerning the word מלאך (messenger, angel), the IInd part of this work, chap. VI, and ibid., chap. XXXIV, wherein the author explaineth the whole passage from Exodus to which he here alludeth.
fn.743.sub_0: The visible manifestation of the Divinity consisteth, according to the theologians, in a light which God causeth to appear in a place and which is a miraculous creation; it is this light which is called Schekhînâ (שכינה, majesty) or cabôd (כבוד, glory), and which appeareth in the place that God chooseth particularly to make His presence known. Saadia likewise speaketh of this created light which God caused to appear in the sanctuary to glorify that place (להגדיל המקום ההוא); vide Beliefs and Opinions, bk. II, chap. 8 (Berlin edit., fol. 33 a). Cf. Ahron ben-Eli, Tree of Life, ch. LXIII (Leipzig edit., p. 72). Speculations of this kind go back in general to the ancient Karaites, who took for guides the Muslim theologians of the sect of the Motazalites, and it was through the impulse of the Karaites that Saadia and other Rabbanites approached this manner of questions (vide infra, ch. LXXI). The Karaite Abu-’Ali (Jepheth), in his Arabic commentary upon Exodus (chap. 19, v. 20), speaketh at length of the manner in which the manifestation of God upon Sinai must be understood; one readeth there the following passage relative to the cabôd or the created light: וד׳לף אנה אמתחאל אן יבון אלכ׳אלק ג׳ל ועלא אלר׳י לא יוצף ולא חי ולא תחויה אלאמבנה̈ בל לא יג׳וז אן יקאל פיה אנה פי אלעאלם ולא כ׳ארג׳א ענה אד׳ הד׳א מן אוצאף אלמכ׳לוקין אלד׳ין תחתוי עליהם אלאמכגה̈ ותלזמגם אלאעראצ׳ ואד׳א כאן הד׳א הכד׳א פלא שך פי אן וירד יי ישיר בה אלי מכ׳לוק מחדוד וחצ׳רה̈ מוצ׳ע פי ראשׁ ההר “In truth, it is impossible to admit that it is here a question of the Creator, who can be neither qualified nor defined, and who could not be enclosed within space. Nay, more, one could not say of Him that He is in the world, nor that He is outside the world; for such qualifications would suit created things, which are enclosed in space and subject to accidents. This being so, there is no doubt that, by the words: And the Lord came down, etc., there is indicated a thing created and limited, and its local presence upon the summit of the mountain.” Cf. infra, p. 290, note 2.
fn.743.sub_1: According to the opinion which Maimonides setteth forth elsewhere concerning miracles in general, one must see in the said created light, as well as in all that occurreth in a miraculous manner, the effect of the primitive will of God, who, from the moment of Creation, hath disposed things in such wise that, under certain given circumstances, there might be produced extraordinary phenomena which seem to us to depart from the general laws of nature. Thus, therefore, miracles are the results of certain physical dispositions established by God at the epoch of Creation, and not the effect of a momentary will; for there can arise no change in the divine will, which is eternal and immutable. Vide what the author saith in this regard in the last of the Eight Chapters serving as an introduction to the treatise Aboth (Porta Mosis of Pococke, p. 240), and cf. the IInd part of this work, towards the end of chap. XXIX. Vide also infra, chap. LXVI, p. 296, note 1.
fn.745: The author having here expressed himself with overmuch conciseness, we have been constrained to depart somewhat from the text the better to convey his thought; the literal translation would run: or rather, all that is outside of him glorifieth him.
fn.746: The text exhibiteth יעט֞ם without a suffix; likewise, there is read in the manuscripts of the version of Ibn-Tibbon יגדיל, whilst the printed editions have יגדילהו.
fn.747: By these latter words, the author maketh allusion unto the celestial spheres, which possess life and apprehension, yet lack the power of speech. Vid. the II<sup>nd</sup> part of this work, chap. V.
fn.748: In divers manuscripts there is read: אנה דבח וקאל כד֞א כמא קאל, that he laudeth and saith such and such a thing, even as it hath been said, etc.; the version of Ibn-Tibbon rendereth this same reading: שהוא שבח ואמר כך כמו שאמר.
fn.749: That is to signify, that the bones afford us the conviction that no being is similar unto Him who hath so wisely disposed them, and it is as though they expressed themselves in this regard by means of words.
fn.750: The author here mentioneth two of the most difficult questions which he hath treated hitherto (vid. chap. LVII), and he intendeth to signify that the reader, after having followed him through subjects so profound and so subtle, hath scarce need that one should explain to him the question which formeth the subject of the present chapter. Having concluded the discussion upon the attributes and the names of God, the author addeth, in this chapter and in the two following, some observations anent the speech and the writing ascribed unto God, and concerning that which must be understood by the rest of the seventh day of creation.
fn.751: According to the ancient Rabbins, the Torah or the Law revealed to Moses had been created long anterior to the creation of the world (that is to say, it subsisted from all eternity in the designs of the Creator, being foreordained to enlighten successively the whole of the human race); vid. Bereshith Rabba, 1st section; Babylonian Talmud, Shabbath, fol. 88 b, and passim.
fn.752: That is to signify: that the divine speech, a thing real and objective which existeth without the soul of the prophet, is a miraculous creation, God miraculously causing the air to resound with tones that strike upon the ear of the prophet. Vid. Saadia, Beliefs and Opinions, book II, chap. 8 (Berlin edit., fol. 33 b): וענין הדבור שהוא ברא דבור הגיע באויר אל שמע הנביא או העם “By speech (divine) it must be understood that God created words which reached the ear of the prophet or of the people through the medium of the air.” Likewise Abu-Ali (commentary on Exodus, at the commencement of ch. XX): ואנמא אלכ֞אלק תבארך יהרה אלבלאם פי אלהוא כמא ישא ויקרע בה אר֞ן אלממאמעין “The Creator causeth speech to arise in the air, according to His will, in such wise as to strike the ear of those who listen, etc.” R. Jehuda ha-Levi expresseth himself in the same sense (Khozari, book I, § 89): וכן יצטיר האויר המגיע אל אזן הנביא בצורות האותיות שהם מורות על הענינים שהוא חפץ להשמיעם אל הנביא או אל ההמון “The air, having reached the ear of the prophet, is modified in accordance with the forms of the letters which indicate the matters that God willeth to make the prophet or the people hear.” This same question likewise occupied the ancient Musalman theologians, who sought to resolve it in diverse manners. Vid. Pococke, Specimen hist. Arab., p. 217; Shahrastani, Germ. transl., vol. 1, pp. 42 and 43; Schmölders, Essai etc., pp. 187, 188, and 198. Concerning the opinion of our author, cf. supra, p. 286, note 3, and infra, p. 296, note 1.
fn.753: Literally: as He created all that He hath created and produced.
fn.754: Literally: minds were therefore led etc… by that (which was said) that God had spoken to them etc. The word באן (بِأَنَّ) is connected to the verb פאַרשרת, and there must be understood that it was said, as if there were באן קיל אן; Ibn-Tibbon hath added the word באמרם.
fn.756: Literally: to the language (expressed) by means of the tongue.
fn.757: That is to say: in order that he may receive impressions which he should have need to express by speech.
fn.758: Vide supra, chap. XLVI, pp. 165 and 166. Instead of נבהנא, several manuscripts bear בינא; likewise Al-’Harizi: כמו שביארנו.
fn.759: According to Moses of Narbonne, the author would allude to Saadia and to the grammarian Ibn-Janâ’h; in truth, Saadia, in his Arabic version of the Pentateuch, ever translateth the words ויאמר אלהים (Genesis, chap. I) by وشاء الله, and God willed.
fn.760: All the works of creation issued from nothingness only through this divine word itself; consequently, there did not yet exist any being to whom this word could be addressed, and the words God said can signify nothing else save God willed. — Instead of אלאקאויל, certain manuscripts bear אקאליל אלאמר; likewise Ibn-Tibbon: מאמרי הצווי.
fn.761: The word אִמְרֵי being here employed in the sense of דִּבְרֵי, and as the object of the verb דִּבֶּר, it thence resulteth that the roots ԃאמר and דבר are synonymous.
fn.762: Literally: that their existence was natural, and not artificial. — The author, desiring to set forth in this chapter that by the writing of God engraved upon the Tables of the Law is understood, as by word of God, the eternal and immutable will of the divinity, must first show that the words work of God, applied unto the Tables, designate in general a work of nature, that is to say, a work created at the same time as all the other works of creation, and not a work newly produced in a certain moment, like unto artificial things.
fn.763: That is to say, the attribution contained in the words works of the Eternal, and by which all that nature produceth is attributed unto the Creator.
fn.764: The author signifieth that Onkelos, who, in his Chaldaic version, seeketh ever to cause the anthropomorphisms of the Hebrew text to disappear, hath here departed from his habitual method, whilst preserving the expression of the original.
fn.765: Here is the sense of this entire passage: Onkelos, in permitting the words finger of God to remain in his version, must have considered the word finger as designating something material brought into relation with God, and not something inherent in the divine essence, such as the will; he must, consequently, have had for the words finger of God an interpretation analogue to that which he giveth to other expressions wherein something material is related unto God. Thus, for example, for the words the mountain of God (Exodus, iii. 1), Onkelos putteth: the mountain upon which was revealed the glory of God; for the rod of God (Ibid., iv. 20), he saith: the rod wherewith miracles had been wrought from God; and likewise the author supposeth that, in the thought of Onkelos, the words finger of God designate an instrument which miraculously engraved upon the Tables the commandments of God, and which, like unto the Tables themselves, was part of the works of creation.
fn.766: See Mishnâ, IVth part, treatise Abôth, chap. V, § 6. The words הכתב והמכתב, which both signify writing, have been diversely interpreted; several commentators have seen in כתב the forms of the letters traced upon the Tables, and in מכתב the manner in which these letters were traced, legible from all sides of the Tables. We have been constrained here to adopt the interpretation which our author himself giveth in his Commentary on the Mishnâ, and which he precedeth with a general observation upon the pre-existence of the ten things in question and of all other miracles (Cf. supra, chap. LXIV, p. 287, at the end of the note). fn.785: In other words: he is the thought, the subject who thinks and the object that is thought, that is to say, he is absolute thought having itself as its object. The famous proposition mentioned by the author, which was extensively developed by the Arabic philosophers, goes back to Aristotle, who, in his Metaphysics (Book XII, ch. 7 and 9), explains that in every intellect in act, and consequently in the prime mover, which is absolute energy, there is always perfect identity between that which thinks and that which is thought. The prime mover, or God, is the supreme thought thinking itself; in him, thought is its own object, and the divine thought, says Aristotle, is the thought of thought (αὑτòν ἄρϰ νοει̃, εἴπερ ὲστὶ τὸ ϰράτιστον, ϰαὶ ἔστιν ἡ νόησις νοήσεως νόνσις, ch. 9).— The author, after having insisted at length in the preceding chapters on the necessity of removing from God every kind of attribute and everything that might compromise his unity and absolute simplicity, shows in this chapter that the proposition in question implies no multiplicity in the divine idea, and that, within it, the intellect, the intellector and the intelligible are one and the same thing. Here, as elsewhere, the author follows in the footsteps of the Arabic Peripatetics, and notably Ibn Sīnā, his usual guide. Cf. the analysis of Ibn Sīnā's philosophy given by Shahrastānī, in his History of Religious and Philosophical Sects, p. 376 ff. of the Arabic text (German trans., vol. II, p. 255 ff.).

fn.793.sub_0: The author here addresses a subject which, as he himself states at the end of this chapter, can only be well understood by those familiar with Peripatetic philosophy, and particularly the part relating to the soul and its faculties. Without entering here into developments that would exceed the limits of a note, it will be necessary, for a better understanding of the author's reasoning, to briefly recall the Aristotelian theory of intelligence and the developments this theory received among the Arab philosophers whom our author took as guides. — In considering the various faculties of the soul enumerated by Aristotle, we notice a successive progression from the less perfect to the more perfect, such that each higher faculty supposes the lower faculty, whose action it renders more complete, and that one is to the other what energy or act is to potency, or what form is to matter. One can distinguish three main faculties of the soul: nutrition (τὸ θρεπτιϰόν sc. μόριον), to which the life of plants is limited; sensation (τὸ αἰσθητιϰόν), which belongs to all animals, and reason (τὸ διανοητιϰόν), which belongs to man alone (Treatise on the Soul, book II, chap. 2); the third faculty cannot exist without the second, nor the latter without the first. Nutrition has material things as its object; through this faculty, the animal assimilates external things themselves, whereas through sensation it receives only the forms of things, just as wax receives only the form of the seal, and not its matter. Reason, or thought, is to intelligible things what sensation is to sensible things; but through the senses we know only individuals or individual forms; we know that things are, but we do not know why they are; it is reason that recognizes general forms and causes. The soul, says Aristotle, that is to say, the intelligent part of the soul, is the place of forms (τόπος εἰδῶν).
fn.793.sub_1: Required to dominate everything, reason has no particular bodily organ; it must be impassible, that is to say, not affected by external things, but capable of receiving the form of objects. These forms it does not possess at first in act, that is, in full reality, but only in potency (Ibid., book 3, chap. 4). Just as in all beings one distinguishes on the one hand matter, or what is in potency, and on the other hand form, or the cause that makes what is in potency pass into act, so it is necessary that these differences be found in the rational part of the soul or in the intelligence. Aristotle thus distinguishes two intellects, one passive (νοῦς παθητιϰός), the other active (νοῦς ποιητιϰός). The passive intellect holds the middle ground between sensation and imagination, on one hand, and the active intellect, on the other; it is the latter especially that is separate (from the lower faculties of the soul), impassible, unmixed with anything whatsoever, being in act by its very essence (ϰαὶ οὗτος ὁ νοῦς χωριστὸς ϰαὶ ἀπαθὴς ϰαὶ ἀμιγής, τῇ οὐσίᾳ ὢν ἐνεργείᾳ. Ibid., chap. 5). Aristotle does not tell us clearly where this active intellect comes from, nor how it is perceived by the passive intellect; but he seems to see in it something divine, which comes from without through the first mover. See the treatise on the Generation of Animals, book II, chap. 3: λείπεται δὲ τὸν νοῦν μόνον θύραθεν ἐπεισιέναι ϰαὶ θεῖον εἶναι ϰ. τ. λ.; cf. Trendelenburg, Arist. de Anima, page 496. It is by the aid of this active intellect that every individual intelligence accomplishes the work of thought, and, passing from potency to act, it appropriates the forms of things and identifies itself with them. These intelligible forms, the object of thought, are themselves thought; for the intellect in act cannot be affected by something outside of itself, and it must draw from within itself what it has as its object. The intellect, therefore, in its entelechy or in its full reality, thinks itself. See Aristotle, Metaphysics, book XII, chap.
fn.793.sub_2: 7: αὑτὸν δὲ νοεῖ ὁ νοῦς ϰατὰ μετάληψιν τοῦ νοητοῦ νοητὸς γὰρ γίγνεται θιγγάνων ϰαὶ νοῶν ὥστε ταὐτὸν νοῦς ϰαὶ νοητόν. Cf. Treatise on the Soul, book III, at the end of chap. 4. Such is, in substance, Aristotle's theory; the obscurity that prevails in this theory, notably regarding the nature of the active intellect and its union with the passive intellect, has given rise, among commentators, to long discussions and the most diverse opinions, and the Arab philosophers, confounding here as elsewhere the theories of Aristotle with those of his Neoplatonic commentators, have elaborated, on the subject that concerns us, a new doctrine which subsequently spread among the scholastics. Here, in summary, is the theory of the Arab philosophers, who differ among themselves on several essential points. The speculative faculty or theoretical reason, the highest among the faculties of the rational soul (see above, page 210, note 1), receives the impression of forms isolated from matter, whether they be general forms that it abstracts from material and individual things, or immaterial and imperishable beings, which are in themselves abstract forms (as, for example, the separate intelligences). This faculty, called intellect (عقل) par excellence, develops gradually, passing through various degrees where the lower is to the higher what matter is to form, or what potency is to act. The Arab philosophers generally distinguish three degrees of development, or three intellects: 1st The hylic intellect or material intellect (العقل الهيولانى), which is the simple disposition that the intellect has to abstract forms; it is a simple potency that has not yet begun to pass into act, and which is called hylic because it can be compared to matter (ὕλη) disposed to receive form. This hylic intellect is the νοῦς παθητιϰός of Aristotle (العقل المنفعل) in all its abstraction.
fn.793.sub_3: The opinions of the Arab philosophers are divided on the nature of the hylic intellect: some, invoking the authority of Alexander of Aphrodisias, see in it only a pure disposition (استعداد) attached to the other faculties of the soul, and which is perishable like them, and this opinion is adopted by Maimonides (see below, chap. LXX); others, taking Themistius as their guide, maintain that, since the passive or hylic intellect must, according to Aristotle, be unmixed (ἀμιγής) with the other faculties of the soul, it must be a disposition having for its substratum a substance separate from the other faculties; for, they say, if the intellect in potency were only a simple disposition attached to the other faculties of the soul, it would have for its substratum something belonging to another genus than itself; but what is disposed to perceive intelligible things can itself only be an intellect. Ibn-Roschd, recognizing on the one hand what is inadmissible in Alexander's opinion, also sees difficulties in admitting the other opinion, according to which there would be a separate and eternal substance whose being would consist only in a disposition and a simple potency (δύναμις); he therefore chooses a middle term, by combining the two opinions, as we have explained elsewhere (see the article Ibn-Roschd in the Dictionnaire des sciences philosophiques, Vol. III, pages 166 and 167). 2nd The intellect in act (العقل بالفعل); this is the intellect that has succeeded in abstracting form from matter, that is to say, which has succeeded in distinguishing, in individual things, that which constitutes their general form, or that by which a thing is what it is. 3rd The acquired intellect (العقل المستفاد); this is nothing other than the intellect in act having become in a sense the property of man, when intelligible forms are always present in his intelligence, and he can identify himself with them at any moment without making new efforts.
fn.793.sub_4: Having arrived at this level, human intelligence always has as its object pure intelligible forms; its object is the knowledge of its own being and that of the immaterial beings outside of it, and it rises to the knowledge of the separate intelligences and of God. In this state, it becomes in a sense a substance entirely separate from the body (see below, at the end of chap. LXXII). Between the intellect in act and the acquired intellect, some Arab philosophers also place the intellect in capacity (العقل بالملكة); they seem to mean by this the intellect in act having become a capacity (ἕξις, cf. above, page 195, notes 1 and 2), and before it has actually reached the level of the acquired intellect (cf. the book Ta’rifât cited in Freytag's Dictionary, under the word عقل, and the Analysis of the philosophy of Ibn-Sînâ, in Shahrastânî, p. 418 of the Arabic text, and Vol. II, page 317, of the German translation). This is a subtle distinction, whose scope is not well understood, and which, it appears, has not been generally admitted; Ibn Falaquera, in enumerating the different intellects (see the Appendix to the Moreh ha-Moreh, at the beginning of chap. I, page 141), does not speak of the intellect in capacity (השכל בקנין). — Studies and philosophical speculation, although they are necessary for the development of the hylic intellect, would not be sufficient on their own to bring it to the levels of the intellect in act and the acquired intellect; like everything that is only in potency, the intellect needs, in order to pass into act or entelechy, a cause that is outside of itself, and this cause is the universal active intellect (العقل الفعال), the last among the intelligences of the spheres (see Part II of this work, chap. IV, and cf. Ibn-Sînâ, in Shahrastânî's work, page 426; German trans., Vol. II, p. 328).
fn.793.sub_5: It is through the influence of this active intellect that the acquired intellect is formed, considered as its emanation (hence, in the Hebrew versions, השכל הנאצל, the emanated intellect), and which succeeds, in certain chosen men, in identifying itself completely with the universal active intellect (cf. above, page 277, note 3, and my article Ibn-Roschd, loc. cit., pages 167 and 169). — Various details of this theory, of which we thought it necessary to present the whole here, will be discussed in other places. It is understandable that its obscurity has given rise to numerous divergences of opinion; the hypotheses, sought as far as regions inaccessible to the human mind, left a free career for the imagination, and the most enlightened Arab philosophers could not fail to abandon here the true ground of philosophical speculation, to lose themselves in reveries. 'Not a single one,' says Ibn Falaquera, 'has a well-fixed opinion on this subject, and we often see the same author change his opinion and say in one work something entirely different from what he said in another.' See Moreh ha-Moreh, book II, chap. 25 (page 111).
