If, then, the action of the agent intellect is not always manifested in an equal manner, one must not conclude from this that it can be sometimes in potentiality and sometimes in actuality; for it is essentially energy, and the interruption of its action has its cause in external obstacles. See the second part of this work, chap. XII and chap. XVIII. — The word חרכה̈ (حركة) does not have the meaning here of motion, but that of agitation or perturbation.
fn.808: In other words: the divine essence is the thought that has itself as its object; it is at once the thought, the thinking subject, and the thought object.
fn.809: Literally: we have often repeated this subject in this chapter, because minds are very far removed from this conception.
fn.810: More literally: and taking as a comparison the sensible, in the imaginative faculty. The words ואכד׳ מתל אלמחמום are somewhat obscure; I pronounce them: وأَخْذِ مَثْلِ الْمَحْسُوسِ, considering the genitive أَحَدٍ as depending on the prefix in بالتخيل, so that وأخذُ would be for وَأَخَذَ. It is also in this sense that Ibn Tibbon seems to have understood the word אכד׳, which he translates into Hebrew with a verbal noun; his version reads ולקיחת משל המוחש. Al-Harizi translates: והנני מדבר על דמיון המורגש וכו׳; it can be seen that he took the word אכד׳ for a verb أَحَدٍ; but his translation is not very intelligible. The meaning is: I do not think that you will allow yourself to be troubled by the imagination, and that you will compare the subject in question with purely sensible things, calling to your aid the imaginative faculty, which should not intervene in what belongs to the domain of the intellect. The author addresses his disciple (see above, p. 3), stating that he is sure of being well understood by him; otherwise he would not have addressed this treatise to him, which was composed only for those who have studied philosophy.
fn.811: The Arabic text expresses the word cause here and further on by two different words, علة and سبب, which the two Hebrew versions render as עלה and סבה; these two words, in the philosophical terminology of the Arabs, correspond to the Greek word αἰτία or αἴτιον (Aristotle, Metaph., V, 2, and passim), and are completely synonymous, as Ibn Rushd says in his Epitome of the Metaphysics, book I (Hebrew version): הסבה והעלה שני שמות נרדפים והנה יאמרו על הסבות הארבע אשר הם הפועל והחומר והצורה והתכלית 'Sabab and 'illa are two synonymous names which are said of the four causes, namely: the efficient, the matter, the form, and the end.' — The designation first cause, mentioned here by the author, very familiar to Arabic philosophers and Scholastics, is closely linked to the system of Aristotle, who shows us in the first mover, or in God, the ultimate term at which our intelligence necessarily arrives by ascending the series of beings and causes. This first cause is, according to Aristotle, a necessary condition for science, which would be impossible if causes extended to infinity; for the unlimited eludes science. See Physics, book VIII, chap. 5; Metaphysics, book II, chap. 2; book XII, chap. 7 ff. — This chapter, like the preceding one, serves as a complement to what the author has said about attributes; it shows that God is at the same time the efficient cause, the formal cause, and the final cause of the universe, and that these three causes, in Him, are completely identical and designate only a single thing, that is to say, His very essence even.
fn.812: See above, p. 5, note 1 and below, chap. LXXI.
fn.813: The existence of the cause as such necessarily implies that of the effect, and as soon as one calls God the first cause, one declares by that very fact that the world, which is the effect of this cause, has always existed. This reasoning of the Mutakallimun is much the same as that made by Plotinus when he says that by calling God the cause, we say something that applies not to him, but to us, because we derive something from him, while he remains in himself: ἐπεὶ καὶ τὸ αἴτιον λέγειν οὐ κατηγορεῖν ἐστὶ συμβεβηκός τι αὐτῷ, ἀλλ’ ἡμῖν, ὅτι ἐχομέν τι παρ’ αὐτοῦ, ἐκείνου ὄντος ἐν αὑτῷ (Enneads, VI, 9, 3). Cf. Ritter, Geschichte der Philosophie, vol. IV, p. 579. — The words ואן אלעאלם לה, which are found in most of the Oxford manuscripts, mean: and that the world is his, that is to say, that it is in a necessary relationship with God, and that its existence is a condition for that of God. Ibn Tibbon translates: ושהעולם מאתו, and that the world comes from him, which is not entirely exact. Al-Harizi makes a true misinterpretation by translating: וכי העולם עלה, and that the world is a cause. He perhaps followed an incorrect reading (ואן אלעאלם עלה̈), which is indeed found in one of the two Leiden manuscripts, while the other reads: ואן ללעאלם עלה̈, and that the world has a cause. This last reading, although less in disagreement with the passage as a whole, is also incorrect.
fn.814: More literally: furthermore, they do not even conceive the idea of an agent as an agent except by the fact that he is prior to his action; that is, they believe that the very idea attached to the word agent implies priority.
fn.815: Literally: its effect necessarily exists by its existence as a cause in act. In Ibn Tibbon's version, instead of במציאות העלה, one should read במציאותה עלה.
fn.816: The editions of Ibn Tibbon's version add here the words וכשיבנה אז הוא בונה בפעל, and when he builds, he is an architect in act. These words are found neither in the Arabic text nor in the manuscripts of Ibn Tibbon's version; they were evidently added by copyists, and this because of a misunderstanding to which this same version gave rise, which, a little further on, reads אז הוא נבנה, instead of אז הוא בונה, so that, without the added words, something would be missing from this passage as a whole, since no mention would be made of the architect in act. Cf. the following note.
fn.817: Ibn Tibbon's version reads נבנה (built or constructed); it appears that the Hebrew translator read מבני here instead of בנא, or else that he thought he should pronounce this last word بِنِسَاءٍ (construction), and not يَشَاءُ (architect). He did not notice that the words כמא אן מאדה̈ דלך אלבית קבל אן יבני בית באלקוה̈ should be considered as a parenthesis, and he imagined that the words פענד מא יבני were its continuation, so that he considered this last verb יבני as a passive verb (دِيُوبَنْدِي), referring to the house, whereas it is an active verb (يُبْنَى), referring to the architect. In truth, a Leiden manuscript supports Ibn Tibbon's version, for it reads בית (house), instead of בנא; but this is only an arbitrary and unintelligent correction. — Al-Harizi was more exact here, rendering בנא as architect (בנאי); but he entirely omitted, in his version, the words that we consider a parenthesis.
fn.818: That is, for every being except the first mover, or God.
fn.819: Cf. Aristotle, Physics, book II, chap. 7, where these four causes are designated as follows: ἡ ὕλη (matter), τὸ εἶδος (form), τὸ κινῆσϰν (that which moves, or the moving cause), τὸ οὗ ἕνεϰα (the why or the final cause). The formal cause, which makes a thing be what it is and which forms the essence of the thing, is also called τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι and οὐσὶα (see Posterior Analytics, II, 11; Physics, II, 3; Metaph., I, 3); the moving cause is also called τὸ ποιοῦν, that is, the efficient, and the final cause is called τὸ τέλος, the end (Metaph., V, 2 and passim), and it is to these two words that the Arabic terms الغاية الفاعل correspond.
fn.820: Cf. Aristotle, Post. Anal., book I, chap. 13 (Bekker ed.); Metaph., book VIII, chap. 4.
fn.821: That is to say, that God is simultaneously the efficient cause, the formal cause, and the final cause of the world. The idea of the prime mover, which is not moved and which is pure energy, excludes the material cause; the latter is often presented by Aristotle as that which exists by necessity (τὸ ἐξ ἀνάγϰης), and is opposed to the three other causes, representing movement and true being, and which is summed up in a single cause, which is the end (τὸ οὗ ἕνεϰα). See Physics, book II, chaps. 7-9, and cf. the treatise On the Parts of Animals, book I, chap. 1. Likewise, the idea of the soul, which is entelechy, excludes the material cause; this is why Aristotle says that the soul is the cause according to the three modes of cause (Treatise On the Soul, book II, chap. 4).
fn.822: Literally: or if it (the world) results from it necessarily, that is to say, if the existence of the world is a necessary consequence of that of God, so that the world would be eternal, and not created by the free will of God.
fn.823: The question at issue here is treated at length in the II<sup>nd</sup> part of this work.
fn.824: See the passages from Aristotle indicated above, p. 313, note 1.
fn.825: Literally: even if whoever of the proximate efficients did it, did it.
fn.826: Al-Harizi's version has והיא הצורה האחרונה, that this be that final form; one likewise reads in one of the Leiden manuscripts: הי אלצורֳה, instead of הי אשארֳה ללצורֳה. Ibn Falaquera (Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 37) also deletes the word אשארֳה allusion; but Ibn Tibbon's version conforms to the reading we have adopted.
fn.827: Aristotle shows, in several places in his Metaphysics, that prime matter and prime form are neither born nor perish. In all being, birth (γένεσις) and destruction or corruption (φθορά) are nothing other than change; what is born is born from something (which is the matter), by receiving the form (by which alone it is what it is), and it perishes by losing its form. It is therefore clear that the idea of matter, like that of form, excludes birth and destruction; for, in order for matter or form to be born or perish, each of the two would have to be composed, in turn, of matter and form, which would extend to infinity if one did not stop at a first matter and a first form, which, consequently, can neither be born nor perish. — Maimonides seems here particularly to have in mind a passage from the VIIth book of the Metaphysics (chap. 8), where Aristotle says, in summary, this: Since what is born is born by something (the efficient cause) and from something (the matter), and becomes something (through the form), the efficient cause makes neither the matter alone nor the form alone. For example, he who makes a bronze sphere makes neither the bronze nor the spherical form in itself, but he gives this form to the bronze, which is its substratum. If the efficient cause actually made this form in itself, the latter in turn would be born from something and would also be composed of matter and form, and births (γενέσεις) would continue to infinity. It is thus clear that the form, or what in sensible things can be called the figure, is not born; there is therefore no birth for the latter nor for the what in itself (τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι), which is always born in something else, whether by art, or by nature or by a faculty. Here are Aristotle's own words: εἰ οὖν ϰαὶ τοῦτο ποιεῖ αὐτό (i.e., τὸ εἶδος), δῆλον ὅτι ὡσαύτως ποιήσει ϰαὶ βαδιοῦνται αἱ γενέσεις εἰς ἄπειρον. φανερὸν ἄρα ὅτι οὐδὲ τὸ εἶδος, ἢ ὁτιδήποτε χρὴ ϰαλεῖν τὴν ἐν τῷ αἰσθητῷ μορφήν, γίγνεται, οὐδ’ ἔστιν αὐτοῦ γένεσις, οὐδὲ τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι. τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν ὃ ἐν ἄλλῳ γίγνεται ἢ ὑπὸ τέχνης ἢ ὑπὸ φύσεως ἢ δυνάμεως. See also Metaph., VII, 15; VIII, 3, 5; XII, 3. We see that what is at issue here is indeed, as Maimonides says, every form in general, or physical form, inseparable from matter, and not only the absolute prime form, or the prime mover.
fn.828: God, while setting the celestial sphere in motion and giving it form, is nonetheless entirely distinct from this sphere, as our author will explain in other places. See the following chapter, and Part II<sup></sup>, chap. IV.
fn.829: In this passage, we have had to deviate slightly from the Arabic text, the construction of which is irregular and even somewhat illogical. The meaning is that God is called the ultimate form, because He causes the principles of all that exists to be, which are remote from the causes we recognize as immediate.

fn.864.sub_0: The Arabic text of this passage is quite obscure; here is an approximate word-for-word translation: And likewise they have proved, for these (other) things they have enumerated, that, being (in) a relation with God, they are with Him. The word ענדה (at his place or with him) does not refer to God, but to the heaven ’Arabôth, and it would have been more regular to construct the Arabic sentence thus: וכדֹלך אמתדלוא עלי אנ תלכ אלתי עדוהא הי ענדה ללה תעאלי (i.e., באנהא נסבֹה (בכונהא מנסובֹה. Instead of נסבֹה (نسبة) which most manuscripts contain, some have נסבת (נُסִבَتْ), and one of the Leiden manuscripts has מנסובֹה (منسوبة); these last two readings appear to have been substituted for the word נסבֹה to facilitate the understanding of the passage. The meaning is: that the doctors, to prove that the other things they have enumerated also exist in ’Arabôth, limit themselves to citing biblical passages where these things are directly attributed to God; for nothing emanates from God except through the mediation of ’Arabôth, which, as has been seen, is the instrument by which God governs the universe. Thus, for example, to prove that ’Arabôth contains treasures of life, these words of the Psalmist are cited: For with you is the source of life (Ps. 36:10); for the treasures of peace, this passage is cited: And he called it (the altar) The Eternal God of peace (Judges 6:24); for the treasures of blessing: He shall receive the blessing from the Lord (Ps. 24:5), and so on. See ’Haghîghâ, l. c. — In the editions of Ibn Tibbon's version (with the exception of the editio princeps), our passage is translated twice, first literally, then in a manner that conveys the meaning more clearly; the second translation is expressed in these terms: ובן הביאו ראיה על השאר שהם בערבות מהיותם מיוחסים לשם יתעלה (the words שהם אצלו, which the editions add, are repeated from the first translation and must be deleted).

fn.871: That is to say, the metaphysical subjects discussed in the preceding chapters, which were designated by the rabbis under the name Ma‘aseh Merkavah (see the preceding chapter, and above, p. 9). — Before expounding the doctrines of the philosophers regarding the existence of God, His unity, and His incorporeality in Part IIe of this work, the author will provide, in the final chapters of this Part Ie, an exposition of the system of the Mutakallimun. The present chapter, serving as an introduction to this exposition, contains some historical indications regarding the origin of the said system, the influence of which is felt among certain Jewish theologians of the East. The author suggests at the beginning of this chapter that the philosophical sciences had been cultivated by the ancient Jews, and that the metaphysical subjects in question were not familiar to them solely through religious tradition. Whatever the value of this assertion may be, it conforms to the opinion of several ancient authors, and I have shown elsewhere that this opinion has been supported by pagan, Christian, and Muslim writers. See my article Juifs, in the Dictionnaire des sciences philosophiques, vol. III, p. 352, and the notes I appended to it in the Archives israélites, issue of March 1848 (all published separately in German, with additions, by Drr B. Beer, under the title: Philosophie und philosophische Schriftsteller der Juden, Leipzig, 1852, 8vo, p. 7 and 96). In Maimonides’ time, the said opinion was generally accepted, as seen in the following passage from Ibn Rushd, toward the end of his Destruction of the Destruction (Hebrew version): לא יםפק אחד שהנה היו בבני ישראל חכמים רבים וזה גלוי מהםפרים אשר ימצאו אצל בני ישראל המיוחםים אל שלמה ולא םרה החכמה ענין נמצא בԁאנשי הנבואה והם הנביאים ע״ה “No one doubts that there were many philosophers among the Israelites, and this is evident from the books found among the Israelites and attributed to Solomon. Science has continually existed among inspired men, who are the prophets.”

fn.876: Ibn Tibbon's version reads וםפקות נופלות בלשון המחבר במפר ושגגה תתחבר לו. It is clear that the translator took אלמדון for a passive participle (المدوّن) meaning that which was drafted in writing; it is in this same sense that this word was rendered by Al-Harizi. The words ושגגה תתחבר לנ (the error that was joined to it) would mean, according to several commentators, the faults of copyists that were added to the obscurity of the drafting; but the Arabic word سہوُ rather designates an error of thought or opinion, a mistake. It seems preferable to us to consider אלמדון as an active participle المدون, meaning redactor; the words ומהו יצחבה literally mean and the mistake or the error that accompanied him, that is to say, which was in the mind of the redactor.
fn.877: See Deuteronomy, ch. XVII (vv. 8-12), and Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, preface.
fn.878: The word אלמשאחחה̈ (as read in all the manuscripts), or better אלמשאחה̈ (الْمُشَاحَة), is the verbal noun of the IIIrd form of فبشر, having the sense of being stingy with something, carefully abstaining.
fn.880.sub_0: The word kalam (كلام), which means word, discourse, also designates a science that formed among the Muslims as early as the 2nd century of the Hegira, and whose goal was to combat the doctrines of heterodox sects and later those of the philosophers, by using against its adversaries the weapons of dialectic and reasoning borrowed from philosophical schools. This science can be called dogmatics, or rational theology, and it has much analogy with Christian scholasticism. Kalam developed especially since the introduction of Peripatetic philosophy among the Arabs, and it will be seen further on (ch. LXXIII et seq.) what doctrines were established by this science and how they proceeded to demonstrate the truth of the principal religious dogmas, particularly those establishing the unity and immateriality of God and Creation. As for the name kalam, the Arabs themselves do not agree on its origin; according to some, this science was so named because it primarily discussed what was meant by the divine word or by the word (kalam) attributed to God (cf. below, p. 343, note 3); according to others, the word kalam is merely an imitation of the word mantiq (منطق), which also means speech, or discourse, and by which philosophers designated one of the principal branches of their doctrine, namely, logic. See Shahrastani, History of Religious and Philosophical Sects, Arabic text, p. 18 (German trans., vol. I, p. 26); cf. Pococke, Specimen hist. ar., p. 195. From the word kalam comes the verb takallam (تكلم), having the sense of professing kalam, and whose participle mutakallim, in the plural mutakallimun, designates the partisans of kalam.
fn.880.sub_1: Having regard for the meaning of word that the word kalam possesses, the Hebrew translators called this science חכמת הדבר and designated the Mutakallimun under the name Medabberim (מדברים), which the Latin translators, in turn, rendered as loquentes. One may also see what I have said on kalam in the Dictionnaire des sciences philosophiques, vol. I, art. Arabes (pp. 169 and 174), and in my Notice on R. Saadia Gaon, p. 16 et seq. (Bible by M. Cahen, vol. IX, p. 88 et seq.). — The two Hebrew translators did not fully grasp the meaning that the word אלכלאם has in our passage, and they took it in its primitive sense of word or discourse; Ibn Tibbon translates: מדברי ענין היחוד, and Al-Harizi: מדבריהם בענין היחוד. Following the words we have just cited, one should read in Ibn Tibbon's version: ומה שנתלה בזה הענין, as found in the manuscripts and the editio princeps; in the other editions, it was erroneously put as: ומה שנתגלה מזה הענין.
fn.881: It is known that the title of Gaon גאון (pl. Geonim) is that held by the heads of the Jewish academies of Babylon under Arabic rule, from the end of the 7th until around the middle of the 11th century. The period of the Geonim coincides with that of the development of kalam among the Arabs; the example set by Muslim theologians was followed by certain Jewish doctors of the East who, like the Mutakallimun, sought to support religious dogmas through philosophical speculation and laid the foundations of a systematic and rational theology. It was the doctors of the Karaite sect who first entered this path and themselves adopted the name Mutakallimun (see the Khozari, book V, § 15), without, however, admitting all the hypotheses of Muslim kalam, which will be set forth further on (ch. LXXIII). Some Rabbanite doctors among the Geonim imitated the example of the Karaites (cf. above, p. 286, note 3, and p. 290, note 2). We have remaining, in the Book of Beliefs and Opinions of Rabbi Saadia Gaon, an important monument of what can be called Jewish kalam, and it is to this celebrated doctor that Maimonides here appears to allude, as Moses of Narbonne observes in his commentary on our passage. In vol. III of the Dictionnaire des sciences philosophiques, art. Juifs (pp. 355-357), I have given some other details on this subject. I will further add that Arabic authors of the 10th century expressly speak of Jewish Mutakallimun. Al-Masudi cites several whom he had personally known (see Silv. de Sacy, Notices et Extraits des manuscrits, vol. VIII, p. 167). Isa ibn Zara‘a, a Christian Arabic author of Baghdad, speaking in his theological treatises of a certain Abu al-Khayr Dawud ibn Mushaj, says that he was one of the principal Jewish Mutakallimun and a profound thinker (...من متكلّمي اليهود وكان متقدّماً فيهم نظّارا). See Arab. ms. of the Biblioth. imp., ancient collection, no. 98, fol. 40 b and 42 a.
fn.882: The sect of the Mutazilites (المعتزلة), whose name means separated or dissidents, was founded by Wasil ibn Ata (born in the year 80 of the Hegira, or 699-700 CE, and died in 131, or 748-749 CE). Wasil, a disciple of Al-Hasan al-Basri (of Basra), having separated (اعتزل) from the school over some religious dogma, became a school leader himself and established a doctrine whose elements were borrowed from various previous sects (cf. Shahrastani, p. 18 ff.; Ger. trans., vol. I, p. 25 ff.; Pococke, Specimen hist. ar., p. 211 ff.). The Mutazilites, subdivided into several branches, all agree on the following two points: 1. Man has perfect freedom in his actions; he does good and evil of his own accord, and thus has merits or demerits. 2. God, being absolutely one, has no attributes distinct from His essence (cf. above, p. 209, note 1). It is because of these two principal points of their doctrine, aimed at establishing the absolute justice and unity of God, that the Mutazilites refer to themselves by the name أصحاب العدل والتوحيد (partisans of justice and unity). These are precisely the same expressions that the Arabic historian Al-Masudi uses to designate the doctrine of the disciples of Anan (see de Sacy, Notices et Extraits, loc. cit.; Chrest. ar., vol. I, pp. 349-351), which proves that the Karaite theologians took as their primary model the Muslim doctors of the Mutazilite sect. In agreement with Maimonides, the Karaite author Aaron ben Elijah expressly says that the Karaite scholars and a portion of the Rabbanites followed the doctrines of the Mutazilites (see עץ חיים or Tree of Life, Leipzig edition, p. 4).
fn.883: The Ash'ariyya or Ash'arites are the disciples of Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Isma'il al-Ash'ari, of Basra (born around the year 880 CE and died in 940). The latter, raised in the principles of the Mutazilites and already one of their leading doctors, publicly declared one Friday in the Great Mosque of Basra that he repented of having professed heretical doctrines, and that he recognized the pre-existence of the Quran, the attributes of God, and the predestination of human actions. The Ash'arites therefore admitted, without evasion, attributes of God distinct from His essence and denied human free will. It can be seen that their doctrine was diametrically opposed to that of the Mutazilites; they nevertheless made some reservations to avoid falling into anthropomorphism and to avoid denying every kind of merit and demerit in human actions (see the art. Arabes in the Dictionnaire des sc. philos., vol. I, p. 176, and cf. above, p. 186, note 1). Several details of the Ash'arite doctrine will be explained later, ch. LXXIII (Props. 6, 7 etc.); on the absolute fatalism professed by this sect, see Part III of this work, chapter XVII (3rd opinion).
fn.884: Literally: and that they believed it to be a demonstrative thing, that is to say, they believed that the opinions of the Mutazilites were truths that could be rigorously demonstrated.
fn.885: It seems to follow from what Maimonides says here that before him there had existed in Andalusia or in Muslim Spain a certain number of Jewish theologians or philosophers (cf. above, ch. XLII, p. 149, and ibid., note 1), but that already by his time only a small number of works by a few recent writers remained of the philosophical literature of the Jews of Spain. Those that still remain today generally justify the judgment passed by our author, with the exception of two who made various borrowings from the Mutakallimun. Solomon ibn Gabirol, of Malaga, left us in his Source of Life an important document proving that as early as the 11th century, and before Peripatetic philosophy had found a worthy representative among the Muslims of Spain, the Jews of that country had successfully engaged in philosophical studies and had addressed the highest metaphysical questions; and from that same period there were also writers in Spain who felt compelled to defend religion against the encroachments of philosophy. Cf. my Notice on Abu al-Walid Marwan ibn Janah, p. 81 ff. (Journal asiatique, July 1850, p. 45 ff.). Around 1160, Abraham ben David of Toledo, an opponent of Ibn Gabirol, undertook in his work entitled The Sublime Faith to reconcile religion and philosophy, and one recognizes in him a great admirer of Aristotle's philosophy, which he brings into religious questions to roughly the same extent as Maimonides. Around the same time, Judah Halevi of Castile had, in his famous Kuzari, declared war on philosophy, in which he was deeply versed; but at the same time he had rejected the reasoning of the kalam, which he regarded as useless subtleties (see his said work, book V, § 16). Among his contemporaries, Moses ben Jacob ibn Ezra seems to belong to the philosophical school, while Joseph ibn Tsaddik was in various respects under the influence of the kalam (cf. above, p. 209, note 1). This same influence is notable at the end of the 11th century in the famous work of Bahya ben Joseph of Saragossa, entitled Duties of the Hearts; in Book I, which treats the unity of God, we find several arguments borrowed from the Mutakallimun (see especially chapter V), although, with respect to divine attributes, Bahya shows himself in complete agreement with the philosophers (cf. above, p. 238, note 1).
fn.886: The author alludes to the ecclesiastical writers, Greek and Syrian, who, from the 6th century onwards, had to defend Christian dogmas against the increasingly dominant Peripatetic philosophy and against the numerous heresies resulting from that same philosophy. The defenders of religion used the weapons of dialectics that the study of Aristotle's philosophy had placed in their hands. Cf. Brucker, Hist. crit. philos., vol. III, p. 534; Ritter, Geschichte der Philosophie, vol. VI, p. 458 ff. (Philos. chrét., book VII, ch. 1). The same method, as the author will explain, was followed by the Muslim Mutakallimun, who were acquainted with the writings of several writers of the Greek Church, such as John Philoponus, John of Damascus, and others, and who were even better positioned to draw from the writings of the Christian theologians of Syria and Mesopotamia. Christian scholars, both Nestorian and Jacobite, lived in great numbers among the Muslims, who owed them their knowledge of Greek philosophy and science. Cf. Wenrich, De auctorum Graecorum versionibus et commentariis syriacis arabicis etc., pp. 7-22; E. Renan, De Philosophia peripatetica apud Syros, Paris 1852.
fn.887: Literally: when the Christian nation had embraced (within itself) these nations [and the assertion of the Christians is what is known] etc. The word מלה̈ (ملة), nation, primarily designates a large religious community. Instead of דעוי (assertion), some manuscripts have the verb אדעוא (ادّعوا); likewise Ibn Tibbon: וטענו הנוצרים מה שכנר נודע, and the Christians affirmed (or maintained) what is known. The author is referring to the mysteries of the Incarnation and the Trinity.
fn.888: This author is John Philoponus, surnamed the Grammarian, who flourished in Alexandria in the 6th and 7th centuries; his commentary on Aristotle's Physics bears the date of the year 333 of the Era of Diocletian, or of the Martyrs, which corresponds to the year 617 CE (see Fabricius, Biblioth. gr., vol. X, p. 640, 4th edition). The discourses of Philoponus to which Maimonides alludes here are, no doubt, his Refutation of Proclus' treatise on the eternity of the world, and his Cosmogony of Moses.
fn.889: Abu Zakariyya Yahya IBN-ADI, a Jacobite Christian from Tikrit in Mesopotamia, lived in Baghdad in the 10th century. He was a disciple of Al-Farabi and became famous for his Arabic translations of several works by Aristotle and his commentators. According to the Tarikh al-hukama of Al-Qifti, he died on August 13 in the year 1285 of the Seleucids (974 CE), aged 81. Cf. Abu al-Faraj, Hist. dynast., Ar. text, p. 317, Lat. version, p. 209. Ibn Adi also composed theological writings in which he sought to reconcile philosophy with Christian dogmas; thus, for example, he saw in the Trinity the unity of the intellect, the intelligent, and the intelligible (cf. above, chapter LXVIII), which are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit (see Hammer, Encyklopädische Übersicht der Wissenschaften des Orients, p. 423). It would seem that Maimonides was not well acquainted with the era in which Ibn Adi had lived and that he believed him to be more ancient, since he seems to suppose that the first Muslim Mutakallimun had drawn from his writings.
fn.890: Literally: everything that the one who chose believed to be useful to him.
fn.891: See below, chap. LXXIII, props. 1 and 2.
fn.892: Most of the Oxford manuscripts read אלם, and this word was taken by Ibn Tibbon in the sense of to suffer, to be sick or affected by something ألم, for he translates it as נחלו (i.e., נֶחֱלוּ, niph’al of הלה). In the two Leiden manuscripts, we find עלם علم, and it is this reading that is expressed by Al-Harizi, who has נודעו; in a manuscript of Ibn Tibbon's version (Oratoire collection, No. 46), we likewise read ידען instead of נחלו. Neither of the two versions expresses the true sense of the Arabic text, where one should read أَلَمْ (IVth form of الله), a verb which means to enter, approach, or engage in something; cf. above, chap. XXVIII, לאילּם בהדֿא אלמעֿני פֿלדֿך לא, that is why he does not engage in this question (fol. 31b of our text and p. 96 of the translation), where Ibn Tibbon renders the verb ירושלם by הבנים עצמו.
fn.893: That is to say, their time was closer to that of the ancient philosophers, to whom they were linked by several ties. This, at least, is how this passage was understood by Al-Harizi, who translates: כי החבמים ההם היה זמנם קרוב לדור הפילוםופים. However, according to some commentators, the sense would be that the Greek theologians stood closer to the philosophers, meaning they did not deviate so much from their doctrines; the Arabic text, as well as Ibn Tibbon's version, indeed allows for this interpretation, and it is also favored by a variant in some Arabic manuscripts which have אלפלספח, of philosophy, instead of אלפלאםפה̈, of the philosophers.
fn.894: All the Arabic manuscripts have והי in the feminine, referring to אשיא; the two Hebrew versions have והוא.
fn.895: וגירהא can grammatically refer only to the word אלמעגׄזאת, and the same applies to the word וזולתם in the Hebrew versions; however, we believe the author inadvertently used וגירהא instead of וגירה, and that this word refers to אלקול. In this way, the use of the feminine והי, mentioned in the preceding note, is also justified.
fn.896: The author alludes to the discussion that arose among Muslim theologians regarding the divine speech addressed to the prophets, and particularly to Muhammad. According to some, the speech of God is eternal, and the Qur'an, in which it is contained, has existed from all eternity; according to others, it is created in the subject in which it is revealed, and which clothes it in letters and sounds. See Pococke, Specimen hist. ar., pp. 217 ff.; Shahrastani, pp. 30 and 156 (Ger. trans., vol. I, pp. 42 and 236); cf. above, p. 290, note 2. It is also in this sense that Ibn Tibbon explains the word דבור, with which he renders here the Arabic word בלאם; in some manuscripts of his version, we read this note by the translator: רוצה בו דבור השם לנביאים כי האריבו לדבר במהותו אם הוא קדמון או מחודש 'He means the speech of God (addressed) to the prophets; for they (the Muslims) have discussed at length the question of whether it is eternal or created.'
fn.897: Literally: certain hypotheses, by means of which hypotheses, which they had chosen, they supported the things in which they had engaged.
fn.898: Literally: of that which has been set down in it. The words ממא ממיא אחצה פיהא פיהא are rendered in Ibn Tibbon's version (according to the editions) as ממה שחובר בהם לה, of that which has been COMPOSED in this regard by it, that is, of what has been recorded in writings; we prefer the reading of several manuscripts which contain ממה שהוצע לה.
fn.899: All the manuscripts contain אלאול in the singular, which is irregular.
fn.900: Literally: that there was no need at all to establish or deny this thing, regarding what is necessary for the foundations of religion.
fn.901: Literally: did not perceive and did not know that the matter was not as they believed.
fn.902: Literally: to establish what one sought to establish, and to deny what one sought to deny.
fn.903: That is: They even denied harmless propositions as soon as they realized that, through a series of consequences, they could lead to a proposition dangerous to religion.
fn.904: Moses of Narbonne expresses surprise that the author cites Themistius here (a 4th-century commentator on Aristotle) instead of citing Aristotle himself, who, he notes, discussed this subject at length in Book Γ (Book IV) of the *Metaphysics*, where he expresses himself as follows: 'If every thought and every opinion were true, everything would necessarily be both true and false at once; for many people think the opposite of what others think, and believe that those who do not share their opinion are in error.' This means (Moses of Narbonne adds) that things would have to be simultaneously true and false if they conformed to human opinions; for people often hold opposing views on the same subject. The passage alluded to is found in Book IV, Chapter 6 of the *Metaphysics*, where Aristotle, refuting Protagoras’s doctrine (that man or individual opinion is the measure of all things), writes: εἴτε γὰρ τὰ δοϰοῦντα πάντα ἐστὶν ἀληθῆ ϰαὶ τὰ φαινόμενα, ἀνάγϰη πάντα ἅμα ἀληθῆ ϰαὶ ψευδῆ εἶναι. πολλοὶ γὰρ τἀναντία ὑπολαμβάνουσιν ἀλλή-λοις, ϰαὶ τοὺς μὴ ταὐτὰ δοξάζοντας ἑαυτοῖς διεψεῦσθαι νομίζουσιν, ϰ. τ. λ. After citing several other passages from the same chapter, Moses of Narbonne adds: 'It seems to me that the author (Maimonides), in composing this treatise, particularly consulted the moderns.' It appears indeed that Maimonides, in his study of Peripatetic philosophy, did not always return to the primary sources, but limited himself to the analyses of commentators; among these, Themistius was one of the most highly regarded among the Arabs, and it was primarily through his works and those of Ibn Sīnā that many Arabic scholars studied Aristotelian philosophy. Cf. Shahrastānī, loc. cit., pp. 312 and 326 (German trans., vol. II, pp. 160 and 181).
fn.905: Dialectic and sophistry deal with the same types of questions as philosophy, and their object is being. But, Aristotle says, dialectic only examines whereas philosophy knows; sophistry appears to be (science) without actually being so: ἔστι δὲ ἡ διαλεϰτιϰὴ πειραστι-ϰὴ περὶ ὧν ἡ φιλοσοφία γνωριστιϰή ἡ δὲ σοφιστιϰὴ φαινομένη, οὖσα δ’οὔ. *Metaph.*, Book IV, chap. 2.
fn.906: אלמתשרעון (properly: those who occupy themselves with the Law) means the same thing as אהל אלשריעה̈; see above, p. 68, note 3.
fn.907: In the version of Ibn-Tibbon, one must add, after מחבוריהם, the word ודבריהם, which is found in the manuscripts of this version and in that of Al-Harizi; the sense is that one can be convinced of it, either by their own works or by what is reported concerning them.
fn.908: Literally: and that we do not fight for this with the sword. There is perhaps here an ironic allusion to the manner in which Islamism sought to propagate its doctrines.
fn.909: Literally: and we shall say thereupon everything by which it is possible to argue, that is to say, we will produce all the arguments that can be alleged in favor of the novelty of the world, or at least against its eternity. See Part II, ch. XV et seq.
fn.910: The word أصوليون designates those who occupy themselves with the roots (اصول) or the fundamental doctrines of religion; it is these roots that form the subject of kalam, while the branches (فروع), that is to say, everything that is secondary, and notably practices, are within the domain of jurisprudence (فقه). See Pococke, Specimen hist. ar., text of Abu'l-Faraj, p. 16; Shahrastani, p. 28 (German trans., vol. I, pp. 38 and 39).
fn.911: The Hebrew expressions הִפּוּךְ עוֹלָם and שִׁנּוּי סִדְרֵי בְרֵאשִׁית, which the author uses here, are borrowed from well-known Talmudic idioms; e.g.: עוֹלָם הָפוּךְ ראִיתִי, Bab. Talm., tractate Pesahim, fol. 50 a; נִשְׁתַּנּוּ לוֹ סִדְרֵי בְרֵאשִׁית, ibid., tractate Shabbat, fol. 53 b; גְּדוֹלָה חִבָּתָן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁהַקָּבָּ״ה מְשַׁנֶּה סִדְרֵי בְרֵאשִׁית בִּשְׁבִיל טוֹבָתָן Shemot Rabbah, sect. 38.
fn.912: Here is the author's reasoning: If one admits that the world is created, it follows undoubtedly that a creator exists; but one thus succeeds in establishing nothing other than the simple existence of God, whereas by admitting the eternity of the world, one will have rigorous demonstrations to establish at the same time the immateriality, unity, and immutability of God, as will be seen in the first chapters of Part II of this work. It is therefore necessary first to borrow the arguments of those who profess the eternity of primary matter, so that no doubt remains regarding the true nature of the Supreme Being, except to subsequently refute the hypothesis of the eternity of matter. One can easily sense the flaw in this reasoning; it contains the implicit admission that the believer who accepts the dogma of Creation ex nihilo must accept the unity and incorporeality of God as objects of religious faith and renounce all demonstration in this regard. This is how Ibn Falaquera (Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 43) expresses himself on our passage: "One can here object: How can one wish to demonstrate such an important subject by means of something doubtful, and even more so if this thing is not true? For if the premises of the demonstration are not true, how can the conclusion be true, and how can one with such premises form a demonstration that is not doubtful?... Undoubtedly, this could not have escaped our master, who has wisely arranged all his words." Cf. above, p. 29, note 1.
fn.913: Literally: That is why you will always find in what I have composed on the books of FIQH (or of the Talmud), when it happens that I speak of bases (or of fundamental principles), etc. Instead of קואעד, one of the Oxford manuscripts (Uri cat., no. 359) bears קואעד אלשריעה̈, bases of religion. It is this reading that has been followed in the two Hebrew versions; that of Ibn-Tibbon has יסודות הדת, and that of Al-Harizi יסודות האמונה. Ibn-Falaquera (Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 43) put פנה מפנות התורה, which would be in Arabic: קאערה̈ מן קואער אלשריעה̈.
fn.914: Literally: and that another may claim it never to have been built.
fn.915: That is to say, I have all the more reason to act in this manner.
fn.916: That is to say, those of the existence, the unity, and the incorporeality of God.
fn.917: The manuscripts read ילתגֹון and further on פילתגֹוא לתואליף; we deemed it necessary to write, in both passages, يلحقون, because the construction indicates that this verb comes from the root لجأ, which means to have recourse, to be reduced to something. In the manuscripts, the ו and the י hamzated are often omitted. Cf. above, p. 50, note 3.
fn.918: See the II<sup>nd</sup> part, chap. XIX.
fn.919: The author appears to allude here to the Vth of the proofs of the Mutakallimūn enumerated further on, chap. LXXIV.
fn.920: That is to say, to deny obvious things. The word مكابرة denotes an obstinate denial, a discussion whose aim is not truth, but dispute and contradiction. See the Appendix of the Moreh ha-Moreh, chap. III (p. 152); men of science, says Ibn Falaquera, call one who denies the obvious سكابر العيان. Cf. the book Ta’rifāt, cited in Freytag's Dictionary, under the root كبر.
fn.921: Ibn Tibbon's version reads: ואם אי אפשר ובו׳, ALTHOUGH there is no possible means for this; this version conforms to one of the Leiden manuscripts, which reads ואן instead of אן.
fn.922: That is to say, the questions of the existence, the unity, and the incorporeality of God, and that of the creation of the world.
fn.923: Plato already, in the Timaeus, presents the universe as a single individual, as an animated and organic whole having a spherical shape, and this is also the basis of Aristotle's cosmology, set forth in the treatise On the Heavens and in that On the World. The comparison the author is about to establish between the organism of the universe and that of the human individual is merely the reproduction of an idea very widespread among Jewish writers of all periods, which has its source in the doctrines of Pythagoras and Plato rather than in those of Aristotle. The idea of the macrocosm and microcosm, which appears here and there in the allegories of the Talmud and the Midrashim, was especially developed in the book Aboth of Rabbi Nathan (chap. 31) and in the book Yezirah, and accepted by several Jewish philosophers of the Middle Ages; see, e.g., the Extracts from the Source of Life by Ibn Gebirol, book III, §§ 6 and 44, and the Olam Katan, or the Microcosm, by R. Joseph Ibn Zaddik (recently published by Mr. Ad. Jellinek, Leipzig, 1854, in-8vo), book II, 1st section. In our author, the comparison is intended only to establish the individuality of the universe; it is limited to ingenious parallels and has nothing of the symbolic and mystical character that the Kabbalists and certain moralists have given to the theory of the microcosm. — The author will present in this chapter the main points of physics, as it was taught in the Arabic schools; Aristotle's theories are supplemented and developed here and there by those of Ptolemy, Galen, and the Neoplatonists. We cannot enter into the details of the various theories summarized by the author, and we must limit ourselves, in our notes, to clarifying certain points whose understanding is particularly necessary for the reader of this work. Various details relating to Peripatetic cosmology and the Ptolemaic system will be more fully explained by the author himself in the IInd part of this work, and it would be useless to dwell on them at this time.
fn.924.sub_0: On the humors, see below, p. 366, note 4. — The spirits are subtle fluids which, according to the hypotheses of ancient naturalists, have their seat in various organs of the animal body and contribute to the manifestations of the soul's different faculties. The three types of spirit correspond to the three faculties of the soul admitted by the ancient physicians, which are the natural faculty, the vital faculty, and the psychic (or animal) faculty. See the Canon of Ibn Sina, book I, fen. 1, ch. 6 (Arabic text, p. 38; Latin version, vol. I, p. 76); cf. Maimonides, Eight Chapters, at the beginning of chapter I, and the IIIrd part of this work, toward the end of chapters XII and XLVI, where the author alludes to these three faculties. Here is how Maimonides himself, in one of his medical treatises, explains the theory of the spirits and their different types, according to the ancient physicians: הד׳ה אלתי תסמיהא אלאטבא ארואחא הי אבכ׳רה̈ לטיפה̈ מוז׳ודה פי ז׳סם אלחיואן מבדאהא ומעט׳ם מאדתהא מן אלהוא אלמסתנשק מן כ׳ארז׳ פבכ׳אר אלדם אלמוז׳וד פי אלכבד ופי אלאורדה̈ لا נאבתה̈ מנהא יסמי אלוח אלטביעיה̈ ובכ׳אר אלדם لا מוז׳וד פי אלקלב ואלשריאן יסמי אלוח אלחיואניה̈ ואלבכ׳אר אלמוז׳וד פי בטון لا דטאג ומא ינבעת׳ מנה פי מסאם لا אעצאב יסמי רוחא נפסאניה̈ ומבדא אלז׳מיע ואכת׳ר מאדתה מן אלהוא אלמסתנשק מן כ׳ארז׳ פאד׳א כאן הד׳א لا הוא עפנא או מנתנא או כדרא תגירת תלך لا ארואח כלהא וז׳רי אמרהא עלי כ׳לאף מא ינבגי ֗֗֗֗ וכלמא כאנת אלוח אלטף כאן תגירהא בתגיר אלהוא אכת׳ר פאלוח لا טביעי אגלט׳ מן אלוח لا חיואני ואלחיואני אגלט׳ מן אלנפסאני פענד תגיר אלהוא איסר תגיר יתגיר חאל אלנפסאני תגירא ישער בה ולד׳לך תז׳ד כת׳ירא מן אלנאס קד ישערו בנקץ אפעאלהם אלנפסאניה̈ ענד פסאד אלהוא אעני אן יחדת׳ להם בלאדה̈ פהם וקצור אדראך ונקצאן חפט׳ ואן כאנת אפעאלהם אלחיואניה̈ ואלטביעיה̈ לא ישער פיהא בתגיר 'What physicians call spirits are subtle vapors that exist in the body of the animal and which derive their origin and their principal matter from the air drawn from outside by respiration.
fn.924.sub_1: The vapor of the blood existing in the liver and in the veins that originate from it is called the natural spirit or physical (φυσικὸν πνεῦμα); the vapor of the blood existing in the heart and in the arteries is called the vital spirit (ζωτικὸν πν.); finally, the vapor found in the cavities of the brain and that which spreads from it into the channels of the nerves is called animal spirit (ψυχικὸν πν.). The origin of all (these spirits) and their principal matter come (as we have said) from the air drawn in by respiration; if, therefore, this air is corrupted, or foul-smelling, or murky, all these spirits are altered and are no longer what they ought to be... The more subtle the spirit is, the more it is altered by the alteration of the air. Now, as the natural spirit is thicker than the vital spirit, and the latter thicker than the animal spirit, it follows that at the slightest alteration of the air, the animal spirit will undergo a perceptible alteration. This is why you will find many men in whom a weakening of the animal or psychic functions (that is, the functions depending on the animal spirits) is observed when the air is corrupted; I mean that it happens to them to have dull intelligence, difficult understanding, and a weakened memory, although no alteration is noticed in their vital and natural functions.' Cf. Galen, De Hippocr. et Plat. placitis, book VII, chapter 3, and above, p. 111, note 2. — The passage we have just cited is found at the beginning of book IV of the treatise titled في تدبير الصحة (On the Regimen of Health), which Maimonides composed at the request of Al-Malik al-Afdhal, son of Saladin, and whose Arabic original, copied in Hebrew characters, is in the Imperial Library (see Hebrew mss. of the old collection no. 412, fol. 107 a.b, and no. 411, fol. 57 b and 46 a). The Hebrew version of this treatise, by R. Moses Ibn Tibbon, was published in the collection titled כרם חמד, vol. III (Prague, 1838, in-8vo), p. 9 et seq. There also exists a Latin version of it which has been printed several times.
fn.926: That is to say, by a fifth element, which is ether and which forms the substance of the celestial spheres. See above, p. 247, note 3, and cf. the IInd part, chaps. II, XIX, and passim.
fn.927: The pronoun והו refers to אלגסם אלכאמם. In the editions of Ibn Tibbon's version, the plural והם is an error; the manuscripts have והוא.
fn.928: That is to say, the center of the earth, which, in the system of the ancients, is the common center of the entire universe.
fn.929: The author refers to the eccentrics, which, in the Ptolemaic system, serve to explain certain inequalities in the motion of the stars.
fn.930: The author speaks here of the hypotheses of the ancients regarding the two opposing motions, one of which is the diurnal motion, from east to west, imparted to the planets and the fixed stars by the movement of the superior sphere; the other is the motion that the stars perform, in certain periods, from west to east. Cf. our author, in his Abridgment of the Talmud, Yesôdé ha-Tôrâ, chap. III, § 2, and Isaac Israeli, Yesôd ’Olâm, book II, chap. 1 and 7. We shall have the opportunity to return to these theories in Chapter IV of Part II.
fn.931: By including the eccentrics, three spheres were attributed to the Moon, three to Mercury, and two to each of the other five planets, which, along with the sphere of the fixed stars and that of the diurnal motion, brings the number to eighteen.
fn.932: Under the designation of sphere of convolution, the Arabs refer to the epicycle, which, in the Ptolemaic system, is a small sphere in which the star is fixed and whose center moves, on the surface of the large sphere, along the circumference of a great circle called the deferent circle (because it carries the epicycle). Cf. the treatise Yesôdé ha-Tôrâ, chap. III, § 4. From the beginning of the 12th century, the Arab astronomers of Spain recognized the implausibility of this hypothesis, by which Ptolemy seeks to explain certain anomalies in the motion of various planets. Ibn-Bâdja was the first to speak out against the hypothesis of epicycles, and Ibn-Tofail rejected both the eccentrics and the epicycles (see my article Tofail in the Dict. des sc. philos., vol. VI, p. 907). This is why Maimonides says here that the question of epicycles must be submitted for examination; he himself addresses this question in chap. XXIV of Part II. Shortly thereafter, Abu-Is’hâk al-Bitrôdji, or Alpetragius, attempted to substitute other hypotheses for those of Ptolemy.
fn.933: The author refers to the sphere of the Moon.
fn.934: The author summarizes here Aristotle's theories on the elements. See the treatise On the Heavens, book IV, chap. 3 and following; Physics, book IV, chap. 5; cf. the treatise Yesôdé ha-Tôrâ, chap. III, §§ 10 and 11.
fn.935: The author will return to this question in Chapter IV of Part II<sup></sup>; the objective he proposes here does not require the immediate solution of this question.
fn.936: Instead of יכון, one of the Leiden manuscripts has יהבון, in the Vth form; likewise Ibn-Tibbon and Ibn-Falaquera (Moré ha-Moré, p. 45): שיתהוה, whereas Al-’Harizi has יהיה. The same Leiden manuscript has מנהא, which would refer to the elements; Ibn-Tibbon and Al-’Harizi indeed have מהם, in the plural; but the suffix in מנה refers to אלמכֿתלט, the mixture, and Ibn-Falaquera also has ממנו, in the singular.
fn.937: According to Aristotle's theories, the first transmutations of elementary substances are exhalations and vapors, which produce the various phenomena above the earth and within the interior of the terrestrial globe; see Aristotle's Meteorology, books I-III. Vapors and exhalations that find no outlet contribute first to the formation of minerals (see ibid., at the end of book III), and then gradually to that of plants and animals. Cf. the account of Al-Kazwēni in Silv. de Sacy's Chrestomathie arabe, vol. III, p. 389 ff., the citation of the Ayīn Acbéri, ibid., p. 454 ff., and the analysis of Ibn-Sīnā's Physics in the work of Schahrestāni, p. 413 (German trans., vol. II, p. 310). See also Part IIe of this work, chap. XXX.
fn.938: That is to say, that which receives the form, or which is capable of receiving it.
fn.939: Literally: in the "where," that is, in relation to the category of ποῦ; for, as the author stated above, the celestial bodies undergo no change except that of position.
fn.940: The word בכתרר (by repetition) is rendered in Ibn-Tibbon's version by בהשתנות (by change); this reading, which is also found in the manuscripts, is perhaps an error for בהשנות.
fn.941: As Ibn-Falaquera observes (Moré ha-Moré, p. 48), it is not accurate to say that the heart moves (for it has no movement of locomotion, but only of pulsation); according to him, the author intends to speak of the movement of the blood passing from the heart into the arteries.
fn.942: Instead of תוליד, one of the Leiden manuscripts has הרכיב, and it is this latter reading that the two Hebrew versions reproduce, as well as the Moré ha-Moré (p. 46), which have בהרכבת.
fn.943: The author means, as he explains himself in chap. XXX of Part IIe, that the birth and destruction of sublunar things occur under the influence of the variation of light and darkness, or of heat and cold; this variation results from the revolution of the stars, as a result of which light and heat are alternately communicated to and withheld from different parts of the earth. — The suffix in לנורהא ודורתהא is irregular; for it can only refer to the word אלפלד, which is at the beginning of the sentence, and it would have been more regular to write לנורה with the masculine suffix. It is perhaps for this reason that Ibn-Tibbon used הגלגלים in the plural, although all the Arabic manuscripts have אלפלד in the singular. One must necessarily understand in לנורהא the word אלאפלאך or אלכואכב. In most editions of Ibn-Tibbon's version, the word לנורהא is rendered by אחר יושחם, whereas one should read אחר אורם, as found in the manuscripts and the princeps edition.
fn.944: All the Arabic manuscripts have או; Ibn-Tibbon and Ibn-Falaquera read איי, which they rendered as כלומר; but this reading does not offer a suitable meaning.
fn.946: That is to say that God, who is one, created only a single being that is likewise one. The author here alludes to a question he will address in chap. XXII of Part II, and which we touched upon above, p. 211, note 2.
fn.947: Ibn-Tibbon's version is distorted here in the editions by several printing errors; the manuscripts and the editio princeps read: כאן אי אפשר שימצאו חלקי העולם קצתם מבלתי קצתם בזה המציאות המיושב אשר דבָרֵנו בו.
fn.948: By this is meant the primary faculty of the soul, which is seated in the brain; it is designated as that which guides and governs the animal body (τὸ ἡγεμονιϰὸν, or τὸ βασιλεῦον ϰαὶ ἐπ τάσσον). See Galen, Definitiones medicæ, CXIII (Kühn ed., vol. XIX, p. 378). This faculty sometimes bears the name nature, as Galen states when discussing the different meanings of the word φὺσις, ibid., XCV (p. 371): φὺσις ϰαὶ ἡ διοιϰοῦσα τὸ ζῶον δύναμις λέγεται. Cf. Cicero, De natura Deorum, II, 9.
fn.949: That is to say, the celestial spheres and the stars, which do not perish, whereas in sublunary things only the species are preserved and individuals perish.
fn.950: The author means that there is no consensus on the question of whether this faculty that governs the universe comes directly from God or is communicated through the mediation of the intelligences of the spheres; this question will be treated elsewhere. See Part II<sup></sup>, chaps. X and XII.
fn.951: More literally: … have as their goal the need to which it is constrained for its food.
fn.952: The suffix in ופיה refers to the body (בדן). Only one of our manuscripts has the incorrect reading ופיהא, which was reproduced by the Hebrew translators; Ibn-Tibbon and Ibn-Falaquera have ובהם, and Al-Harizi ויש מהם.
fn.953: Literally: to its being (or to its nature) that was intended. The suffix in כונה (its being) seems to me to refer to the body, like that of ופיה (see the preceding note); the sense is that various incidental elements, resulting from the material quality of certain parts of the body, are joined to the formation of the body, in which everything is constituted for a specific purpose and according to a specific plan.
fn.954: That is to say, because these things are merely incidental.
fn.955: The words אלתפאצ̇ל בין אלאשכ̇אץ signify that individuals surpass one another, and that the things in question are found in much greater quantity in some than in others.
fn.956: On the word אכ̇ת̇רי, cf. above, p. 300, note 2.
fn.957: The word כד̇לך corresponds to the words וכמא אן, just as, which are found at the beginning of this long sentence, and which we have omitted in our translation in order to make the construction of the sentences less cumbersome.
fn.958: Literally: in which there is only a small variation, according to the measure of the extent of the species in its quality and quantity; that is to say, according to the limits that nature has fixed, regarding quality and quantity, for the species in question. On the word ערץ̇, see above, p. 236, note 2.
fn.959: Literally: but are attached to the nature of general generation and destruction. The author means that these species are produced by nature without intention and without a specific purpose, and that they are formed as a result of certain accidents resulting from the general physical laws governing the part of the universe subject to generation (γένεσις) and to destruction or corruption (φθορά).
fn.960: Literally: whose individuals are stable or permanent; that is to say, bodies that remain individually constituted within each individual.
fn.961: Ancient physicians count four principal humors in the human body, which are blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile. These humors do not have, like the limbs, an individual existence; for they are mixed, and it is sometimes one, sometimes the other, that predominates. The nature of the mixture constitutes the temperament, which is either sanguine, phlegmatic, bilious, or melancholic. See Galen, Definitiones medicae, LXV-LXX (ed. by Kühn, vol. XIX, p. 363 et seq.). Cf. Sprengel, Versuch einer pragmatischen Geschichte der Arzeneykunde, vol. II, p. 164.
fn.962: That is to say, the matter of the spheres or the ether, the spheres and the stars, which have an individual permanence in the universe.
fn.963: Since everything is composed of the four elements, the elements exist everywhere as element in general, but not as such an element in particular.
fn.964: Literally: And just as the faculties of man that produce his birth and his duration as long as he lasts.
fn.965: That is to say, in the sublunar world, where everything is subject to the perpetual change of birth and destruction, by opposition to the superior world, where nothing is born nor perishes.
fn.966: By the attractive faculty, each part of the animal body extracts from food and attracts to itself the parts that suit its nature; by the retentive or coercive faculty, the various parts of the body retain this attracted substance; by the digestive faculty, they prepare it to be converted into their own substance; finally, by the expulsive faculty, the body rejects the residues that do not suit its organization. Cf. Al-Kazwini, in the Chrestomathie arabe of Silv. de Sacy, vol. III, p. 487-488; Sprengel, loc. cit., p. 162.
fn.967: That is to say, provided that the matter is of the kind that the animal body can assimilate and that it is of a nature to be attracted by the attractive faculty and absorbed by the body.
fn.968: The word خسف designates an upheaval of the ground as a result of which mountains and entire cities are sometimes swallowed into the earth; according to Arab physicists, this upheaval, related to earthquakes, takes place when the vapors enclosed in the heart of the globe emerge violently, tearing the ground and carrying earthy matter with them, so that vast subterranean cavities are formed and the ground subsides. See Al-Kazwini, Adjayib al-makhloukat, published by Mr. Wüstenfeld (Göttingen, 1849, 4to), p. 149. It is by inadvertence that earlier, in ch. LIV (p. 220), the word خسوف was rendered by inundations.
fn.969: With these last words, the author alludes to the incursions of marine and subterranean waters, phenomena that sometimes accompany earthquakes, and which Aristotle discusses in the IInd book of the Meteorology (towards the end of chapter VIII): ἤδη δὲ καὶ ὕδατα ἀνερράγη γιγνομένων σεισμῶν, κ. τ. λ.
fn.971: Literally: As for man alone, if one were to suppose an individual, etc.
fn.972: Literally: so that he governs by it (i.e., by this motive faculty) what is outside of him (i.e., outside the principal organ). The author refers to the motive faculty communicated by the first mover to the superior sphere which sets all the other spheres in motion.

fn.974: That is to say, all the principal parts of the universe which govern the other parts or communicate certain faculties to them.

Ibn Falaquera's version is more accurate; it reads (in the manuscripts of the Moreh ha-Moreh): לנדיבות טבע ומעלת יצירה לא לתוחלת גמול.

fn.977: See above, ch. LXIX, p. 320, note 1; ch. LXX, p. 325; Part II<sup></sup>, ch. IV.

fn.980: Literally: Many doubts arise here, and there is ground for the critic to criticize and for the caviler to cavil.

fn.982: That is to say, let him accept, as if by tradition, what we have said regarding the constitution of the universe in general, and let him construct upon it his proofs to demonstrate the four questions in point.

fn.984: Literally: I begin to report what I promised to report and explain, that is, the propositions of the Motécallemîn and their demonstrations concerning the four questions mentioned at the end of the preceding chapter.

fn.986: That is to say, the existence of atoms; see above, p. 185, note 3.
fn.987: The word آن‏, in the language of the Mutakallimūn, denotes an indivisible particle of time, which is to time what the geometric point is to space. It is the moment or the ideal point intermediate between what comes before and what comes after, and which Aristotle calls τὸ νῦν; cf. above, p. 199, note 1.
fn.988: Literally: that the reason (or nature) of capacities is also that of their privations; that is to say, that what we consider as the privation of a certain quality or capacity (ἕξις) is likewise a real and positive quality.
fn.989: That is to say, as will be seen below, it is sufficient, for a thing to be possible, that one can form an idea of it, and it is not necessary for the real being to conform to this idea.
fn.990: Literally: there is no difference between etc.
fn.991: In other words: it matters little whether it concerns an infinite number of things existing simultaneously, or a series of things existing successively one after another.
fn.992: Literally: and that many of their objects of perception escape them.
fn.993: The hypothesis of atoms, to which that of the void is intimately linked, was borrowed by the Motécallemîn from the ancient Greek philosophers, as the author observed earlier (p. 342). However, in restoring the hypotheses of Democritus and Epicurus and adding that of the atoms of time, the Motécallemîn, far from fearing the consequences, sought to align this doctrine with the dogma of creation ex nihilo, by removing eternity from the atoms and assuming them to have been created by God. It was in roughly the same form that atomism reappeared later in the doctrine of Gassendi. — See also, on these propositions of the Motécallemîn, Aaron ben-Elijah, Tree of Life, chap. IV.
fn.994: According to this view, each atom in itself becomes quantitative as a result of composition. Cf. the objections of Saadia, Beliefs and Opinions, book I, chap. 4 (Berlin edition, fol. 10 b): והשלישית שאני מרחיק ואחשוב לשקר ..... הצטיירות מה שאינו לא ארוך ולא רחב ולא עמוק עד שיהיה ממנו האורך והרוחב והעומק ·
fn.995: That is to say: atoms join one another, but do not form a mixture; for, being indivisible, they are not susceptible to merging through fusion.

Al-Harizi’s version has האחיס, the brothers; it is clear that this translator pronounced אלאכ׳ואן (الاخوان), which is absurd. — The author means that the Motécallemîn avoid using the word فساد, corruption or destruction (φθορά), because, in all physical transformations, atoms remain indestructible; they therefore prefer to designate all transformations by the word كون, birth. All physical appearances are reduced by them to these four phenomena: union, separation, motion, and rest. Cf. Schmölders, Essai sur les écoles philosophiques chez les Arabes, p. 167 ff.
fn.997: That is to say, they are not the same from all eternity, such that their number cannot change. fn.998: That is to say, the privation of the atom, or the void, and how they generally understand privation or non-being. See propositions II and VII.
fn.999: See above, chap. LXXI, p. 349, note 1. fn.1000: The word מלא (מַלָּ), which is found in all the manuscripts, is a vulgar form for מלאן.
fn.1001: The manuscripts read ילתגֹון; see above, p. 351, note 4.
fn.1002: Literally: They knew necessarily. Ibn Tibbon’s translation is inaccurate; instead of וידענו, one should read ידעו.
fn.1003: That is to say, in the Physics; the Arabs designate Aristotle's Physics under the title السماع or السماع الطبيعي, corresponding to the Greek title: φυσικὴ ἀκρὸασις (physica auscultatio). — The author refers to the VIth book of the Physics (chap. 1 et seq.), where Aristotle explains that what is continuous cannot be composed of indivisible parts, and where, after having established the continuity and divisibility of magnitude or extension (μέγεθος or μῆκος), of time and of motion, he demonstrates that these three continuous things are linked together by a mutual connection, and that what is said of one of them is necessarily also said of the others. Maimonides has particularly in mind the following passage from chapter II: ἔτι δὲ καὶ ἐκ τῶν εἰωθότων λόγων φανερὸν ὡς εἴπερ ὁ χρόνος ἐστὶ συνεχής, ὅτι καὶ τὸ μέγεθος, εἴπερ ἐν τῷ ἡμίσει χρόνῳ ἥμισυ διέρχεται καὶ ἁπλῶς ἐν τῷ ἐλάττονι ἔλαττον · αἱ γὰρ αὐταὶ διαιρέσεις ἔσονται τοῦ χρόνου καὶ τοῦ μεγέθους. καὶ εἰ ὁποτερονοῦν ἄπειρον, καὶ θάτερον, καὶ ὡς θάτερον, καὶ θάτερον, κ. τ. λ.
fn.1004: That is to say: according to the hypotheses of the Mutakallimun, time would be something positive and real, composed of perceptible elements succeeding one another in a certain order (Cf. Schmölders, Essai, etc., p. 163 et seq.); but in reality, time has only two parts, one of which no longer exists and the other of which is not yet, for the present moment (τὸ νῦν) is only an ideal limit between the past and the future and cannot be considered as a part of time capable of serving to measure it. See Aristotle, Physics, book IV, chap. 10, and cf. above, p. 199, note 1.
fn.1005: Literally: Motion is the translation of a simple substance from among these particles (moving) from one simple substance to a (another) simple substance adjacent to it; that is to say: according to the Mutakallimun, when a body moves, each of the atoms of this body touches, step by step, the atoms of the path it must traverse; from which it follows that all motions are equal, and that, if they appear slower or faster than one another, it is due to a greater or lesser number of intervals of rest interrupting the motion.
fn.1006: That is to say: if it is objected to them that, in the rapid motion of the arrow, one cannot admit intervals of rest, as they are forced to do. For, if they claimed that this is indeed a continuous motion without any interval of rest, they would be obliged to admit that the motions of two arrows are always absolutely equal, which is equally inadmissible.
fn.1007: The author refers to what he stated above regarding the manner in which the Mutakallimun explain motion.
fn.1008: One necessarily arrives at this result as soon as one denies the continuity of extension, as the atomists do. By considering the square as a discrete quantity, composed of a number of atoms = a 2, the number of atoms contained in each of the sides, as well as in the diagonal, will be = a. Let, for example, the square be composed of sixteen atoms arranged in the following order: ם one will have in all directions, in horizontal and:::: vertical lines as well as diagonally, four atoms; and, since the atoms are all equal and equally close to one another, it necessarily follows that the diagonal is equal to each of the sides of the square, which is absurd. This is one of the principal arguments cited by the Arabic Peripatetics against the atomism of the Mutakallimun; Al-Ghazali, in his Maqasid al-Falasifa (at the beginning of the Metaphysics section), enumerates six, among which the one we are discussing appears in fourth place. Two of Al-Ghazali's arguments are cited by Mr. Schmölders (Essai etc., p. 224); they are the first and the sixth.
fn.1009: Literally: The matter is divided with ITS regard into two parts. I refer the suffix in פיהא and in בעצׄהא to the word אלהנדסה̈ (geometry), and not to the word בראהין (demonstrations), as Ibn Tibbon did, who puts the suffix in the plural (קצתם ,בהם); it is evident, from the words ובעצׄהא תכון בראהינה, that the suffix in בעצׄהא cannot at all refer to the demonstrations.

I and II), commensurable magnitudes (σύμμετρα) are called المشتركة and incommensurable ones (ἀσύμμετρα), المتباينة. — It is easily understood, from what has just been said regarding the diagonal of the square, that under the hypothesis of atoms there can be no question of demonstrating the theories of commensurable and incommensurable magnitudes, of rational and irrational lines, etc., and almost all geometrical demonstrations become impossible.

fn.1014: These are the three sons of Musa Ibn-Shakir, named Muhammad, Ahmad, and Al-Hasan, who flourished in the middle of the 9th century. They promoted the introduction of Greek sciences among the Arabs by every means and became famous themselves for writings on various mathematical sciences. The book known under the title حيل or Devices contained, it seems, ingenious inventions relating to various branches of mechanical science (عام الرحيل), and notably to hydraulics and pneumatic machines, which were based on the hypothesis of the horror of a vacuum. Cf. Hammer, Encyclopædische Übersicht der Wissenschaften des Orients, pp. 340 and 508. On the Beni-Shakir, see the notice in the Tarîkh al-Hukamâ, in Casiri's Biblioth. arab. hisp., vol. fn.1031: According to this latter opinion, which is that of the Mu'tazilites, it would not be enough for the destruction of the world for God to refrain from creating accidents in the atoms, but it would be necessary for God to create specifically the accident of destruction, without however this accident being in a subject or a substance; for if it were in a subject, it would be the combination of being and non-being, which is impossible. — Ibn Rushd has highlighted everything that is absurd in this hypothesis, which, he says, does not deserve serious refutation. First, destruction and non-being are synonyms, and if God does not create non-being, he does not create destruction either. Furthermore, an accident without a substratum is in itself an absurd thing; and besides, how can one imagine that non-being produces non-being? See Destruction of the Destruction, IInd question, where one finds other details relating to this VIth proposition of the Mutakallimun.
fn.1032: Literally: would set itself up as an adversary, or would rise up against.
fn.1033: Literally: which color we believe has penetrated the fabric, while, they say, it is not so at all.
fn.1034: Ibn Tibbon's version adds these words here: לא זו בלבד אמרו אבל אמרו גם כן, and they did not only say that, but they said further. fn.1035: Literally: who set in motion CUSTOM; that is to say, God willed that this should occur habitually, without making it a law of nature. The Mutakallimun thus claimed to destroy every kind of causality, in order to attribute everything that happens in the world directly to the sole will of God. This opinion found a fervent champion in Al-Ghazali (see my article Gazâli in the Dict. des sc. philos., vol. II, p. 511). Ibn Rushd showed that this hypothesis of custom is something elusive and meaningless. Custom, being a capacity acquired by repeating an action several times, cannot be attributed to God, an immutable being in whom no change can occur. Nor can it reside in beings in general; for custom, in its true sense, can only be attributed to an animate being, and if it is attributed to an inanimate being, it means the same thing as nature or natural law. Finally, it cannot be made into something subjective residing in our judgment, which would have the habit of judging things in a certain way; for this judgment itself is the action of the intellect, which is also subject to a natural law. See Destr. of the Destruction, XVIIth question, and cf. Ibn Falaquéra, Moré ha-Moré, p. 57.
fn.1036: The word נילג׳ (نيلج) is generally used in the East to designate indigo, which gives the color blue; if, therefore, the author speaks here of the color black, it is perhaps in the sense of the Mutakallimun, according to whom blue is a kind of black. They generally count only five colors: white, black, red, yellow, and green; white and black are the fundamental colors, the others being only a more or less intense portion of black on a white background. See Schmölders, Essais etc., p. 167.

fn.1055: That is to say, everything in nature is composed of simple substances, or atoms, and their accidents, and not of matter (ὕλη) and form, as the philosophers say; and even what the latter call physical forms, that is, the forms that constitute genera and species and make up the essence of things, are likewise nothing but simple accidents created in the atoms.
fn.1056: Literally: so that the difference between an individual of such a species and an individual of another species is like the difference between one individual and another of the same species; that is to say, no generic or specific difference exists, and every difference between any two individuals is purely accidental, and not essential; for physical forms, as we have seen, are nothing but simple accidents.
fn.1057: The words עלי מא יתוהם, according to what one imagines, refer to the throne (العرش, cf. above, p. 95, note 1), in which the common people see something real, but which, according to our author, is only an image of the divine majesty, or sometimes designates the superior sphere. See above, chs. IX and LXX.
fn.1058: As, for example, figure and color, which are accidents borne by quantity, and time, which is an accident borne by that of motion.
fn.1059: More literally: if they flee this (i.e., if they refuse to admit that accidents bear one another), it is because it would follow that this second accident could only exist in the substance after the first accident has preceded it, which they do not wish to admit for certain accidents, etc. The meaning of this passage is as follows: the Mutakallimun do not want to admit, as the philosophers do, that there are certain accidents which are linked to the substance only through the medium of other accidents, such as figure and color through the medium of quantity; they maintain, on the contrary, that all accidents in general are borne immediately by the atoms and serve to determine the substance, that is, to form its essence and to make it what it is; for it was seen in the preceding proposition that it is the accidents that determine the genera and species and that physical forms are likewise accidents (Cf. above, p. 398, note 1). They therefore strive to present, as existing in the substance itself or in the atoms, those accidents which are evidently borne by other accidents.
fn.1060: All the manuscripts bear אלתקדיר (with daleth); Ibn Tibbon, who uses הימוד, appears to have read אלתקריר (with resh).
fn.1061.sub_0: The verb جوّز signifies to allow to pass, and, figuratively, to judge admissible or permitted, and the word تجهيز, which is its verbal noun, is used by the Mutakallimun as a technical term to designate the famous proposition stating that everything the imagination can picture is also admissible (جائز) to the reason, that everything in the universe could be other than it is, and that nothing is impossible, provided that an idea of it can be formed. Cf. Maimonides, Eight Chapters, or Introduction to the treatise Aboth, ch. Ist (Porta Mosis of Pococke, p. 188).—One must truly be surprised to see an author of our day assert with confidence that not only are there very essential errors in the alleged enumeration that Maimonides provides here of the principles of the Mutakallimun, but that even what he calls their primary foundation—namely, that there is no certain knowledge of things, since the contrary can always exist and be thought in our understanding—is entirely erroneous and diametrically opposed to dogmatic doctrine (Schmölders, Essays, p. 135). The same author insinuates that Maimonides only knew the doctrines of the Mutakallimun through the false reports of their adversaries; but it follows from Maimonides' own declaration that he perfectly knew the doctrines in question, and here, as everywhere else, his assertions are based on a serious and thorough study of the most authentic sources; see the beginning of chapter LXXIV. It is sufficient, moreover, to read the Destruction of the Destruction of Ibn Rushd, which contains numerous details on the Mutakallimun, and where one finds all the propositions enumerated by Maimonides. These two illustrious men must have been at least as well informed as the more recent authors that Mr. Schmölders may have consulted. As for this Xth proposition, which Maimonides calls the basis of the science of Kalam, it is so essential to the system of the Mutakallimun that it is impossible to separate it from it. Ibn Rushd also returns to it on several occasions.
fn.1061.sub_1: We content ourselves with citing here a single passage, where Ibn Rushd (speaking of the principle of causality denied by the Mutakallimun, and notably by the Ash'arites, who see in all phenomena and in all actions that occur in the world the immediate intervention of the Creator) expresses himself thus: והניחו עם זה כל הנמצאות פעולות עוברות ולא יראו שיש בם סדר ולא ערך ולא חכמה גזר אותם טבע הנמצאות אבל האמינו שכל נמצא אפשר שיהיה בחלוף מה שהוא "They have, with this, posited as a principle that all existing things are admissible facts (and not necessary), and they do not admit that there is in them either order, or proportion, or wisdom, resulting from the nature of things. They believe, on the contrary, that everything that exists could be other than it is." See Destr. of the Destruction, IIIrd question (Hebrew trans., MS of the Oratory collection, no. 93, fol. 243 a). Cf. Moses of Narbonne, Commentary on the Moreh Nevukhim, Ist part, at the end of ch. LIII; Ibn Falaquera, Moreh ha-Moreh, I, chs. LXXIII and LXXIV (pp. 58 and 63); Ritter, Geschichte der Philosophie, vol. VII, p. 737.

Ibn-Sīnā believed he was justified in maintaining that, as souls have neither place nor position, nothing prevents their number from being infinite. Ibn-Roschd, arguing against those who claimed to demonstrate the dogma of Creation by means of that of the permanence of souls, admitted by the philosophers, first refuses to admit with Ibn-Sīnā the existence of these individual substances, pure forms without matter; for he adopts on the permanence of the soul the opinion of Ibn-Bādja, which will be discussed shortly.
