We know of no one who has made a distinction in this regard between that which has position and that which has none, except for Ibn-Sīnā alone.... But these are vain childishness; for the philosophers reject the existence of the actual infinite, both for the corporeal and for the incorporeal, because it would follow from this that there is an infinite larger than another infinite. Perhaps Ibn-Sīnā only intended to accommodate the multitude in what they were accustomed to hearing regarding the soul, etc."
fn.1181: The author addresses himself here, as in many other passages, to his disciple, to whom he dedicated this work.
fn.1182: That is to say, abstract beings entirely separated from corporeality, in Greek τὰ ϰεχωρισμένα (Arist., treatise On the Soul, book III, chap. 7). Cf. above, pp. 373 and 374.
fn.1183: See Part II of this work, introduction, XVIth proposition, and cf. Abridgment of the Talmud, treatise Yessōdē ha-Tōrā, chap. II, § 5. See above, at the end of chap. LXXII (p. 373), and cf. p. 328, note 4.
fn.1184: That is to say: the totality of all souls forms only one unity. This doctrine of the unity of souls was professed by Abu-Becr ibn-al-Çâyeg, or Ibn Bajja, in his Letter of Farewell (رسالة الوداع) and in other writings. See the commentary of Moses of Narbonne on our passage, and Ibn Falaquera, Moré ha-Moré, p. 65. — Averroes proclaims the same doctrine: 'Zeid and 'Amr,' he says (loc. cit.), 'are numerically two, but they are one by their form, which is the soul; now, if the souls of Zeid and 'Amr were numerically distinct, as their persons are, their souls would be two in number, but a unity by form, so that the soul would have a soul. Since, therefore, the soul of Zeid and 'Amr is necessarily one by form, and since that which is one by form receives numerical multiplicity or division only through matter, it follows that if souls do not die with the bodies, they necessarily form, after having separated from the bodies, a numerical unity.' Developed by Averroes in several of his writings, this doctrine caused a great sensation among the Christian theologians of the 13th century; Albert the Great refuted it in a specific work entitled: Libellus contra eos qui dicunt quod post separationem ex omnibus animabus non remanet nisi inlellectus unus et anima una (see Alberti Opera, vol. V, p. 218 et seq., Jammy edition).

Ibn Tibbon's version reproduces the same error; it reads בל איש ····· אין תכלית להם. Al-Harizi thought he could do better by putting אין לו תכלית, so that it would have to be translated: every individual, etc. ... is infinite, which is obviously a contradiction.
fn.1187: That is to say: they show in this manner that he who professes the eternity of the world necessarily arrives at the result that there are infinities larger than one another, which is absurd.
fn.1188: That is to say: they apply the same reasoning to the celestial sphere, which, starting from two different epochs and previously, will have accomplished revolutions obviously more numerous than one another, and yet both of which are infinite. Cf. Khozari, book V, §18, article 1st.
fn.1189: Slower revolutions are obviously fewer in number than those that are faster, and yet both, in the hypothesis of the eternity of the world, would be infinite. Cf. Khozari, loc. cit..
fn.1190: That is to say: they apply the same reasoning further to accidents of every kind, occurring successively one after the other, and which, in the hypothesis of the eternity of the world, would form an infinite series.
fn.1191: The author's observation applies generally to the various cases just enumerated; he means that, both in the series of creatures of the same species and in the series of the revolutions of the spheres and in that of accidents, and, in general, in the infinite by succession or by accident, one not only counts as actually existing all individualities and all particular manifestations that have ceased to exist, but one also envisions them as delimited things, such that they can be counted as an infinite multitude of units in this infinite series that one wishes to establish. By the words and as if they were delimited things, the author specifically indicates the revolutions of the celestial spheres, which the Mutakallimun also consider as a numerical multitude composed of well-defined units, whereas in reality circular motion has neither beginning nor end, and consequently, the movements of the spheres cannot be numbered. Cf. above, p. 425, note 1. As for the words ذات بداة, which literally mean having a beginning, and which we have rendered as delimited things, here is how the author himself explains them in his letter to Samuel ibn Tibbon: דׄאת בדאה̈ מענאהא אנהם יטׄנון אמורא להא אבתדא מחדוד לאן כל מא הו מוגׄוד בגׄמלתה מחדוד אלטרפין הו אלדׄי יקאל פיה אנה דׄאת בדאה̈ והו אלדׄי ימכן א׳ן יזאד עליה או ינקץ מנה אמא מא יחדתׄ אאולא אולא וליס פיה מבדא מחדוד מתׄל אלմרכאת אלדוריה̈ פלא יתצור פיה זיאדה̈ ולא נקףצאן «The words ذات بداة mean that they believe they see there things having a determinate beginning; for anything that exists as a whole limited at both extremities is called ذات بداة, and it is this which can be increased or decreased. But, in that which arises little by little and which has no determinate beginning, such as, for example, circular motions, one cannot imagine either increase or decrease.» It was on the advice of the author himself that Ibn Tibbon rendered the words in question as דברים שיש להם התחלה מסוימת.

fn.1193: Literally: struck the brain or on the head. The true reading is دمغ, i.e.: he struck it upon its brain, an expression similar to that of the Doctors: מחו לה אמוחא. This is how the Arabs use the verb دمغ, with the direct object, when speaking of someone who has struck a person on the head so as to cause them to perish. I intended to say by this that Abu Nasr demonstrated the flaw of this proposition which the Mutakallimūn adopted as an important principle.' — Of eight manuscripts that we consulted, only two contain דמג; the other six have the reading אדמג, which the author himself declares to be erroneous. As for the expression מחו לה אמוחא, perfectly analogous to the Arabic verb دمغ, the Talmudists likewise employ it when speaking of a proposition whose invalidity has been shown. See Babylonian Talmud, tractate Megillah, fol. 19 b; cf. tractate Soferim, chap. 2, § 11.
fn.1194: Literally: and he revealed the locations of the error in all its particulars, as you will find clear and evident, upon an examination devoid of partiality, etc. The verb تعصب means to defend something ardently, to grow heated for or against an opinion, to show partiality. The principal argument is indicated by our author himself in these words: and as if they were delimited things. See the note on these words and cf. Ephodi’s commentary on the words ובבר הבה.
fn.1196: One sees that the proofs alleged by the Mutakallimūn to establish the existence of God are of the kind that have been called physical proofs. It might appear that the methods enumerated in this chapter, and notably the Ist and IInd, are based on the principle of causality, and yet it has been seen that the Mutakallimūn reject this principle in an absolute manner. But the contradiction is only apparent. For the Mutakallimūn, indeed, the proof of the existence of the Creator results immediately from each newly produced or created thing, which, according to them, requires the direct action of the divinity to pass from non-being to being; and if, to reach the Creator, they have us ascend through a series of creations that seem to produce one another, it is only to show that the series of transformations would be infinite if one did not stop at a first creation, and that even those who admit a series of causes and effects in nature are forced to stop at a first created thing which has no other cause than the will of the Creator. For them, nothing is caused, but everything in nature is made or created; thus they carefully avoid using the word cause in their arguments and refuse to adopt the designation first cause used by the philosophers to designate God. See above, at the beginning of Chapter LXIX. — Several of the methods enumerated in this chapter were adopted in substance by Jewish theologians of the Middle Ages; cf. Saadia, Beliefs and Opinions, Book I, chap. 1; Bahya, Duties of the Hearts, Book I, chap. 5. The Karaites especially imitated, on this point as on many others, the arguments of the Arabic kalam. See Judah ha-Levi, Kuzari, Book V, § 18.
fn.1197: It will be seen from what follows that these two methods (to which three others are added) are indirect; for they demonstrate the unity of God by showing that the supposition of the contrary, or of dualism, leads to the impossible or the absurd. It is difficult to render exactly the two Arabic terms used by the Mutakallimūn to designate these two methods; both words are verbal nouns of the VIth form indicating reciprocity. The verb تمانע means to hinder one another, to be an obstacle to one another; Ibn Tibbon doubtless attached the same meaning to the word המנעות which he uses in his version, while Al-Harizi commits a misinterpretation by translating: דרך הנמנע, the method דה of the impossible. Bahya, who provides a demonstration of the unity of God combining the 1st and 5th methods of the Mutakallimūn, likewise employs the word تهازع in the sense we have just indicated; see Duties of the Hearts, Book I, ch. 7 (7th demonstration), where one reads, in the original Arabic: ולו גׄאז אן יכון אכתׄר מן ואחד לאמכן אן יכון בינהם תמאנע ואכׄתלאף פי כׄלקה̈ אלמכׄלוקין (the Hebrew version reads: ואלו היה אפשר להיות יותר מאחד היה אפשר שתהיה ביניהם מחלוקת בבריאת הברואים). — The verb تغاير means to differ reciprocally, and expresses the non-identity of two things. In the editions of Ibn Tibbon’s version, one reads: דרך ההמנעות ודרך ההשתנות והחלוק; the word והחלוק is found neither in the manuscripts nor in the editio princeps. Some manuscripts read: ודרך ההשתנות ודרך החלוף והחלוק; it is evident that Ibn Tibbon’s version rendered the Arabic word אלתגאיר in two different ways and that copyists brought the two translations together, one of which was probably written in the margin.

fn.1255: See chap. LXXIV, 6th method. — All the manuscripts carry לאמבאן וגׄודה ועדמה, except for one of the two Leiden manuscripts, which has only לאמבאן וגׄודה; according to this latter reading, one should translate: "its existence being (only) possible," i.e., not being a necessary thing. This reading was reproduced by the two Hebrew translators; Ibn Tibbon has לאפשרות מציאותו, and Al-Harizi, בעבור שמציאותו אפשרית.
fn.1256: The construction of this sentence is irregular; here is a near word-for-word translation: For all the forms and measures of a possible existence (are so) in the sense that something had (initially) not existed and that it subsequently existed; it is of this that one will say, etc.
fn.1257: The words וְלֹא לְמַרְגֵּחַ are found in only one of the Oxford manuscripts (Uri, no. 359) and are also not rendered in Ibn Tibbon's version; but these words seem necessary to me to complete the sense, and the negation לא, which in all the manuscripts (except in one of the Leiden MSS) precedes the word למכ״צץ, sufficiently indicates that something is missing here. Al-Harizi translates: לא יצטרך למגביל אשר יבריע המציאות על האפימה.
fn.1258: That is to say: God, according to the proponents of corporeality, is, just as He is, the necessary being; everything in Him, the attribute as well as the essence, is of absolute necessity, and nothing in Him presupposes a prior being that has determined Him in such or such a manner.
fn.1259: Literally: consider (פתאמל) ... the condition of these thinkers (i.e., of the Mutakallimun) and what happened to them and on their part.
fn.1260: In the editions of Ibn Tibbon's version, שהוא was mistakenly used; the MSS have שהם.
fn.1261: That is to say: one who, to avoid an evil, falls into an even greater evil.
fn.1262: Literally: they have destroyed the nature of being.
fn.1263: Literally: After having completed (expounding) the ultimate goal of their words; that is to say, after having made known in substance the opinions and demonstrations of the Mutakallimun.
fn.1265: Literally: our own method in that to which true speculation has led us to complete, etc.
fn.1266: That is to say: After having first reasoned under the hypothesis of the eternity of the world, I shall return to this very hypothesis and engage in a discussion with the philosophers on this subject.
fn.1267: All Arabic mss. read עלי ברהאן כל ואחדהּ מנהא. Ibn Tibbon deviates slightly from the original, translating: כבר עשה ··· מופת על כל אחת מהן. Al-Harizi's version reads: כבר בדק ··· על מופת כל אחת מהן.
fn.1268: That is to say, which we provisionally concede to them as an hypothesis; see below the <small>XXVI</small><sup>th</sup> proposition, and cf. vol. 1, p. 350, note 1.
fn.1269.sub_0: On infinity in general, see Aristotle, Physics, book III, ch. 4-8; Metaph., book II, ch. 2; book XI, ch. 10. Aristotle shows in these various passages that, in nature, the infinitely great in actuality, that is to say infinite extension, is inadmissible, and he admits as infinite only the infinitely small or the infinite divisibility of space, which he designates (as well as the infinity of abstract number) as potential infinity. Consequently, the universe itself, which is the most extended body, is limited in space (see the treatise On the Heavens, book I, ch. 7, where Aristotle says in conclusion: ὅτι μὲν τοίνυν οὐκ ἐστὶ τὸ σῶμα τὸ τοῦ παντὸς ἄπειρον ἐκ τούτων φανερόν). The most general demonstration of this first proposition is given in the very definition of body; Aristotle observes that from a logical point of view (λογικῶς), the existence of an infinite body is inadmissible: for, if the idea one has of a body is to be limited by surfaces, there can be no unlimited body, whether intelligible or sensible (εἰ γάρ ἐστι σώματος λόγος τὸ ἐπιπέδῳ ὡρισμένον, οὐκ ἂν εἴη σῶμα ἄπειρον, οὔτε νοητὸν οὔτε αἰσθητόν. Physics, III, 5, Metaph., XI, 10). From a physical point of view, Aristotle shows that an infinite body could be neither composite nor simple: 1. If it were composite, the parts of the composition would be either infinite or finite; now it is evident that they could not be infinite, for the infinity of each necessarily excludes that of the others; but neither could they be finite, for they would be consumed by the infinite and would disappear completely before it. 2. Neither could an infinite body be simple; for none of the elements, each of which has its determined region, is infinite, and there exists no sensible body outside the elements that unites them all, as several physicists have believed.— Another physical proof (which is linked in a way to the logical proof) is this: "Every sensible body is in space. The species and differences of space are: up and down, front and back, right and left. These distinctions do not exist solely in relation to us and by position, but are grounded in the whole itself."
fn.1269.sub_1: However, they could not exist in the infinite." (See Physics, loc. cit. at the end of ch. 5). Ibn Sina and other authors, Arabic and Jewish, multiplied the demonstrations of the propositions enumerated by Maimonides. Abu Bakr Muhammad al-Tabrizi, who wrote a commentary on the twenty-five propositions, went into great detail to demonstrate their truth. This 1st proposition was demonstrated by the Arabs in several different ways. We shall cite here a demonstration borrowed from Ibn Sina: Let the magnitude supposed to be infinite be a line AB أ ج ب; we may suppose that this line extends to infinity on both sides or only on one side B. In the latter case, let us imagine that from the finite side a part AC is cut; we will then have two lines, AB and CB, each of which will be infinite on side B and finite on the other side. Now, if we apply point C to point A, one of two things will happen: either line CB will extend to infinity like line AB, and then we will have AB—AC=AB, which is impossible, for the part cannot be equal to the whole; or line CB will extend less than line AB, and then it will be finite on side B, which is contrary to the hypothesis. If line AB is supposed to be infinite on both sides, it can be cut at any point so as to make two lines, each of which will be infinite on one side and finite on the other, and the demonstration will be the same as the one just given. Cf. Shahrastani, p. 403 (German trans., vol. II, pp. 295 and 296). — We cannot reproduce the proofs alleged for each of the propositions enumerated here by Maimonides, and we must limit ourselves to indicating the places from which our author drew these various propositions. As will be seen, they are not all borrowed from Aristotle, and several are taken from the works of Ibn Sina, which, as we have already stated elsewhere, are the principal source from which Maimonides drew his knowledge of Peripatetic doctrines. On this first proposition and the following two, see also the 1st part of this work, ch. LXXIII, 11th proposition, and the notes we have appended there (vol. I, pp. 413 and 414).
fn.1270: This second proposition states of discrete magnitude what, in the first proposition, was stated of continuous magnitude. Actual numerical infinity is as inadmissible as infinite extension: for the units that compose discrete quantity can together form a continuous quantity, and it is clear that, since the latter cannot be infinite, the former cannot be either. Moreover, as the commentator Shem-Tob observes, the demonstration we gave for the first proposition, according to Ibn Sina, can be directly applied to this proposition. Indeed, by decreasing the supposedly infinite discrete quantity by a certain number of units, the remainder will be either infinite or finite; now, if it were infinite, the part would be equal to the whole, which is impossible; if it were finite, the whole would likewise be finite, which is contrary to the hypothesis.
fn.1271: It has already been seen that, according to our author, the inadmissibility of the infinite by succession is not demonstrated. See vol. I, pp. 414 and 415, and cf. below at the 26th proposition.
fn.1272: This proposition was developed by Aristotle in the Metaphysics, Book II, Ch. 2, where it is shown in general that, in the four species of causes, one necessarily arrives at a final term, and that these causes cannot continue to infinity: Α’λλὰ μὲν ὅτί γ’ ἐστὶν ἀρχή τις καὶ οὐκ ἄπειρα τὰ αἴτια τῶν ὄντων, οὔτ’ εἰς εὐθυωρίαν οὔτε κατ’ εἶδος, δῆλον, κ. τ. λ. Cf. Volume I of this work, p. 313, note 1.
fn.1273: See Aristotle, Metaphysics, Book XII, Ch. 2: Εἰ δὴ αἱ μεταβολαὶ τέτταρες, ἢ κατὰ τὸ τί ἢ κατὰ τὸ ποιὸν ἢ ποσὸν ἢ ποῦ, καὶ γένεσις μὲν ἡ ἁπλῆ καὶ φθορὰ ἡ κατὰ τόδε, αὔξησις δὲ καὶ φθίσις ἡ κατὰ τὸ ποσόν, ἀλλοίωσις δὲ ἡ κατὰ τὸ πάθος, φορά δε ἡ κατὰ τόπον, εἰς ἐναντιώσεις ἂν εἶεν τὰς καθ’ ἕκα-στον αἱ μεταβολαὶ, κ. τ. λ. Cf. Physics, Book III, Ch. 1: Μεταβάλλει γὰρ τὸ μεταβάλλον ἀεὶ ἢ κατ’ οὐσίαν, ἢ κατὰ ποσόν, ἢ κατὰ ποιόν, ἢ κατὰ τόπον. One sees that by change (μεταβολή), one must understand the mutual passage of opposites into one another, and it must not be confused with the idea of motion, which, as Aristotle says elsewhere, applies only to the categories of quantity, quality, and place, and not to that of substance. See Physics, Book V, at the end of Ch. 1, and at the beginning of Ch. 2. Cf. the treatise On the Soul, Book I, Ch. 3, § 3, where Aristotle speaks of four species of motion, which fundamentally only form three, belonging to three categories, namely: φορά, to the category of place, ἀλλοίωσις, to that of quality, φθίσις and αὔξησις to that of quantity. However, in the six species of motion (κινήσεως) enumerated at the beginning of Ch. 14 of the Categories, Aristotle also includes generation and corruption (γένεσις καὶ φθορά), which apply to the category of substance. The four others are: increase (αὔξησις), decrease (μείωσις = φθίσις), alteration (ἀλλοίωσις) and change of place (κατὰ τόπον μεταβολή); the first two species relate to the category of quantity, the third to that of quality, and the fourth to that of place. One sees that this passage of the Categories corresponds exactly to that of the Metaphysics, and that Aristotle used the word κίνησις there in the broader sense of μεταβολή. Cf. below, note 2.
fn.1274: It was seen in the preceding note that in general the changes in question here, with the exception of the first, are also designated as motions; but this is only because fundamentally all these various changes are in some sense local motion: πᾶσαι γὰρ αἱ λεχθεῖσαι κινήσεις ἐν τόπῳ (Treatise on the Soul, loc. cit.); thus, for example, in growth and decrease, local motion can be attributed to the different parts of the body. Cf. below the 14th proposition. — All editions of Ibn Tibbon's version add here the words: ועל שאר השנויים בכלל, and to other changes (it applies) in general; the manuscripts of the version do not have this addition. Cf. at the beginning of Ch. I.
fn.1275: The author reproduces here the definition that Aristotle gives of motion. And here, the word motion embraces all species of changes mentioned in the preceding proposition; as much the change of birth and corruption, which occurs instantaneously and so to speak without motion, as other changes, which occur gradually and through actual motion. In this sense, therefore, motion is the change that can be designated, in the most general way, as the passage from potentiality to actuality. See Aristotle, Physics, Book III, Ch. 1: ὥστε κινιήσεως καὶ μεταβολῆς ἐστὶν εἴδη τοσαῦτα ὅσα τοῦ ὄντος. διῃρημένου δὲ καθ’ ἕκαστον γένος τοῦ μὲν ἐντελεχείᾳ τοῦ δὲ δυνάμει, ἡ τοῦ δυνάμει ὄντος ἐντελέχεια, ᾗ τοιοῦτον, κίνησίς ἐστιν, κ. τ. λ. Cf. Metaphysics, Book XI, Ch. 9.
fn.1276: The author speaks here of motion *par excellence*, that is to say, of local motion.
fn.1277: The various distinctions the author makes here in local motion are borrowed from Aristotle and are intended to show that all particular motions, whatever they may be, have their source in a first eternal motion on which they depend. What is moved, says Aristotle, is so either in itself (καθ’ αὑτό) or accidentally (κατὰ συμβεβηκός). In that which is moved accidentally, he distinguishes things that could also be moved in themselves, such as the parts of an animal body and the nail in a ship, and other things that are always moved accidentally, such as whiteness (in the body) and knowledge (in the soul): for these only change place along with the thing in which they are found. Finally, in that which is moved in itself he further distinguishes what is moved by itself and what is moved by another thing, what is moved naturally and what is moved by violence and against nature (βίᾳ καὶ παρὰ φύσιν). See Aristotle, Physics, Book IV, Ch. 4 and Book VIII, Ch. 4; cf. the treatise On the Soul, Book II, Ch. 3 (§§ 2 and 3), and the treatise On the Heavens, Book III, Ch. 2.
fn.1278: See Aristotle, Physics, Book VI, at the beginning of Ch. 4: Τὸ δὲ μεταβάλλον ἅπαν ἀνάγκη διαιρετὸν εἶναι. The demonstration given by Aristotle can be summarized as follows: Everything that undergoes a change passes from one state of things to another; it cannot be for a single instant in either of the two states, for then it would not change; but it also cannot be in only one of the two states, for then either it would not yet be changing, or it would already be changed. It is therefore necessary that it be partly in one and partly in the other, and consequently it is divisible.
fn.1279: The fifth proposition establishes that every motion is a change; consequently, everything that is moved undergoes change and is necessarily divisible. Aristotle, who had already established the divisibility of extension, time, and motion (cf. Volume I of this work, p. 380, note 2), shows, in the chapter cited in the preceding note, that divisibility must also apply to that which is moved: Ἐπεὶ δὲ πᾶν τὸ ϰινούμενον ἔν τινι ϰινεῖται ϰαὶ χρόνον τινά, ϰαὶ παντός ἐστι ϰὶνησις, ἀνάγϰη τὰς αὐτὰς εἰναὶ διαιρέσεις τοῦ τε χρόνου ϰαὶ τῆς ϰινήσεως, ϰαὶ τοῦ ϰινεῖσθαι, ϰαὶ τοῦ ϰινομένου, ϰαὶ ἔν ᾧ ἡ ϰίνησις, ϰ. τ. λ. Cf., Book VIII, chap. 5 (Bekker ed., p. 257 a, line 33): Ἀναγϰαῖον δὴ τὸ ϰινούμενον ἄπαν εἶναι διαιρετὸν εἰς ἀεὶ διαιρετά, ϰ. τ. λ.
fn.1280: As, for example, the geometric point and the intellect, which have no essential motion, but only accidental motion. This thesis, which the author adds here as a corollary, is a necessary consequence of what precedes. However, Aristotle entered into some detail to demonstrate that the indivisible is immobile in itself, and has only an accidental motion; he notes in particular that if one admitted the motion of the point, one would thereby establish that the line is composed of points and time of small instants or present moments (ὲϰ τῶν νῦν), which is false. See Physics, Book VI, chap. 10, at the beginning: Λέγομεν ὅτι τὸ ἀμερὲς οὐϰ ἐνδέ-χεται ϰινεῖσθαι πλὴν ϰατὰ συμϐεϐηϰός, ϰ. τ. λ. And further on: ῶστ’ οὐϰ ἐνδε-χεται τὸ ἀμερὲς ϰινεῖσθάι οὐδ’ ὅλως μεταϐάλλειν, ϰ. τ. λ.
fn.1281.sub_0: This proposition, stated in too concise a manner, has been found obscure, and when taken in an absolute sense, has met with objections (see the commentary of Moses of Narbonne). This is how it should be understood: Anything that does not have within itself the principle of its motion, but to which an accidental motion is imparted by an external cause that can cease to exist, will necessarily be at rest when that cause ceases, as, for example, a passenger on a ship, who is moved only because he is accidentally in a moving thing that can stop moving (cf. Aristotle, On the Soul, Book I, chap. 3, § 2). What proves that Maimonides understands this proposition in this way is that further on, at the beginning of chap. I, in demonstrating that the first mover cannot be considered the soul of the celestial sphere, he applies this VIIIth proposition to the human soul, which is moved accidentally with the body by an external cause, either by seeking what is suitable for it or by fleeing what is contrary to it. Therefore, the Arab commentator Al-Tabrizi is wrong to object to this proposition of Maimonides that there are certain motions which, although accidental, are nonetheless perpetual, such as, for example, the diurnal motion from east to west imparted by the ninth sphere to the eight lower spheres, which is contrary to their own essential motion from west to east; or as the circular motion of the sphere of fire and the other elements, whose essential motion is in a straight line (cf. Vol. I of this work, pp. 357-359). It is evident that these accidental motions, having as their cause an essential and perpetual motion, must themselves be perpetual. The proposition in question here appears to relate to a passage from the treatise On the Heavens (Book I, end of chap. 2), where Aristotle establishes that above the four elements which, by their nature, have a straight-line motion, there is a simple substance of another nature that has circular motion.
fn.1281.sub_1: Now, he observes, this motion must be inherent to the nature of this substance; for it would be astonishing and entirely unreasonable if this motion, which alone is continuous and eternal, could be contrary to nature, since generally what is contrary to nature is quickly destroyed: Eἰ δὲ παρὰ φύσιν φέρεται τά φερόμενα ϰύϰλῳ τὴν περὶξ φοράν, θαυμαστὸν ϰαὶ παντελῶς ἀλογον τὸ μόνέν εἶναι συνεχῆ τάυτην τὴν ϰὶνησιν ϰαι ἀίδιον, οὖσαν παρὰ, φύσιν · φαίνεται γὰρ ἔν γε τοῖς ἀλλοις τάχιστα φθειρόμενα τὰ παρὰ φύσιν. The Arabic version, which rendered the words contrary to nature (παρὰ φύσιν) as accidental, better explains the terms of Maimonides' proposition. Here is how the passage we have just cited was paraphrased in Ibn Rushd's Middle Commentary on De Caelo et Mundo, Book I, Summa IV, Demonstration 5 (Hebrew version): והוא שזאת התנועה הסבובית שהיא סביב האמצע לא המלט משתהיה לזה הגשם טבעית או מקרית ושקר הוא שתהיה מקרית בי התנועה המקרית אי אפשר שתמצא תמידית אין תכלית לה ושהצעת זה יוצאה מכל הקש כי אԃנחנו רואים הדברים המקריים כלים אובדים.
fn.1282: This proposition was developed at length by Aristotle, who, in order to establish the existence of an unmoved first mover, shows that that which moves, if it is not the first mover itself, can only be an intermediary cause of motion, which is necessarily itself moved by another cause. It follows naturally that a physical body can communicate motion to another body only by being moved itself. See Phys., Book VIII, chap. 5; cf. Metaph., Book XII, chap. 6.
fn.1284: That is to say, the form which constitutes the genus or the species, and which makes a thing what it is. Cf. Vol. I, p. 398, and Ibid., note 1.
fn.1285: That is to say: what is called a force in a body can be either an accident, such as, for example, heat and cold in bodies which, by their nature, are neither hot nor cold; or a physical form, such as, e.g., the heat or the fiery nature of fire, or the coldness of ice. The word قوة (power), which the Arab philosophers use in the various senses that Aristotle attributes to the word δύναμɩς, must be taken here not in the sense of possibility or capacity for being as opposed to act (ἐνέργεɩα), but in its primitive and absolute sense which Aristotle defines as "the principle from which emanates the motion or the change produced in another thing insofar as it is another thing" (Metaph., Book V, chap. 12, beginning and end), or in other words in the sense of force or active faculty. This force can be found outside the body upon which it acts, or within that body itself; and in the latter case, it is a force in a body.
fn.1286: The manuscripts have עשר here and in the following propositions; we have written עשרה̈ more correctly.
fn.1287: Here is the more precise meaning of this proposition: among the accidents or qualities that subsist only in the body, there are some that divide with the body, such as, for example, the heat of a hot body or the color inherent in a body; for each part of the body retains the same heat and the same color. Others do not follow the division of the body, such as, for example, the shape, which does not always remain the same when the body is divided. On the other hand, even among the things that constitute or complete the being of the body, there are some that cannot be divided in any way, neither in reality nor even in thought, and such are notably the rational soul and intelligence; others, like certain physical forms, divide with the body to which they belong. — By the soul and the intelligence, the author means not only the rational soul of man and the hylic intellect, but also the souls of the celestial spheres and the intelligence by which they conceive the particular aim of their movement: for it will be seen later (chap. IV) that the author, according to Ibn Sina's theory, attributes to the celestial spheres not only a soul, but also a thought inherent in them, which must not be confused with the separate intelligences that are the object of desire of their respective spheres, and which determine their movement.
fn.1288: Aristotle, after having established that the first mover is not moved, intends to show that it has neither parts nor extension. Starting from the already demonstrated proposition that there is no infinite extension or magnitude, he shows that the first mover cannot be a finite magnitude, for the movement emanating from it being infinite, it would follow that in a finite magnitude there can be an infinite force; now, this is impossible, for the infinite force would have to produce its effect in a time less than that which would be necessary for any finite force to produce the same effect—that is to say, the infinite force would produce its effect in no time or instantaneously, which is inadmissible, for every transformation occurs in a certain amount of time. Should it be said that the infinite force will also produce its effect in a certain amount of time? But then one could find a finite force which would produce the same effect in the same amount of time, and it would follow that this finite force would be equal to an infinite force, which is impossible. Such is in substance the demonstration by which Aristotle establishes that in a finite magnitude there cannot be an infinite force. See Physics, book VIII, ch. 10 (Bekker ed., p. 266 a): ὅτι δ’ὅλως οὐϰ ἐνδέχεται ἐν πεπε-ρασμένῳ μεγέθει ἄπειρον εἶναι δύναμιν, ἐϰ τῶνδε δῆλον. ϰ. τ. λ.
fn.1290: The first three kinds of changes enumerated above (Prop. IV) all indicate the passage from one state to another opposite state; now, the two opposite states are necessarily separated from each other by an interval of time, and consequently the change is not continuous. Nothing similar occurs in the fourth kind of change, or in local motion, which alone can be continuous. See Arist., Phys., book VIII, ch. 7 (p. 261 a): ὅτι μὲν οὖν τῶν ἄλλων ϰινή-σεων οὐδεμίαν ἐνδέχεται συνεχῆ εἶναι, ἐϰ τῶνδε φανερόν. Ἅπασαι γὰρ ἐξ ἀντι-ϰειμένων εἰς ἀντιϰείμενά εἰσιν αἱ ϰινήσεις ϰαὶ μεταϐολαί, ϰ. τ. λ. Cf. ibid., book V, chap. 4 (p. 228 a, b.): Κεῖται γὰρ τὸ συνεχές, ὧν τὰ ἔσχατα ἕν... πολλαὶ οὖν ϰαὶ οὐ μία ἡ ϰίνησις, ὧν ἐστὶν ἠρεμία μεταξύ.
fn.1291: In local motion itself, only circular motion is truly continuous; for motion in a straight line, being unable to continue to infinity, will necessarily have a stopping point from which it will turn, to take another direction or to return in the opposite direction. See ibid., book VIII, chap. 8, at the beginning: ὅτι δ’ἐνδέχεται εἶναί τινα ἄπειρον, μίαν οὖσαν ϰαὶ συνεχῆ, ϰαὶ αὕτη ἐστὶν ἡ ϰύϰλῳ, λέγωμεν νῦν... ὅτι δὲ τὸ φερόμενον τὴν εὐθεῖαν ϰαὶ πεπερασμένην οὐ φέρεται συνεχῶς, δῆλον. ’Α’ναϰάμπτει γὰρ, τὸ δ’ ἀναϰάμπτον τὴν εὐθεῖαν τὰς ἐναντίας ϰινεῖται ϰινήσεις. See also Metaphys., book XII, chap. 6, where our proposition is stated in these terms: Κίνησις δ’οὐϰ ἔστι συνεχὴς ἀλλ’ ἢ ἡ ϰατὰ τόπον, ϰαὶ ταύτης ἡ ϰύϰλῳ.
fn.1292: The manuscripts have ואולהא in the masculine, instead of ואולאהא.
fn.1293.sub_0: In this proposition, the author establishes that local motion (certainly that which, in the preceding proposition, was designated as the only one that is continuous) is prior according to nature to all other motions and changes; and by prior according to nature one must understand, in accordance with Aristotle's definition (Metaph., book V, chap. 11), that which can be without other things being, but without which other things cannot be. The terms of this proposition are drawn from Aristotle's Physics, book VIII, chap. 7 (Cf. book VII, chap. 2), although the author, it seems to me, does not strictly follow the reasoning of the Stagirite. It was seen above, p. 6, note 2, that according to Aristotle, the idea of motion applies to the categories of quantity, quality, and place. Now, he says, of these three kinds of motion, that of place is necessarily the first: for it is impossible for there to be growth without there having first been transformation. Transformation is change into what is opposite; but when there is transformation, there must be something that transforms and which causes, for example, that which is hot in potentiality to become hot in act. Now it is evident that the mobile [agent] of this transformation is sometimes closer and sometimes further from the thing to be transformed, and that the transformation cannot take place without local motion; the latter, consequently, is the first among the motions. Further on, Aristotle establishes by other proofs that local motion, although it is the last to develop in the individual beings of this world, is the first in the universe and even precedes the birth (γένεσις) of all things, which is followed by transformation and growth (μετὰ γὰρ τὸ γενέσθαι πρῶτον ἀλλοίωσις ϰαὶ αὔξησɩς; Phys., VIII, 7, page 260 b, line 32).
fn.1293.sub_1: One might initially find it surprising that Maimonides places transformation before generation and corruption; however, it appears that our author considers transformation from a more general perspective—that is, not only in relation to the category of quality, as in the IVth proposition, but also in relation to generation, which is itself in some sense a transformation of matter by form, a transformation effected by an agent more or less remote, which needs to draw closer to the matter to be transformed. It is also in this sense that Averroes explains the passage in the Physics. See the Works of Aristotle with the Commentaries of Averroes, folio ed., vol. IV, fol. 180 c: «Deinde dicit: Et manifestum est quod dispositio motoris tunc non currit eodem modo, sed forte quandoque erit propinquior alterato et quandoque remotior, etc. Id est, et quia primum alterans, quod non alteratur, non alterat semper, sed quandoque, necesse est ut non habeat se cum alterato in eadem dispositione, sed quandoque appropinquetur ei, et alteret, et quandoque removeatur, et non alteret: et propinquitas, et distantia non est, nisi per translationem: ergo translatio præcedit naturaliter alterationem, scilicet quod, cum utraque fuerit in actu: deinde alterans alteravit, postquam non alterabat: necesse est ut alterum moveatur in loco aut alterans, aut alteratum, aut utrumque. Si autem alterum fuerit generatum, aut utrumque, et posuerimus hoc esse causam ejus, quod quandoque alterat, et quandoque non, manifestabitur quod translatio debet prœcedere eodem modo, cum alteratio etiam prœcedat generationem; generatio enim aut est alteratio aut sequitur alterationem.»
fn.1294: It is, as Aristotle expresses it, something of motion (τῆς ϰινήσεώς τι). On this proposition, see vol. I of this work, p. 199, n. 1, and p. 380, n. 2.
fn.1295: That is to say, everything that is not moved, but is itself the cause of motion, or in other words, everything that is outside the celestial sphere, such as God and the separate intelligences. See Arist., Treatise On the Heavens, book I, chap. 9: Ἀμα δὲ δῆλον ὅτι οὐδὲ τόπος οὐδὲ ϰενὸν οὐδὲ χρόνος ἐστὶν ἔξω τοῦ οὐρανοῦ..... ϰίνησις δ’ ἄνευ φυσιϰοῦ σώματος οὐϰ ἔστιν · ἔξω δὲ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ δέδειϰται ὅτι οὔτ’ ἔστιν οὔτ’ ἐνδέχεται γενέσθαι σῶμα, ϰ. τ. λ. Cf. Phys., book IV, chap. 12: Ὥστε φανερὸν ὅτι τὰ ἀεὶ ὄντα ᾗ ἀεὶ ὄντα, οὐϰ ἐστὶν ἐν χρόνῳ, ϰ. τ. λ.
fn.1296: Literally: In everything that is not a body, numeration cannot be conceived… Cf. Arist. Metaph., book XII, chap. 8: Α’λλ’ ὅσα ἀρι-θμῷ πολλά, ὕλην ἔχει, ϰ. τ. λ.
fn.1297: That is to say, the different matters or the subjects in which they are found.
fn.1298: See vol. I of this work, p. 434, and ibid., notes 2, 3, and 4, and below, at the beginning of chap. 1, page 31, note 2.
fn.1299: See Arist., Phys., book VII, chap. 1: Ἅπαν τὸ ϰινούμενον ἀνάγϰη ὑπό τινος ϰινεῖσθαɩ. Aristotle demonstrates this proposition by arguing primarily from the infinite divisibility of that which is moved (See the VIIIth prop.), which does not allow one to stop at any part of the moved thing to find therein the moving principle of the whole; from which it follows that this mover is necessarily something other than the whole of the moved thing. Cf. book VIII, chap. 6, toward the end.
fn.1300: See Arist., Phys. book VIII, chap. 4. After having distinguished that which is moved accidentally along with something else from that which is moved in itself (ϰαθ’ αὑτό), Aristotle adds: Τῶν δὲ ϰαθ’ αὑτὰ τὰ μὲν ὑφ’ ἑαυτοῦ τὰ δ’ ὑπ’ ἄλλου... ϰινεῖται γὰρ τὸ ζῷον αὐτὸ ὑφ’αὑτοῦ, ϰ τ. λ.
fn.1301: Instead of אלאג׳סד, which more precisely designates the inanimate body, some manuscripts have אלאג׳סם.
fn.1302: That is to say, the local motion that came to it from the soul.
fn.1303: The Arabic words מן חלקיאה, on the part of or from himself, correspond to the Greek words ὑφ’ ἑαυτοῦ.
fn.1304: In other words: that the motive force inherent in it—by which any part of the moved body receives an essential rather than an accidental motion (as, for example, the motion a hand would receive from an external impulse)—resides in the whole of that body.
fn.1305: This proposition results from the combination of propositions V and XVII. Since motion has been defined as the transition from potentiality to actuality (see Phys., III, 1 and 2; Metaph., XI, 9), and since all motion presupposes a mover other than the thing moved, it follows that everything in potentiality requires an external impulse to pass into actuality. Potentiality is a faculty of acting or a faculty of receiving action (cf. Metaph., IX, 1); in both cases, potentiality passes into actuality only through something external to it. Thus, for example, the artist, who possesses the faculty to produce a work of art, requires external matter to realize this faculty; likewise, bronze, which has the faculty to become a statue, requires the artist's labor for this faculty to be realized.
fn.1306: Thus, for example, that which is of absolute lightness, such as fire, or of absolute heaviness, such as earth, possesses not only the faculty to move—the former upward, the latter downward—but this faculty or potentiality is always in act, unless there is an obstacle that prevents natural motion and produces a contrary motion.
fn.1307: If, for example, someone removes a column supporting a heavy object so that the object falls, it can be said in a sense that it is he who caused the object to fall by removing the obstacle that prevented its heaviness from following its natural law. See Arist., Phys., book VIII, end of ch. 4. Cf. Maimonides, Part IIIe of this work, ch. 10.
fn.1308: Literally: and understand this. Commentators observe that the author adds these words here because of the great significance of this proposition, which seems to overturn the dogma of creation: for since God is absolute energy, always in act, and nothing can place an obstacle to his action, he could not, at a given moment, have created the world, or passed from potentiality to actuality. On this question, see ch. XVIII of this Part IIe.
fn.1309: This proposition and the following two are borrowed from Ibn Sina, who was the first to make, within the concept of necessary being (as opposed to the absolute possible, which comes into being and perishes), this distinction between that which is necessary in itself or the absolute necessary, and that which is necessary through another, being by its own essence in the category of the possible. To the second species belong, according to Ibn Sina, the celestial spheres, in which one distinguishes between potency and act, matter and form, and which derive the quality of necessary beings only from their relationship with the first cause, or God. Ibn Sina departs, in this respect, from Aristotle, who expressly extends the concept of necessary being to that which is eternally moved, or to the celestial spheres, which, he says, are not at all in potency and have no matter properly so called—that is, matter subject to generation and destruction. See Metaph., Book IX, chap. 8: Oὐθὲν ἄρα τῶν ἀφθάρτων ἁπλῶς δυνάμει ἐστὶν ὂν ἁπλῶς οὐδὲ τῶν ἐξ ἀνάγκης ὄντων, καὶ τοι ταῦτα πρῶτα.... διὸ ἀεὶ ἐνεργεῖ ἥλιος καὶ ἄστρα καὶ ὅλος ὁ οὐρανός, κ. τ. λ. Cf. Treatise On the Heavens, I, 2. Ibn Rushd contested Ibn Sina's theory in several places in his works. Cf. my Mélanges de philosophie juive et arabe, pp. 358-359.
fn.1310: Ibn Sina gives as an example the number four, which exists only by virtue of the number two taken twice, and which, consequently, ceases to exist as soon as the number two, which is its cause, no longer exists. See Shahrastani, p. 373 (German trans., vol. II, p. 250), and Al-Nadjah, Metaph., at the beginning of Book II, p. 62.
fn.1311: That is to say, the relationship between cause and effect, or the necessary condition under which alone a given cause produces a given effect. "Everything," says Ibn Sina (loc. cit.), "whose existence is necessary through another is in itself of possible existence: for the necessity of its existence depends on a certain relationship (نسبة), where something other than the very essence of the thing in question is considered." Thus, for example, the sun becomes the cause of day for a part of the earth only when it is in a certain position relative to that part.
fn.1312: That is to say: it has neither an external cause, nor even an internal cause, which would imply a composition. See the following prop.
fn.1313: It is evident, and the author insists upon it very often (See, in vol. I, the chapters on attributes, and hereafter, ch. I), that the absolute and necessary being cannot be composed of two different things, and that thought cannot even distinguish within it two different ideas, or two intelligible things. Consequently, any existence that presents itself in our thought as a composite of two ideas—such as matter and form, for example—cannot be, as it presents itself, necessary in itself, since it is, at least for thought, the result of a composition: for, as Ibn Sina observes, it is impossible to admit that the whole is, by its essence, prior to its parts; rather, it is either posterior to them or exists together with them. See Al-Nadjah, loc. cit., p. 63, line 9.
fn.1314: The concepts of potency and act, of matter and form, are so familiar to the Peripatetics that the proposition in question here requires no explanation. It should only be noted that the author understands by body here not only that which is subject to generation and corruption, but also the celestial bodies; these, according to Aristotle, while having no matter susceptible to generation, do have matter that serves as a substratum for local motion. See Arist., Metaph., IX, 8, at the end, and XII, 2, and cf. Mélanges de philosophie juive et arabe, p. 4, note 1, and p. 18, note 1. Maimonides adopted the opinion of Ibn Sina, who claimed to provide a general demonstration of the existence of matter and form in bodies, applying to all bodies, including the celestial bodies. Cf. Shahrastani, p. 366 (German trans., II, pp. 239-240). This opinion, by which one might be led to attribute also to celestial bodies a being in potency (which would be contrary to Aristotle's theories), was contested by Ibn Rushd; the latter considers the celestial bodies to be simple bodies that find their form or their entelechy in the separate intelligences. Cf. Ibn Falaquera, Moreh ha-Moreh, on this proposition (pp. 71-72).
fn.1315: These three accidents are inherent to every body: one cannot imagine a body without quantity, and it necessarily has limits that constitute its shape; finally, its parts are in a certain position relative to one another, and the entire body is in a certain position relative to what is outside of it.
fn.1316: There is a nuance between potency and possibility; the former may exist only in our thought, while the latter is in things themselves. Thus, we often distinguish between potency and act in a purely conceptual way, even when in reality the two ideas are inseparable from one another; prime matter, for example, is a potency, but this potency exists separately only in thought, for prime matter is inseparable from form. Possibility, on the contrary, is in the object itself and denotes that which can be or not be; thus, for example, bronze can be or not be a statue, and the statue can cease to be what it is by losing its form. Thus, the author, wishing to characterize in this proposition that which at a certain moment may not exist in act, must add to potency the condition of possibility in the very essence of the thing, meaning that everything that is in potency—not only in our thought, but because the thing itself contains the idea of the possible—can also be conceived as not existing in act at a certain moment. In short, this proposition amounts to what Aristotle said, namely that everything that is possible can not be in act, and consequently it can be and not be. See Metaphysics, Book IX, chap. 8 (Brandis ed., pp. 187-188): Ἔστι δ’ οὐθὲν δυνάμει ἀΐδιον..... Τὸ δυνατὸν δὲ πᾶν ἐνδέχεται μὴ ἐνεργεῖν· τὸ ἄρα δυνατὸν εἶναι ἐνδέχεται εἶναι καὶ μὴ εἶναι. An explanation that the author himself gave regarding this XXIIIrd proposition is cited in Moreh ha-Moreh (p. 72, lines 9-18): ופירש בו מורנו ז״ל כי הדבר בהיות תאר מהתארים וכו׳. This explanation is taken from the letter addressed by Maimonides to R. Samuel ibn Tibbon, which we have mentioned elsewhere (cf. vol. I, p. 23, note 1). — One will see in chap. I (in the fourth speculation) the application the author makes of this proposition to demonstrate the necessity of tracing back to a first mover, in which there is absolutely no concept of possibility.
fn.1317: The words שי מא are rendered in Ibn Tibbon's version by the words דבר אחד, which one must be careful not to render here as a single thing, and which have the sense of something or any thing whatsoever. These two words, omitted in almost all editions, are found in the editio princeps. Ibn Falaquera rightly replaced them with דבר מה, and Al-Harizi with שום דבר.
fn.1318: This proposition, which forms one of the principal points of Peripateticism, needs no explanation. Potentiality is the principle of contingency or the faculty of becoming something, and this faculty is necessarily in a substratum, which is matter. Everything subject to any change whatever has matter (πάντα δ’ ὕλην ἔχει ὅσα μεταϐάλλει, Metaph., XII, 2). We have already seen that Aristotle also attributes to the celestial spheres a certain matter as a substratum for the motion of translation. Cf. above, p. 20, n. 1.
fn.1320: The editions of Ibn Tibbon's version read הצורה ההיא; the word ההיא must be deleted, as it is not in the manuscripts.
fn.1321: That is to say, which disposes a particular matter to receive a specific particular form, such as, for example, the artist who gives bronze the form of a statue.
fn.1322: Literally: And already that which is necessary to expound concerning all this has been expounded. The author refers to the detailed explanations given by Aristotle in the Physics and in the Metaphysics.
fn.1323: See Metaph., Book XII, chap. 6: Πῶς γὰρ ϰινηθήσεται, εἰ μηθὲν ἔσται ἐνεργείᾳ σἴτιον; Οὐ γὰρ ἥ γε ὕλη ϰινήσει αὐτὴ ἑαυτήν, ἀλλὰ τεϰτονιϰή, ϰ. τ. λ.. Cf. ibid., Book I, chap. 3: Οὐ γὰρ δὴ τό γε ὑποϰείμενον αὐטὸ ποιεῖ μεταϐάλλειν ἑαυτό.
fn.1324: Most of the manuscripts read מעקולאת without the copulative ו, and likewise both Hebrew versions, as well as the Moreh ha-Moreh, have מושכלות as an adjective for הקדמות מופתיות, so that one would have to translate: demonstrative propositions, intelligible at first sight; but then the form מעקולאת would be incorrect, for the adjective should have the feminine singular form מעקולה̈. I therefore consider this word as a neuter noun, in the sense of intelligibilia, so that the words מעקולאת אול signify, as always, primary notions or axioms. These words could not be a simple apposition to the words מקדמאת ברהאניה̈; for demonstrative propositions could not be qualified as axioms. I have therefore added a copulative ו, and I have written ומעקולאת, as it is indeed found in one of the two Leiden manuscripts (no. 221).
fn.1325: Literally: by what we have summarized of their arrangement or of their enumeration. The word במא depends on מעקולאת, the (notions) intelligible through, etc.
fn.1327: All the mss. contain ושרחה in the singular, as does Al-Harizi's version: ופירותו, while Ibn Tibbon's version has the plural ופירותיו, and its commentaries. It is known that Greek commentaries on the Metaphysics were few; the Arabs knew only an incomplete commentary by Alexander of Aphrodisias on the XIIth book and a paraphrase by Themistius on this same book. This is how Ibn Rushd expresses himself in this regard at the beginning of his introduction to book XII of the Metaphysics (Hebrew version, ms. from the Oratory collection, no. 114, fol. 139 a): לא ימצא לאלכסנדר ולא למי שאחריו מהמפרשים פירוש במאמרי זאת החכמה ולא ביאור אלא בזה המאמר כי אנחנו מצאנו לאלכסנדר בו פירוש משני שלישי המאמר ומצאנו לתמסמטיוס בו ביאור כפי הענין ·
fn.1328: All the mss. I have been able to consult contain וחתביין אבער טמקדמאת; this reading is confirmed by Ibn Tibbon's version, which contains ולבאר הרחוקות שבהקדמות. It appears, however, that the Hebrew translator had a doubt here about which he consulted the author; for here is what we read in the letter addressed by Maimonides to R. Samuel Ibn Tibbon: אלמקדמה̈ אלכ"ה ט̇ננת אן פיהא נקצ̇א ולא נקץ̇ פיהא בל נצ̇הא כמא ענדכם ואנמא תקדיר אלכלאם הד̇א ליס גרץ̇ הד̇ה אלמקאלה̈ נקל כתב אלפלאספה̈ פיהא אלא תביין בעץ̇ אלמקדמאת . "You supposed that, in the XXVth proposition, something was missing; but nothing is missing there, and on the contrary the reading is as you have it. My words state nothing other than this: The purpose of this treatise is not to transcribe the books of the philosophers in it, but to explain certain propositions." — If these are indeed Maimonides' words, and if there is no error in the sole manuscript we have of the letter in question, the sentence should be continued as follows: or rather to report the propositions that are within our reach, etc. — Al-Harizi's version contains אלא לבאר ההקדמות הרחוקות והקרובות שאנו צריכים עליהם וכו׳. This version, in any case, is inaccurate; but the word אלא offers a trace of the reading given in Maimonides' letter.
fn.1330: Literally: Until what we intend to set forth has been set forth.
fn.1331: See especially Phys., bk. VIII, ch. 1, where Aristotle establishes the eternity of motion as a necessary consequence of the eternity of time, which, as Aristotle expresses it, is the number of motion: Eἰ δὴ ἐστὶν ὁ χρόνος κινήσεως ἀριθμὸς ἢ κίνησις τις, εἴπερ ἀεὶ χρόνος ἐστίν, ἀνάγκη καὶ κίνησιν ἀΐδιον εἶναι. Cf. Metaph., XII, 6: ’Αλλ’ ἀδύנהτον κίνησιν ἢ γενέσθαι ἢ φθαρῆναι · ἀεὶ γὰρ ἦν · οὐδὲ χρόνον. κ. τ. λ. See also above, the XVth proposition and the passages indicated in the accompanying notes.
fn.1332: That is to say, the body of the celestial sphere, which is above the four elements, and whose substance has been designated by the name ether. See the treatise On the Heavens, bk. I, ch. 2 and 3, Meteor., bk. I, ch. 3, and cf. Vol. I of this work, p. 247, n. 3, and 425, note 1. — The expression fifth body (πέμπτον σῶμα) is common among the commentators of Aristotle. See, for example, Simplicius, on the treatise On the Heavens, bk. I, ch. 3 (Scholia in Aristotelem, collected by Brandis, p. 475 a). Aristotle himself rather employs the expressions τὸ ἄνω σῶμα (treatise On the Soul, II, 7, and passim; cf. the commentary by Trendelenburg, p. 373 ff.), τὸ πρῶτον σῶμα (On the Heavens, II, 12), τὸ πρῶτον στοιχεῖον (Meteorol., I, 2 and 3). It is undoubtedly this celestial substance that was the subject of Empedocles' work entitled "On the Fifth Substance" (περὶ τῆς πέμπτης οὐσίας) and which, it seems, was refuted by Plutarch in a work mentioned by Lamprias. Cf. Sturz, Empedocles agrigentinus (Lipsiae, 1805, 8vo), p. 73.
fn.1333: Thus, for example, the circular motion of each of the celestial spheres, considered in itself, is caused by a motion of the same kind that precedes it; the generation of the elements and their motion proceed from the circular motion of the celestial spheres, which is not of the same kind.
fn.1334: See Phys., Book VIII, chap. 2. After discussing this objection, drawn from the movement of animals, which appears to be spontaneous and not to proceed from any movement coming from the outside, Aristotle observes that this is only a false appearance, and that we always notice, in what composes the animal organism, certain movements whose cause should not be sought in the animal itself, but in what surrounds it from the outside, such that there are external movements that act upon the intellectual and appetitive faculties: ὁρῶμεν γὰρ ἀεί τι ϰινούμενον ἐν τῷ ζῴῳ τῶν συμφύτων.... οὐδὲν οὖν ϰωλύει, μᾶλλον δ’ ἴσως ἀναγϰαῖον τῷ σώματι πολλὰς ἐγγίγνεσθαι ϰινήσεις ὑπὸ τοῦ περιέχοντος, τούτων δ’ ἐνίας τὴν διάνοιαν ἢ τὴν ὄρεξιν ϰινεῖν, ϰ. τ. λ. Cf. the treatise On the Motion of Animals, chap. 6: ὁρῶμεν δὲ τὰ ϰινοῦντα τὸ ζῷον διάνοιαν, ϰαὶ φαντασίαν ϰαὶ προαίρεσιν, ϰαὶ βούλησιν, ϰαὶ ἐπιθυμίαν · ταῦτα δε πάντα ἀνάγεται εἰς νοῦν ϰαὶ ὄρεξιν. — To better understand the terms that Maimonides reports here in Aristotle's name, we will further cite the passage from the Physics according to the Arabo-Latin version with the explanation of Ibn Rushd (Works of Aristotle with the commentaries of Averroes, vol. IV, f. 161, col. 3): "Semper enim invenimus aliquid moveri in animali, quod est naturale in eo; et causa istius motus animalis non est anima ejus, sed aer qui continet animal in eo, quod reputo. Et cum dicimus ipsum moveri a se, non intendimus omni motu, sed motu locali. Et nihil prohibet, immo dignum est ut sit necessarium, ut in corpore fiant plures motus a continente, quorum quidam movent voluntatem et appetitum, et tunc ista movebunt animal secundum totum." Here is how Ibn Rushd explains the end of this passage: "Et dixit et nihil prohibet, etc., id est et necesse est ut principium motuum animalis sit ex continente: immo hoc est necessarium. Et quia posuit quod in corpore animalis fiunt plures motus ex continente, narravit quomodo accidit ex istis motibus ut animal moveatur in loco, et dixit quo rumquædam moventur, etc., id est, et hoc est ita, quod in animali fiet ab eo, quod accidit sibi, opinio, voluntas, et appetitus ad motum, aut ad expellendum nocumentum contingens ex continente, aut ad inducendum juvamentum. Et intendit hic per opinionem aliquid commune virtuti imaginativæ, et rationali. Animali enim non accidit appetitus, nisi ex imaginatione; e.g., that when it suffers and when it fears, it flees; and when appetites are removed, it rests; or, when fatigue occurs to it, and it desires rest." On imagination, see also below, at the beginning of chap. IV.
fn.1335: See Phys., VIII, 1 (p. 251 a). Aristotle, after recalling the definition of motion given above, adds that, even without this definition of motion, everyone will grant that regarding every motion, it is necessary that what moves be capable of moving, such as being capable of transforming what is transformed, and capable of changing the place of what is transported, so that a thing must be combustible before burning, and capable of igniting before it ignites. (ὥστε δεῖ πρότερον ϰαυστὸν εἶναι πρὶν ϰάεσθαι, ϰαὶ ϰαυστιϰὸν πρὶν ϰάειν). According to Ibn Rushd (loc. cit., f. 155, c. 3), this passage means nothing other than that motion (which, according to Aristotle, is the entelechy of a mobile thing insofar as it is mobile) must exist in potentiality in every mobile thing. But the Arabic commentator informs us that Al-Farabi understood this passage in the sense that every power must temporally precede the act, not only in motion, but generally in everything that occurs: "Dico secundum hanc expositionem intellexit Alpharabius et alii hoc capitulum, scilicet quod induxit definitionem motus ad declarandum potentiam esse ante actum; et hoc non est proprium motui, secundum quod est motus, sed est proprium novo facto secundum quod est novum factum, scilicet ut potentia et posse novi præcedat ipsum secundum tempus." It is evident that Maimonides borrowed the terms of Al-Farabi's explanation, which Ibn Rushd declares erroneous: "Et hoc quod dixit et sine hac definitione, etc., hoc decepit homines in hoc: et existimaverunt ipsum declarare potentiam esse ante actum in tempore, et ipse intendebat dicere quod non dicitur moveri nisi illud in cujus natura est motus, scilicet corpus mobile: et quod non invenitur in immobili."
fn.1336: That is to say, the celestial sphere, which is a finite body.
fn.1337: That is to say, one can admit the existence of the infinite in number (See the 2nd prop.), provided that the units composing it do not exist simultaneously, but successively, one after another, such as, for example, the moments that succeed each other in time and the successive and uninterrupted motions of the celestial sphere. See vol. I, chap. LXXIII, pp. 413-415.
fn.1338: Literally: That he does not decide (or determine) that his proofs for them are a demonstration.
fn.1339: See on this question chap. XV of this Part II.
fn.1340: Literally: The force of their words (i.e., what ultimately results from them) is that this is, according to them, a first notion; that is to say: they generally consider it a simple axiom that the infinite by succession is impossible. Cf. vol. I, p. 416. — All the manuscripts read אנהא ענדהם, and the feminine suffix of אנהא must be taken in a neuter sense, or else referred to an implied word מקדמה̈, i.e., the proposition which declares the infinite by succession inadmissible. Ibn Tibbon's version has שהוה in the masculine, while Al-Harizi's has שהיא in the feminine.
fn.1341: That is to say, the existence, incorporeality, and unity of God.
fn.1342: In this chapter, the author provides various demonstrations of the existence of a unique and immaterial God. His demonstrations are of the type referred to as physical or cosmological, and which lead us from the contingent existence of the world to the conception of a necessary being. His proofs are primarily based on motion; it is demonstrated that, since inert matter cannot move itself, and the causes of motion cannot regress to infinity, it is necessary to acknowledge a first mover that is itself immobile. The argumentation is, in substance, borrowed from Aristotle (Phys., Book VIII, ch. 5 et seq.; Metaph., Book XII, ch. 6 and 7); but it has been, on various points, supplemented and modified by Arabic philosophers, and one will recognize, notably in the 3rd Speculation, theories specific to Ibn-Sīnā.
fn.1343: That is to say, the matter of all sublunar things. The two Hebrew versions (cf. Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 74), according to which the words ההוה והנפמדו refer to matter, are incorrect; instead of החמר הזה, one should write חמר זה without the article, and consider חמר as a construct state, of which זה is the complement.
fn.1344: The author means, I believe, that the motion proper to sublunar things stops there, to be continued by an impulse emanating from a motion of another kind.
fn.1345: That is to say, everything in this lower world that serves as a proximate or immediate mover, and disposes particular matter to receive a particular form. See above, the XXV<sup>th</sup> proposition.

He says, in substance, that the XII<sup>th</sup> proposition applies in an absolute manner only to a divisible force (such as, for example, the heat of fire, which spreads only to a certain limited distance), whereas certain indivisible forces found in a finite body are not necessarily finite; thus, for example, human thought rises beyond the ninth sphere, and it is not demonstrated that it has a limit, although it is found in a finite body. It was therefore necessary here, to show that the prime mover of the sphere could not be a force diffused within it, to join the XII<sup>th</sup> and XI<sup>th</sup> propositions together as premises. The author will then show that this mover also cannot be an indivisible force.

fn.1373: In the universe, it is the matter of that which is born and perishes; or, for example, in the movements emanating from the soul, of which the author spoke above, the stone that is moved by the hand, and which no longer moves anything else.
fn.1374.sub_0: This demonstration appears to be based on a passage from Aristotle's Physics, which may be summarized as follows: Three things may be considered in motion: the thing moved, the mover, and that by which the latter moves. That which is moved does not necessarily communicate motion; that which serves as an instrument or intermediary communicates motion at the same time as it receives it; finally, that which moves without being an instrument or intermediary is itself immobile. Now, since we see (in the universe), on the one hand, that which is moved without having within itself the principle of motion—that is, without moving anything else—and on the other hand, that which is simultaneously moved by another and the mover of another, it is reasonable, if not necessary, to admit a third thing which moves without being moved. See Phys., Book VIII, ch. 5 (Bekker ed., p. 256 b): τρία γὰρ ἀνάγκη εἶναι, τό τε κινουμένον, καὶ τὸ κινοῦν, καὶ τὸ ᾧ κινεῖ. κ. τ. λ. In the Metaphysics, Book XII, chap. VII, Aristotle summarizes himself in these terms: ἔστι τοίνυν τι καὶ ὃ κινεῖ, ἐπεὶ δὲ τὸ κινούμενον καὶ κινοῦν, καὶ μέσοντοίνυν ἐστί τι ὃ οὐ κινούμενον κινεῖ, ἀΐδιον καὶ οὐσία καὶ ἐνέργεια οὖσα. Alexander of Aphrodisias explained this passage in nearly the same terms used by Maimonides in this second demonstration; and it is evidently from Alexander that our author borrowed his argumentation, as well as the proposition he places at the head as having been stated by Aristotle himself. Alexander's explanation was cited by Averroes in his large commentary on the Metaphysics. We reproduce it from the Latin version of this commentary (folio ed., f. 149 verso): "Alexander said: This is the reason why [there is] some mover [which] is not moved, and it is stated briefly and as a reminder of what was said in the last [book] of the Physics. And it is founded upon two propositions, one of which is that every composite of two things, of which one can exist by itself, the other will also possibly exist by itself, unless the composition be of substance and accident; for example, because hydromel is composed of water and honey, and honey is found by itself, it is therefore necessary that water be found by itself. And, because we find something moved and moving as if composed of a mover and a moved, and we find something moved by itself and not moving, it is manifest that it is necessary for there to be some mover and not moved."
fn.1374.sub_1: "This mover, therefore, is immune from potentiality, and exists in no matter." As for the proposition attributed by Maimonides to Aristotle, some commentators have objected that, in what is composed of substance and accident, one cannot imagine the existence of the accident alone, although evidently the substance can exist alone. This objection fails due to the express condition set by Alexander: nisi compositio sit substantiæ et accidentis. Maimonides, in copying Alexander, perhaps omitted this condition through inadvertence.
fn.1375: The author means that this demonstration does not, strictly speaking, belong to Aristotle, but that it is he who provided its main elements. It is when he wishes to demonstrate the eternity of the world as a whole that Aristotle enters into details on the idea of the perishable and the imperishable, and on that which, in itself, is or is not subject to birth and corruption; see especially the treatise On the Heavens, Book I, chap. X et seq. It will be seen that this third demonstration is based on the theories of Ibn-Sīnā.
fn.1376: These words are missing in several editions of the Hebrew version, where it is necessary to add, along with the editio princeps, או יהיו בולם הוות נפמדות.
fn.1377: The author, questioned by the translator Ibn Tibbon on the precise meaning of this passage, explains himself roughly as follows in the letter cited above: When the possible is said of a species, it must actually exist in certain individuals of that species; for, if it never existed in any individual, it would be impossible for the species, and by what right would it then be said to be possible? If, for example, we say that writing is a possible thing for the human species, it is necessarily required that there be men who write at some time; for, if it were maintained that there is never any man who writes, that would be to say that writing is impossible for the human species. It is not the same for the possible said of an individual; for, if we say that it is possible for this child to write or not to write, it does not follow from this possibility that the child must necessarily write at any moment. Thus, the possible said of a species is not, strictly speaking, in the category of the possible, but is in some way necessary. — This explanation is still insufficient to fully grasp the conclusion the author is about to draw from this proposition, namely, that all beings would necessarily have perished. There is perhaps an obscure point here on which the author did not wish to pronounce himself more clearly, as the commentator Ephodi indicates. Cf. the introduction to the first part, Vol. I, p. 28, VIIth cause. According to the indications of the commentator Shem-Tov, the author's thought would be as follows: the possibility attributed to an entire species is, like the species itself, an eternal thing; one cannot, strictly speaking, attribute a possibility to an eternal thing, and for it, everything that is possible will be at the same time necessary. — In short, it appears the author intended to say that the hypothesis of contingency for the universality of beings is inadmissible; and if he did not clearly state this thesis, it is perhaps because he feared offending certain readers by explicitly admitting that this demonstration, which he says is the strongest, is based on the principle of the eternity of the world.
fn.1378: The author intends to speak of the celestial sphere, which is of a necessary existence and not subject to contingency, although it does not have within itself the necessary cause of its existence, according to the distinction made by Ibn-Sīnā (see above, the XIX<sup>th</sup> proposition), and to which the author returns in the remainder of this demonstration.
fn.1379: The author, by the word קאל, dixit, evidently alludes to Ibn-Sīnā, who, as we have already stated (p. 18, n. 3), was the first to distinguish, in being, between that which is necessary in itself and that which is so by another. Cf., on the demonstration that follows, the analysis of Ibn-Sīnā's Metaphysics in Shahrastānī, pp. 375-376 (German trans. Vol. II, pp. 253-255).
fn.1380: The author here makes reservations regarding the celestial sphere, in which, as will be seen later, he does not wish to see, with Aristotle, an uncreated being.

fn.1382: Some manuscripts have here the incorrect form אלעשריניה, which Ibn Tibbon imitated in Hebrew as העשרימיה.
fn.1383: In other words: As soon as necessary existence were supposed to belong to several beings, these would form a species characterized by necessary existence, and, consequently, the idea of a necessary being would be that of the species and would no longer belong to the essence of each of these beings.
fn.1384: That is to say, the Divinity cannot be composed of two principles, neither similar nor contrary to one another.

fn.1390: It must be remembered that, according to Ibn-Sinâ, whose theories the author has adopted, the other separate intelligences are, in relation to their own essence, in the category of the possible, and only derive from their cause or from God the quality of necessary beings; they do not form an absolute unity, for they can be numbered as causes and effects. fn.1391: The demonstration that the author is about to give is borrowed from the Motécallemîn, as can be seen in the first part of this work, ch. LXXV, IInd method (vol. I, p. 443).

fn.1393: Cf. vol. I, p. 314, and ibid., note 1.
fn.1394: This method aims to demonstrate that, every body being composite, God, who is absolute simplicity, could not be a body. It consists of two distinct demonstrations. In the first, based on the XXIInd proposition, the body is considered from the point of view of its composition of matter and form, which presupposes an efficient, and which, consequently, does not allow any body, whatever it may be, to be seen as the absolute being, independent of any cause. In the second demonstration, the body is considered as a composite being, from the point of view of its divisible quantity, its composition of substance and accidents, and its quality of being complex, in which there is both the idea of corporeity in general and that of any determined body.
fn.1395: Literally: because it is two by the expression (or the term); for the word body contains the idea of corporeity in general, and the idea of a particular body in particular.
fn.1396: That is to say, the one based on creation ex nihilo, which the author will explain further on, after having provided details on the celestial spheres and the intelligences.

The proofs alleged for the existence of God are thus among those based on imperfect definitions, where the prior is defined by the posterior. See Vol. I of this work, p. 190, and ibid., notes 3 and 4. Cf. Mélanges de philosophie juive et arabe, pp. 192 and 193.
fn.1399: See the preceding chapter, at the end of the 3rd speculation, where the author has shown that, the existence of the necessary being having been established, it is easy to demonstrate that this being is one and incorporeal.

fn.1414: That is to say, the opinions of Aristotle.
fn.1415: Cf. the treatise On the Heavens, Book II, chap. 2, where Aristotle calls the heaven a living being, having in itself a principle of movement (ὁ δ’οὐρανὸς ἔμψυχος ϰαί ἔχει ϰινήσεως ἀρχήν). Elsewhere, however, Aristotle seems to attribute the circular motion of the heaven, like the rectilinear motion of the elements, to a nature inherent in the celestial body (Ibid., Book 1, ch. 2), and at other times, he attributes it to a desire awakened in it by the supreme intelligence, toward which it is attracted (Metaph., XII, 7). Here, as in the theory of the different intellects (see vol. I, p. 304 ff.), the obscurity and vagueness prevailing in Aristotle's theories have given rise to various interpretations. The Arabic philosophers, and notably Ibn Sina, combining the opinions of the Neoplatonic commentators with astronomical theories, formed, regarding the movement of celestial bodies and the order of the spheres and Intelligences, the doctrine developed by Maimonides in this and the following chapters, which has been contested on various points by Ibn Rushd. II, p. 261 ff.); Al-Nadjâh, or Abridgment of the Philosophy of Ibn Sina (following the Canon), p. 71 ff.; Averroes, Epitome in libros Metaphys. Aristotelis, tract. IV. Cf. Albert the Great, De Causis et processu universitatis, lib. I, tract. IV, cap. 7 and 8, and lib. II, tract. II, cap. 1 (opp. omn., vol. V, p. 559 ff., p. 586 ff.); Saint Thomas Aquinas, De Substantiis separatis, cap. II (opp. vol. XVII, fol. 16 verso ff.)
fn.1416: That is to say, the local motion of the celestial sphere.
fn.1417: The principle of motion proper to the elements, which is gravity or levity, is designated by Aristotle as a nature (φύσις) inherent in the elements. These move in a straight line, sometimes according to their nature (ϰατὰ φύσιν), as for example earth downward and fire upward, and sometimes, by an external force, contrary to their nature (παρὰ φύσιν). See the treatise On the Heavens, I, 2; III, 2; IV, 3, and passim. Cf. above, p. 8, note 1, and p. 10, note.
fn.1418: Cf. the <sup>1st</sup> part of this work, chap. <small>LXXII</small> (vol. I, p. 359).
fn.1419: The verb تصورُ is derived from صورة, form, and signifies, according to the book Ta’rîfât, حصول صورة الشى فى العقل, to receive in the intellect the form of a thing. The infinitive, which we translate here as conception, could also be rendered as thought or idea (cf. vol. I, p. 116, note 3); in the Arabic versions of Aristotle, the words τὸ νοεῖν, νόησις and νόημα are often rendered by تصوّر بالعقل, or simply by تصوُّر. See, for example, the treatise On the Soul, Book I, chap. 1 (§ 9): Μάλιστα δ’ ἔοιϰεν ἰδίῳ τὸ νοεῖν; in Arabic: والذى يشبه ان يكون يخصها هو التصور بالعقل (Hebrew MS of the Imperial Library, old collection, no. 317, fol. 104 recto, col. b). Ibid., chap. 4 (§ 14): ϰαί τὸ νοεῖν δή; in Arabic: والتصور بالعقل (same MS, fol. 113, col. d). Metaph., Book XII, chap. 7: ἀρχὴ δὲ ἡ νόησις; Hebrew version: וההתחלה הוא הציור בשבל; Latin-Arabic version (folio, fol. 150, col. a): «Principium autem est imaginatio per intellectum.» The word تصور also indicates the simple notion (νόημα), in which there is neither truth nor falsehood, and in this sense it is opposed to تصديق (affirmation), indicating the combination of thoughts (σύνθεσις νοημάτων), in which there is error and truth. See Arist., Categories, chap. 2 beginning, and chap. 4 (II) end; treatise On Interpretation, chap. I; treatise On the Soul, Book III, chap. 6 (§ 1); and ibid. the commentary of Averroes (folio edition, fol. 171, col. c).
fn.1420: That is to say, an intelligence that it possesses within itself, similar to the rational faculty of man, and which must not be confused with the separate intelligence that is outside the sphere. Cf. Part Ist of this work, ch. LXXII (pp. 373-374).
fn.1421: Cf. Aristotle, Metaph., bk. XII, ch. 7 (Brandis ed., p. 248): Ẻπιθυμητὸν γἁρ τὸ φαινόμενον ϰαλόν, βουλητὀν δὲ πρῶτον τὸ ὂν ϰαλόν. In accordance with the doctrine of Ibn Sina, Maimonides considers God and the other separate Intelligences as the final causes of the movement of the celestial spheres, which, as has been seen, possess within themselves the immediate efficient causes of their movement, namely their souls and their intellects.

fn.1425: That is to say, none of his contemporaries.
