fn.1428: Literally: to that in which we were.
fn.1429.sub_0: As we have said, the author, in this enumeration of the Intelligences, followed Ibn Sina, who, besides the supreme Intelligence, or God, admits ten Intelligences, the first of which, emanating directly from God (cf. below, ch. XXII), is that of the sphere of diurnal motion, which surrounds the entire universe, and the last of which, emanating from the Intelligence of the lunar sphere, is the active intellect. See Avicennæ opera, Metaph., IX, loc. cit.: «Si autem circuli planetarum fuerint sic quod principium motus circulorum uniuscujus-que planetarum sit virtus fluens a planeta, tunc non erit longe quin separata sint secundum numerum planetarum, non secundum numerum circulorum; et tune eorum numerus est decem post primum (that is to say, God). Primum autem eorum est Intelligentia quæ non movetur, cujus est movere sphæram corporis ultimi (that is to say, the diurnal sphere). Deinde id quod sequitur est quod movet sphæram fixarum. Deinde sequitur quod movet sphæram Saturni. Simililer est quousque pervenitur ad Intelligentiam a qua fluit super nostras animas; et hæc est Intelligentia mundi terreni, et vocamus eam Intelligentiam agentem.» Ibn Rushd, identifying the sphere of diurnal motion with that of the fixed stars, admits only eight spheres. See Epitome in libros metaph., tract. IV (fol. 182, col. a): «Tandem apud me est remotum quod inveniatur orbis nonus sine stellis; nam orbis est stellarum gratia, quæ sunt nobilior pars ejus…. Orbis autem qui movet motum magnum est nobilior cæteris or-bibus; quapropter non videtur nobis quod sit sine stellis, immo apud me est impossibile.» According to this, there would be in total only nine separate Intelligences, the last of which, as in Ibn Sina's theory, is the active intellect. This, therefore, according to the theory of the Arabs, is in a close relationship with the Intelligence of the lunar sphere, from which it emanates directly, but with which it must not be identified. — [In my Mélanges de philosophie juive et arabe, at the beginning of page 332 (cf. also pp. 165 and 448, and Vol. I of this work, p.
fn.1429.sub_1: 277, and note 3), I expressed myself on this matter in an inaccurate manner, and I should have said: «From the last of these separate Intelligences, which presides over the movement of the sphere closest to us (that of the moon), the active intellect emanates, etc.»] — The passage from Ibn Rushd (loc. cit., fol. 184, col. d), which has often been cited to show that, according to this author, the active intellect is itself the mover of the lunar sphere (see Ritter, Geschichte der philosophie, Vol. VIII, p. 148), is thus phrased in the Hebrew version: והשכל הפועל הוא יםודר מםוף אלו המניעים במדרגה ונניחו מניע גלגל הירח. The word מםוף seems to me to be an inaccurate translation of the Arabic words من آخر , and it should be translated as follows: «The active intellect emanates from the last of these movers in rank (i.e., from that one of these movers which by its rank is the last), which we assume to be the mover of the sphere of the moon.» To leave no doubt in this regard, I shall cite here a passage from Moses of Narbonne's commentary on Al-Ghazali's Maqāṣid, towards the end of the IInd part, or of the Metaph., where the theory of the spheres and their intelligences is set forth (according to Ibn Sina) (see Hebrew MS. of the Oratory collection, no. 93, fol. 179 a): ואמנם בן רשד ובל הפילוםופים מודים שהשבל הפועל בלתי מניע לגלגל רק שהוא עשירי לשבלים הנפרדים לפי בן רשד והשבל הראשון בבלל והוא עשירי לשבלים העלולים מבלתי מנוה במחוייב המציאות לפי אבוחמד. «Ibn Rushd and all the philosophers agree that the active intellect is not the mover of any celestial sphere. But, according to Ibn Rushd, it is the tenth of the separate Intelligences, if the first Intelligence (or God) is also included; whereas, according to Abu Hamid (al-Ghazali), it is the tenth of the caused Intelligences, without counting the Necessary Being (i.e., the first absolute cause, or God).»—Cf. Albert the Great, De Causis et processu universitatis, bk. I, tract IV, ch. 8 (Opp. Vol. V, p.
fn.1429.sub_2: 562 a): “Moreover, after the Intelligence of the lunar sphere and the lunar sphere itself, which (as Aristotle says) is in some way terrestrial, there is an Intelligence that illuminates above the sphere of the active and passive [elements], whose light it diffuses in the active and passive, which illuminates above the souls of men, and whose power is conceived in the seeds of generated and passive things.”
fn.1430: Literally: and that which brings forth (or causes to pass into actuality) must be of the same species as that which is brought forth.
fn.1431: The editions of the Hebrew version of Ibn-Tibbon contain: יחם בל שכל נבדל המיוחד לגלגל ההוא; one sees that the equivalent of the Arabic words בכל פלך is missing. In the MSS of this version, one reads, as in that of Al-Harizi: המיוחד בגלגל לגלגל ההוא; the word בגלגל renders the Arabic word באלפלך, which some Arabic MSS contain instead of בבכל פלך.
fn.1432: That is to say, for Aristotle, to whom our author attributes the basis of the theory he has just explained.
fn.1433: Literally: but (it is) as (when) it burns through an intermediary, etc.—Ibn-Tibbon, having taken the words פכמא אן in their ordinary sense of just as, wrote, to complete the sentence, כן הגלגל (likewise the sphere), while all the Arabic MSS simply contain ואלפלך (and the sphere).

One cannot admit that Maimonides, in a work intended for Jews, intentionally reproduced an expression from the Quran. The entire passage is undoubtedly borrowed from one of the Arabic philosophers, probably from Ibn Sina or Al-Ghazali. The latter, speaking of the philosophers, expresses himself in these terms (Destruction of the Philosophers, XVIth question, Heb. version): וכבר חשבו שהמלאכים השמימיים הם נפשות הגלגלים ושהמלאכים הנקראים כרובים המתקרבים הם השבלים המופשטים. “They claim that the celestial angels are the souls of the spheres, and that the approaching angels, called cherubim, are the abstract (or separate) Intelligences.” Cf. Averroes, Destr. destructionis, disputat. XVI, at the beginning. — Regarding the identification of angels with the separate Intelligences, see below, chap. VI.
fn.1435: In other words: As the Intelligences do not constitute diverse essences, distinct from one another, such that they could be numbered as diverse units, it follows that they can only be so insofar as they are the causes and effects of one another; so that God is the immediate cause only of the first Intelligence, which in turn is the cause of the second Intelligence, and so on. See the <small>XVI</small><sup>th</sup> of the propositions placed at the head of this II<sup>nd</sup> part.
fn.1436: That is to say, the lunar sphere.
fn.1437: Literally: The existence of the separate Intelligences culminates in this one.
fn.1438: That is to say: Since, on the one hand, the first Intelligence has in common with the others that it sets its respective sphere in motion, and since, on the other hand, all the intelligences are distinguished from each other in that they are the causes and effects of one another, one can distinguish in the first, as in all the others, two different ideas, for it is at the same time the mover of the first sphere and the efficient cause of the second Intelligence; it is therefore composite, and it cannot be considered as the necessary Being, who is of an absolute simplicity. Cf. chap. XXII of this IInd part.
fn.1439: Here, in almost all editions of the version of Ibn-Tibbon, the word וראיותיו is missing, which is found in the MSS and in the editio princeps.
fn.1440: Instead of עׂבלם, which all editions of Ibn-Tibbon’s version have here, one must read סבלם, a verbal noun from the verb סבל, which, like the Arabic verb احتمل, has the sense of to bear, sustain, be admissible or possible. The suffix pronoun refers to its proofs.

fn.1442: Literally: who praise and glorify Him; and what praise! and what glorification!
fn.1443: Literally: one who would believe that this is the language of the state or of the attitude; that is to say, the mute and figurative language that, in our thought, we attribute to objects. “The expression لسان الحال,” says Silvestre de Sacy, “is a metaphor used when speaking of things whose sight alone proves as well and often better than all words the truth of a fact. This is why we say in English: The facts speak clearly. Thus the Arabs say that a man's thinness, his gaunt and haggard appearance, his worn and torn clothes, say, by the language of their state, that he has been the plaything of misfortune, and implore for him the commiseration of generous men.” See Chrest. ar. (2nd edition), vol. I, p. 461. Maimonides means that those are far from the truth who imagine that in the words of the Psalmist it is a matter of a language that exists only in the poet's imagination and that he attributes to the heavens metaphorically; for the celestial spheres, as living and intelligent beings, really have a language within themselves, and not only in our thought, although their language does not consist of words. — The words לשון הענין, by which Ibn-Tibbon’s version renders the Arabic words לסאן אלחאל, are barely intelligible; Al-Harizi, to suggest the true meaning, used: לשון הענין הנראה מהם.

fn.1447: For example, in the morning prayer: פנות צבאות קדושים וכו׳, “the leaders of the hosts of saints, exalting the Almighty, continually tell of the glory and holiness of God.”

One can respond with Joseph ibn Kaspi that here it is a matter of a distinction in the very nature of the vision, which may occur to a man either in a waking state or in a dream. For Abraham, the vision was clear and distinct, whereas for Lot it was confused: one was awake, the other was dreaming; but in each type of vision, the appearance of a human figure is inferior to that of an angel; that is to say, the perception of a sublunary being is below the perception of the superior Intelligences, called angels.

According to some commentators, the author refers to a passage from Ezekiel (ch. I, v. 24): And I heard the sound of their wings, like the sound of great waters, like the voice of the Almighty. It is more than probable that he had in mind a Talmudic passage, which we cite in the following note.
fn.1500: The author undoubtedly refers to a passage from the Babylonian Talmud, treatise Yoma, fol. 20 b, where the following is read: שלש קולות הולכין מסוף העולם ועד סופו ואלו הן קול גלגל חמה וקול המונה של רומי וקול נשמה בשעה שיוצאה מן הגוף "Three voices resound from one end of the world to the other; these are: the voice of the solar sphere, the tumult of the city of Rome, and the cry of the soul as it leaves the body." Cf. Bereshith Rabbah, sect. 6 (fol. 5, col. d).
fn.1501: See Babylonian Talmud, treatise Pesahim, fol. 94 b: חכמי ישראל אומרים גלגל קבוע ומזלות חוזרין וחכמי אומות העולם אומרים גלגל חזזר ומזלות קבועין "The sages of Israel say: The sphere remains fixed and the stars revolve; the sages of the nations of the world say: the sphere revolves and the stars remain fixed." Aristotle also links the opinion of the Pythagoreans with that which attributes movement to the stars themselves and not to the sphere in which they are fixed. See Treatise on the Heavens, book II, chap. 9: ὅσα μὲν γὰρ αὐτὰ φέρεται, ποιεῖ ψόφον ϰαὶ πληγήν. ὅσα δ’ἐν φερομένῳ ἐνδέδεται ἢ ἐνυπάρχει, ϰαθάπερ ἐν τῷ πλοίῳ τὰ μόρια οὐχ οἷόν τε ψοφεῖν, ϰ. τ. λ.. According to Aristotle, who opposes the opinion of the Pythagoreans, the stars remain fixed in their respective spheres, which carry them along in their movement. See ibid., chap. 8.
fn.1502: These words are not found, in our editions of the Talmud, following the passage from Pesahim that we quoted in the preceding note; thus some Jewish authors have expressed their surprise at this citation by Maimonides. See R. Azariah de' Rossi, Me’or Enayim, chap. XI (Berlin ed., f. 48), and the Sefer ha-Berit (Brünn, 1797, 4to), Part I, book II, chap. 10 (fol. 14 b). However, several authors state with Maimonides, and by citing the same passage from the Talmud, that, on this point, the sages of Israel admitted defeat to the sages of other nations. See Isaac Arama, Akedah, chap. XXXVII (Presburg ed., 1849, 8vo, vol. II, fol. 39 a); David Gans, in his astronomical work titled Nehmad ve-na'im, §§ 13 and 25. The latter, after quoting the passage from the treatise Pesahim, adds that the great astronomer Tycho Brahe had told him that the sages of Israel were wrong to admit defeat and to adopt the opinion of the pagan scholars, which was obviously false. — It must be assumed that the words quoted by Maimonides were found, at least in his time, in certain mss. of the Talmud; other authors who quote them may have taken them from Maimonides' work without verifying the citation.
fn.1503: Literally: that for which the demonstration has been verified and established.
fn.1505: Literally: merely counted the single globe, encompassing several spheres. This phrasing is irregular and quite obscure, and it is undoubtedly to make it clearer that Ibn-Tibbon added the words: וחשבוהו לאחד, and they considered it one. The sense is: "They often counted a certain globe as one, although it encompassed several spheres."
fn.1507: The reading we have adopted in our text, although somewhat irregular, is that of most of the mss. In one of the Leiden mss. It would have been more regular to put, instead of the 1st כרה̈, the plural אכר, and this is what Al-Harizi did, who translates: היה מונה כידורי הככבים בלם אחד.
fn.1508: All the mss. have פלך in the singular; it would have been more regular to say מַלְכִּי, in the dual.
fn.1509: Literally: for there is no demonstration that indicates to us the order of these two globes.
fn.1510: The author insists on this point, which must be established, as will be seen later, to include all the spheres within four globes, which, according to the author, are indicated by the four living creatures of Ezekiel. Cf. the following chap. and Part III, chap. II.
fn.1511: See Almagest, or Great Composition of Ptolemy, book IX, ch. I.
fn.1512: Literally: then came later men (or moderns) in Andalusia. Ibn-Tibbon's version bears: אנשים אחרים other men, which is inaccurate; one should have said אנשים אחרונים, as Al-Harizi has it.
fn.1513: The author refers to the كتاب الهيئة or book of astronomy by Abu Muhammad Jabir ibn Aflah, an author who flourished in Spain at the beginning of the 12th th century, and who is often cited by the scholastics under the name of Geber. Ibn Aflah's work is an abridgment of the Almagest; but the author, on several important points, departs from Ptolemy, and notably contests the latter's opinion regarding the position occupied by the planets Venus and Mercury. Cf. my Mélanges de philosophie juive et arabe, pp. 519-520. The Arabic original of Ibn Aflah's work exists in the library of the Escorial, and the Hebrew version in the Imperial Library of Paris. See my Notice sur Joseph-ben-Iehouda in the Journal Asiatique, July 1842, p. 15, note 3. A Latin version by Gerard of Cremona has been published: Gebri filii Afla hispalensis de Astronomia libri IX, etc. Norimbergae, 1533. I have provided a French extract concerning one of the inequalities of the moon in the Comptes rendus des séances de l’Académie des sciences, vol. XVII, pp. 76 et seq. See also, on this work, Delambre, Histoire de l’Astronomie du moyen âge, p. 179 et seq., and on the question of the planets Venus and Mercury, ibid., p. 184. Delambre states in conclusion (p. 185) that it is not possible to decide during what period Geber lived; but the epoch can be specified by our very passage; for we know that Maimonides, who says he was associated in his youth with the son of Ibn Aflah or Geber, was born in 1135. Ibn Rushd or Averroes, born in 520 of the Hegira (1126), when speaking in his Abrégé de l’Almageste of this same question regarding the planets Venus and Mercury, expressly says that Ibn Aflah lived in the same century. The Hebrew version reads: והאיש שהיה בדורנו והוא בן אפלח אלאשבילי וכו׳ (Cf. Moré ha-Moré, p. 89).
fn.1514: On this philosopher, also known by the name Ibn Bajja, see my Mélanges de philosophie juive et arabe, pp. 383 et seq.
fn.1515: The author likely means that these arguments were copied by students during the lessons given to them by the disciple of Ibn al-Sayigh.
fn.1516: The author uses here the word كُرَةُ, corresponding to our word globe, which he employs, as seen above, to designate a compact set of several spheres (أفلاك) nested within one another, as is notably the case here for the globe containing the spheres of the five planets. In several passages, we have had to avoid using the word globe, which would apply more to the body of the star itself than to the sphere in which it revolves.
fn.1517: That is to say, which is nearest to the terrestrial globe, the center of the universe.
fn.1518: Literally: Therefore, the number of figured spheres shall be... their number (I say) shall be four spheres. All the manuscripts have at the beginning of the sentence the verb פתבון in the feminine, making it agree with אלאבר, and we have followed the reading of the manuscripts; but it would be more correct to write פיבון or to delete the word עדר. Ibn Tibbon (in the manuscripts) and Ibn Falaquera (Moré ha-Moré, p. 90) reproduced the error of the Arabic text by translating ויהיו מספר הכדורים. As for the name figure given to the stars, it applies mainly to the signs of the zodiac, called by the Arabs صور الكواكب. Cf. Hammer, Encyclopädische Uebersicht der Wissenschaften des Orients, p. 373. Moses of Narbonne points to the passage in the Centiloquium of Ptolemy (no. 9), where it is stated that the forms or figures, in what is born and perishes, are affected by the celestial figures (τὰ ἐν τῇ γενέσει καὶ φθορᾷ εἴδη, πάσχει ὑπὸ τῶν οὐρανίων εἰδῶν). The same commentator observes that Maimonides intends to allude to the faces of the living creatures from Ezekiel's vision, chap. I, vv. 6 and 10, which would designate the figures of the stars.
fn.1520: The author adds a note here to observe that the word mazzal, which usually designates a constellation or one of the signs of the zodiac, is also used generally in the sense of star or planet.
fn.1521: See loc. cit. fol. 8, col. a. It is clear that in this latter passage, the word mazzal means planet; for the text of the Midrash expressly says that the mazzal which completes its course in thirty days is the moon, and the one which completes it in thirty years is Saturn. It also mentions the sun, which completes its revolution in twelve months, and Jupiter, which completes it in twelve years.
fn.1522: The word الكسوف, being, which is used in the sense of γένεσις, here designates in general the beings of sublunary nature.
fn.1523: Literally: nevertheless, the force of such a star is also specific to such a species.
fn.1524: That is to say, of an animal body; for in the animal as well, the different members and their faculties are under the immediate influence of certain particular forces, although the entire body is dominated by a general force which has been called the directing faculty of the animal body. See vol. I, chap. LXXII, p. 363, and ibid., n. 5.
fn.1525: What the author says here regarding the influence of the moon, not only on the tides but also on the rising of river waters, is a hypothesis already found among some ancients. In the surviving writings of Aristotle, there is scarcely any slight allusion to the flux and reflux of the sea. See Meteorology, book II, ch. 1 (§ 11) and ch. 8 (§ 7), and the note on the first of these two passages in the edition by Mr. J. L. Ideler (Leipzig, 1834, 8vo), vol. I, p. 501. Only in the treatise On the Universe (at the end of chap. 4) is there mention of the relationship said to exist between the tides and the phases of the moon; but it does not appear that the Arabs were acquainted with this treatise, the authenticity of which is at least doubtful. What Maimonides says here (probably following Ibn Sina) seems to be borrowed from Ptolemy's Quadripartitum, book I, at the beginning; we cite the Latin version by Camerarius: “Ipsi fluvii nunc augescunt, nunc decrescunt, secundum lunarem splendorem, ipsaque maria impetu diverso pro eo ac ille oritur aut occidit, feruntur.”
fn.1526: This idea had already been put forward, as a mere conjecture, by Ibn Sina, who says that this sublunary matter, which encompasses the four elements, emanates from the celestial bodies, either from four of them or from a certain number (of bodies) comprised in four classes; it is also possible, he adds, that it emanates from a single celestial body and that its division is due to causes unknown to us. See the passage from Ibn Sina cited by Ibn Falaquera, Moré ha-Moré, p. 90.
fn.1527.sub_0: The four astronomical terms used here by the author are borrowed from Ptolemy's theories on the motion of the planets. By اختلاف, one designates the anomaly or the inequality of a celestial body; the word رجوع designates the apparent retrogradation (προνήγησις) of the five planets, as opposed to their direct motion (ὑπόλειψις) designated in Arabic by the word استقامة, rectitude; finally, by إقامة, is meant what Ptolemy calls the station (στηριγμός) of these same planets, that is, the position where the motion of the celestial body appears to stop. Cf. Almagest, book XII, chap. I. In the Arabic version of the Almagest (Hebrew ms. of the Imperial Library, old collection, no. 441), the terms προνήγησις and ὑπόλειψις are rendered more accurately, the first by تقدّم, moving forward, the second by تأخر, remaining behind. Later, the Arabs substituted the first of these two terms with رجوع, retrogradation, and the second with استقامة, rectitude. Indeed, since the periodic motion of the planets occurs from west to east, the planet, when it appears to retrograde, i.e., when it appears less advanced in longitude, is forward in relation to the diurnal motion from east to west; the more advanced it is in longitude in relation to the periodic motion, the further behind it is in relation to the diurnal motion. Delambre, to explain the two terms used by Ptolemy, expresses himself thus (Notes on the Almagest, following the edition by Abbé Halma, vol. II, p. 16): "One says of a star that precedes another at the meridian, which passes it before him, which moves at its head, that it is προηγούμενος; of a star that passes after him, that it is ἑπόμενος."
fn.1527.sub_1: "But the one that passes first at the meridian is less advanced in longitude; the one following it, ἑπόμενος, which remains behind, ὑπολειπόμενος, is on the contrary more advanced in longitude; thus a star is προηγούμενος when its longitude decreases and it retrogrades; προνήγησις in the language of the Greeks, therefore, corresponds to retrogradation; it is the same motion considered in relation to two different points, just as, in the theory of curves, one may at will place negative abscissas either to the right or left of the center indifferently." — The terms retrogradation and rectitude introduced by the Arabs are also found in the Epitome of the Almagest by Ibn Aflah, book VIII, where the Hebrew version, which alone we can consult, uses for the former the word חזרה, and for the latter the word יושר. It is probably in the work of Ibn Aflah that Maimonides took these terms (cf. above, p. 81).
fn.1528: That is to say: the earth has a sluggish motion and only with difficulty receives the action and the mixing of the other elements.
fn.1529: The author undoubtedly refers to the passage of the Midrash cited at the beginning of this chapter.
fn.1530: See the details that the author gave earlier, chap. IV, and which he will summarize again here. — On the prophetic visions that the author applies to these four causes, Cf. vol. I, chap. XLIX, p. 179, and ibid., note 2, where I did not express myself with accuracy regarding the third and fourth causes; the third is the intellect that our author (along with Avicenna) attributes to each sphere, and the fourth is the separate intelligence or the respective mover of each sphere.
fn.1531: That is to say, as Aristotle demonstrated in the Physics and the Metaphysics. Cf. the introduction, XIIIth proposition, above, p. 13, and ibid., n. 3.
fn.1532: In other words: for motion to be perpetual and continuous, it must necessarily be circular.
fn.1533: For this passage and for what follows, cf. vol. I, chap. LXXII, pp. 360, 363-364, and 368. We prefer to use here the word force instead of the word faculty, which we used in chap. LXXII of the first part.
fn.1534: The editions of Ibn Tibbon's version generally bear במלאכה מחשבית; one should read במלאכה כמחשבית (as in the mss. and the editio princeps), that is to say, במלאכה כמלאכת המחשבת. Ibn Falaquera translates: במלאכה כמו האומנות (Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 91). The Arabic word المهنية designates the faculty by which man possesses the arts; this is how Maimonides himself defines elsewhere the word مُهَنَّى. See the end of the first of the Eight Chapters (in Pococke's Porta Mosis, p. 189), where Ibn Tibbon renders this word as מלאכת מחשבת. Cf. vol. I of this work, p. 210, n. 1.
fn.1535: This passage is not found in our editions of the Midrash Tanhuma, which, as is known, are very incomplete. The author of the Megalleh Amukot appears to allude to this passage when speaking of the mystery of the four degrees of Jacob's ladder (סוד ד' שבילות בסולם שראה יעקב). See the book Yalkut Reubeni, article מלאך, no. 99.
fn.1536: See, for example, Pirke de-Rabbi Eliezer, chap. IV, where it is said that the throne of God is surrounded by four legions of angels who have at their head four archangels: Michael, Gabriel, Uriel, and Raphael. Cf. the Midrash on Numbers or Bemidbar Rabbah, sect. 2 (fol. 179, col. a).
fn.1537: The word tarshish, which designates a precious stone, is taken here by the rabbis in the sense of sea; now, as the sea, according to rabbinic tradition, constitutes a third of the world, an allusion was found in the passage from Daniel to the size of each of the three worlds, called angels. The three worlds, as will be seen, are: that of the separate intelligences, that of the celestial spheres, and the sublunary world. — The passage that Maimonides interprets here is found in Bereshit Rabbah, sect. 68 (fol. 61, col. b); cf. Babylonian Talmud, treatise Hullin, fol. 91 b.

In the two mountains, commentators have seen either matter and form, or the two firmaments of which the author spoke at the beginning of chap. IX.
fn.1539: The author will return to this at the end of chapters XXIX and XLIII of this second part, without however clearly stating which homonymy he means.
fn.1540: Regarding the Arabic word פקה, see vol. I, p. 7, n. 1. The author refers to his Mishneh Torah (repetition of the law) or Epitome of the Talmud; the explanation he indicates here is found in book I, treatise Yesode ha-Torah, chap. 2, § 3.
fn.1541: In the editions of Ibn Tibbon's version, the word למעלה is superfluous; it is not found in the mss.

The Arabic text leaves some uncertainty; the words ולא קלבה could also be linked to what precedes, and in this case one should translate: '...he will not need to tire his body or his heart; he will be free of agitation, but he will naturally descend to the lowest degree.'
fn.1544: That is to say: it does not seek to provide rigorous demonstrations for all its theorems; for it is sometimes content with certain hypotheses suitable for explaining the phenomena, such as, for example, the hypotheses of epicycles and eccentrics.
fn.1545: Literally: there are those that are demonstrable subjects (i.e., of which it can be demonstrated) that they are so.
fn.1546: Literally: a sphere of circumvolution. See on this term vol. I, p. 358, n. 2.
fn.1547: In other words: the astronomer makes suppositions that are undemonstrable in themselves, with the goal of justifying the anomalies observed in the movement of the stars and showing that fundamentally this movement remains circular and always uniform; all that is required of him is that his suppositions satisfy the observations.
fn.1548: The text says: He proposes; the subject of the verb is צאחב אלהיאה̈, the astronomer.
fn.1549: See Almagest, book III, chaps. 3 and 4. Ptolemy shows that the apparent anomaly of the sun can be explained as well by the hypothesis of an epicycle as by that of an eccentric circle; but he finds it more reasonable to adhere to the hypothesis of the eccentric, because it is simpler and because it supposes only one movement, rather than two.
fn.1550: Instead of עולנא (properly: we trust in, we are certain), several mss. have עמלנא or עלמנא, readings which do not offer a suitable sense here. Moreover, the preposition עלי, which follows the verb, also speaks in favor of the reading we have adopted.
fn.1551: That is to say: even if one were to admit that each of the fixed stars is in a particular sphere, this would in no way disrupt the classification we have adopted, by dividing all the celestial spheres into four groups, in relation to the four species of forces emanating from them.

This latter reading, which means to limit, was followed by the two Hebrew translators; Ibn Tibbon has לגבוׄל, and Al-Harizi להגבלת. The reading we have adopted is preferred by Ibn Falaquera; See Moreh ha-Moreh, appendix, p. 154.
fn.1554: The verb פיץׄ (فيض), which we are obliged to render in different ways, properly means: to pour out, to shed, to flow, to emanate. See on this expression the following chapter, and vol. I, p. 244, n. 1.
fn.1555: By the principles or origins of the celestial spheres, one must understand the intelligences.
fn.1556: Literally: the existence, the goal, and the end of this giver are not solely, etc.
fn.1557: Of the two words ענה מנה, which are found in all the mss., the first refers to the fortune (אלמאל), and the second to the person (אכׄר), literally: of whom there remains on his part.
fn.1558: That is to say, each separate intelligence, in producing the intelligence that is below it, causes another production to emanate from it, which is one of the celestial spheres.
fn.1559: That is to say, the doctors, who carry and propagate the tradition. Cf. above, page 65, n. 3.
fn.1560: Most of the mss., and the best ones, carry חכמנא, and it must be pronounced حكمنا (plur. of حكمة). fn.1569: Cf. above, p. 6, n. 2, and p. 7, n. 2.

fn.1574: That is to say, the last of the separate intelligences, which is the active intellect.
fn.1575: Ibn Tibbon translates: ככל אשר יזדמן דבר; this version is criticized by Ibn Falaquéra (Moré ha-Moré, appendix, p. 154), who prefers to translate: כל דבר שהוא מוכן. Al-Harizi's version reads: בעוד שיזדמן דבר מוכן, whenever a prepared thing is encountered.
fn.1576: Cf. Ibn Gabirol, The Source of Life, book V, § 64 (Mélanges de philosophie juive et arabe, p. 138).

fn.1580: Literally: The intention is rather the understanding of the meaning of the emanation which is predicated of God and of the intelligences—that is to say, the angels—because they are incorporeal.
fn.1581: That is to say, according to their respective positions relative to one another.
fn.1582: Literally: It is through this that one entered into the judgments of the stars or into astrology. fn.1583: The word ונמדתדל, and we guide ourselves, was not rendered in the Hebrew versions. Al-Harizi ends this chapter with the words נשכיל ונלך באורח משור. Ibn Falaquéra (Moré ha-Moré, p. 94) translates the final words thus: נשכיל וינחה אותנו ויורנו השכל.
fn.1584: Literally: the opinions of men concerning the eternity of the world or its novelty, among all those who have admitted that a God exists, are three opinions. — For אלאה מוזֹוד, the manuscripts generally have אלאהא מוזֹודא, in the accusative, which is incorrect.
fn.1585: Literally: and likewise everything that is drawn from it (as a consequence) in the mind. Ibn Tibbon translates: וכן כל מה שיעלה בשכל; this version is rightly criticized by Ibn Falaquéra (Moré ha-Moré, Appendix, p. 154), who observes that the Arabic verb ינזֹר (يَنْجَرُّ) resembles the Hebrew form יִגָּרר (niphal of גרר, to drag or draw), and that it is not appropriate here to translate the Arabic word דהן, which means mind or thought, by שכל, intelligence.
fn.1586: That is to say, although it does not fall under the category of quality, like blackness, whiteness, and most accidents.
fn.1587: See above, p. 15, the <small>XV</small><sup>th</sup> proposition, and the notes.
fn.1588: Literally: so that its thing (or its idea) has made them perplexed.
fn.1590: Literally: but in one state after another (another) state. Ibn Tibbon translates: אבל ישתנה מענין אל ענין. One of the Leiden manuscripts (no. 18) has: יתגיר פי חאלה̈ בעד חאלה̈; but, this construction being incorrect, I believe that the copyist took the liberty of adding a word here (יתגיר), following the Hebrew version, as he has done in other places.
fn.1591: See Genesis 21:33, and cf. Vol. I, p. 3, note 2.
fn.1592: Literally: that any being whatever having matter and form should be born from the absolute non-being of this matter, nor that it should perish into the absolute non-being of this matter. All manuscripts have on both occasions תלך אלמאדה̈, this matter; likewise, the versions of Ibn Tibbon and Al-Harizi: החמר ההוא. In Ibn Falaquéra's Moré ha-Moré, both in the printed edition (p. 95) and in the manuscripts, one reads אותה הצורה, this form; but this reading is inadmissible.
fn.1593: Ibn Tibbon's version adds the words כנושא אחד in the same subject. Indeed, these words are understood in the Arabic text; for there is truly a contradiction only when assuming two contraries united at the same instant and in the same subject. Cf. Part I, chap. LXXV, at the end of the first method (p. 443) and Part III, chap. XV.
fn.1594: See Part III of this work, chap. xv.
fn.1595: Editions of Ibn Tibbon's version generally read אם כן; one should read אבל, as found in the manuscripts.
fn.1596: See Phys., book VIII, chap. 1, where Aristotle says that Plato alone considered time as born; it was born, he said, at the same time as the heavens, which themselves are born: ἅμα μὲν γὰρ αὐτὸν τῷ οὐρανῷ γεγονέναι, τὸν δ’ οὐρανὸν γεγονέναι φησίν. It will be noted that Aristotle says only that, according to Plato, the heavens were produced, but not that they must perish; elsewhere Aristotle even expressly says that, according to the Timaeus, the heavens, although born, are imperishable and will last forever (see the treatise On the Heavens, book I, at the end of chap. 10). It is therefore incorrect for Maimonides to say here and later (chap. XV and XXV) that, according to Plato, the heavens are born and subject to corruption. Cf. Ibn Falaquéra, Moré ha-Moré, p. 95.
fn.1597: See the Timaeus, p. 28 B-C: Γέγονεν (ὁ οὐρανός) · ὁρατὸς γαπτός τέ ἐστι καὶ σῶμα ἔχων, πάντα δὲ τὰ τοιαῦτα αἰσθητά, τὰ δὲ αἰσθητά, δόξῃ περιληπτά μετὰ αἰσθήσεως, γιγνόμενα καὶ γεννητά ἐφάνη. — Maimonides might have read the Timaeus, of which there existed an Arabic translation entitled קלאב קטימאווס (See Wenrich, De auctorum graecorum versionibus, etc., p. 118). Almost all Arabic manuscripts, as well as the two Hebrew versions, have לטמאוס, to Timaeus; we have reproduced this reading, although it contains an inaccuracy. In one of our manuscripts, we read more precisely: פי בתאבה טימאוס (without ל), in his book Timaeus; likewise in Moré ha-Moré, loc. cit.: בספרו טימיאוס.
fn.1598.sub_0: It can be seen that, according to Maimonides, the difference between Plato and Aristotle is this: that the latter admits not only the eternity of prime matter, but also that of motion and time; whereas Plato, while admitting the eternity of matter and chaos, nevertheless believes that the world, as it is, had a beginning, that the heavens were, like sublunary things, produced from chaos, and that consequently motion and time had a beginning. It is in this sense that Plato's opinion was generally interpreted by the Arabs and the Scholastics, and it is in this sense also that one of the most learned adherents of the new Platonic school of Italy expresses himself. This is how Leone Ebreo speaks on this question (Dialoghi di amore, III, Venice edition, 1572, fol. 145 et seq.): «Concedendo tutti gli huomini che’l sommo Dio genitore et opifice del mondo sia eterno, senza alcun principio temporale, son divisi nella produttion del mondo, se è ab eterno, o da qualche tempo in quà.
fn.1598.sub_1: Molti dei filosofi tengono essere prodotto ab eterno da Dio, e non havere mai havuto principio temporale, così come esso Dio non l’ha mai havuto, et di questa opinione è il grande Aristolile, et tutti i peripatetici… Ma gli fideli, et tutti quelli che credono la sacra legge di Moise, tengono che’l mondo fusse non ab eterno produtto, anzi di nulla creato in principio temporale, et ancora alcuni dei filosofi par que sentino questo; per quali è il divino Platone, che nel Timeo pone il mondo essere fatto et genito da Dio, produtto del chaos, che è la materia confusa, del quale le cose sono generate… È ben vero che lui fa il chaos, di che le cose sono fatte, eterno, cioè eternalmente produtto da Dio, laquai cosa non tengono gli fideli; perche loro tengono che fino all’ hora della creatione solo Dio fusse in essere senza mondo, et senza chaos, et che l’omnipotentia di Dio di nulla tutte le cose in principio di tempo habbia produtto, che in effetto non par già chiaramente in Moise, che’l ponga materia coeterna a Dio.— Sono adunque tre opinioni nella produttione del mondo da Dio: la prima d’Aristotile, che tutto il mondo fue produtto ab eterno; la seconda di Platone, che solamente la materia, o chaos, fue produtto ab eterno, ma il mondo in principio di tempo; et la terza delli fideli, che tutto sia produtto di nulla in principio di tempo.» — But one recognizes from our passage that in the time of Maimonides, as in all eras, opinions were divided on the true sense of Plato's doctrine; and, indeed, Plato's poetic language and the mythical veil under which he often presents his doctrines only too well justify this divergence of opinions. While several of the oldest Platonists, and later the Neoplatonists, claimed that Plato had admitted, like Aristotle, the eternity of the world, others on the contrary (notably some Christians, such as Clement of Alexandria) went so far as to maintain that Plato had professed the doctrine of creation ex nihilo, considering God to be the author not only of the order of the world, but of matter itself. The same divergence is still observed among the scholars of our day. On this subject, see Zeller, Die Philosophie der Griechen, vol. II, p. 508 et seq. (2nd ed. Tübingen, 1859), and Henri Martin, Études sur le Timée de Platon, vol. II, p. 179 et seq.
fn.1598.sub_2: This latter scholar, after a thorough examination of the texts, arrives at conclusions that agree with the opinion of Maimonides and Leone Ebreo, namely that, according to the Timaeus, 1. God did not create the prime matter of bodies, that is, the indeterminate substance; 2. he did not even create secondary matter, that is, eternal chaos; 3. he produced the order of the world, but not from all eternity. — The distinction between incorporeal prime matter and corporeal chaos is of no interest to us here, any more than the question of how Plato understood prime matter and in what way his doctrine, in this regard, differs from that of Aristotle. Suffice it to say that Plato admits an eternal principle opposed to the idea, as blind necessity is to reason, non-being to being, the variable and the multiple to the permanent and the absolute one. But this is not the ὕλη of Aristotle, that being in potentiality which necessarily calls for form to become being in actuality; for, according to Plato, it is with consciousness and freedom, and not by necessity, that the idea realizes itself in the indeterminate substratum, which it causes to pass from confusion to order. The term ὕλη is itself unknown to Plato, although Aristotle uses this term when speaking of his master's doctrine. This confused and indeterminate substance that the idea orders and in which it manifests itself is called by Plato: that which receives the imprint (τὸ ἐϰμαγεῖον), that in which things are born, the place, space, etc.; it is also presented as the mother or the receptacle and the nurse of all generation; and Plato himself says (Timaeus, p. 49 a) that it is a species quite obscure and very difficult to understand. Cf. Ritter, Geschichte der Philosophie, vol. II, p. 347 et seq.; Brandis, Handbuch der Geschichte der griechisch-römischen Philosophie, vol. II, A, p. 297 et seq.; Zeller, l. c., p. 457 et seq.; Henri Martin, l. c., vol. I, p. 16 et seq.
fn.1599: Literally: has never ceased and will never cease (to be) thus.
fn.1600: The words ולא יטרי פיה טאר (literally: and nothing fresh will happen there, or nothing new) are not expressed in Ibn Tibbon's version; that of Al-Harizi reads: ולא יתחדש בו מתחדש ממה שאין בטבעו ולא יוסיף בו תוספת שהיא חוץ מן הםברא בשום פנים.
fn.1601: In the editions of Ibn Tibbon's version, one must add here the words הווים נפםדים, which are found in the manuscripts and in the editio princeps.
fn.1602: The author alludes to the ancient atomists, according to whom the birth and destruction of things consist in the aggregation and separation of atoms. Cf. vol. I of this work, p. 378.
fn.1603: Literally: whose refutation has already been demonstrated.
fn.1604: That is to say, some thinkers even consider creation ex nihilo as a necessary and perfectly demonstrable thing. The author is evidently alluding to the Mutakallimun, who are often designated by the name אהל אלנטׄר. See vol. I, p. 184, note 3, and ibid. chapter LXXIV.
fn.1605: All the manuscripts have פי תביין ותלכׄיץ; Ibn Tibbon's version has only בביאור; that of Al-Harizi reads לברר ולבאר.
fn.1606: The author addresses, as in other places, the disciple for whom he wrote this work. Cf. vol. I, p. 312, n. 3.
fn.1607: Literally: and if the objection or the doubt, in that which we object or which we make doubtful against it in one of them (i.e., the opinions), is well established. Instead of נרד או, several manuscripts read נריר אן; but the two Hebrew versions confirm the reading we have adopted and which is also required by the sense of the sentence.
fn.1608: The author will cite seven demonstrations by which the Peripatetics believed they could establish the eternity of the world. These seven demonstrative methods were cited, following Maimonides, and refuted by Albertus Magnus. See Summa Theologiae, part II, tractate I, question IV, section 3 (Opp., vol. XVIII, p. 58): "De septem viis quas collegit rabbi Moyses, quibus probatur mundi aeternitas."
fn.1609: The author intends to refer to the motion of the celestial sphere. In the editions of Ibn Tibbon's version, the word התנועה is missing here; the manuscripts contain: ר״ל התנועה המוחלטת.
fn.1610: This demonstration is based on Aristotle's reasoning in book VIII, chapter I of the Physics.
fn.1611: See the XV<sup>th</sup> of the propositions placed at the beginning of this II<sup>nd</sup> part (p. 15).
fn.1612: This demonstration is taken from book I of the Physics, chapter 9, where Aristotle shows that only relative matter is perishable—that is, that which is matter for something else without being so in itself. Absolutely prime matter—that is, that which is potency and substratum in an absolute sense—cannot be subject to birth and corruption; for if it were born, it would necessarily have a substratum from which it was born—that is, a substratum of a nature identical to its own, such that it would have existed before being born: ὡς μὲν γὰρ τὸ ἐν ᾧ, ϰαθ’ αὑτὸ φθείρεται (ἡ ὕλη). τὸ γὰρ φθειρόμενον ἐν τούτῳ ἐστὶν ἡ στέρησις. ὡς δὲ ϰατα δύναμιν οὐ ϰαθ’ αὑτὸ ἀλλ’ ἄφθαρτον ϰαὶ ἀγένητον ἀνάγϰη αὐτὴν εἶναι, εἴτε γὰρ ἐγίγνετο, ὑποϰεῖσταί τι δεῖ πρῶτον, τὸ ἐξ οὗ ἐνυπάρχοντος τοῦτο δ’ἐστὶν αὐτὴ ἡφύσις, ὥστ’ ἔσται πρὶν γενέσθαι.
fn.1613: For, as prime matter must receive form, which comes to it through motion, one necessarily traces back to the eternal motion of the celestial sphere, by which the eternity of the world has been demonstrated.
fn.1614: Motion in a straight line is directed toward a point opposite the starting point, whereas circular motion is always directed toward its starting point, so that no kind of contrariety or opposition can be indicated therein. Cf. above, chap. IV, p. 53.
fn.1615: See the treatise On the Heavens, book I, chapter 3, where Aristotle, speaking of the celestial body that has circular motion, expresses himself as follows: ὁμοίως δ’ εὔλογον ὑπολαβεῖν περὶ αὐτοῦ ϰαὶ ὅτι ἀγένητον ϰαὶ ἄφθαρτον ϰαὶ ἀνανξὲς ϰαὶ ἀναλλοίωτον, διὰ τὸ γίγνεσθαι μὲν ἅπαν τὸ γιγνόμενον ἐξ ἐναντίον τε ϰαὶ ὑποϰειμένου τινός, ϰαὶ φθείρεσθαι ὡσαύτως ὑποϰειμένου τέ τινος ϰαὶ ἐναντίου ϰαὶ εἰς ἐναντίον, ϰαθάπερ ἐν τοῖς πρώτοις εἴρηται λόγοις. ϰ. τ. λ. Cf. Phys., book I, chap. 5.
fn.1616: See the treatise On the Heavens, book I, chap. 10 et seq.; in chapter 12 (page 283 a, Bekker ed.), Aristotle summarizes in these terms: τὸ δὴ φάναι μηδὲν ϰωλύειν γινόμενόν τι ἄφθαρτον εἶναι ϰαὶ ἀγένητον ὂν φθαρῆναι… ἀναιρεῖν ἐστὶ τῶν δεδομένων τι.
fn.1617: Albertus Magnus (loc. cit., pp. 58-59), without reproducing the entire demonstration, presents its conclusion as follows: "Tertia via est sumpta de natura cœli, cujus materia elongata est a generatione et corruptione; propter quod omnes antiqui convenerunt, quod cœlum esset locus Dei. Manente autem cœlo nunquam defuit motus ejus; manente motu, nunquam cessavit mundus producere animalia et plantas. Substantia orbis et motus sine initio manserunt, et manent, et manebunt sine fine; ergo mundus sine initio mansit, manet, et manebit sine fine."
fn.1618: We have shown above, p. 27, n. 1, that the proposition in question rests only on an interpretation of a passage from Aristotle accepted by Al-Farabi, but which Ibn Rushd declares to be erroneous. — Albertus Magnus (loc. cit. p. 59) also points out that this IVth method does not belong to Aristotle, but to his Greek and Arabic commentators; however, he is undoubtedly mistaken in also counting Averroes among those who accepted it.
fn.1619: That is to say: If one were to admit a God who was the creator of the world, this God could not be the absolute agent always in act; such an agent presupposes the eternity of the action, and, consequently, the eternity of the world. Cf. above, chap. I, fourth speculation (p. 43).
fn.1620: In the editions of Ibn Tibbon's version, a few words of this last sentence are missing; the manuscripts contain: וזהו כמו כן קשה מאד וזהו אשר צריך כל משכיל להתירה ולהראות סודו.
fn.1621: Properly: of the things that invite or call.
fn.1622: The word המקרים in the editions of Ibn Tibbon's version is an error; the manuscripts contain המביאים.
fn.1623: See, e.g., the treatise On the Heavens, book I, at the end of chap. 4: ὁ δὲ θεὸς ϰαὶ ἡ φύσις οὐδὲν μάτην ποιοῦσιν. On the Parts of Animals, book IV, chap. 13: ….. ἐπεὶ οὔτε περίεργον οὐδὲν οὐδὲν μάτην ἡ φύσις ποιεῖ.
fn.1624: Literally: and there is no extreme (perfection) after him. Ibn Tibbon translates: ואי אפשר טוב ממנו, and it is not possible that there be anything better; Al-Harizi translates literally: ואין אחריו תכלית
fn.1625: Literally: In the Eternity that has not ceased. Instead of אלאזל, eternity, one of the Leiden manuscripts (no. 18) contains אלחאל the state; similarly Ibn Tibbon: בענין אשר לא סר. Al-Harizi translates: ולא חדש חרוש מקודם.
fn.1626: I must note that for the numerals מיי אלף (مِنْ أَلْفِ), none of the manuscripts I was able to consult present the spelling I have adopted. Some of these manuscripts contain מנוין אלאף, others מיין אלאף. The plural אלאף (آلاف) is here contrary to the rules of Arabic grammar; as for the form מיין (مدين, genitive pl.), it was probably written thus by Maimonides himself; however, I felt it necessary to substitute the construct state متى, though I admit I have never encountered this form.
fn.1627: Literally: And (one proceeded) also by way of argumentation from what is generally known, or admitted. This sentence has no verb, and one proceeded must be understood; the author means that the dialectical syllogism was employed, which has as its basis the consensus of the totality or the majority of men, and which starts not from principles of absolute truth, but only from probable opinions (ἐξ ἐνδόξων). See Aristotle, Topics, book I, chap. 1, and cf. vol. I, p. 39, n. 1.
fn.1628: That is to say, the perpetuity of the Heaven. — See the treatise On the Heavens, book I, chap. 3: ἔοιϰε δ’ὅ τε λόγος φαινομένοις μαρτυρεῖν ϰαὶ τὰ φαινόμενα τῷ λόγῳ πάντες γὰρ ἄνθρωποι περὶ θεῶν ἔχουσιν ὑπόληψιν ϰαὶ πάντες τὸν ἀνοτάτω τῷ θείῳ τόπον ἀποδιδίασι, ϰαὶ βάρβαροι ϰαὶ Ἕλληνες, ὅσοι περ εἶναι νομίζουσι θεούς, δῆλον ὅτι ὡς τῷ ἀθανάτῳ τὸ ἀθάνατον συνηρτημένον. Averroes, in his large commentary (folio ed., vol. V, f. 9, col. b), says in explaining this passage: "Et cum dixit quod sensus testatur rationi, in hac ratione incœpit dare significationes ex propositionibus famosis (ἐξ ἐνδόξων) apud plures gentes, etc."
fn.1629: That is to say, by dialectical syllogisms.
fn.1630: Instead of כ״פית (خَفِيَتْ) (several manuscripts contain כ״פאת, for خَفَتْ), which is merely a very common spelling error in verbs whose 3rd radical is a quiescent letter. Cf. vol. I, page 24, at the end of the note.
fn.1631: The author undoubtedly had in mind the passage from Book VIIIth (ch. 1) of the Physics, which we cited above, p. 109, n. 1; however, the citation is not verbatim.
fn.1632: Literally: by the fact that the physicists who preceded thought likewise.
fn.1633: The words בעד ד̇לך, after that, were not rendered in Ibn Tibbon's version.
fn.1634: See the treatise On the Heavens, Book I, at the beginning of chap. 10: Τοὺτων δὲ διωρισμένων λέγωμεν μετὰ ταῦτα πότερον ἀγένητος ἢ γενητὸς καὶ ἄφθαρτος ἢ φθαρτός. — It would be pointless to dwell on the phrasings of the Arabic version that Maimonides had before him; a striking example of the manner in which it paraphrased the Greek text will be seen shortly.
fn.1635: In Ibn Tibbon's version, the words הווים נפסדים must be deleted; the best manuscripts of this version have only בהתהוות השמים. In some manuscripts, however, one reads: בהיות השמים הווים נפמדים, and similarly in one of the Leiden manuscripts (no. 18), בכון אלסמא כאאינה̈ פאסדה̈; but this variant must be attributed to the lack of understanding of the copyists, who do not comprehend the meaning of the Arabic word كُون used here in the sense of λὲνεσις.
fn.1636: Literally: by conceding to him what he concedes to himself regarding the accuracy of the arguments. — One would hardly recognize, in the citation just read, the Greek text to which it corresponds (loc. cit.: ἅμα δὲ καὶ μᾶλλον ἂν εἴη πιστὰ κ. τ. λ.), of which the following is a literal translation: "What is about to be said will appear more credible to those who have first heard the justifications of the opposing reasons; for it would hardly befit us to appear to judge in absentia. Indeed, those who wish to pronounce a sufficiently true judgment must be arbiters and not adversaries." However, the accuracy of Maimonides' citation, according to the Arabic version, is guaranteed for us by the Arab-Latin version, which, in turn, has poorly paraphrased the Arabic terms. See the Works of Aristotle with the commentaries of Averroes, folio edition, vol. V, f. 32, col. d: "Et nos cum hoc fecerimus, tune sermo noster erit dignior ut recipiatur apud eos qui sont bonæ discretionis (vel considerationis in discretione ipsorum, vel intellectu); et maxime, cum audierint rationes contradicentium primo. Et jam scimus quod cum nos dixerimus in aliquo, necesse est ut sic sit, aut sic visum est nobis, et cum hac opinione et necessitate non dixerimus rationes contradicentium in eis, tunc minus erunt recipiendæ apud audientes ex distinguentibus propositiones signorum, et contemplationes intellectuum; et oportet qui voluerit judicare vere, ut non sit contradicens. Et odiens eum qui contradicit: sed oportet esse diligentem ipsum et pacificum ei. Et ex pacificatione est ut concedat ei, sicut concederet sibi de sermonibus recte et de scientia apud terminos demonstrationum". — The Latin version of the treatise On the Heavens, attributed in the printed edition to Paul the Israelite, is, for the most part, identical to that of Michael Scot, which is found in several manuscripts of the Imperial Library.
fn.1637: Editions of Ibn Tibbon's version generally have הדעת; one should read דעת, without the article, as found in the editio princeps.
fn.1638: The author refers to those who admit that the heaven had a temporal beginning, but that it was formed from an eternal matter, and that upon perishing, it returns to this matter; that is to say, it is in the same conditions as sublunar things. See chap. XIII, the <small>II</small><sup>nd</sup> opinion.
fn.1639: That is to say, we do not share Aristotle's opinion, although from a certain point of view it is closer to the truth.
fn.1640: Literally: without realizing that he has demonstrated. The author says ironically that, since Aristotle does not present his proofs as true demonstrations, it is possible that he himself did not realize the full force of his arguments.
fn.1641: Literally: that the methods for finding proofs on these matters leave their doors closed before us.
fn.1642: That is to say, in all these matters there is no principle, no axiom, that can serve as a starting point for a demonstration.
fn.1643: See Topics, Book I, ch. 11: ...... ϰαὶ περὶ ὧν λόγον μὴ ἔχομεν, ὄντων μεγάλων χαλεπὸν οἰόμενοι εἶναι τὸ διὰ τί ἀποδοῦναι, οἷον πότερον ὁ ϰόסμος ἀΐδιος, ἢ οὔ. — Instead of or which appear grave to us, one should say, according to the Greek text: because they are grave. All the Arabic manuscripts of the Guide carry או הי עט̇ימה̈ ענדנא; in the Arabic version of the Topics (Ar. MS of the Imperial Library, 882 a, f. 247 b), one reads: اذ هي عظيمة لظנنا .
fn.1644: Moses of Narbonne was already no longer acquainted with the work of al-Farabi alluded to here: the author, he says, is content to cite it briefly because it was very well known then; but it has not reached us.
fn.1645: Cf. Galen, De Hippocratis et Platonis placitis, Book IX, chap. 7 (Kühn ed., vol. V, p. 780), where Galen treats as idle and useless the question of knowing whether the world is born or not. Οὐ γὰρ δή, ὥσπερ γεγονέναι τὸν ϰόσμον ἢ μὴ γεγονέναι, ζητεῖν ἄχρηστον, οὕτω ϰαὶ περὶ προνοίας ϰαὶ θεῶν.
fn.1646: The author is referring to the manner in which Aristotle expresses himself in the various passages cited in this chapter, and he means that nothing can be inferred from these vague expressions, by which the opinion of the eternity of the world is neither confirmed nor destroyed or cast into doubt.
fn.1647: Literally: because their discourse is not in the path of instruction (methodical). The word مَعْرِضُ , place where one meets, is used, like مَجْرَىٰ , in the sense of way, manner, method.
fn.1648: Literally: the soul weakens in the belief of, etc.
fn.1649: Instead of יקבל, one of the two Leiden manuscripts (no. 18) carries יטלק; the other (no. 221) has יטלב
fn.1651: That is to say, the world was not created, as we say, but is eternal.
fn.1652: The text says: being possible, that is to say, as in this question both hypotheses are possible...
fn.1653: Literally: It will be accepted by me on the part of prophecy. Here again the author has expressed himself in an elliptical and somewhat illogical manner; for it is not the question that he accepts, but the solution.
fn.1654: On the word ترجيح, see vol. I, p. 428, note 3.
fn.1655: Cf. on this passage, vol. I, p. 226, and ibid., note 3.
fn.1656: The verb تمحل does not come here from the root محل, but must be considered as a denominative verb, derived from مُحَال, an inadmissible, absurd thing, just as from مَكَان, place, one forms the verb تمكن, to fix oneself in a place. See my Notice on Abu’l-Walid, etc., pp. 188 and 189 (Journal Asiatique, November-December 1850, pp. 410 and 411).
fn.1657: Literally: suppose then, regarding what we have given as an example, that, etc. פאפרץ̇ must be considered an imperative (فَافْرِضْ); in Ibn Tibbon's version, instead of ונניח, the MSS have, more accurately, והנח. The supposition that the author is about to make refers to the example of the formation of the fetus, which he cited above.
fn.1658: فِطْرَة signifies natural, natural disposition one brings at birth. Cf. Appendix to the Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 149 (first note on chap. II of Part I).
