See the Appendix to the Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 154. Al-Ḥarizi translates in the same sense: והתעסקו אנשים, men occupied themselves. Indeed, the author has not expressed himself with all the desirable clarity; perhaps he meant that the father went, with several servants to a solitary island, to complete his child's education there.
fn.1660: Literally: and he will establish the demonstration against all these true things, (to show) that they are impossible.
fn.1661: Ibn Tibbon has: כים סתום, a closed purse; this translation was rightly criticized by Ibn Falaquera (Appendix to the Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 154), who observes that the Arabic word ספיק does not mean firm, but strong, coarse or thick. Al-Ḥarizi has כלי קשה.
fn.1662: Literally: that it has been such from such, that is to say, it has had such a form that developed from another such form.
fn.1663: The author refers to the methods by which Aristotle demonstrates the eternity of the world, and which are enumerated in chap. XIV.
fn.1664: See chap. XIV, the second method.
fn.1665: That is to say: It is indeed true, as Aristotle says, that it was not born from something; but nothing prevents us from admitting that it emerged from absolute nothingness.
fn.1666: In other words: it is as it must be to correspond to the idea of prime matter; for, after having emerged from nothingness, it is absolutely without form.
fn.1667: That is to say: although in our thought it is a matter without form, in reality it exists only with form; for, immediately after its production, forms succeed each other within it incessantly and give way to one another.
fn.1668: See chap. XIV, the first method.
fn.1669: That is to say, we can grant this, without it resulting in a proof against our system of creation.
fn.1670: Literally: for we maintain that, after movement has existed according to that nature upon which it was fixed, it is unimaginable that it could have been born and perish by a total birth and a total corruption, as partial movements which are born are born, and as partial movements perish. The author has expressed himself in a convoluted and unclear manner. The sense is: We admit with Aristotle that the universal movement of the world is of such a nature that it could not have been born from a prior movement that caused it to pass from potentiality to actuality, as occurs in partial movements, for example in that of animals. But we do not conclude from this that universal movement is eternal; for, while it is true that it could not have had a prior movement as its cause, it could nevertheless have had a beginning and have been created by God. It is in this sense that Albert the Great refutes the first method of Aristotle, and he summarizes his refutation in these terms: 'Et de hac via constat, per antedicta, quod non probat motum non incepisse per creationem, sed quod non incepit per mutationem et motum. ' See Summa theologiae, part II, tract. I, quest. IV, partic. 3 (opp. vol. XVIII, p. 58, col. b).
fn.1671: The author refers to time, which is also discussed in this first method.
fn.1672: The author refutes here, in passing, an argument drawn from the circular movement of the celestial sphere; since this movement has no starting point, it has been claimed that one can conclude from this that it must be eternal. This argument is not included in the methods of chap. XIV.
fn.1673: See chap. XIV, the fourth method.
fn.1674: See chap. XIV, the third method.
fn.1675: The author means: We grant to Aristotle that in the heaven, as it is, there is no contrariety by reason of which it must perish, and that, consequently, it could not have been born as sublunar things are born; but neither do we say at all that it was born and composed like the latter; and it does not follow from Aristotle's thesis that God could not have created it, by bringing it out of nothingness into absolute simplicity.
fn.1676: The words הנמצא לו, which the editions of Ibn Tibbon's version add here, are found neither in the manuscripts of that version, nor in that of Al-Ḥarizi.
fn.1677: The author is no doubt alluding to the discussion between the school of Shammai and that of Hillel, reported in the Babylonian Talmud, treatise Ḥagigah, fol. 12 a.
fn.1678: See below, chap. XXX, where the author explains at length various details of the creation.
fn.1679: That is to say, on the subject treated in the present chapter, which aims to show that Aristotle's arguments prove nothing against creation.
fn.1680: That is to say, a being of a different nature, which is the Divinity.
fn.1681: In Ibn Tibbon's version, the Arabic word רומנא, desire, effort, was rendered by מחשבתנו, our thought; Ibn Falaquera (loc. cit.) observes that it must be translated by השתדלותנו. Al-Ḥarizi has בקשתנו.
fn.1682: The author alludes to the reproach he himself addressed to the Mutakallimun, namely, that their system is in open revolt against the laws of nature. See Part I, chap. LXXI, p. 349 et seq.
fn.1683: See chap. XIV, methods V, VI, and VII.
fn.1684: Literally: is the one by which we would be forced, according to their opinion, to admit that, etc.
fn.1685: See chap. XIV, the fifth method.
fn.1686: Literally: The refutation of this doubt is very evident.
fn.1687: Literally: This thing does not follow, etc.; that is to say: the reasoning by which it is concluded that the agent who sometimes acts and sometimes does not act must necessarily have passed from potentiality to actuality—this reasoning, I say, can only apply to a body composed of matter and form.
fn.1688: The author refers to a short treatise by Al-Farabi, titled كتاب العقل والمعقولات, which was published in Latin under the title: De Intellectu et intellecto (See my Mélanges, etc., p. 350, and ibid., n. 2). The passage the author is about to cite is found near the end of this treatise. — Recently, a young German rabbi, Mr. Michael Rosenstein, published, as a doctoral dissertation, the Hebrew version of this work, accompanied by a Latin translation and several notes: Abû-Nassr Alfarabii de intellectu intellectisque commentatio, etc., Breslau, 1858, octavo.
fn.1689: Cf. Vol. I, p. 311, and ibid., note 4.
fn.1690: That is to say, the person who believes that by arguing from the active intellect, I have employed sophistical reasoning, and that there is no analogy between this intellect and God.
fn.1691: The author means: From the similarity we established between God and the active intellect, we did not conclude that action, in both cases, depends on the disposition of matter, nor that God's action could, like that of the active intellect, be occasionally interrupted by obstacles arising in matter. Cf. Vol. I, loc. cit., where the author states that God is always intellect in act, and that His perception experiences no hindrance from Himself or from any other source. It will be seen later that Maimonides seeks the cause for why God created at a particular moment solely in the divine will.
fn.1692: The author has not completely finished his thought, implying the following: Consequently, God also could have not acted from all eternity and could have created the world at a certain time, without there being grounds to maintain that in creating the world, He would have passed from potentiality to act, which would suppose an efficient cause prior to Him.
fn.1693: See Chapter XIV, the sixth method.
fn.1694: Ibn Tibbon translates: ולא יבא; Ibn Falaquera (Moreh ha-Moreh, Append., p. 154) rightly observes that one should say ולא יוכן, or ואינו נאות. In Part III, Chap. VIII, Ibn Tibbon more accurately renders the words אלמאד̇ה אלמהאח̈יה as החמר הנאות.
fn.1695: That is to say: if one were to suppose that God created the world at a certain time, having then willed what He had not willed before, would this not be to attribute change to Him?
fn.1696: The editions of Ibn Tibbon's version have התבאר in the preterite; it should read יתבאר in the future, as found in the manuscripts.
fn.1697: That is to say, that from this second method no conclusion can be drawn to oppose our system and demonstrate its inadmissibility.
fn.1698: That is to say: Everything that divine wisdom decides must take place immediately; for what it decides is necessary and cannot for a single moment fail to exist.
fn.1699: See Chapter XIV, the seventh method.
fn.1700: Literally: Just as we are ignorant of His wisdom which required that..., so we are ignorant of His wisdom in that He (God) brought into existence, etc.
fn.1701: Ibn Tibbon's version, which reads דרך החכמה ההיא ומשפטה, is not entirely accurate; Al-Harizi translates more precisely: חק החכמה ההיא וחיובה.
fn.1702: The author means: We cannot even say that God's wisdom is determined by His will, or vice versa; for, in our view, will and wisdom in God are one and the same thing, both being His very essence. Cf. Vol. I, Chap. LIII, pp. 214 and 215.
fn.1703: See Part III, Chapters XIII and XVII, and cf. Part I, Chapter LXIX, pp. 321, 322.
fn.1704: That is to say, the absurdity implicitly attributed to us by this final demonstration of the eternity of the world.
fn.1706: That is to say, according to the opinion that admits a Creator God.
fn.1707: Literally: What is attached to his opinion in terms of absurdities. The suffix in ראיה (his opinion) refers to Aristotle, or to the preceding words: מן יקול באלקדם, the one who maintains eternity.
fn.1708: The author here addresses the direct proofs that can be alleged in favor of creation ex nihilo; he combats Aristotle's system, according to which everything in the universe follows an eternal and immutable law, and he shows that, particularly in the movements of the celestial spheres, one cannot fail to recognize the action of a free will acting with intention and not by necessity. Maimonides shows the implausibilities resulting from Aristotle's system, and he particularly emphasizes the difficulties presented by certain passages of the treatise On the Heavens. This chapter is one of the most important in the discussion Maimonides enters into against the Peripatetics. Since Moses of Narbonne answered several of the author's objections and thereby weakened, in the eyes of some contemporaries, the effect this chapter was intended to produce, Isaac Abravanel explained it in a specific commentary, accompanied by several dissertations. This commentary, titled עמים חדשים, The New Heavens, had remained unpublished; it was published for the first time by Wolf Heidenheim, Rödelheim, 1828, quarto.
fn.1709: Cf. Vol. I, Chap. LXIX, pp. 313-314.
fn.1710: Literally: Before they were proposed, or before they were the object of design; that is to say: The intention that willed things to be in such and such a manner, even though they could have been otherwise, necessarily had to precede these things, and consequently they would not always have been as they are.
fn.1711: That is to say: There are things naturally impossible and which it does not depend on God to change, because it is in their very nature to be impossible, such as, for example, the combination of contraries in the same subject and at the same moment, or the construction of a square whose diagonal is equal to its sides. See Part III of this work, Chap. XV, and cf. above, p. 108.
fn.1712: Literally: That it is (or that it exists) by the design of a (being) having an intention.
fn.1713: Literally: of their principles which they only endeavored to set forth in order to reveal determination. The author means that all the propositions of the Mutakallimun are solely intended to establish that it is the divine will that determines everything in the universe. On the meaning of the word determination, see Vol. I, p. 426, note 3. — Ibn Tibbon's version is here absolutely unintelligible; it reads: אשר אמנם השתדלתי להציעו להמציא הביאור. Ibn Falaquera (Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 100) translates more accurately: אשר השתדלו להציעם להמצאת הסגול; likewise Al-Harizi: אשר השתדלו להציעם כדי להמציא ההגבלה. It is evident from the critical notes of Ibn Falaquera (Append., p. 154) that the manuscripts of Ibn Tibbon also carried הביאור, as further on: וכונו בהם הביאור; probably the latter had in his Arabic text אלתלכ̇יץ instead of אלתכ̇ציץ. As the note by Ibn Falaquera is very corrupt in the printed edition, we reproduce it here more correctly: לאיג̇אד אלתכ̇ציץ העתיק להמציא הביאור והעתקתו להמציא הסגול או ההתיחד כי אינו ביאור.
fn.1714: Literally: Only as for them, there is no difference for them between the particularization of this plant by the color red, to the exclusion of whiteness, or by sweetness to the exclusion of bitterness, and the particularization of the sky by this figure it possesses, to the exclusion of the square and triangular figure. In other words: They do not differentiate between sublunary things, which are subject to certain physical laws explaining their particular properties, and celestial bodies, whose particularities cannot all be explained by a natural law, and in which one recognizes the will of God, who freely preferred one state of affairs over another.
fn.1715: That is to say, by propositions that deny every law of nature and all causality, and that attribute the particularities of all things, both sublunary and celestial, to the direct and immediate intervention of the Deity. See especially the VIth proposition of the Motécallemîn (Vol. I, Ch. LXXIII, p. 388 ff.)
fn.1716: The version of Ibn Tibbon reads: שהחמר, and that of Al-Harizi: כי החמר; likewise one of the Arabic manuscripts of Leiden (no. 18): אן אלמאדה̈. One should read: אן כל מאדה̈, as found in the other manuscripts.
fn.1717: These are the forms of the four elements, each of which has two qualities: fire is hot and dry, air is hot and moist, water is cold and moist, and earth is cold and dry. See my Mélanges de philosophie juive et arabe, p. 88, note 1, and the passages from Aristotle and Galen indicated therein.
fn.1718: That is to say: by the four qualities which, combined in pairs, constitute the four forms of the elements, matter becomes a fourfold elementary body for everything composed of this matter. — The verb צארת and the suffix in מנהא refer to הלך אלמאדה̈, this matter. The two Hebrew translators have put the verb and the suffix in the plural; Ibn Tibbon has: היו יסודות למה שהורככב מהם; Al-Harizi: נעשו יסודות לכל מה שהורכב מהם. According to these versions, the two feminine forms would refer grammatically to the four forms (ארבע צור), which would be irrational; for what constitutes the four elements is not the forms, but rather the universal matter, endowed with the elementary form.
fn.1719: The verb اختاط means to intermingle, that is to say, to form a confused mixture (μίξις), whereas by امتزج, one denotes a mixture where the various elements are distributed throughout with perfect equality, an equal and proportioned mixture (κρᾶσις).
fn.1720: That is to say, the different regions occupied by the four elements. See Vol. I, p. 134, note 2, and p. 356.
fn.1721: See Vol. I, p. 247, note 3, and above, p. 25, note 1.
fn.1722: According to Abravanel, the author is alluding to the commentators on Aristotle, and notably to Themistius. The latter had observed that the definition Aristotle gives of body, namely that it is what has length, breadth, and depth (treatise On the Heavens, Book I, Ch. I), does not apply exactly to celestial bodies; for, since these are of an absolute simplicity, the dimensions are not determined there, as in sublunary bodies, by the corporeal form supervening upon matter, but are always present there in actuality and are inherent to their matter. They are therefore dimensions of another nature, forming bodies of another nature, and consequently it is only by homonymy that the names dimension and body are applied simultaneously to the heaven and to sublunary things. See Abravanel, Schamaïm ’hadaschîm, fol. 4.
fn.1723: As was stated above (Ch. XII), bodies act upon one another only by their form; whenever, therefore, there is a difference in the respective action exerted by certain bodies, it must be assumed that their forms are different.
fn.1724: See Aristotle, treatise On the Heavens, Book IV, Ch. 4 and 5.
fn.1725: Literally: But the form of each sphere differs from the form of the other sphere.
fn.1726: The ancients, believing the earth to be immobile and generally not admitting its rotation about its axis (Almagest I, 6), had to seek another way to explain how the sun and all the planets accomplish, in twenty-four hours, a movement from east to west around the earth, opposed to the various movements proper to them and which they accomplish in longer or shorter periods, traveling from west to east toward those fixed stars that arrive later at the meridian. It was thus believed that the superior sphere, called the diurnal sphere, alone had a natural movement from east to west, in which it carried with it the spheres of the seven planets, which did not prevent the latter from accomplishing their own periodic movement from west to east. See Almagest, Book I, Ch. 7, and cf. Vol. I of this work, p. 357, note 3. As for the diurnal sphere, there are some among the Arabs who identify it with that of the fixed stars, while others make it a ninth sphere devoid of stars. See above, p. 57, note 3.
fn.1727: Literally: As He ordered for us (or arranged) the existence of what is below the sphere. The editions of Ibn Tibbon's version read: גלגל הירח, the sphere of the moon; but the manuscripts read simply הגלגל, and likewise all the Arabic manuscripts, אלפלכ.
fn.1728: Literally: And by the determination of a determinant. See Vol. I, p. 426, note 3.
fn.1729: The author refers to the superior sphere which, as has been seen, moves from east to west. He is evidently alluding to a passage in the treatise On the Heavens, Book II, Ch. 5, where Aristotle seeks to indicate the reason why the heaven moves from left to right; just as, he says, in rectilinear movements (of the elements) the one directed upwards is the most noble, so in the circular movements of the celestial spheres, it is the one directed forward or toward the right. It would therefore appear that Aristotle is speaking here of the movement of the planets rather than that of the superior heaven; for forward (εἰς τὸ πρόσθεν), or toward the right, means toward the east. Cf. ibid., Ch. 2: δεξιὸν γὰρ ἑκάστου λέגוμεν, ὅθεν ἡ ἀρχὴ τῆς κατὰ τόπον κινήσεως · τοῦ δ’ οὐρανοῦ ἀρχὴν τῆς περιφορᾶς, ὅθεν αἱ ἀνατολαὶ τῶν ἄστρων, ὥστε τοῦט’ ἂν εἴה δεξιόν, οὗ δ’ αἱ δύσεις, ἀριστερόν. But Maimonides' assertion is based on the Arabic version, which, as is recognizable from the Arabo-Latin version, had significantly altered the Greek text. The final sentence of Ch. V (βέλτιστον γὰρ κινεῖσθαι ἁπλῆν τε κίνησιν καὶ ἄπαυστον, καὶ ταύτην ἐπὶ τὸ τιμιώτερον) is paraphrased as follows in the Arabo-Latin version (fol. 55, col. b): 'Melius enim et nobilius est ut cœlum moveatur semper sine cessatione, et quod motus ejus sit ex nobilissimo locorum, quod est dextrum. Manifestum est igitur quare cœlum movetur ex oriente ad occidentem, et non e converso.'
fn.1730: See ibid., chap. 10, where Aristotle says that, since the spheres of the planets have a motion opposite to that of the superior heaven, the one closest to the latter has the slowest motion, the one farthest from it has the fastest motion, and likewise the motion of the others is, because of their respective distance from the superior heaven, slower or faster: …. εὔλογον ἤδη τὸ μὲν ἐγγυτάτω τῆς ἁπλῆς καὶ πρώτης περιφορᾶς ἐν πλείστῳ χρόνῳ διιέναι τὸν αὑτοῦ κύκλον, τὸ δὲ πορρωτάτω ἐν ἐλαχίστῳ, κ. τ. λ. — Thus, the periodic revolution of Saturn lasts thirty years, that of Jupiter twelve years, and so on until the revolution of the moon, which is completed in less than a month.
fn.1731: See ibid., chap. 12: ἡ μὲν γὰρ πρώτη μία οὖσα πολλὰ κινεῖ τῶν σωμάτων τῶν θείων, αἱ δὲ πολλαὶ οὖσαι ἓν μόνον ἑκάστη · τῶν γὰρ πλανωμένων ἐν ὁτιοῦν πλείους φέρεται φοράς, κ. τ. λ. Cf. Metaph., book XII, chap. 8, where Aristotle cites the opinions of Eudoxus and Callippus on the various spheres that must be assumed for each planet to explain its motion.
fn.1732: Isaac Abravanel reports on this passage, which is quite obscure, the interpretation of another author, which seems extremely forced to me (see Schamaïm ’hadaschim, fol. 6). This author believes that Maimonides, by saying that there are faster spheres that are above those with a slower motion, intends to speak, on the one hand, of the periodic motions proper to the respective spheres of each planet, and, on the other hand, of the motions of the apogees of the planets inferior to it; for the precession of these apogees is almost as slow as that of the sphere of fixed stars. Now, it is evident that the sphere of Saturn, for example, is closer to the eighth sphere than the apogee of Jupiter, and even more so than those of Mars and the other planets; likewise, the sphere of Jupiter is higher than the apogee of Mars, and so on. If Maimonides then says that there are spheres with equal motions, although they are above one another, the same author thinks he refers to these same apogees which all, it seems, have equal motions, with the exception of those of Mercury and the moon; or else, the periodic revolutions of the sun, Venus, and Mercury, which were believed to be of equal duration. — But it is not probable that Maimonides compared motions of such a diverse nature. It is possible that in saying that certain spheres with faster motion are above those with slower motion, he refers to the planet Mercury, which, according to an opinion that seems probable to him (see above, chap. IX), is located above the sun, and whose true periodic motion is shorter than that of the sun; for a duration of about ten months was attributed to it. (See Abravanel, loc. cit.) By the planets with equal motions and whose periodic revolution is completed in the same or nearly the same amount of time, Maimonides perhaps means Venus and the sun. However, we dare not affirm anything in this regard; for there is much divergence in the data found among Arabic astronomers concerning the periodic revolutions of Mercury and Venus, and it would be necessary to know which data were adopted by Maimonides. Cf. Almagest, book IX, chap. III ff.
fn.1733: More literally: Regarding the opinion (which admits) that the matter is by necessity.
fn.1734: See below, chap. XXIV, where the author highlights everything that is implausible and contrary to nature in the hypotheses of epicycles and eccentrics.
fn.1735: All the MSS have עקולנא, and Ibn Tibbon’s version (editio princeps) has שכלינו in the plural, our intellects; but the word عُقُولُ should perhaps be considered here as a verbal noun.
fn.1736: The MSS generally read: אלמסאיל אלגׄזילה̈ אלשריפה̈, and Ibn Tibbon’s version has: השאלות המעולות הנכבדות; but two Arabic-Latin versions of Aristotle’s text have, one quæstiones disputabiles, the other quæstiones topicas, which suggests that their Arabic text read: المسائل الجدلية. It appears that this reading was also found in some Arabic MSS of the Guide, and that it was later adopted by Ibn Tibbon; for, in a MS of the latter's version (Hebrew MS of the Imperial Library, no. 238, fol. 185 a), we read: השאלות המחלקיות הנכבדות, and these words are accompanied by the following gloss: פי׳ כי מלאכת מחלוקת הנצוח יש לה להניח שאלות בכל דבר ולבקש אמתתם והיא כהצעה למלאכת המופת לבוא ולבאר האמת בהם.
fn.1737: This passage is taken from the treatise On the Heavens, book II, chap. 12, where Aristotle examines the following two questions: 1. Why the respective motions of each planet do not increase in proportion to their distance from the superior sphere, which has only a single motion? For we see, on the contrary, that the sun and the moon have fewer motions than the planets situated above them, although the latter are farther from the center and closer to the superior sphere. 2. Why the superior sphere has a large number of stars, while each of the inferior spheres has only one? — The Arabic version is but a very free paraphrase of the Greek text, of which we content ourselves with citing the beginning: δυοῖν δ’ ἀπορίαιν οὔσαιν, περὶ ὧν εἰκότως ἂν ὁστισοῦν ἀπορήσειε, πειρατέον λέγειν τὸ φαινόμενον. This means: “Since there are two difficulties that could rightly perplex anyone, one must try to say what seems to us to be the case.” We see that the words τὸ φ ανόμενον, id quod videtur, were paraphrased in Arabic by what our intellect, our science, and our opinion allow. Maimonides thus took unnecessary pains by explaining further on, in a very subtle manner, what Aristotle meant by the three words intellect, science, and opinion; for not a single one of these words is found in the Greek text. — The two Arabic-Latin versions of the treatise On the Heavens do not have the word intellect. That of Michael Scot (published under the name of Paul the Israelite) reads: “Et volumus modo perscrutari de duabus quæstionibus, de quibus oporlet perscrutatorem perscrutari; et dicemus in eis secundum nostram scientiam et nostram opinionem.” The other version, anonymous and unpublished (Latin MS of the Imperial Library, Saint-Victor collection, no. 872, fol. 147), has the following terms: “Volo autem nunc inquirere de duabus quæstionibus inquisitione sufficiente; convenit autem ut inquirat de his inquisitor. Dicam ergo in utrisque secundum summam scientiæ nostræ et nostræ sententiæ.”
fn.1738: The author means that, since the reasons Aristotle gives (in the treatise On the Heavens) for the various motions of the planets appeared insufficient, it is likely for this reason that he assumes for each sphere a separate intellect, which contributes to determining its particular motion. The passage alluded to is found in book XII of the Metaph., chap. VIII.
fn.1739: See above p. 153, note 1. Regarding the reason why the spheres move more slowly as they are closer to the superior (diurnal) sphere, Aristotle expresses himself in these terms (On the Heavens, II, 10): τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἐγγυτάτω μάλιστα ϰρατεῖται, τὸ δὲ πορωτάτω πάντων ἥϰιστα διὰ τὴν ἀπόστασιν. The meaning is: that the spheres closest to the diurnal movement, which goes from east to west, are most influenced by this movement, so that their opposite movement from west to east is weaker; and on the contrary, those that are furthest from the diurnal movement are less hindered in their opposite movement, which is, consequently, stronger and faster. — This reasoning, indeed, appears rational (εὔλογον), as Aristotle says. If Maimonides finds it strange and astonishing, it is probably because the slowness or speed of the periodic movement of the spheres (from west to east) is not proportional to their respective distance from the superior sphere, or else because, in his view, there is a certain sphere faster than another, which nonetheless is situated above the latter. The word מסתגרבה̈, strange, is not rendered in the Hebrew version of Ibn Tibbon, nor in that of Al-Harizi.
fn.1741: According to Abravanel (loc. cit., fol. 8 a), Maimonides intends to speak of the retrograde motion of the nodes of the planets, which goes from east to west. Indeed, it is hardly possible to explain this passage otherwise; for none of the planetary spheres has a natural movement from east to west. As spheres were imagined for each movement, they were also attributed to the retrograde motion of the nodes. Thus the Arabs give the nodes of the moon a sphere they call فلك الجوزهر, which Jewish authors render as גלגל התנין (see Yesôd ’olâm, book III, chap. VIII). Now, the movement of the nodes of the planets that are above the moon is extremely slow and almost imperceptible compared to the movement of the nodes of the moon, which, according to Maimonides, traverse 18°, 44′, 42″ in one year (see Abridgment of the Talmud, tractate Kiddush ha-hodesh, chap. XVI, § 2). But, according to the principles laid down by Aristotle, the spheres that move from east to west should have a faster movement as they are closer to the diurnal sphere and more influenced by the latter. Such appears to be the sense of Maimonides' objection, however subtle it may seem. On nodes and their movements, cf. Riccioli, Almagestum novum, vol. I, part I, p. 502.
fn.1742: That is to say: The diversity observed in the movement of the spheres could have been traced back to a physical cause, just as one can explain, from a physical point of view, why the four elements occupy different positions, some toward the center, others toward the circumference.
fn.1744: See above chap. VIII, p. 78, and ibid., note 4.
fn.1745: That is to say, the matter of the stars and that of the spheres.

fn.1747: The author means that it would be quite astonishing if the star were fixed in its sphere as a result of a physical and necessary law, and that this can only be explained by the will of the Creator acting freely and with a certain intention.

fn.1751: See vol. I, chap. LXX, p. 324.
fn.1754: See above p. 152, note 3, and p. 153, n. 1.

fn.1784: This proposition, which Maimonides borrowed from Avicenna, was not stated by Aristotle; however, in the latter's writings, one finds several passages that could have given rise to it. Thus, for example, Aristotle says in the Physics (Book VIII, chap. VI end) that what is not moved (the first mover), remaining simple and always the same, will only be able to produce a single simple motion (ὸ ὃ’ἀϰίνητον, ὥσπερ εἴρηται, ἅτε ἁπλῶς ϰαὶ ὡσαύτως ϰαὶ ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ διαμένον, μίαν ϰαὶ ἁπλῆν ϰινήσει ϰίνησιν). In the Metaphysics (Book XII, chap. VIII towards the end), it is said that the first unmoved mover being one in idea and in number, it follows that what is moved always and continuously is also one; and that, consequently, there is only one heaven (ἓν ἄρα ϰαὶ λόγῳ ϰαὶ ἀριθμῷ τὸ πρῶτον ϰινοῦν ἀϰίνητον ὄν · ϰαὶ τὸ ϰινούμενον ἀεὶ ϰαὶ συνεχῶς ἓν μόνον · εἷς ἄρα οὐρανὸς μόνος). See, on this subject, my Mélanges de philosophie juive et arabe, p. 360 ff. — The author will show in this chapter that the entire scaffolding of the successive emanation of the Intelligences and of the spheres, according to the theory of Aristotle (or rather of Avicenna), does not suffice to explain the multiplicity and diversity that reign in the world, but that all difficulties disappear as soon as one admits a creator God, having created the world by his free will.
fn.1785: There is an apparent contradiction here with what the author said of fire in chap. But all the effects of fire that the author enumerates in the passage in question, he attributes, in reality, to one of the two simple qualities of fire, namely, heat.
fn.1786: This proposition and the following two are not borrowed from Aristotle; the author states them as axioms against which no objection could be raised.

fn.1788: The editions of Ibn Tibbon's version bear הראשון, which is only a printing error; the mss. have האחרון.

fn.1791: That is to say: it would no longer suffice to consider each Intelligence as composed of two simple elements or of two kinds of thoughts, but it would be necessary for one of these two elements to be itself composite in order to serve as the cause for the two species of matter and form that are in the sphere and the star.
fn.1792: Literally: And this, if the matter of all the stars were one; that is to say, the hypothesis of a composite element existing in the separate Intelligences, from which the matter of the spheres and that of the stars would emanate; this very hypothesis, I say, would only suffice if one assumed that the matter of all the stars is one and the same.

In short, the meaning of this sentence is: when comparing two opposing hypotheses to examine which of the two appears more doubtful, it is not a matter of determining which side has the greater number of doubts, but rather of weighing the improbabilities that would result from each of the two hypotheses, and seeing which of the two is more contrary to the laws of nature.
fn.1812: The editions of Ibn Tibbon's version add here the words על אמתתם, which are not found in the MSS.
fn.1813: Literally: so that you may know the doubts in their reality.

fn.1819: See above, ch. XIX, p. 155, and ibid., note 2.
fn.1820: Literally: that man has encompassed through science the order, etc.
fn.1821: Throughout this chapter, Maimonides particularly addresses the disciple for whom he originally composed the Guide (see the beginning of Part I). fn.1822: Literally: it is that, with regard to the regularity of the movements and the conformity of the course of the stars with what is seen, everything follows two principles.
fn.1823: Ancient astronomers, in order to explain the apparent inequalities of planetary movements, made them move, sometimes in eccentrics, that is, in spheres whose center deviates from that of the zodiac or the earth, and sometimes in epicycles, that is, in small secondary spheres carried by large concentric or eccentric spheres, and whose center is supposed to move on the surface of the large sphere along the circumference of a great circle called the deferent (See Almagest, book VI, ch. 3). These purely geometric hypotheses, very ingenious and at the same time very complicated, remained one of the bases of astronomical science throughout the Middle Ages. They became obsolete with the discovery of the elliptical orbits of the planets and the laws of attraction. From the beginning of the 12th century, Arab philosophers were troubled by how improbable Ptolemy's hypotheses appeared and their lack of conformity with the physical principles and theories of motion developed by Aristotle. Attempts were made to substitute other hypotheses for them; but no system was successfully developed that could compete with that of Ptolemy (See my Mélanges de philosophie juive et arabe, pp. 412, 430, 520 et seq.). These attempts had no success among astronomers, and Maimonides himself, who here attacks Ptolemy's hypotheses from a philosophical point of view, does not hesitate, in his treatise Kiddousch ha-’hodesch, or on the fixing of the new moons, to admit them in their full extent and to take them as the basis for his astronomical calculations.

fn.1828: Cf. above, p. 82, where the author says he studied with one of the disciples of Abu-Bakr Ibn-al-Sayigh.

fn.1835: On the form of the imperative ארי, see Vol. I, p. 19, n. 2.

fn.1837: This proposition is quite obscure. Here, it seems to me, is its meaning: Since the celestial spheres are all exactly nested within one another, without any vacuum between them (see Vol. I, pp. 356-357), it is necessary that, of two spheres having different centers, the higher or larger one forms a thick vault on one side over the smaller one, while, on the other sides, it will form an envelope around the small interior sphere whose thickness will decrease in proportion to the distance between the two centers. It is then evident that, whenever the large sphere moves around an axis other than the one passing through the two centers, it will always carry the small one along by its movement. But if the movement of the large sphere occurs around the axis passing through the two centers, it will not be hindered by the interior sphere, which can always remain in the same position; so that the large sphere can rotate around the surface of the small one without carrying it along by its movement. — Ibn Tibbon expressed himself inaccurately by saying: הקוטר העובר בין שני המרכזים; instead of בין, it should have been על.
fn.1838: For, if there were a sufficient vacuum inside the large sphere, its movement, around whatever axis, would no longer be hindered by the small one, which, consequently, would no longer be forced to move with it.
fn.1839: That is to say, of the hypothesis of eccentric spheres, which supposes the existence of spheres with different centers nested within one another.
fn.1840: This hypothesis allows for the assumption of an interval between the two spheres, which, no longer linked to one another, remain free and independent in their respective movements. The void is supposed to be filled by spherical bodies that do not participate in the life and movements of the celestial sphere, and which vary in form according to the void they must fill. R. Levi ben-Gerson, who adopts this hypothesis, calls such a body: גשם בלתי שומר תמונתו. See Mil’hamoth Adonaï, Book V, Part IInd, chap. 2.
fn.1841: This is the famous Arabic astronomer Thābit ibn Qurra (commonly called Thebit), a Sabian from Harran, who died in 901. On this astronomer, see d’Herbelot, Bibliothèque orientale, folio edition, p. 1015; Casiri, Biblioth. arab. hisp., vol. I, p. 386 ff. Maimonides cites him again in the IIIrd part of this work, chap. XIV, where he attributes the same theory of intermediate bodies to him.
fn.1842: The author is referring to the deviations of these two planets in latitude. The theory alluded to is set forth in the Almagest, Book XIII, chap. I ff. Cf. Al-Farghāni, Elementa astronomica, chap. XVIII. The Arabic words ميل and انحراف correspond to the Greek words ἔγϰλισις and λόξωσις; Delambre thinks that the first of these two words designates the inclination of the eccentric to the zodiac, and the second, the inclination of the epicycle to the eccentric. See the notes on the Almagest, edited by Abbé Halma, vol. II, p. 25. The Hebrew version of Ibn Tibbon does not translate the word אנחראף. Al-Harizi has הנטיה והיציאה.
fn.1843: Delambre (loc. cit.) expresses himself in much the same way regarding the difficulty of this theory: "This entire chapter," he says, "is difficult to understand and impossible to remember. One cannot form a precise idea of this whole theory except by examining the tables in which it is contained. This remark applies more or less to everything that follows, up to the tables."
fn.1844: Literally: has manifested impotence in this; that is to say: he has declared that man is incapable of forming a correct idea of it.
fn.1845: This passage, taken by Maimonides from the Arabic version of the Almagest (Book XIII, chap. 2), differs slightly from the Greek text, which reads: Καὶ μηδεὶς τὰς τοιαύτας τῶν ὑποθέσεων ἐργώδεις νομισάτω, σκοπῶν τὸ τῶν παρ’ ἡμῖν ἐπιτεχνημάτων κατασκελές · Οὐ γὰρ προσήκει παραϐάλλειν τὰ ἀνθρώπινα τοῖς θείοις. "Let no one believe that such hypotheses are difficult (to accept), considering the harshness of the contrivances employed by us; for it is not fitting to compare human things to divine things."
fn.1846: The words אלא מא ד״ברת לך are missing from the Leiden MS, no. 18, and both Hebrew translators have likewise omitted them, although they are necessary for the meaning of the sentence.
fn.1847: Cf. above, p. 187, n. 1, and the IIIrd part of this work, chap. XIV. We find no information anywhere concerning the astronomer Al-Kabīcī, nor his treatise On Distances, and we do not know how he demonstrated the distances between the centers of the eccentrics and the center of the zodiac, taking the semi-diameter or radius of the earth as a unit. The astronomer in question is undoubtedly the same one whom the Scholastics frequently cite under the patronymic name Alkabitius, and who, according to Albertus Magnus, was called Abdilazil, or more correctly ‘Abd al-‘Azīz. See Speculum astronomiae, chap. V and XI (Opp. vol. V, pp. 659 and 663). The Biblioth. Imp. [Imperial Library] possesses several MSS containing an Introduction to Astrology by Alkabitius, which begins with these words: Postulata a Domino prolixitate vitae Ceyfaddaula, id est gladii regni (MS from the Sorbonne collection, no. 976). From this it can be concluded that our astronomer lived at the court of Sayf al-Dawla, ‘Alī ibn Hamdān, in Aleppo, and, consequently, that he flourished in the first half of the Xth century of the Christian era. Cf. the Bibliographical Dictionary of Hajji Khalifa, ed. Flügel, vol. V, p. 473. The two works indicated by the Arabic bibliographer under nos. 11,681 and 11,682 appear to me to be identical. The first, which was dedicated to Sayf al-Dawla, is anonymous; the second is attributed to ‘Abd al-‘Azīz ibn ‘Uthmān al-Kabīcī. Both bear the title Introduction to Astrology. — As for the name القبصي, it may be pronounced Al Kabīcī or Al-Kobéicī; Ibn Tibbon’s version might justify this latter pronunciation, for it reads הקבאייצי.
fn.1848: The words כי לפי דעתו, which are also found in the MSS of this version, must be deleted from Ibn Tibbon's version, as they are contrary to the construction of the Arabic sentence.
fn.1849: That is to say, by that of the eccentric or by that of the epicycle. All the MSS have אצלין, without the article, and likewise Ibn Tibbon: באחד משני שרשים; Al-Harizi העיקרים, with the article.
fn.1850: The author alludes here to an ingenious observation by Ptolemy (Almagest, Book V, chap. 5) concerning the oscillatory movement of the line of apsides or of the diameter of the moon's epicycle, which forms a corollary to the two inequalities of eccentricity and evection. See my Notes on the discoveries attributed to the Arabs concerning the inequalities of the moon's movement (Comptes-rendus des séances de l’Académie des sciences, vol. XVI, p. 1444 ff., and vol. XVII, p. 76 ff.), and the memoir by M. Biot in the Journal des Savants, October 1843, p. 623 ff.
fn.1851: That is to say, the moment the eclipse begins, and the extent of the obscured surface. The masculine suffix in מקאדירה (Ibn Tibbon ושעורו), its measures, refers to the word אט׳לאמהא, their obscuration; some MSS have ומקאדירהא, and their measures, the suffix referring to the eclipses, and likewise, Al-Harizi’s version and some MSS of Ibn Tibbon’s have ושעורם.
fn.1852: See Ptolemy, Almagest, Book XII, chap. I ff. and cf. above, p. 86, n. 2.
fn.1853: That is to say: the astronomer, as such, is not concerned with whether his hypotheses are admissible or not from a philosophical point of view, but only with whether they suffice to explain the phenomena. Cf. above, chap. XI, pp. 92, 93.
fn.1854: Ibn al-Ṣā'igh meant that Aristotle perhaps knew of the hypothesis of eccentricity but believed it to be useless, because he thought that the position of the sun could just as well be found by means of homocentric spheres, by assuming a certain inclination. Cf. above, p. 57 note 1.
fn.1856: Literally: man encompasses nothing of it, except for this small dose of mathematics.
fn.1857: The masculine verbs בעד and עלא refer to the Heaven; the noun אלסמא is of common gender, and the author most often puts the adjectives and verbs referring to it in the feminine.
fn.1858: The reading of this passage is uniform in all the manuscripts, except that the words אנה דלנא are missing in one of the Leiden manuscripts (No. 18). Al-Harizi's version agrees perfectly with the reading of our Arabic manuscripts; it states: והראיה הכוללת המצואה מהם על מניעם הוא דבר אשר לא יגיעו דעות בני אדם אליו. Ibn Tibbon adds after מניעם the words אבל שאר ענינם, which essentially modifies the sense of this sentence, which would be translated as follows: "The general proof that can be drawn from them is that it proves to us (the existence of) its mover; but the rest of what concerns it (that is, the heaven) is a thing to the knowledge of which human intelligences cannot arrive." Ibn Tibbon's reading seems justified by other passages of this treatise, where the author expressly states that the Heaven generally proves to us the existence of a prime mover, although we cannot give an exact account of the laws of motion. See, e.g., Part I, ch. IX, and above, ch. II and ch. XVIII, p. 144.
fn.1859: Literally: the extreme point (that is, the strongest proof) of my preference for the search for truth is to have manifested and declared my perplexity in these matters. In Ibn Tibbon's version, one must write: שאני בארתי והגדתי בלבולי באלו הענינים, as it is in the editio princeps.

The author means that the texts relating to the creation of the world could be interpreted allegorically, just as those which seem to imply that God is a corporeal being must be. The word تأويل designates the allegorical interpretation of the sacred text, while the explanation of the literal sense is designated by the word تفسير.
fn.1861: More literally: and it is necessary to interpret everything whose literal sense is refuted by a demonstration and which is known to require an interpretation.
fn.1862: Literally: by other modes of preference; that is, by justifying in various ways the preference one would give to this contrary opinion.
fn.1863: On the meaning of the verb عطر, cf. Vol. I, p. 115, note 1. — All the Arabic manuscripts have the infinitive תעטיל here, although the two preceding verbs are in the participle. The two Hebrew versions have the participle ומבטלת.
fn.1864: By the word باطן, internal (in Hebrew תוך), the Arabs designate the allegorical sense of the words of the Qur'an, as opposed to ظاهر, external, which designates the literal sense. From this comes the name Batenis (الباطنية or اهל הבאטן), that is, partisans of the allegorical sense, a mystical Muslim sect that formed under the influence of Neo-Platonic doctrines and which has much analogy with the Jewish Kabbalists. See on this sect, its names, and its various branches, Shahrastani, History of Religious and Philosophical Sects, Arabic text published by Mr. Cureton, p. 147 et seq. (German trans. by Mr. Haarbrücker, Vol. I, p. 221 et seq.).
fn.1865: See above, ch. XIII, p. 107 et seq.
fn.1867: That is, in the sense of this opinion of Plato.
fn.1868: Most manuscripts have ויגׄד in the active form, as does Al-Harizi: וימצא לו דמיונים רבים. We preferred to write ויוגׄד, in the passive, a reading we found in only one of our manuscripts, but which is confirmed by Ibn Tibbon's version, ויֹ֬צאו לו וכו׳
fn.1869: The text unnecessarily repeats the words: הדׄא אלראי אלאכׄר to this other opinion; instead of אלאכׄר, some manuscripts have איצׄא, as does Ibn Tibbon: גם כן.
fn.1870: That is: why did He not cause it so that, by a natural feeling, we were inclined to do what He commanded and to abstain from what He forbade, if it is true that His sole purpose was that we should do such a thing and abstain from such another?

fn.1873: In most editions of Ibn Tibbon's version, the words על הקדמות are missing here, which are found in the editio princeps.
fn.1874: See the Pirke R. Eliezer, ch. III. Maimonides' citation is somewhat abbreviated.
fn.1875: Ibn Tibbon's version has רחוק; it should have been מגונה. Al-Harizi translates: זאת דבה גדולה ורעה.
fn.1876: The author means that R. Eliezer, in this case, would have affirmed the eternity of prime matter, which he would designate allegorically by the light of his garment and by the snow from beneath the throne of glory.
fn.1877: Literally: Except that it would be according to Plato's opinion; that is: he would have affirmed the eternity of matter, though in a sense not as contrary to religion as is Aristotle's opinion. See above, ch. XIII, second opinion.
fn.1878: The ancient Rabbis enumerate seven things created before the creation of the world, among which is the throne of glory. See Bereshit Rabba, sect. 1, (fol. 1, col 2); Babylonian Talmud, Pesahim, fol. 54 a; Nedarim, fol. 39 b. Cf. the Kuzari, Book III, § 73, and the Akedah, ch. 101.
fn.1879: On the meaning of the word תאויל, see above, p. 196, note 1. Ibn Tibbon uses the Hebrew word פירוש in the same sense, as observed by Ibn Falaquera in the Appendix to Moreh ha-Moreh regarding our passage (p. 154):
fn.1880: See Part <sup>I</sup> of this work, ch. IX.
fn.1881: Ibn Tibbon's version lacks clarity here due to its excessive literalness; the word אמונתו is the object of יבלבל, and היודע, an adjective of בעל הדת, has the sense of learned. The Hebrew sentence should be constructed in this manner: יבלבל מאד מאד אמונת בעל הדת היודע. The author means that this passage causes great embarrassment to one who is both an orthodox theologian and a man of science. Al-Harizi translates: ועל דרך כלל הוא דבר משבש דעת המאמין בתורה וישחית לאיש החכם אמונתו מאד מאד.
fn.1882: According to Moses of Narbonne, the author means that by this expression, Rabbi Eliezer evidently designates a pure and brilliant matter, and not an attribute of God.
fn.1883: Cf. my Miscellany of Jewish and Arabic Philosophy, pp. 144-145, where I reported a curious explanation of this passage, attributed to Emperor Frederick II.
fn.1884: For the understanding of this passage, see Part <sup>I</sup> of this work, ch. XXVIII, where the author goes into great detail on this subject.
fn.1885: See Bereshit Rabba, sect. 12 (fol. 11, col. 1). Cf. Babylonian Talmud, treatise Yoma, fol. 54 b.
fn.1886: The author emphasizes this subject because there is a divergence of opinions in this regard, not only among the doctors (see loc. cit.), but also among the philosophers; for the Platonists, and especially the Alexandrians, admitted a single matter which, being of extreme subtlety at its origin, becomes successively more and more condensed. Among the Jewish philosophers, it is Ibn Gabirol who professes this opinion in his Fons Vitae.
fn.1887: Literally: but its destruction, after having been born and formed, is not, according to us, etc.
fn.1888: Literally: Let that not oblige us, or let it not follow for us; that is to say, that this reasoning cannot be applied to the opinion we have maintained.
fn.1889: In the editions of Ibn Tibbon's version, הטבעי is a printing error; one must read טבעי, without the article.
fn.1890: That is to say, it did not exist in the form it has now; for all sublunar things are born from one another, and they all arise from the mixing of the elements. — In the editions of Ibn Tibbon's version, the word כן, which is found in the manuscripts, is missing here after נמצא.
fn.1891: That is to say, it does not perpetually preserve the form it has now; for things that are born eventually lose their forms and return to their primary elements.
fn.1892: In Ibn Tibbon's version, one must read או בגזרת חכמתו; the conjunction או is missing in most editions but is found in the editio princeps.
fn.1893: See what was said concerning the throne of glory in the preceding chapter. — All the manuscripts contain בל אלנץ בתאבידה, an elliptical phrase in which the verb קאל must be understood. Ibn Tibbon supplied this ellipsis by translating: אבל הכתובים אומרים בנצחותו.
fn.1894: It has already been seen elsewhere that our author attributes immortality only to the souls of the righteous, or of superior men, that is to say, to those who in this life have reached the degree of the acquired intellect, while the souls of the impious, or those who have not sought to perfect themselves here below through virtue or science, are doomed to destruction. See Vol. I, p. 328, note 4. And cf. the Mishneh Torah, Book I, treatise Teshuvah (On Repentance), chap. VIII, §§ 1-3.
fn.1895: More literally: As those whose belief is widespread believe, concerning the people of paradise. The author is clearly alluding to Muslim fables concerning the delights of paradise. — Cf. on this passage, Maimonides, Commentary on the Mishnah, Part 4, introduction to the 10th (11th) chapter of treatise Sanhedrin.
fn.1896: Most manuscripts have: מן טׄאהר; some: מן טׄאהר נץ. The editions of Ibn Tibbon's version contain: מפשוטו כל דבר; one should read: מפשוטו של דבר.
fn.1897: The verb יִשָּׂאח' (يُشَاحّ) is here the passive aorist of the 3rd form of the root شيخ, having the sense of to settle accounts strictly with someone, to be stingy or rigorous, to yield nothing to someone. It is in the same sense that the Talmudists use the verb הקפיד, and it is by this verb that Maimonides himself, in his letter to Ibn Tibbon, translates our Arabic verb: סאלתני כיף יתרגׄם פלא ישאחח תתרגׄס אין בזה הקפדה. — In most manuscripts, the verb in question is written ישאחח, probably to make the root more recognizable. In the introduction to Kitāb al-Lumaʿ, the Oxford manuscript likewise has אלמשאחחה̈, for المشاحة. See my Notice on Abu'l-Walid, p. 133 (Journal asiatique, Nov.-Dec. 1850, p. 355).
fn.1898: Ibn Tibbon's version adds here the words ויציאה מעקרי הדת, the equivalent of which is found in none of our Arabic manuscripts, nor in Al-Harizi's version. fn.1899: Most manuscripts have וגׄב; one of the Leiden manuscripts (No. 18) has נגׄד, as does Al-Harizi: כמו שנמצא, as we find it. Ibn Tibbon's version combines the two readings: כמו שנמצא שחייבוהו; Ibn Tibbon had doubtless placed one of the two verbs in the margin, which copyists later joined together.
fn.1900: See Vayikra Rabbah, sect. 28 (fol. 168, col. 4); Midrash Koheleth, at chap. I, v. 3. Maimonides' citation, as often happens, differs slightly from our editions of the Midrashim, which read: שמצאו בו דברים שהם נוטים לצד מינות.
fn.1901: Literally: Toward opinions foreign to the opinions of the Law.
fn.1902: That is to say: those who did not know how to separate the eternity of the world from its perpetual duration had to explain these words of Ecclesiastes in the sense that the earth will have the duration fixed for it in advance by the Creator.
fn.1903: In the editions of Ibn Tibbon's version, the verse יְיָ מֶלֶךְ עוֹלָם וָעֶד (Ps. 10:16) is cited here.
fn.1905: That is to say, the heavens and their laws.
fn.1906: The editions of Ibn Tibbon's version contain כי אי אפשר המצא דבר מביא לשנויים. The words המצא דבר are not in the manuscripts and were added only for greater clarity.
fn.1907: Literally: It is also as if he had wanted to give a goal to what exists, or to excuse what is changed, by saying, etc.; that is to say: it seems that Solomon, by the final words of this verse, wanted to indicate the goal God had in creating the world, or else to justify the change that the laws of nature seem to undergo, at certain times, through the intervention of miracles. — The words תכלית כונה, in Ibn Tibbon's version, are a double translation of the Arabic word גאיה̈; one of the two words should therefore be deleted.
fn.1908: Cf. on this expression, applied to Moses, Vol. I, p. 216, note 2.
fn.1909: Ibn Tibbon translates: על נתיצת עם; Al-Harizi says more precisely: על עקירת מלכות, for the Arabic word دولة, which Ibn Tibbon often translates as עם or אומה, nation, means dynasty, empire.
fn.1910: The verb כור, in the 1st and 2nd forms, means to wrap the head (with a turban). In the Quran, كُوِّرَتْ is said of the sun (chap. LXXXI, v. 1): إِذَا الشَّمْسُ كُوِّرَتْ. Commentators do not agree on the meaning of this passive verb; it is explained as to be obscured or enveloped, to set, to be effaced. See the Commentary on the Maqamat of Hariri, p. 313. Maimonides attaches to it the idea of upheaval or destruction, as he himself says in his letter to R. Samuel Ibn Tibbon: ואלסמא כורת באלכאף ומעני אלתכויר אבארה̈ אלסמא 'One must read כורת with a kaf. This verb is said of the destruction of the heaven.'
fn.1911: That is to say: it was turned upside down.
fn.1912: Saadia translates in the same sense: ואדׄ יבער אללה האולא אלנאסי, and behold, God will remove these men (the Israelites).
fn.1913: Literally: I will make you see the truth and the demonstration of it; that is to say: I will demonstrate to you through examples that what I am saying is true.
fn.1914: Ibn Tibbon has: והשמים נהפכים עליו; perhaps he read, in his Arabic text, מנקלבה̈ instead of מנטבקה̈.
fn.1915: The Paris manuscript (no. 237) contains מתממא, in finishing.
fn.1916: Similarly Saadia: פיכ׳זא אלקמ ריון ויכ׳יב אלשמסיון.
fn.1917: See vol. I, p. 111, note 2, and p. 355, note 1.
fn.1918: The verb اقبال, IVth form of the root قول, or قيل (See the Commentary on the Maqamat of al-Hariri, p. 6), means to cancel a bargain, to release someone from an engagement, to forgive him; hence, أقال عثرته, he raised him from his fall, both literally and figuratively. XVI: ועת׳רוא עת׳רה̈ לא אקאלה̈ להם מנהא, which Ibn Tibbon translates: כשלו כשלון אין תקומה להם ממנו, literally, and they have made a false step (or a fall) from which they cannot recover.
fn.1919: The words וסקוט בכ׳ותהם וכ׳מול חט׳וט׳ עט׳מאיחם are rendered, in Ibn Tibbon's version, as והשפלם ושחות גדוליהם. It can be seen that this translator has neglected the words בכ׳ות and חט׳וט׳. I, p. 52, note 2); he observes at the same time that כ׳מול has here the sense of disappearance, vanishing: וזו המלה (חטף) היא בפרק כ"ט מהחלק השני ובמול חטףות עצמיותיהם העתיק ושחוה גדוליהם ולא העתיק זו המלה והעתקתו וההתעלם מעלות גדוליהם כי במול הההעלם הפך הראות ומלת במול שהוא הההעלם הורה על ענין שהוא יתעלם הכבוד והמעלה.

XLVII: אלאסתעאראת ואלאג׳אזאת, metaphors and hyperboles. The word تغاي, the verbal noun of the VIth form, is also used in the same sense. See my edition of the Commentary of R. Tanhum on Habakkuk, p. 33, and note 13 b, p. 98.

fn.1922: All Arabic manuscripts have ותנסי תלך, which Ibn Tibbon and Al-Harizi render as וישכחו הראשונים.
fn.1923: One must delete from Ibn Tibbon's version the words וימלאו את הארץ, which are expressed neither in the Arabic text nor in Al-Harizi's version.

fn.1925: Literally: Measure it (or compare it) with what I have cited.
fn.1926: This sentence is missing in the editions of Ibn Tibbon's version; one must add, according to the manuscripts: כבר אמר יואל זה על יום בוא הארבה עליהם.

fn.1994: This is to explain one enigma by another; for the author does not tell us what, in his view, is the meaning of R. Akiba's obscure words, which have been the crux of interpreters. This whole paragraph in general is very obscure, and it seems that Maimonides intended to conform strictly to Talmudic prescriptions by speaking only in guarded terms about the Ma’aseh Bereshith (see the Introduction to this work, Vol. I, p. 10). It appears that our author, combining the words of Genesis and Peripatetic theories, admitted the existence of the three elements of fire, air, and water between the moon's orbit and our atmosphere, forming spheres that surround our globe. These spheres contain the sublunary prime matter clothed in elementary forms; these are only elements in potentiality, which, in our atmosphere, become elements in actuality. In the 3rd sphere, or water, a separation was formed called the firmament (רקיע); the upper part remained water as an element in all its abstraction, while the lower part became water properly speaking, which fills the cavities of the earth. It would thus be, according to our author, the upper water, the moist and cold element, that R. Akiba designated by the words pure marble, and he would have meant that one must be careful not to see in it water similar to that here below. This seems to me to be the sense of this obscure paragraph as a whole. However, according to Moses of Narbonne and some other commentators, the lower water, the water of the seas, is itself what constitutes the element of water; while by the upper water, Maimonides is supposed to mean the middle layer of air. According to the Arabian Peripatetics, air is divided into three layers: the first, near the element of fire, is hot and dry, giving rise to various meteors, such as comets, shooting stars, thunderbolts, etc.; the second, in the middle, is cold and moist, and the vapors that rise into it descend as rain, snow, or hail; the third, near the earth, is heated by the reverberation of the sun's rays. According to the commentators, it is this last layer of air that Maimonides would have considered the separation, or firmament, which separates the lower water, or that of the seas (which is itself elementary water), from the upper water, or the second layer of air, which is only potential water. It would thus be the latter of which R. Akiba intended to speak in saying that it should not be called water. See the commentaries of Moses of Narbonne and Shem-Tob on our passage, and the commentary of Isaac Abravanel on the Pentateuch, on verse 6 of the 1st chapter of Genesis, 4th opinion.

fn.2020: By the Hebrew words מגלה סוד, the author alludes to a passage in Proverbs 11:13.
fn.2021: The author has in view a passage from Bereshith Rabbah, sect. 8, at the beginning (fol. 6, col. 2), where it is said that Adam was created at once male and female, and that he had two faces (דיו פרצופין) turned in two directions; cf. fn.2023: Ibn Tibbon's translation אחד מחלקיו (one of its parts) is inexact; see Ibn Falaquera, loc. cit..
fn.2024: The author means: It is clear that this narrative contains a certain philosophical idea; he contents himself with indicating it, but does not deem it appropriate to explain it clearly. According to the commentators, the author saw in this narrative an allusion to the union of matter and form, which in our thought are two distinct things, but which in reality are always united together and which the creative word brought forth from nothingness at the same instant. The author seems to allude to the same idea in Ch. VI of the first part, by saying that the word ISHA (woman) was used metaphorically for anything destined and ready to join with another thing, which indicates prime matter destined to receive form, or the male (ISH), and which we separate in our thought.
fn.2027: Here again, the author does not give an opinion on the philosophical idea he believes is hidden beneath this narrative and indicated by the names used therein. According to the commentators, the word נָחָשׁ, serpent, indicates the imaginative faculty and is related to the word נַחַשׁ which designates divination, in which the imagination plays a significant role; the name Sammael is said to come from the verb סמא, to blind, and would indicate the appetitive faculty, or concupiscence, which blinds man; finally, God who laughs at the camel (serpent) and its rider is the intellect.
fn.2028: It must be remembered that God says to the serpent: And I will put enmity between you and the woman, between your seed and her seed (Genesis 3:15). As we have just stated, the serpent represents the imaginative faculty; the author seems to wish to indicate here this allegorical meaning: that the imagination does not directly affect the intellect, represented by Adam, and that it only disturbs the latter through an intermediary, which is either matter or the sensible faculty, represented by Eve.
fn.2029: That is to say, by striking it on the head.
fn.2030: The commentators offer only unsatisfactory explanations of the allegory the author may have had in mind in this last passage; the most plausible seems to me to be that of Shem-Tob, who expresses it roughly as follows: The offspring of the woman, or the human being, through his rational and speculative faculty, or through his intellect, triumphs over the imagination, which has its seat in the head and destroys its phantoms. However, the imaginative faculty and the passions arising from it often strike man at the heel, that is to say, they prevent him from moving forward, from developing his intellectual faculties, and from arriving at the conception of intelligible things.
fn.2031: More literally: Of the number of astonishing passages, etc., is what they say. All the MSS have והו קולהם, as does Ibn Tibbon: והוא אמרם; since these words are the consequent of the words ומן אלאקאויל, it would have been more correct to write הו without the conjunctive ו. It is likely the author himself who wrote והו through inadvertence. As for the word פהמת, Ibn Tibbon considered it a passive verb (فُهِمَتْ), the subject of which is פצול, and translated it as וכשיובנו; however, the verb תעג̇ב that follows clearly shows that it should be pronounced فَهِمْتَ, an active verb, of which פצול is the object.
fn.2032: See Babylonian Talmud, Shabbath, fol. 146 a; Yebamoth, fol. 103 b. According to Maimonides, the sense of the passage appears to be this: the imaginative faculty, by awakening the passions, taints man with impurity; the Israelites, by receiving a moral law that subdued their passions, purified themselves of this impurity, with which the pagans remained constantly tainted.
fn.2033: The verb תדבר must be pronounced تَدَبُّر, imperative of the fifth form, and Ibn Tibbon incorrectly translated it as והנהיג (MSS והנהיגו). Al-Harizi rendered it better as והעיר מחשבתך לזה.
fn.2034: See Bereshith Rabbah, sect. 15 (fol. 13, col. 2); Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot, chap. I, and the commentary Yefeh Mareh, ibid., § 4.

The word קורה, which means beam, is used here in the sense of tree trunk.
fn.2036: Instead of ההשאלה, which the editions of Ibn Tibbon's version have here, one should read ההשלמה, as found in the MSS of that version and that of Al-Harizi.
fn.2037: Here again, one can only catch a glimpse of the allegorical meaning the author found in the words of the doctors. What is most probable is that he saw in the tree of life science, which is the true life of the human soul. This science encompasses a span of five hundred years' journey, that is to say, it extends over everything that exists below the sphere of the moon; for according to the rabbis, there is a journey of five hundred years from the earth to the sky or to the last of the celestial spheres: מן הארץ עד לרקיע מהלך חמש מאות שנה (Babylonian Talmud, Hagigah, fol. 13 b; cf. Part III of this work, chap. XIV). These sublunary things, which alone are completely accessible to human science, are designated by the trunk of the tree; its branches, which extend far beyond the sphere of the moon, represent the science of the celestial spheres and metaphysics, of which man can acquire only a more or less imperfect knowledge. Cf. the commentaries of Ephodi and Shem-Tob.
fn.2038: See Bereshith Rabbah, sect. 15, at the end, where, after reporting the opinions of several doctors on the species to which the tree of knowledge belonged, the opinion of R. Joshua ben Levi is cited, who said that the tree of knowledge should never be precisely designated, so that no man could know the fruit that led to sin.
fn.2039: To understand this passage, one must remember the distinction the author established, in chap. II of Part I, between the knowledge of true and false and that of good and evil. The intellect, through which man knows truth and falsehood, was given to man from the moment of creation, and it is this that made him like God; but the knowledge of what is beautiful or ugly, good or evil, is only a consequence of man's sin and the loss of his state of innocence. According to the author, therefore, the passage from the Midrash just cited means that it is not God who directly reveals to man, by giving him intellect, the knowledge of what is beautiful or ugly, proper or improper, and that the objects of this knowledge would not exist for him if he had not sinned and were not led away by his desires and evil inclinations.
fn.2041: Ibn Tibbon (MS) has לא אמרו זה הלשון, which is a misinterpretation; for the word אלנץ here designates the biblical verse. Al-Harizi says more accurately אין זה הפסוק להעלותו וכו׳.
fn.2042: That is to say, in a moral situation that elevated him above all beings here below, and it is this situation that is allegorically designated by the words Garden of Eden.
fn.2043: The verb אמהל is in the passive أَمْهِلْ. Ibn Tibbon's translation, שהאריך (for שהאריך אף), is not entirely accurate; some MSS have שנמחל. Al-Harizi translates: ואם האריכו חיי המתגבר והרוצח.
fn.2044: The author limits himself to inviting the disciple to meditate on the symbolic meaning of the names of Kain, Hebel, and Scheth, and on the allegories contained in the biblical narrative. The silence kept by the author regarding his true thought has given rise to various explanations; commentators generally agree in seeing the three sons of Adam as symbols of different faculties of the rational soul. Kain represents the faculty of practical arts, necessary for the preservation of the body, of which one of the main ones is agriculture; the name Kain, which the biblical text relates to the verb kanâ (to acquire), means acquisition, possession. Hebel represents reflection, which judges the appropriateness of actions from a moral perspective, and which determines the governance of the individual and of societies, represented by the image of the shepherd. The name Hebel, which means vanity, indicates that the faculty of reflection, although superior to that of the practical arts, is a vain and perishable thing; for what remains of man after death is intelligence alone, represented by Schéth, who alone among the sons of Adam resembled his father, created in the image of God, as the author observed in Part I of this work, Chap. VII. If Kain kills Hebel in the field, this indicates that the man who lives outside of social habits and laws does not possess exact notions of what is just or unjust and yields to violence. See the commentaries of Moses of Narbonne and Ephodi; and cf. the passage by Maimonides on the rational part of the soul, cited in vol. I of this work, p. 210, note 1. See also, on our passage, the commentary of Isaac Abravanel on the Pentateuch, Genesis, Chap. 4, verses 1-8.
fn.2045: That is to say, that words are a matter of pure convention, and that they did not originate in the very nature of the things they serve to designate. This is what results, according to the author, from the passage in question, where the naming of all beings is attributed solely to the will of Adam, who invents names at random.
fn.2046: The author seems to allude to a passage from the Midrash, where it is said that Adam's wisdom, that is, his knowledge of natural things, was superior to that of the angels; for the latter were ignorant of the nature of sublunar things and did not know how to call them by their names, whereas Adam knew how to give each animal the name that naturally suited it and characterized its being: אמר לזה נאה לקראתו שור ולזה ארי ולזה סוס ולזה חמור ולזה גמל ולזה נשר וכן כלם שנאמר ויקרא האדם שמות לכל הבהמה וגו׳. See the Midrash Tanhuma, Book of Numbers, section הקת (Verona edition, fol. 77, col. 1); Bereshith Rabba, sect. 17 (fol. 14, col. 3). The words לזה נאה לקראתו וכו׳, this one it is appropriate to call, etc., are explained by Isaac Abravanel in these terms: לפי שלא היו אותם השמות מוסכמים כפי הרצון כלבד אבל מונחים ונגזרים באופן נאות לטבעיהם ולצורותיהם "Because these names were not simply conventional and arbitrary, but established and derived in a manner suited to the nature of the objects and their forms." See Abravanel's dissertation on the wisdom of Solomon, chap. 2, in his commentary on the Book of Kings, chap. III, v. 6 ff. (Commentarius in prophetas priores, Leipzig, 1686, fol. 210, col. 3). This opinion of the ancient rabbis, which is challenged here by Maimonides, is also adopted by R. Judah ha-Levi, in his Kuzari, book IV, § 25 (Buxtorf edition, p. 303).
fn.2047: By heaven, what must be understood here is the whole of the universe.
fn.2049: The author means that this verb is never used when referring to the creation of heaven and earth, or of the universe as a whole; for, speaking of the earth alone, one also says יוצר ארץ (Isaiah, XLV, 18), which the author undoubtedly interpreted as יוצר הרים.

What caused the error is that it was not noticed that the word והאדון forms a second biblical citation.
fn.2052: Literally: And this inclines toward the belief in the eternity of a certain matter. fn.2057: That is to say: they suffice for the intelligent and learned reader whom the author had in view.
fn.2058: That is to say: Through all that has been said previously on the importance of the dogma of creation, you could already understand, by yourself, why the law of the Sabbath has been so often repeated in the Pentateuch, and why the one who transgresses it is punished with the most severe penalty, that of stoning, a penalty which was indeed applied one day by the legislator himself, as the book of Numbers reports, chap. xv, v. 32-36. — This chapter on the Sabbath is connected, as a natural complement, to all that the author has said regarding the Creation, which is symbolically represented by the solemn rest of the seventh day of the week.

It is thus that the author said above (chap. XIII, p. 107), in speaking of the Creation, that it is the second principle after that of the unity of God.
fn.2060: The author alludes, it seems to me, to conversations he had with his disciple on the motives that one can suppose for certain precepts relating to religious practices. See what he says in this regard in Part III of this work, chap. XXVII and passim.

fn.2063: That is to say: The two causes indicated in the two Decalogues are justified by the consequences that will be discussed.
fn.2064: Literally: a general benefit for the confirmation of speculative opinion and for the well-being of the bodily state. Most manuscripts read: פי צחיח אלראי אלנטֿרי. fn.2065: We believe, with Isaac Abravanel, that the author saw a certain relation between the three opinions on prophecy and the three opinions he reported above (chap. XIII) on the origin of the world; for one cannot assume that he only intended to speak of the triplicity of opinions on the two subjects, which is entirely accidental and would not have deserved the author's insistence. According to Abravanel, the first opinion on prophecy—that of the common mass of believers—is analogous to the first opinion on the origin of the world, which makes everything emanate from the sole will of God, without admitting any kind of prime matter or pre-existing substratum capable of receiving form. The second opinion on prophecy corresponds to the third on the origin of the world, or to that of the Peripatetics. The latter, admitting nothing supernatural, see in prophecy only the development and entelechy of a faculty that the entire human species possesses in potentiality, just as, according to them, there is in the universe a pre-existing matter that has received form from all eternity. Finally, the third opinion, which attributes prophecy to a pre-existing faculty developing through the divine will, is analogous to that which Plato professes on the origin of the world, according to which the world, emerged from eternal chaos, had a temporal beginning and was ordered by the free will of God. See Isaac Abravanel's commentary on various parts of the Moreh Nevukhim, published by M. J. Landau, IInd fascicle (Prague, 1832, 4to), fol. 20; cf. Isaac Arama, ’Akedah, chap. 35.

By the word الجاهلية, the author designates, in accordance with the usage of Arabic authors, the state of peoples who have not been instructed by a divine revelation, or the era of paganism.

fn.2074: The opinion that the author is about to present, and which he considers the orthodox opinion, is far from being that of the principal Jewish theologians, who generally believe that the high faculties possessed by prophets come to them from the will of God, and not from a certain innate nature, מצד הבורא ולא מצד עצמם, as Saadia says (Book of Beliefs and Opinions, book III, chap. 4, end). fn.2079: That is to say, in the Mishneh Torah, or Abridgment of the Talmud, book I, tractate Yesode ha-Torah, chap. VII.

fn.2081: According to the rabbinic commentaries, the word grandeurs, in the words of Jeremiah, designates the prophecy that Baruch aspired to and for which he had prepared himself. It would thus follow from this passage that, by divine will, the gift of prophecy can be refused even to those who are worthy of it by their natural qualities and who have worthily prepared themselves for it. However, the author adds, it would be permissible to see in the words of Jeremiah the express declaration that Baruch was not sufficiently prepared, and that it was too great an ambition on his part to wish to be a prophet, so that the passage from Jeremiah could not serve as proof for the thesis just maintained. — The commentators are surprised that the author thus refutes himself the only biblical proof he has alleged in favor of his thesis, and they see in it the implicit admission that he preferred to admit the opinion of the philosophers without any restriction. But the author expressly says that those who would understand the passage from the book of Jeremiah and that of Lamentations (II, 9) in the sense that natural aptitude and preparation alone are sufficient to form a prophet, would find many other passages, both in Holy Scripture and in the writings of the doctors, that would prove that, by divine will, the gift of prophecy can be refused even to one who is perfectly prepared for it. Abravanel cites the example of the seventy elders, who prophesied when the spirit rested upon them, but who did not continue (Numbers 11:25), which proves that they ceased to prophesy as soon as the divine will prevented them: likewise the prophets Hosea (XII, 11) and Amos (3:8) evidently make prophecy depend on the word of God or on His will. See Abravanel, l. c., fol. 20 b.
