See Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat, fol. 30 b: אין השכינה שורה לא מתוך עצבות ולא מתוך עצלות; cf. Maimonides, Yesodei ha-Torah, chap. VII, § 4, and below, chap. XXXVI (p. 287).
fn.2083: The verb ינבי is evidently active يَنْبِي having as its subject the word אללה understood and as its object אברהם, and the two Hebrew translators wrongly translated it as a neutral or passive verb, one by שינׇּבא and הנבא, the other by שיתנבא; we have therefore written חמארא and צׄפדעא in the accusative, although the mss. bear חמאר and צׄפדע, without א.
fn.2084: That is to say: divine power only grants the gift of prophecy when it has become possible through good preparation. All the mss. have קדרה̈ אלאלאה, which Ibn Tibbon rendered by גזרת השם ית׳, taking קדרה̈ in the sense of קדר; Al-Harizi has: כה האלוהי.
fn.2085: The author means that one should not conclude from this passage that certain men are predestined to prophecy by the sole will of God, without their needing intellectual or moral preparation.
fn.2086: Jeremiah says: I do not know how to speak, for I am a young man, נער; from which one might infer that, although an inexperienced young man, he could be entrusted with a prophetic mission, and that he needed no preparatory study. To answer this objection, the author cites some examples proving that the Hebrew word NA’AR also sometimes designates a man of mature age. It designates, in effect, the servant, of whatever age, like the Greek word πϰῖς and the Latin word puer; but this sense cannot apply to the passage in Jeremiah, and the author's explanation is evidently strained.
fn.2087: The author seems to be alluding to the words of Pharaoh's chief cupbearer (Genesis 41:12), who designates Joseph as NA’AR, or young man, although he was then nearly thirty years old (cf. ibid., v. 46).
fn.2088: All the mss. bear: אחד ותׄמאנין; we have more correctly written אחדי in the feminine, for one must understand סנה̈. Further on, the mss. incorrectly bear ארבעה̈ עשר, for ארבע עשרה̈; likewise מאיה̈ ועשרה̈ for מאיה̈ ועשר, and סבעה̈ for סבע.
fn.2089: The editions of Ibn Tibbon's version have כל מגיד בעולם; instead of בעולם, one must read בנעלם as the mss. have it. Al-Harizi translates: כל מודיע העתידות.
fn.2090: It appears evident to us that the word רויה̈ (رؤية) must be taken here in the sense of رؤيا, dream, and Ibn Tibbon wrongly rendered this word by מחשבה, thought. The true dream is what Aristotle calls εὐθυονειρία. See my Mélanges de philosophie juive et arabe, p. 95, note 1.
fn.2091: The word מחיצה, which properly signifies partition, separation wall, compartment, is here used figuratively to designate the different degrees of perception. See Mekhilta or rabbinic commentary on Exodus, at chap. 19, verse 24 (Venice edition, fol. 25, col. 1), and the commentary of Rashi on the same passage of Exodus; cf. Abravanel, commentary on Exodus, chap. 19, 13th question.
fn.2092: That is to say: The people did not hear distinctly, and in their entirety, all the divine words that reached the ear of Moses. — In Ibn Tibbon's version, the words גׄמיע and הו כלה have not been reproduced; however, the first of these words is rendered in the mss. and in the commentaries, which have: כל המגיע למשה. Some mss. bear קול המגיע, which is an error. Al-Harizi translates: לא היו כל הדברים המגיעים למשה מגיעים לכל ישראל.
fn.2093: See Mekhilta, on the verse וידבר אלהים (Exodus 20:1): מלמד שאמר המקום עשרת הדברות בדבור אחד חזר ופרשן דבור דבור בפני עצמו.
fn.2094: Literally: not the distinction of the discourse.
fn.2095: That is to say: the first two commandments, one beginning with the words I am the Eternal your God, and the other with the words you shall have no other gods, all the Hebrews present before Mount Sinai heard them pronounced by God Himself. See Babylonian Talmud, tractate Makkot, fol. 24 a; Midrash on the Song, or Shir ha-Shirim Rabbah, fol. 3, col. 2. — According to this passage, therefore, the first two commandments would be an exception to the principle the author has just laid down, since the whole people directly heard every word from the voice of God, without needing the mediation of Moses.
fn.2096: That is to say: these are perfectly demonstrable philosophical principles, for which one does not need a prophetic revelation.
fn.2097: Here is the meaning, according to the author, of this passage from Deuteronomy: you were shown the way in order to know, that is to say, to recognize, solely through the path of the intellect and science, that God exists and that there is no other God besides him.
fn.2098: The eight other commandments concern things that do not belong to the domain of the intellect, and which could not be the object of a demonstrative syllogism; they concern virtues and vices, good and evil, which belong to the domain of probable opinions, or even purely traditional matters, such as the fourth commandment regarding the Sabbath. On the meaning of the word אלמשהוראת, see Vol. I, p. 39, note 1.
fn.2099: The verb استقل here has the sense of أجمل, to support, to bear, to admit, to allow; the author means that it is the opinion which, according to the texts, is admissible.
fn.2100: That is to say: a single prolonged sound, without any interval. See Mekhilta, loc. cit. (cf. Yalkut, Vol. I, no. 285): אח כל הדברים מלמד שאמר המקום עשרת הדברות בדבור אחד מה שאי אפשר לבשר ודם לומר כן. Cf. Midrash Tanhuma, section יתרו (fol. 51, col. 3): אמרו ז״ל שעשרת הדברות כלן בקול אחד יצאו מפי הגבורה וכו׳. I believe that in the Arabic text (קול ואחד), קול should be considered a Hebrew word meaning voice, sound. It is also in this sense that it was understood by Ibn Tibbon, who has: קול אחד, while Al-Harizi translates: דבור אחד. Immediately following, the words והו אלקול are rendered in Ibn Tibbon's version as והוא המאמר, and in Al-Harizi's as והוא הדבור. However, in Ephodi's commentary, one reads וזהו הקול.
fn.2101: The author thus considers admissible the opinion of certain doctors, who say that all the Israelites heard the first two commandments proclaimed by the divine voice itself. But, according to the principle he established at the beginning of the chapter, he believes that Moses alone heard them distinctly, whereas for the people it was only a confused sound of a voice; this means that even of these purely intelligible and perfectly demonstrable things, Moses had a clearer and deeper understanding than all the other Israelites. If what was said for the first two commandments is explained in this sense, it must be assumed that, regarding the eight other commandments, the people no longer even heard the confused sound they had heard initially, and that these commandments were simply reported to them by Moses, in the name of God, like all the other commandments of the divine law. But, whether one admits that the people heard the entire Decalogue directly from the divine voice, or that they heard only the first two commandments, what the author primarily wishes to establish is that the people heard this divine voice only confusedly and that the words did not distinctly strike their ears.
fn.2102: Literally: The doctors mentioned this, supporting it, etc. The author refers to that prolonged and confused sound of a voice that the Israelites heard during the proclamation of either the entire Decalogue or only the first two commandments. See Mekhilta, loc. cit., Yalkut, Vol. I, no. 285, and Vol. II, no. 783: שלא כמדת הקדוש ברוך הוא מדת בשר ודם בשר ודם אינו משמיע ב׳ דברים כאחד אבל מי שאמר והיה העולם אמר עשרת הדברות בדבור אחד שנאמר אחת דבר אלהים וידבר אלהים את כל הדברים האלה לאמר.
fn.2103: Here, the two Hebrew translators considered קול as an Arabic word and rendered it, one as מאמר, the other as דבור; however, the result of the whole is that it is still a question of the divine voice heard by all the Israelites, which inspired such terror in them. After the proclamation of the commandments, says the author, they no longer heard this divine voice, but only the sound of thunder. In the passage from the Midrash that the author cites (Shir ha-Shirim Rabbah, loc. cit.), it is stated that, according to R. Joshua ben Levi, the Israelites only heard the first two commandments proclaimed by the mouth of God, but that, according to the other doctors, they heard the entire Decalogue; all thus agree in saying that by the voices mentioned before and after the Decalogue, one should not understand the divine voice, but the sounding of horns and thunder. — By מדרש חזית, one designates the Midrash on the Song of Songs, which begins with the citation of the verse חזית איש מהיר במלאכתו (Prov. 22:29).
fn.2104: The author again speaks here in the sense of those who say that the Israelites themselves directly heard only the first two commandments, an opinion the author has judged admissible and which he ultimately seems to adopt. See above, p. 270, note 4.
fn.2105: The words אעני תלך אלאצואת were not rendered in the versions of Ibn Tibbon and Al-Harizi, nor are they found in the Leiden MS, no. 18.
fn.2106: Literally: saw. Cf. Vol. I, Ch. XLVI, p. 161.
fn.2107: See Vol. I, Ch. LXV, p. 290, and ibid., note 2.
fn.2108: With the Hebrew words יצאה נשמתן בשמעו, the author alludes to a passage in the Midrash on the Song of Songs, Ch. V, verse 6 (fol. 19, col. 4): נפשי יצאה בדברו מקול דבורו הראשון שאמר אנכי ה׳ אלהיך. Cf. Yalkut, on the same verse of the Song (Vol. II, no. 988, fol. 179, col. 4): בדבור ראשון יצאה נשמתן של ישראל.
fn.2109: Literally: The whole that we have separated. The author means that Onkelos, through his manner of translating, highlighted the distinction that must be established in this perception, common to Moses and the other Israelites, by indicating that Moses perceived the divine word distinctly and directly through his intellect, which reflected it clearly to him, whereas for the other Israelites it was, in a sense, veiled; for they perceived it only confusedly, and it could not strike their intellect so vividly, as it was clouded by the senses. — According to R. Moses ben Nahman (Commentary on the Pentateuch, Exodus, 20:16), Maimonides' observation concerning Onkelos is poorly founded; he cites in this regard several passages from Onkelos' version where the communication of the divine word to the Israelites is expressed by the words מלל יי (See Exodus, 20:19; Deuteronomy, V, 4, 19, and 21), and another passage where the communication made to Moses himself is expressed by the periphrasis מן קדם יי (See Exodus, 19:19). — Abravanel, to justify Maimonides, observes that in the first four passages, the Hebrew text itself sufficiently indicates that the word was communicated through an intermediary designated by the words heaven (מן השמים) and fire (מתוך האש), and that, consequently, Onkelos was not obliged to use a periphrasis; as for the last passage, it speaks of the divine voice heard simultaneously by Moses and the Hebrew people, and it is for this reason that Onkelos felt obliged to use the periphrasis מן קדם יי here. See Abravanel's Commentary on our chapter, fol. 26 b and 27 a.
fn.2111: Ibn Tibbon's version reads החכמים שבישראל, the wisest in Israel. The word החכמים should be considered a superlative, by which the translator intended to render the Arabic word באטלאק, par excellence or in the absolute sense. Al-Harizi translates: אשר הס חכמי ישראל במלה מוחלטת.
fn.2112: More literally: in a greater measure than what they (the doctors) said of it.
fn.2113: Literally: the truth of this perception and what its state was is what is very hidden from us. The word כֿפי (خَفِي) should be considered a neuter adjective: something hidden.
fn.2114: The author intends to say, not that the messenger, or the angel, referred to in the passage of Exodus, is himself the prophet mentioned in Deuteronomy, but that he designates the active intellect that inspires the prophet. It clearly follows from what the author said above (ch. VII, p. 76) that, in the passage of Exodus, by angel one must understand that of the separate intelligences, or superior forces, through which God communicates with the prophet.
fn.2115: That is to say: what proves that this refers to the superior power in relationship with the prophet, and not an angel who would have marched at the head of the people and revealed himself to them.
fn.2116: Cf. the 1st part of this work, chap. LXIV (vol. I, p. 286).
fn.2117: Literally, to make them know that etc. The conjunction أنَّ, that, serves here to introduce direct speech. Cf. vol. I, p. 283, note 4. Instead of אעלאמא (أَعْلَامًا), the mss. have אעלאם; this infinitive, it seems to me, must be taken adverbially and put in the accusative.
fn.2118: In Ibn Tibbon's version, one must read מעמד instead of במעמד.
fn.2119: See Exodus, chap. 40, verse 38; Numbers, chap. 9, verses 15 and 16.
fn.2120: The verb محمد means to extend, to deploy, to prepare. The meaning is: he will make the land you are to conquer accessible to you. The editions of Ibn Tibbon's version have וישקיט, he will appease; in some mss. one reads ויזמן, he will prepare. Al-Harizi has: ויושיבכם על הארץ.
fn.2121: These words still relate to what was to be done for the taking possession of the conquered country, while the following words relate in general to the rules of conduct they were to observe thereafter. The conjunction ف, in פיעלמכם, indicates that this verb designates a new action, a continuation or consequence of the preceding one. In Ibn Tibbon's version, the words וילמדכם מה שצריך לעשותו may seem a useless repetition of ויודיעכם מה שתעשוהו.
fn.2122: That is to say: by the explanation of the passage Behold, I send an angel before thee, applied to the prophets who would come after Moses, the principle that the author set forth elsewhere and which the following chapter treats has been made known, namely, that the other prophets, before and after Moses, received divine inspiration through an angel, that is to say, through something intermediary, such as the active intellect, or only the imagination. The verb אעטי should be considered, I believe, as a passive preterite (أَعْطَىٰ); as it precedes the subject אלואעדׄה, it could be put in the masculine, even though this subject is feminine; likewise, according to Ibn Tibbon's version, the verb נתן should be pronounced נִתַּן, which is indicated in some mss. by the full spelling: ניתן. In several of our Arabic mss. we read אעטא, which should be considered as a noun of action إِعْطَاء, so that one should translate into Hebrew: ובזה גם כן נתינת היסוד. The word איצׄא, also, is not found in all mss. and has not been rendered in the two Hebrew verses.
fn.2123: That is to say, in a popular language, accessible to everyone, as is that of the Talmudic works of our author.
fn.2124: See the Commentary on the Mishnah, Introduction to the 10th (11th) chap. of the treatise Sanhedrin, seventh article of faith (Pococke, Porta Mosis, p. 169-173); Mishneh Torah or Abridgment of the Talmud, treatise Yesode ha-Torah, chap. VII, § 6. The author points out the following differences: 1. God spoke to all prophets in general only through an intermediary, whereas He spoke to Moses without an intermediary. 2. All prophets had their divine revelations only in dreams or night visions, or in a state of slumber, in which the senses ceased to function; but Moses had his inspirations in a waking state and in full possession of all his faculties. 3. All prophets experienced, during their vision, a convulsive trembling and extreme agitation; Moses was always in a perfect calm. 4. All prophets, although perfectly prepared for divine inspiration, were inspired only at certain times, by a particular grace of the divine will; Moses had the privilege of being able spontaneously and at any hour to call upon divine inspiration.
fn.2125: From one point of view, the name prophet can be considered as a common name, fitting Moses as well as all other prophets; but, from another point of view, it can be considered as a homonymous name, since there is an essential and well-defined difference between Moses and the other prophets. It is therefore what is called an ambiguous or amphibological name. See vol. I of this work, p. 6, note 3, and p. 229.
fn.2126: As for example, Noah, Shem, and Eber.
fn.2127: The author intends to say that, in the passage he is about to cite, the matter is simply stated as a fact, and not presented in the form of a theory.
fn.2128: That is to say: and with all the more reason Moses's perception must have essentially differed from the perception of those who, among the pagan nations, passed for prophets, such as for example Balaam.
fn.2129: Ibn Tibbon's version reads: תמה מהם, or, according to some mss., יתמה מהם, marvelled at them; this translation is inaccurate, as Ibn Falaquera has already observed. See Appendix to More ha-More, p. 155: ימתפהם ענהא העתיק יתמה מהם והעתקתו יבקש ידיעתם והחריזי העתיק ישאל בעדם.
fn.2130: In the editions of Ibn Tibbon's version, the words על צד ההגדה are missing, which are found in some mss.
fn.2131: Ibn Tibbon's version reads: האוהב והשונא הנאות לו והחולק עליו; this is a double translation of the Arabic words אלמואלף לה ואלמכֿאלף עליה.
fn.2132: Ibn Tibbon and Al-Harizi have rendered only one of the two synonymous verbs: בי קשר הנה שני עניינים יחד.
fn.2133: The Leiden ms., no. 18, reads בעדה, after him; likewise Al-Harizi, אחריו.
fn.2135: The author does not clearly express his entire thought. According to the commentators, he indicates by the words ענדהם, for them, and הנאך, there (that is, in those regions), that the miracle was purely local and that one should not think of a real slowing down in the movement of the solar sphere; for such a miracle would have caused a universal catastrophe. Indeed, as the author expressly says elsewhere (Part I, ch. LXXII, p. 362): 'Just as when the heart stops for a single moment, the individual dies, and his movements and faculties cease, so if the celestial spheres stopped, it would be the death of the entire universe and the annihilation of everything within it.' — Maimonides therefore seems to intimate here that, during the battle of Gibeon, the day appeared to the Israelites to extend beyond its ordinary limits because of the great things that had been accomplished; or else that, by a miracle, God had caused a light independent of that of the sun to appear, so that it seemed as if the sun itself had stopped.
fn.2136: Literally: for the singularity of this perception is like the singularity of those acts.
fn.2137: Literally: all this after this degree (of which mention has been made).
fn.2138: Literally: the reality of prophecy and its quiddity.
fn.2139: Ibn Tibbon here renders the word מאדהּ, matter, by ליחה, humor; he does the same in several other passages. See, for example, Part I, ch. LXXII, Arabic text, fol. 102 a, and French trans., p. 368.
fn.2140: Ibn Tibbon did not render the words יגבר פאיתה או; Al-Harizi's version reads: וזה הדבר לא יתכן להשיג מה שאבד ממנו או למלאות חמרונו.
fn.2141: Literally: of its measure, that is, of its volume being too large or too small.
fn.2142: Literally: there is no artifice for this.

fn.2144: The text reads: and that its activity etc.; the conjunction ואן, and that, is connected to the verb עלמת (you know) located at the beginning of the sentence.
fn.2146: That is to say: the inspiration in question is of the same species in dreams and in prophecy, and it differs only in the degree of intensity, being much stronger in prophecy than in dreams. — The verb יכתלף, which is in the masculine singular, refers to פיץ׳, inspiration, and it was erroneous of Ibn Tibbon to render it by the plural יתחלפו.
fn.2148: See Bereshith Rabbah, sect. 17 (f. 14, col. 4), and sect. 44 (f. 39, col. 3).
fn.2149: Literally: before its perfection and before having matured.
fn.2150: Some MSS. have אבתדאה, others אבתדא or אבתדי. fn.2151: Literally: that, if there were a human individual etc. We have found it necessary to modify slightly, in our translation, the first words of this sentence, which begins a long hypothetical period enumerating all the physical and moral qualities required for prophetic inspiration, and whose grammatical complement only begins at the words: פאלשכ׳ץ אלד׳י הדה צפתה (fol. 79 b, line 10). If there were a human individual, says the author, who possessed all the qualities to be enumerated, that individual, led by the action of his perfect imaginative faculty and calling forth through his speculative perfection the inspiration of the active intellect, would undoubtedly perceive divine, extraordinary things, etc. (below, p. 286). — It was all the more necessary, for the sake of clarity, to break up this period, as the author himself lost the thread of it and interrupted himself with a brief digression on a passage from Aristotle's Ethics.
fn.2152: That is to say: in such a way that all the faculties he possesses potentially could develop and pass into reality or actuality.
fn.2153: It should be remembered that, according to Aristotle, virtue consists in avoiding extremes and in knowing how to maintain a reasonable mean in our inclinations, equally distant from excess and deficiency. See Nicomachean Ethics, book II, chapters 5 and 6.
fn.2154: Word for word: that his thought were idle and his desire unoccupied with regard to animal matters.
fn.2155: See Nicomachean Ethics, book III, ch. 13, where Aristotle says, speaking of the sense of touch: Καὶ δόξειεν ἂν δικαίως ἐπονείδιστος εἶναι, ὅτι οὐχ ᾗ ἀνθρωποί ἐσαεν ὑπάρχει, ἀλλ’ ᾗ ζῷα.
fn.2156: The MSS. generally have the vulgar form יתנבוא, some יתנבון; we have written more correctly יהנבאוק .
fn.2157: Literally: not true, or not real; that is, ambitions directed toward vain things, devoid of any true value.
fn.2158: Literally: solely for that, that is, for the sole pleasure of receiving homage and being respected and obeyed. According to Abravanel (loc. cit., fol. 38 a), the author would seem to allude here to the ambitious views of the prophet Muhammad.

fn.2160: It seems to me that by solitary the author here means the sage, who isolates himself from human society in order to remain out of reach of their vices and not to be disturbed in his meditations; this is the sage mentioned by Ibn Bājja in his treatise The Regime of the Solitary. fn.2162: See Pirke Rabbi Eliezer, ch. XXXVIII, and cf. Maimonides, Eight Chapters, or Introduction to the tractate Aboth, ch. VII.

According to Ephodi, the author intended to imply here, without daring to state it clearly, that Moses himself needed, to a certain point, the imaginative faculty in order to predict the future. Abravanel (l. c., fol. 35 a) considers this opinion of Ephodi as a genuine heresy.
fn.2166: See the passages indicated above, p. 277, note 2.
fn.2167: Literally: and this could not continue; the word דֿלך, that, this thing, refers to the prophecy. Al-’Harîzi translates literally: וזה לא היה נוהג; Ibn-Tibbon: ולא התמידה להם, and it did not continue for them.
fn.2168: Literally: what dejection or (what) sadness can exist for a man, in any circumstance (that may be) more serious etc. — Ibn-Tibbon rendered this passage inaccurately, by misunderstanding the meaning of the word איי, which he pronounced أَيّ, and which he rendered by כלומר, namely, whereas it must be pronounced أَيْ; this error led him to add a conjunctive ו to the word אשד and to translate ויותר חזק. fn.2170: That is to say, the instrument of prophecy, which is the imaginative faculty free from all preoccupation.
fn.2171: By the word פֿיץֿ, overflow, emanation, the author understands here the influence that the active intellect exerts on the faculties of man.
fn.2172: Literally: It is that something of it sometimes happens to an individual, in such a way that the measure of this something that happens to him is sufficient to perfect him, and nothing else.
fn.2173: Instead of שלימותו, which most editions of Ibn-Tibbon's version have, one should read השלמתו, as found in the manuscripts and the princeps edition. Al-’Harîzi's version is clearer here; it reads: שיעור יותר ממה שיהיה שלם ויוכל להשלים בו לזולתו.
fn.2174: We have followed the reading offered by most manuscripts, which read: קדר יכון מדבר (מُدَبَّرًا) בגירה. Ibn-Tibbon's version reads: כשיעור שיהיה מנהיג בו עצמו לא זולתו; likewise, Al-’Harîzi: כפי מה שינהיג בו לנפשו לא לזולתו, only as much as is necessary to govern oneself, and not others. Both translators read: קדר יכון מדברא בה נפסה לא גירה, a reading found indeed in the two Leiden mss., and which is more in conformity with the way the author expresses himself above, ch. XI (p. 95-96). According to the reading we have adopted, the sense is: while there are other beings whose entire perfection consists in being constituted in such a way as to receive the influence and direction of beings superior to them. This concerns the inferior beings governed by superior beings, whose forces are communicated to them. See above, ch. X and XI, and the 1st part of this work, ch. LXXII (vol. 1, p. 361).
fn.2175: Literally: because of the paucity (paucitatis) of the thing that overflows; that is to say, because the active intellect does not overflow sufficiently. It goes without saying that this insufficiency cannot be attributed to the active intellect itself, which is always in act and always acts with the same force; but the matter upon which it acts (or the hylic intellect of man) can sometimes not be fit to receive the form, so that the action of the active intellect, which gives the form, finds itself halted or apparently weakened (see above, p. 139, and vol. I, p. 311, note 4). According to Shem-Tob and Abravanel, one must understand by the thing that overflows the rational faculty, which spreads over the imaginative faculty what it has received from the active intellect and which, according to whether it is more or less strong, acts more or less on the imaginative faculty. Abravanel, who could only read Ibn-Tibbon's version, believes he must relate the word ממנו (in ולא ישפע דבר ממנו) to the rational faculty; but the Arabic text which has מנה, in the masculine, does not admit of this explanation.
fn.2176: In the Leiden ms., no. 18, the words כמא בינא וביק גיראני מן אלפלאספה וכאנת אלמתחבילה were omitted, and both Hebrew translators also passed over them. The author intends to speak of what he said in the preceding chapter about the imaginative faculty and the divine emanation spreading first over the rational faculty and then over the imaginative faculty.
fn.2177: Some mss. have וואצֿעוא, with the copulative ו; according to this reading one should translate: It is the class of statesmen, legislators, etc.
fn.2178: Literally: much reciprocal superiority; that is to say, that the individuals belonging to each of these categories differ greatly among themselves by the superiority they have over one another. Ibn-Tibbon's version, which reads יתרון רב מאד, lacks clarity; the sense is: יש יתרון רב מאד לבני אדם זה על זה. At the beginning of this chapter, the words ותתפֿאצֿל עקולנא were more accurately rendered by: ויהיה יתרון שכלינו זה על זה. Al-’Harîzi translates: וידוע כי כל מין משלשת המינים האלה יש יתרון גדול לזה על זה; according to this translation, it would be the three categories themselves that would be declared to have superiority over one another, which is a misinterpretation.
fn.2179: Literally: or else, in a quantity (sufficient) to perfect him (that is to say, the individual to whom it happens), nothing else, or else, in such quantity that there remains (to the individual), after his perfection, enough to perfect others.
fn.2180: The editions of Ibn-Tibbon's version have השכלי; one should read הדברי, as found in the mss.
fn.2181: Ibn-Tibbon did not express the demonstrative pronoun הדֿא; Al-’Harîzi's version reads זה השכל.
fn.2182: Literally: and to extend from the one who receives this overflow to another who receives it after him. The verbs הַמַּהֵר, הַפִּיץ and תנתהי are in the feminine, having as their subject טביעה̈, nature.
fn.2183: Literally: to an individual whom this overflow cannot go beyond.
fn.2184: See above, ch. XI (p. 96), the example of the rich man. Ibn-Tibbon's version reads simply כמו שביארנו; but the Arabic verb מתֿל means to make a comparison.
fn.2185: Literally: even if he were to be damaged in his body. Ibn-Tibbon's version has בעצמו, for כגופו.
fn.2187: The two Hebrew translators omitted the translation of the verb צרח, which is also missing from the Leiden MS, no. 18.
fn.2188: Ibn Tibbon, who has למתום, seems to have read יכֿתם (يختم), with a pointed כֿ; according to him, one should translate: he wished to close his prophetic mission.
fn.2189: That is to say: a certain faculty of the soul that imparts boldness, and which is part of the motive faculties. In our editions of Ibn Tibbon's version, the ו in וגבורה must be deleted. Furthermore, the word גבודה is not well chosen to render the Arabic word إقدام, which means boldness, courage. Ibn Falaquera, while criticizing the use of the word גבורה here, proposes translating it as כח קדימה, and expresses himself thus regarding the faculty designated by this name: וכה הקדימה הוא שיקדים האדם וילך להלחם עם האריה או הדומה ולהכנם במקום דכנה ולא יפחד 'This faculty is that by virtue of which man advances boldly (יקדים) to fight the lion or something similar, or to go without fear into a place of danger.' See the Appendix to the Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 155. Al-Harizi calls this faculty כה אמצה.
fn.2190: Cf. Vol. I of this work, p. 367, and ibid., note 5.
fn.2191: According to Moses of Narbonne and Shem-Tob, the author, through the words with a certain way of thinking, means that one must also join a certain way of seeing to the natural predisposition; depending on whether one believes, for example, that with death everything ends for man, or that a heroic death places man in the rank of superior beings, this natural disposition will be neglected or exercised.
fn.2192: The two Hebrew versions have אלו הכחות, these faculties; but all the Arabic MSS have the singular אלקוה̈.
fn.2193: Literal translation: so that you find in your soul.
fn.2194: Ibn Tibbon translates: מי שדמיונו ומשערו וכו׳. According to Ibn Falaquera, the Arabic words حدס and شعور designate sagacity of mind, or the faculty of suddenly divining the unknown from the known (וענינם אצל חכמי המחקר זכות השכל שמבין הדבר הנסתר מתוך הדבר הנגלה במהירות ובזמן קצר מאד). He criticizes as a grave error the word דמיון, imagination, used here by Ibn Tibbon. See the Appendix to the Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 156, the note on chapter XLV.
fn.2195: Literally: that he can hardly imagine a thing to be, without it being (actually) as he imagined it, or at least in part.
fn.2196: The word קראין (قرأتن, plural of قريظة) means conjectures, combined circumstances. Ibn Tibbon translates this word simply as ענינים, and Al-Harizi as ענינים דבקים. According to Ibn Falaquera (loc. cit., p. 156), this word is used in the sense of premises; for, he says, premises, joined together, give rise to the conclusion. But, while it is true that the author says immediately afterward תלך אלמקדמאת, these premises, it does not follow from this that he uses the word קראין in the sense of premises; he only means that the mind rapidly scans all the circumstances that appeared at different times, and which, for it, are mutually linked in the blink of an eye and serve as premises from which it draws conclusions.
fn.2197: Literally: that it is in no time at all.
fn.2198: Instead of ינדֿר, the Leiden MS, no. 221, bears כֿבר; likewise Ibn Tibbon has יגידו, they announce.
fn.2199: Ibn Tibbon has שהתגבר; but this translation is rightly criticized by Ibn Falaquera (loc. cit., pp. 155–156), who translates: והיא קדימת האיש הנפרד.
fn.2200: The verb ירתע is the apocopated future of the VIIIth form of the root (يرتع) روع.
fn.2201: That is to say: boldness is indispensable to all prophets, although they possess it in varying degrees.
fn.2202: The meaning is: Just as prophets predict things that it is not given to every man to foresee through the sole faculty of divination that we all possess to a certain extent, so too they possess speculative knowledge to which the common man could not rise through philosophical speculation alone.
fn.2203: Literally: this same emanation, that is, that of the active intellect.
fn.2204: Word for word: of things of a real being; that is, things as they are in all their reality.
fn.2206: After having sought to establish, through simple analogy, that the rational faculty must be, like the imaginative faculty, much stronger in prophets than in all other men, the author intends to show, through a more direct proof, that what he has said applies even better to the rational faculty than to the imaginative faculty.
fn.2207: See the preceding chapter, p. 291. — Instead of אלד׳ין, the MSS generally have אלד׳י, which is incorrect.
fn.2208: Literally: and whose traces have remained imprinted in their chimeras.
fn.2209: It is probably through oversight that Ibn Tibbon translated here as מקומות (places, locations) the word that a little further up he himself renders as רשומים (traces), as noted by Ibn Falaquera (Appendix to Moré ha-Moré, p. 156).
fn.2210: Literally: and they appeared to them in such a way that they believed them to be something new.
fn.2211: The author means that it is even possible that the predictions of these so-called prophets are not always based on pure chimeras, but on vague reminiscences that, unbeknownst to them, affect their imagination, appearing to it as a sudden revelation.
fn.2212: Literally: it is one of the places that lead astray and cause to perish; and how many are there of those who claimed discernment who have perished thereby? The author refers to those sudden inspirations by which certain men believe they can claim the gift of prophecy, which are nothing other than reminiscences of old studies and certain very simple and rational ideas. — Ibn Tibbon incorrectly rendered the word אלמהלכה̈ (which cause to perish) as הממיתים (which cause to die), and likewise וכם הלך (and how many perished) as וכמה מתו (and how many died); the Arabic term here designates a moral perdition. Al-Harizi has the words המאבידות and אבדו. The words אלד׳ין ירידון אלתמייז (word for word: those who want discernment) allow for two different interpretations; one can translate: those who claim discernment or good judgment, which is the sense adopted by Ibn Tibbon, who has המחזיקים עצמם כחכמים, who take themselves for wise men; or these words can be understood as: those who seek to discern well, a sense adopted by Al-Harizi, who has רודפי האמת, who pursue the truth.
fn.2213: The text has ומן אג׳ל הד׳א, that is why, words which refer to what the author said about reminiscences mingling with the phantoms of the imagination.
fn.2214: Instead of ענד פיץ׳, the Leiden MS, no. 18, has מן פיץ׳, and it is this reading that the two Hebrew translators express; Ibn Tibbon has באמצעות שפע, and Al-Harizi, משפע.
fn.2215: Maimonides, following the example of the Chaldean version, considers here the word נביא as a noun in the sense of prophet, although it would be more natural to see it as a verb, hiph’il of בוא.
fn.2216: Instead of ממן עלמנאה, the Leiden MS, no. 18, has ממן תקדם, of those who preceded. This reading was followed by the two Hebrew translators; Ibn Tibbon has ממי שקדם, and Al-Harizi, מן הקדומים.
fn.2217: The text says: אן אללה, THAT God. It is known that the conjunction אן is sometimes used to introduce direct discourse; cf. vol. I of this work, p. 283, note 4.
fn.2218: Only one of our MSS, Leiden no. 18, has אלוהי, with the article, as do the two Hebrew versions הנבואה.
fn.2219: See Part I, ch. LXIII, pp. 281-282.
fn.2220: The author has in view these words from the same verse: in order that he may command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the Lord, etc., where it is clearly stated that he limited himself to instructing his own in what they should do to please God, without saying that God had sent him to proclaim such and such a commandment.
fn.2221: See, for example, Bereshit Rabbah, sect. 43 (fol. 55, col. 2, and 56, col. 1), which discusses the school of Shem and Eber. I cannot say whether, in our Midrashim, there is mention of a tribunal or a school of Methuselah; but here and there the great piety of this patriarch and his profound knowledge are mentioned. See e.g., Midrash Abkhir, cited in Yalkut, vol. I, no. 42.
fn.2222: That is: to the descendants of such-and-such, to such-and-such a tribe, or to such-and-such a people.
fn.2223: Literally: who stand straight (or upright) to follow it, which Ibn Tibbon rendered as מי שהתישר להמשך אחריה. Al-Harizi translates more freely: ויבטיחו כל הרודף אחריה והולך בדרכיה.
fn.2224: That is: that this law must always be followed, and that it will never be replaced by another; for, as Scripture says, it does not need to be sought in heaven, nor beyond the seas; it is in our mouth, in our heart, and is perfectly adapted to human nature.
fn.2225: The author plays here on the double meaning of the Arabic word معتدל, which designates that which is equal, in equilibrium, well-proportioned, and figuratively, that which is equitable or just; it corresponds to the Latin words aequus and aequalis, which are likewise used literally and figuratively, whereas the Hebrew word צדיק is used only in the figurative sense. The pun in question here can hardly be rendered in English; however, the words equal and equitable have the same etymology.
fn.2226: The word الرهبانية, which means the life of an anchorite, is rendered in Ibn Tibbon's version by this paraphrase: עבודת המתבודד בהרים הפורש עצמו מן הבשר והיין ודבריס רביס מצרכי הגוף, the worship of one who lives solitarily in the mountains and abstains from meat, wine, and many other things necessary for the body; the word السياحة is rendered as טלטול לעבודה, Wandering life whose object is worship. Al-Harizi's version does not render these two words. — Instead of אלרהכאניה̈, the Leiden MS, no. 18, has אלבראהמה̈, Brahmanism. A MS of Ibn Tibbon's version (Imperial Library, anc. fonds, no. 238, fol. 235 b) has the singular reading במופתיות, which would suggest that אלברהאניה̈ was read in the Arabic text (instead of אלרהבאניה̈), a reading that offers no meaning here.
fn.2227: Instead of אלסאלפה̈, the Leiden MS, no. 18, has אלג׳אהליה̈; likewise, Ibn Tibbon, הסנליות, and Al-Harizi, הסכלוּת, which must be understood here in the sense of pagans. Cf. above, p. 260, note 2.
fn.2228: See Part III of this work, ch. XXXI et seq. — In Ibn Tibbon's version the words עלת טעמי are a double translation of the word תעליל; Al-Harizi has: בטעמי המצות.
fn.2229: That is to say, in their just proportion, maintaining the mean between excess and deficiency. Cf. above, p. 285, note 1. — The suffix in אעתדאלּהא וּחכמתהא evidently refers to the plural אלשראיע (Heb. המצות), and Ibn Tibbon was wrong to put the suffix in the singular: שוויה וחכמתה.
fn.2230: According to the author, these words mean: have I been harsh to Israel through my commandments, like a desert and a land of deep darkness, where the traveler encounters difficulties at every step? Cf. Abravanel's commentary on this verse from Jeremiah: ראו דבר י״י הביטו מצותיו ותורותיו אם יש בהם מעמם וטורח לבעלי התורה, "see the word of the Eternal, that is, see if there is in his commandments and in his laws a burden and a toil for those who possess the law."
fn.2231: Literally: and let the punishment strike the one who carries it out.
fn.2232: In Ibn Tibbon's version, the words גנות רוע are a double translation of the Arabic word רדּילה̈; Al-Harizi has: כפי נבלות מדותיו.
fn.2233: Literally: but it (the law) must be considered with respect to the perfect man, the goal of the law being that all men should be (like) that man. The Arabic MSS read: אן יכון אלנאס כלהס דּלך אלאנסאן; the meaning is: that all men should be identically that man, i.e., perfectly resemble him. Both Hebrew versions have כמו האיש ההוא. — The oldest of the Oxford MSS (Uri, no. 359, cf. vol. I, p. 462) has this singular reading: אן יכון אלנאס כלחס דּלך אלזמאן כאמלין, that all men were perfect at that time.
fn.2234: See Aristotle's Politics, Book I, ch. 1: ἄνθρωπος φύσει πολιτιϰὸν ζῶον. Cf. Part III of this work, ch. XXVII.
fn.2235: Literally: that he be gathered (with his fellow beings).
fn.2236: We observe among all sublunary beings a progression from the least perfect to the most perfect. Besides the four elements, of which all beings are composed, plants possess the vegetative soul, to which, in animals, the vital soul is added; man alone also possesses the rational soul and is thus the most complex and the most perfect of all sublunary beings.
fn.2237: Literally: that you find almost no two individuals who agree, in any way, in one of the species of character traits, except as you find their external forms in agreement. Instead of אלא מא, the Leiden MS, no. 18, has כמא לא, and similarly Ibn Tibbon: כמו שלא תראה; Al-Harizi translates: אלא כשתמצא.
fn.2238: Literally: is brought closer or tends to be brought closer.
fn.2239: Instead of לחיימ, to the limit, to the point, the Leiden MS, no. 18, has the words אלי חד, which have the same meaning; Ibn Tibbon's version has simply עד, until; likewise Ibn Falaquera, Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 116.
fn.2240: That is to say, in most of the moral qualities of the soul.
fn.2241: Literally: as its nature (that of the human species) requires that there be this variation among its individuals.
fn.2242: Instead of the first אלמפרט, which should be pronounced المفرط, some MSS read אלמקצר.
fn.2243: Literally: nevertheless has an entry into what is natural.
fn.2244: That is to say, the prophet and the legislator. Ibn Tibbon has מה שצוה הנביא ההוא, what this prophet prescribed; likewise Al-Harizi, במה שצוה הנביא, and Ibn Falaquera (loc. cit.), מה שאמר אותו הנביא. This translation is justified only by one of our MSS, Leiden no. 18, which reads: בעמל מא גּא בה אלנביא.
fn.2245: Instead of ותרך, the Leiden MS, no. 18, has ותרבה with a suffix. Ibn Tibbon has והניח, without a suffix. At the beginning of the sentence, Ibn Tibbon has ויהיה, while all the Arabic MSS have יכון, without the copulative ו; הקצתו in the editions of Ibn Tibbon is a printing error for הקצת.
fn.2246: In the editions of Ibn Tibbon's version, the words מאת השם are missing here; the MSS read: מה שלא באה נבואה בו מאת השם יום כלל. The translator used the word יום as an adverb, in the sense of never, in imitation of the Arabic adverb يوماً.
fn.2248: See Jeremiah, ch. 28, vv. 1 and following. — At first glance, this example does not seem well chosen, since Hananiah, as well as Zedekiah, is presented as a false prophet, and his words are expressly refuted by Jeremiah. Ibn Caspi, in his commentary entitled עמודי כסף, points out this difficulty in these terms: תמה איך יאמר הר״מ זה כי עליו כתוב כמו על צדקיה כי סרה דבר ובכלל לא מצאתי הבדל בין צדקיה וחנניה. However, in establishing a distinction here between Zedekiah and Hananiah, Maimonides followed the Talmud, according to which the former predicted things he had never heard (מתנבא מה שלא שמע), while the latter predicted what had not been told to him specifically (מתנבא מה שלא נאמר לו), i.e., he merely reproduced a prophecy by Jeremiah, whose meaning he distorted or misunderstood. According to the Jerusalem Talmud (tractate Sanhedrin, last chapter), Hananiah, in predicting that within two years God would break the yoke of the king of Babylon, believed himself to be in agreement with Jeremiah, who predicted seventy years of captivity (Jeremiah 29:10), which, in Hananiah's opinion, had begun during the reign of Manasseh. According to the Babylonian Talmud (same tractate, fol. 89a), Hananiah's words: I will break the yoke of the king of Babylon, were merely a reproduction of Jeremiah's words (49:35): behold, I break the bow of Elam; since, Hananiah reasoned, if the Elamites, who were only auxiliaries of Babylon, were to receive celestial punishment, all the more so the Chaldeans themselves.
fn.2249: That is to say, the regimes or governments founded by a mere legislator. — Several editions of Ibn Tibbon's version have המונחים לא המושמים; instead of לא, one should read ל״א, an abbreviation for לשון אחר (another wording), for the words המונחים and המושמים are two different translations of the Arabic word אלמוצּועה̈. Cf. vol. I, p. 411, note 2.
fn.2250: Literally: that they are laws which they established by means of their reflections.
fn.2251: The verb תחתאגּ is in the second person masculine; the Leiden MS, no. 18, has יחחאגּ in the third person, as does Ibn Tibbon: לא יצטרך.
fn.2252: That is to say, borrowings from the prophets that were intended to be passed off as original works. — The word מנתחלחה̈, which Al-Harizi renders as לקוחים מזולתו, was paraphrased by Ibn Tibbon as follows: שיאמר אומרם שהוא אמרם מלבו ולקחם מזולתו. Cf. vol. I, p. 419, note 1.
fn.2253: In the editions of Ibn Tibbon's version, השגה is a printing error for השגחה.
fn.2254: The word מטּנונה̈, which Ibn Tibbon rendered by the words ראה אותו, is missing in the Leiden MS, no. 18, and was not rendered in Al-Harizi's version, which reads: ושישיגו שום הצלחה בעצת המנהיג ההוא.
fn.2256: The editions of Ibn Tibbon's version have מעויניס; according to the manuscripts, one must read מעייניס.
fn.2257: In Ibn Tibbon's version, the Arabic verb חעקב is rendered by the two verbs ילחקור ולדעת; the manuscripts have ולחקור ולבדוק, which is a double translation of the Arabic verb. Al-Harizi's version contains ולדקדק על פעליו.
fn.2259: The verb פצח, which means to confound or to cover publicly with shame, was rendered in Ibn Tibbon's version as עבר ופרסם. Al-Harizi translates more precisely: וע״כ גלה בה הבורא חרפת כל מתנחלי הנבואה. — After the words כֹּל מַדָּע, whoever arrogated to himself, the gift of prophecy is understood; both Hebrew translators have supplied this ellipsis. The meaning of this sentence is that God confounded the false prophets by unmasking their hypocrisy and making it publicly known that they were debauched men who committed adultery.
fn.2260: Literally: Do you not see Zedekiah etc.?... how they arrogated prophecy to themselves, and the people followed them etc.?
fn.2261: This is what the author seems to find in the words of Jeremiah, cited below: and that they had spoken lying words which I had not commanded them. According to the author, the lie consisted in their attributing to themselves words spoken by other prophets.
fn.2262: That is to say: the intent of what was said in this last paragraph, to distinguish between the true prophet and the plagiarist.
fn.2263: The author means that what Scripture calls מראח, theologians explain by מַרְאֵה הַנְּבוּאָה, that which is seen in the state of prophecy, a prophetic vision.
fn.2264: See II Kings, 3, 15; Ezekiel, 1, 3; III, 22; XXXVII, 1; XL, 1.
fn.2265: A word derived from the verb HAZA (הזה), to see. See Genesis, 15, 1; Numbers, 24, 4 and 16.
fn.2266: See above, at the beginning of Ch. XXXVII.
fn.2267: See Bereshith Rabbah, sect. 63 (fol. 55, col. 2), where R. Levi says, in the name of R. Aba, that God spoke to Rebecca through the mediation of an angel.
fn.2268: Literally: The reporting (or the statement) of the word addressed to the prophets, according to the expression found in the prophetic books, occurs in four ways.
fn.2269: In none of our manuscripts is the verb יצנח preceded by the conjunction אן; and similarly, Ibn Tibbon simply has יגלה. Al-Harizi's version contains שיאמר הנביא.
fn.2270: Both Hebrew translators omitted the imperative אפעל because of its synonymy with אצנע.

To resolve the difficulty, Abravanel (Commentary on the Moreh, II, fol. 40 a) believes that one must refer to the two opinions expressed by the scholars regarding the word אדני, Lord, used in verse 3; according to some, this word replaces the Tetragrammaton of verse 1 and designates God Himself; according to others, it designates one of the three men mentioned in verse 2. According to the first opinion, the vision, in which Abraham represented God Himself, or the supreme cause, in his mind, would have been interrupted by the appearance of the three men, and Abraham, distracted by this appearance, would have prayed to God not to depart from him—that is, he would have made efforts not to be interrupted in his contemplation of the Divinity. According to the second opinion, the appearance of the three men would be identical to that of God mentioned in verse 1; so that verse 2 and those following would merely explain in detail the nature of the divine manifestation of verse 1. Since R. Hayya evidently professes the second opinion, it follows that, according to him, all the details narrated from verse 2 onward are a prophetic vision, in the same way as the appearance of God in verse 1, which would merely summarize the set of details that follow. — Undoubtedly, this is an overly subtle explanation of the simple words of R. Hayya; but it is consistent with the manner in which Maimonides generally interprets the often naive words of the ancient scholars.

fn.2380: Literally: among the other prophets. The author means: among prophets other than Moses, for the latter saw God face to face and God spoke to him mouth to mouth, which means that God manifested Himself clearly to his intellect, without the mediation of the imagination.
fn.2381: On the meaning of the word אחזאל, union, cf. Vol. I, p. 37, note 1.
fn.2382: The Arabic text says אפתעאל, a term designating the VIIIth form of Arabic verbs, which Arabic rabbis use improperly to designate the hithpa'el of Hebrew verbs. See my edition of the Commentary of R. Tanhum of Jerusalem on the book of Habakkuk (in Vol. XII of the Bible by Mr. S. Cahen), p. 94, note 3.
fn.2383: The author means that this verb indicates an intellectual perception which, although under the action of the imaginative faculty, nevertheless retains sufficient clarity and is not dominated by the phantoms of a confused imagination.
fn.2384: Literally: there is the hearing of a speech from God. Ibn Tibbon translated the words סמאע כלאם literally as שֵׁמע דבר; the editors have substituted the verb ישמע for the noun שמע.
fn.2385: The word חדס (حَدُس) designates an opinion based on a simple conjecture, and it is with reason that Ibn Falaquera criticized here the version of Ibn Tibbon, which contains על צד המחשבה. According to Ibn Falaquera, it should be translated as על צד האומד. See Appendix to Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 156, and cf. above, p. 296, note 1.
fn.2386: In other words: it is on the hypothesis that the prophet imagines that God Himself is speaking to him. — This passage, which is quite obscure, especially in the Hebrew version, has perplexed the commentators. Its meaning is evidently as follows: The author, after having declared it improbable that the prophet, in a vision, could believe he hears the word of God, anticipates an objection that might be made, based on certain biblical passages where there is evidently a question of the divine word addressed to the prophet in a vision, such as for example Genesis, ch. 15, vv. 1 and 4. He responds that, according to his purely conjectural opinion, these passages refer only to the divine word addressed to the prophet through the mediation of an unknown voice, a personage, or an angel (which constitute the IXth, Xth, and XIth degrees), whereas in the passage from Numbers 12:6, it is a matter of the immediate word of God that the prophet believes he hears, which can only take place in a dream. However, the author continues afterwards, it would also be permissible to lend the passage of Numbers a more general sense; for it is possible that this passage means that in a vision one never hears any speech of any nature whatsoever, and that one only sees parables; so that it would be necessary to admit that, wherever there is mention of words in a vision, it is a matter of a revelation which, after having begun with a vision, ends in a dream. In this case, the author says in conclusion, there would be only eight degrees of prophecy; for the different degrees of the vision would be reduced to a single one, namely the eighth, where the divine intellect acts upon the prophet, in the waking state, through parabolic visions.
fn.2387: The author means that the literal sense (אלט̇אהר) of the passage in Numbers favors the interpretation he has given it, namely that it only excludes from the vision the immediate word of God that the prophet may believe he hears in a dream.
fn.2389: See Bereshith Rabbah, sect. 17 (fol. 14, col. 4), and sect. 44 (fol. 39, col. 2 and 3).
fn.2390: Word for word: or intelligible unions, that is to say, revelations resulting from the union of the universal active intellect with the prophet's intelligence. — Ibn Tibbon here renders the word אלצאלאת, unions, by השגות, perceptions, which is inaccurate.
fn.2391: All the MSS contain ת̇מאן; but, in the construct state, it is more correct to write ת̇מאני.
fn.2392: That is to say: even if, in the account of the vision, there were a question of a character who had spoken to the prophet, which, according to what was said previously, would not yet constitute the highest degree of prophecy, but only the penultimate degree (the Xth). The author means that, according to this latter interpretation, the vision would form only a single general degree, that of parabolic revelation, in which there would no longer be other gradations to establish, as was done for the dream; for if, in the parabolic vision, mention is also sometimes made of words addressed to the prophet by a character or an angel, this can only be by simple allegory, or to indicate that the vision ended up becoming a dream.
fn.2393: This entire observation seems superfluous to us; for it appears that the author has already explained himself sufficiently above, stating that it is in the dream alone that the prophet can believe he directly hears the word of God. Cf. p. 344, note 3.
fn.2394: That is to say, by the direct influence of the universal active intellect, which communicated itself to the intelligence of Moses, without the imagination having any part in it.
fn.2395: See Mishneh Torah, or Abridgment of the Talmud, treatise Yesodei ha-Torah, ch. VII, § 6, and cf. above, ch. XXXV (p. 277, note 2).
fn.2396: In other words: by examining a single individual of any species, and by recognizing what constitutes its essential form or quiddity, one concludes, by induction, that all individuals of the same species have the same quiddity. — The word צורה̈ here designates a specific form, and Ibn Tibbon incorrectly rendered it as תכונה, constitution. Al-Harizi's version reads: ויודע בי זאת צורת כל איש ממנו.
fn.2397: Word for word: of a single form from among the forms of the accounts of the prophets. The author means, it seems to me, that it is sufficient to have recognized the form of a certain part of the prophet's account to draw conclusions about all parts of that account; if one of the parts of the vision recounted by the prophet is recognized as a parable, all the rest will likewise have a parabolic meaning. The meaning I attribute to our passage seems to emerge from the following example of a dream in which one believes one is taking a journey and where one sees all sorts of imaginary details. Each of the examples the author will cite from Ezekiel and other prophets is recognized as a vision by one of the expressions designating prophetic vision, and from then on all the details reported by the prophet are part of this same vision.
fn.2398: Literally: and it was of its state and its thing (or condition) in such and such a manner. The words כית וכית are found in only one of the MSS I was able to consult, where they were added by a more recent hand. However, the meaning of the sentence requires these words or another similar expression. Al-Harizi's version seems to express the words כית וכית; it reads: והיה עניינו כך וכך. Ibn Tibbon translates: והיה מעניינו מה שהיה, which would suggest that his Arabic copy had מא כאן. The two translators rendered these two words, חאל and אמר, which are nearly synonymous, by the single word עניין. Maimonides might have written: וכאן מן האלה ומן אמרה כד̇לך; the copyists may have omitted the word כד̇לך because this word was repeated immediately after.... כד̇לך הד̇ה אלאמת̇אל.
fn.2399: Literally: which are seen, or which are done, in the prophetic vision, etc.
fn.2400: Ibn Tibbon's version reads: במה שיורה, which is inaccurate. Al-Harizi translates: וכל מה שיחייב המשל ההוא ממעשה וכו׳; here the Arabic verb אקתצ̇י is rendered exactly by שיחייב; but the words וכל מה are an inaccurate translation of the Arabic words פי מא.
fn.2401: The author means that all the details recounted in a prophetic vision, as well as all the acts attributed to the prophet therein, are part of the vision and must not be considered as real facts.
fn.2402: That is to say: some of these details are recounted simply and in an absolute manner, without expressly stating that they belong to the vision, so that the common people take them for real facts. — Instead of בעצ̇הא, the Leiden MS, no. 18, has בעדה, an implausible reading, but one reproduced by Al-Harizi: ובא זכרון זה בספרי הנבואה אחר זה במאמר מוחלט. Instead of the adverb מטלקא (MSS מטלק), several MSS have מטלקה̈, an adjective relating to בעצ̇הא; likewise Ibn Tibbon: קצתם מוחלטים.
fn.2403: For, as the author stated above (ch. XLI, p. 314): "Whenever a passage (of Scripture) says of someone that an angel spoke to him, or that the word of God was addressed to him, this could not have taken place except in a dream or in a prophetic vision." The author here alludes to several passages where one finds the formula ויאמר יי׳ אלי, and the Eternal said to me, and where either actions, movements, or conversations with God are attributed to the prophet. See, e.g.: Jeremiah, ch. 1, vv. 7, 9, 12 and 14; ch. XIII, vv. 6 et seq.; Ezekiel, ch. XLIV. vv. 1 et seq.; Zechariah, ch. 11, vv. 13 et seq.
fn.2404: That is to say, they are real facts, accomplished by the prophet while his senses were functioning and manifesting their full activity.
fn.2405: The verb קאל is a pleonasm that uselessly repeats the verb וד̇כר. Ibn Tibbon did not translate the verb קאל.
fn.2406: Most of our MSS read: צ̇חכה̈ ללספאה וסכ̇ריה̈, and it is this reading that Al-Harizi's version expresses, which reads: לעג לריקים והתול. Instead of צ̇חכּה̈, laughing-stock, some MSS have הָדָא, a target, a reading also held by Ibn Falaquera, who criticizes Ibn Tibbon for having put in his version: דומים לשוטים ולשכורים (see Appendix of Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 156). It is unclear where Ibn Tibbon took the word דומים, similar. As for the word ולשכורים, Ibn Falaquera observes that instead of סכ̇ריה̈ (سُخْرِيَّة) or סכ̇רה̈ (سخرة), which means laughing-stock (לעג וקלס), Ibn Tibbon read סכרה̈, with a כ without a dot, that is, سكرة, plural of سكر, drunkard; but in this case, the construction required וללסכרה̈ or ואלסכרה̈, with the article.
fn.2407: In the editions of Ibn Tibbon's version, these last words are translated twice: ויצום לעשות מעשה השוטים ויצום לעשות מעשה השגעון. The word אלכ̇רק is considered once as a plural (خرق, plural of أُخْرَقُ) and once as a singular in the sense of stupiditiy, dementia; the MSS have only the 2nd version, מעשה השגעון, as does Al-Harizi.
fn.2408: The author refers to the last passage of Ezekiel that he just cited (chap. V, v. 1), in which the prophet is commanded to pass a razor over his head and beard. In doing so, Ezekiel, who was a priest (ibid., chap. I, v. 3), would have twice violated the Law of Moses; for not only is every Israelite forbidden from cutting the corners of their hair and shaving the corners of their beard (Leviticus 19:27), but this prohibition is specifically repeated for priests (ibid., 21:5). — All the Arabic manuscripts of the Guide, as well as those of Ibn Tibbon's version, have: אאו פאת ראש; and it is incorrect that the editions of Ibn Tibbon's version and the manuscript of Al-Harizi have put ופאת ראש.
fn.2409: In Ibn Tibbon's version, instead of מראה נבואה, one should read, according to the Arabic text, במראה הנבואה.
fn.2411: Literally: All these parables (were) in the prophetic vision.
fn.2412: Literally: the matter no longer remains veiled, so as (to suggest) that any part of it had any reality. This phrase refers not only to the example drawn from Hosea, but also to the preceding examples. The author means: as soon as it is clear that all these visions have a parabolic meaning and that they do not concern real facts, there is no longer any reason to doubt any detail or to suppose that a single one of these specific facts actually occurred; unless, the author continues, we are completely incapable of understanding prophetic visions, such that they are for us a sealed book, as Isaiah says.
fn.2413: Literally: unless it had been said of us; that is, we could not fall into such errors unless these words of Isaiah applied to us: And every vision etc.—We have adopted the reading of the great majority of manuscripts, which carry: אלא עינד מא קיל פינא; Ibn Tibbon: אלא כשנאמר בהם; he therefore read פיהם instead of פינא. The Leiden manuscript, no. 18, has פיה in the singular; but this reading, like that of Ibn Tibbon, seems to us to present more difficulties than our own. The manuscript of the Hebrew supplement of the Imperial Library, no. 63, written by the hand of R. Saadia ibn Danan, carries: אלא עינד מן קיל פיה, except for him of whom it was said; that is, there can be no doubt in this regard except for those of whom Isaiah spoke in the cited passage. This reading, indeed, offers a simpler meaning; but it is precisely for this reason that it appears suspicious to us, and we can only see in it an arbitrary correction of the original text. In the manuscript of Al-Harizi's version, this entire phrase is missing.
fn.2415: Literally: and how then (would it have attained) the rank of miracles?
fn.2416: Ibn Tibbon's overly literal version, שישיג בשופטי ישראל, is not clear enough, and the editors have completely altered the meaning by writing כשופטי instead of בשופטי. Al-Harizi translated better: ותכלית מעלתו שהיה נמנה בשופטי ישראל.
fn.2417: See Babylonian Talmud, tractate Rosh ha-Shanah, fol. 25 a, b, where it is said that, in a verse of the first book of Samuel, chap. XII, v. 11, three of the least important men of the world (קלי עולם), Jerubbaal (Gideon), Bedan (Samson), and Jephthah, were contrasted with the three most important men of the world (חמורי עולם), namely Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, mentioned together in Psalm 99:6.
fn.2418: The author probably alludes to what he said in the previous chapter (1<sup>st</sup> degree) regarding the judges of Israel, whom he places in a rank far inferior to that of the true prophets.
fn.2420: The example of Zechariah that the author is about to cite follows what he said regarding the details reported in certain visions of the prophets Ezekiel, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Hosea; for the passage relating to Gideon is merely an observation that the author has inserted here in passing, because Gideon too, in a kind of vision or dream, believed he saw certain specific facts that occurred only in his imagination.
fn.2421: According to the author, it is not God who is presented here under the image of the shepherd, as most commentators believe, but the prophet Zechariah, who, in a prophetic vision, takes the two staffs and performs the symbolic actions discussed below.
fn.2422: The editions of Ibn Tibbon's version have: שהוה עשה כן; one should read, according to the manuscripts, שהוה עשה בו.
fn.2423: That is, it is part of a larger narrative that has a parabolic meaning.
fn.2424: Word for word: that most of the prophecy of the prophets (occurs) through parables. Ibn Tibbon has: שרוב נבואות, "that most of the prophecies." Al-Harizi has, more accurately, נבואת in the singular.
fn.2425: Regarding the word אג’יא أغياء, a verbal noun of the IVth form of the root גזה, see above, page 217, note 1. Ibn Tibbon's version has, for the word ואלאג’יאת, the two words וההפלגות והגוזמות; his Arabic manuscript perhaps contained in addition the word ואלמבאלגאת, just as one reads further on: אג’יא ומבאלג’ה.
fn.2426: The words עלי תחריר strictly mean in an exact manner; that is, if one adhered to the exact meaning of the terms without seeing anything hyperbolic in them. In Ibn Tibbon's version, the words כמשמעם מדוקדקים are a double translation of the Arabic words עלי תחריר. Al-Harizi translates: וכשיובן על השיעור, as if he had read in his Arabic text עלי תקדיר; this reading is indeed found in one of our manuscripts, but it does not offer a plausible meaning.
fn.2427: See Babylonian Talmud, tractate Hullin, fol. 90 b; tractate Tamid, chap. II, § 1.
fn.2428: And, consequently, Og's cubit was larger than an ordinary cubit.
fn.2429: Instead of the dual מהלי, several manuscripts have מת’ל in the singular; likewise Al-Harizi: כמו אורך איש, AS the length of a person, etc. But this is a very grave error, and Ibn Tibbon's version, which has כפל, double, confirms the reading מהלי (for which some manuscripts incorrectly have מלא). The author means that the text of Deuteronomy, by giving Og's bed a length of nine cubits, fixes Og's height at six cubits, which is double the height of an ordinary man. — The ancient Hebrew cubit was approximately 525 millimeters (see my History of Palestine, p. 397), and the length the author attributes here to ordinary height would be 1 meter 575 millimeters; consequently, Og's height would have been 3.15 meters.
fn.2430: All the Arabic manuscripts have אכת’ר, as does Al-Harizi, או יותר מעט. Ibn Tibbon has, by error: או פחות מעט, or a little less. In one manuscript one reads: או פחות או יותר מעט, a little more or less.
fn.2431: Instead of תחריר, which here means exact indication, in full, some manuscripts have תחדיד (with daleth), fixation, determination. Ibn Tibbon translated in this sense: ממדת ימי האנשים ההם; Al-Harizi: מעניין אורך ימי האנשים הקדמונים.
fn.2432: Literally: or else by way of miracle and proceeding in its manner.
fn.2433: The author means that the Chaldean paraphrase of Jonathan, on the passage of Isaiah, is similar to that given by Onkelos on the passage of Deuteronomy (XXXII, 14): יהב להון בזת מלכיהון ושליטיהון וכו׳, He gave them the spoil of their kings and their rulers, etc.
fn.2434: Literally: by this consideration also, you will be saved from the imagination of a being that God has not produced; that is to say: by fully internalizing all that has just been said, you will no longer be liable to imagine the existence of those extraordinary beings that have never existed in the real world.
fn.2435: See the first part, chap. LV, and passim.
fn.2436: This sentence is elliptical; its meaning is as follows: if you did not wish to admit what I have said, then you would have no other means, in order to escape those false ideas of which I have just spoken, than to believe that the words of the prophets are false.—In the version of Ibn Tibbon, instead of או יחשוב (or יֵחָשֵׁב), one should read או החשוב, as Al-Harizi does; all the Arabic manuscripts have תט̇ן in the second person.
fn.2437: Ibn Tibbon has העלם, which is inaccurate. Al-Harizi translates more accurately: כשתתרשל במה שעוררנוך.
fn.2438: Literally: the will of God and His choice or free will. Cf. Part I, chap. LXIX.
fn.2439: The words פי אקאויל are missing in some manuscripts, where one reads תחד̇ף אלאנביא. According to this reading, אלאנביא would be the subject of the verb תחד̇ף, which would be in the active form (تُحْذَفُ), so that one would have to translate: the prophets sometimes omit; but this would not fit with the two following passive verbs: بُسم and ויקאל. However, this reading was adopted by Al-Harizi and by Ibn Falaquera; the former translates: כן ידחו הנביאים לפעמים הסבות ההם האמצעיות ומיחסים זה הפעל לבורא ויאמרו וגו׳; the latter (Moré ha-Moré, p. 117): ומפני זה יחסרו הנביאים אותן הסבות האמצעיות וייוחס לאלוה ית׳ אותו הפעל האישי ויאמר וכו׳. The version of Ibn Tibbon expresses the words פי אקאויל; but the construction of the sentence is slightly modified there.
fn.2440: By אלמחקיקין, those who establish the truth, the author here appears to designate the true philosophers, as opposed to the Mutakallimun, who see in God the immediate cause of every particular fact.
fn.2441: On the expression אהל שריעה̈, cf. Vol. I, p. 68, note 3.
fn.2442: The author here has in mind the exposition of causes given by Aristotle, Phys., Book II, chaps. 3-6. By ذاتية, the author means what is a cause in itself (ϰαθ’ αὑτό), or essentially and by its nature; by اختيارية, arbitrary, he means causes located in a moral choice (προαίρεσις), in a deliberate intention (διάνοια); the word عرضية designates accidental causes (ϰατὰ συμβεβηϰός), and the word اتفاقية designates causes due to chance (ἀπὸ τύχης). Cf. Metaphysics, Book V, chap. 30; Book XI, chap. 8. — The word אחפאקיה is not rendered in the version of Ibn Tibbon; Ibn Falaquera (l. c.) translates: או מקריות הזדמנויות.
fn.2443: The author appears to allude to what Aristotle calls τὸ αὐτόματον, that which happens of itself, the spontaneous, and which he seems to reduce to the acts of animals and the phenomena of inanimate things, which are not the product of a will endowed with free choice: τὸ δ’ αὐτόματον ϰαὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις ζώοις ϰαὶ πολλοῖς τῶν ἀψύχων, ϰ. τ. λ. Phys., Book II, chap. 6. Elsewhere Aristotle says that one can attribute spontaneity to children and animals, but not moral choice or intention: τοῦ μὲν γὰρ ἑϰουσίου ϰαὶ παῖδες ϰαὶ τἄλλα ζῷα ϰοινωνεῖ, προαιρέσεως δ’οὔ. Nicomachean Ethics, Book III, chap. 4.
fn.2444: Ibn Tibbon here has two verbs: כפי מה שהונח והתישב, and likewise Ibn Falaquera (l. c.); the Arabic manuscripts have only the verb קדר.
fn.2445: The author, after having spoken of God's intervention in the will of the irrational animal, in free will, and in the course of natural things or in essential causes, adds this parenthesis to make it understood that it follows necessarily from what has just been said that chance also is a cause that must be traced back to God; for chance (τύχη), according to Aristotle's definition, without being the goal itself, is always related to a goal of nature or to the intention and free choice (προαίρεσις) of a rational being (see Phys., Book II, chap. 5: ἔστι δ’ἕνεϰά του ὅσα τε ἀπὸ διανοίας ἂν πραχθείη ϰαὶ ὅσα ἀπὸ φύσεως · τὰ δὴ τοιαῦτα ὅταν ϰατὰ συμβεβηϰὸς γένηται, ἀπὸ τύχης φαμὲν εἶναι, ϰ. τ. λ. Cf. Metaphys., Book XI, chap. 8, toward the end). One can therefore say that chance is an excess, or an accessory, of the goal aimed at either by nature or by the intention of a rational being (free will); most often, chance participates in this goal, as it may also participate in the animal will, since this will can accidentally become the cause of an effect it did not intend.
fn.2446: Literally: as of the war of a people that dominates over one (another) people. Instead of סלטוא, one of our manuscripts bears טלטוא.
fn.2447: This is inaccurate, as Ibn Caspi observes in his commentary Ammudei Kesef; for the quoted words apply to the army of the Medes and Persians, called to destroy the Babylonian empire.
fn.2448: The version of Ibn Tibbon bears: כאשר סבך השם לו פרנסתו, when God brought about his sustenance; one sees that Ibn Tibbon did not have, in his Arabic text, the word אמראה̈, a woman, and that instead of تَقُوزَةُ, he pronounced تَفَوُّقُهُ.
fn.2449: It would seem that this passage would be better placed among the examples of chance; for the result of the sale of Joseph was quite different from what his brothers had intended to obtain; and indeed, the author further on cites verse 7, which relates to the same fact, among the examples of chance. Some commentators have sought to explain this kind of contradiction by making a subtle distinction between verse 7 and verse 8 (see the commentaries of Ibn Caspi and Efodi). It appears that the author wishes to suggest that Joseph, after having attributed the accidental result of the act originating from his brothers' free will to God in verse 7, corrects himself in verse 8, saying that a result of such high importance could not be purely accidental, and that it was necessarily God Himself who directed the free will of Jacob's sons, so as to make them accomplish, without their knowledge, a great act that was in the plan of His divine providence. Cf. Abravanel's commentary on Genesis, chap. 45, on the two verses in question.
fn.2450: In some mss., this sentence offers slight variants which render it quite obscure: באדכן מעני דלך קיאם בין עלי מא שאבה הדה אלאיצ'אפה מן איצ'א אלקול פקט. Al-Harizi adopted this wording, which he rendered in a poorly intelligible manner: אך ענין זה הסברא גלויה לו לזה הבנין מן המאמר בלבד (read על מה שיזדמן (?שידמה. Other mss. of this version, as well as the editions, confirm the reading we have adopted; but the word הבאים must be deleted in the editions, as it is superfluous and not found in the mss.
fn.2451: Eliezer’s mission intended to seek a wife for Isaac in Abraham’s native land, without Rebecca being directly mentioned; it was by chance that she presented herself first to Eliezer’s choice.
fn.2452: Here again, a chain of fortuitous circumstances is attributed to God, which necessitated David’s departure.
fn.2453: That is to say: natural causes, proceeding from the laws of nature.
