fn.2455: Word for word: and the reality of the matter will manifest itself to you in such a passage as might give cause to suspect a departure from the truth.
fn.2456: Literally: this is the limit of that to which the discourse has led me or arrived. —Instead of אנתהי בי אלקול, some mss. have אנתהי באלקול; some others have בה instead of בי. —In several editions of the Ibn-Tibbon version, one finds, due to a typographical error: אל המאמר או; instead of או, one must read בן, as in the editio princeps.
fn.2457: The words פי הד̇ה אלמקאלה̈, in this treatise, which are found in all the Arabic mss., were not rendered in the Ibn-Tibbon version. The author perhaps intended to suggest by these words that he planned to return to this matter elsewhere; we know, in fact, that he had begun the drafting of a specific work on Prophecy. See Vol. I of this work, p. 15.
fn.2458: The word מקדמה̈ can be translated here neither as Introduction, nor as Preface; for the passage that follows does not serve as an Introduction to this third part of the Guide, but merely contains some observations which the author deemed necessary to place before the first seven chapters, containing the explanation of the Ma’aseh Merkavah or the vision of Ezekiel.
fn.2459: Cf. Vol. I, p. 9, note 2, and Vol. II, p. 50.
fn.2460: That is to say: by addressing myself to the intelligent readers for whom I composed this work and who will be capable of understanding the subtle hints. The Ibn-Tibbon version reads: כפי מה שחובר לו זה המאמר, which is not very clear. Instead of מה, one should write מי, as is indeed found in some manuscripts.
fn.2461: See Babylonian Talmud, tractate Pesahim, fol. 119 a. The words ולמכסה עתיק probably mean: and in order to have luxury garments; the Talmud, as has just been seen, diverts these words from their natural meaning in order to see in them an allusion to those who veil the deep mysteries of the Ma’aseh Merkavah, revealed by God to His elect. The words the Ancient of Days designate God, by allusion to the words of Daniel, ch. 8, verses 9 and 13. — Instead of שגלן, which He has revealed, our editions of the Talmud read שכסה, which He has covered; this variant does not change the essence of the interpretation or the use Maimonides makes of it.
fn.2462: Some mss. have בייא, in the first person; similarly Al-Harizi and the mss. of the Ibn-Tibbon version: בארנו. Accordingly, one should translate: We have already explained.
fn.2463: According to the Ibn-Tibbon version, one should translate: "Even what is understood by him whom God has endowed with intelligence." Al-Harizi translates more literally: אפילו השיעור אשר התבאר ממנו למי שנפתח לו השער מדעתו.
fn.2464: See what the author said on this subject in the first part of this work, ch. <small>XXXIV</small> (Vol. I, p. 127 et seq.).
fn.2465: Word for word: neither little nor much.
fn.2466: Literally: for it had not ceased to be transmitted from one head (of a school) to another. The word צדר here has the meaning of principal, head. The Ibn-Tibbon version, לא נעדר מקבל מפי מקבל, is both obscure and incomplete. Al-Harizi, taking the word צדר here in the sense of chest, heart, translates thus: כי מאז ועד עתה לא חדל להיות מקובל מפה אל פה וחקוק מלב אל לב.
fn.2467: The author evidently distinguishes here two parts of the Ma’aseh Merkavah, one of which he understood approximately (עמאא) and the other of which appeared to him with unquestionable clarity. This distinction is not sufficiently apparent from the Ibn-Tibbon version, which reads: להעירך על מה שאפשר שנודע לי והתבאר אלי בלי ספק במה שהבינותיו מזה. Al-Harizi rendered all the verbs of this sentence well; but the highly essential nuance of the word עמאא, approximately, disappeared in his version, which reads: להעיר אותך על מה שנראה לי והתבאר לי ונודע לי בלי ספק ממה שהבינותי ממנו.
fn.2468: Ibn-Tibbon adds, for clarity, the word המוריש; he translates: או קנאת המוריש ביורש על ירושתו, or jealousy of the testator against the heir for his inheritance.
fn.2469: Literally: added to what opinion requires; that is to say, regardless of the reserve imposed upon me by my own judgment.
fn.2470: The words ד̇א חדם ותכ̇מין are rendered in the Ibn-Tibbon version as בעל סברא; Ibn Falaquera observes that it would be more accurate to translate: בעל עומד ומשער. See the Appendix to Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 156, the note relative to ch. XLV of Part II; and cf. Vol. II, p. 296, note 1, and p. 345, note 6.
fn.2471: Instead of תלקנת, some mss. have تَلَقَّيْتَ, which has roughly the same meaning.
fn.2472: That is to say: this important subject is like the large peg of a tent to which the entire hanging is suspended, or like a column that supports the entire roof of a building. — In the Arabic text, the words a peg etc. are written in Hebrew, which might lead one to believe they are taken from a Talmudic passage relating to the Ma’aseh Merkavah; but I have searched in vain for such a passage, and one must believe that the author simply used a rabbinic locution very common in his time and which served him to characterize the high importance of Ezekiel’s vision. This is also the opinion of Chief Rabbi Klein, whom I consulted in this regard and who pointed out to me a passage from the Jerusalem Talmud, tractate Berakhot, ch. IV (fol. 19 a), where, regarding the elevation of R. Eliezer ben Azariah to the dignity of nasi, it is said: אשרי אדם שיש לו יתד להתלות בה. The words ועמוד שהכל נשען עליו are analogous to these words from the book of Judges (16:26): העמדים אשר הבית נכון עליהם.
fn.2473.sub_0: Maimonides, in approaching his oblique explanation of Ezekiel's vision, in which he seems to find the principal cosmological doctrines of the Arab Peripatetics, deems it necessary to indicate first what is to be understood by the four faces attributed to each of the four 'hayyôth, or animal figures (Ezekiel 1:10), in which he sees the celestial spheres, reduced to four: that of the moon, that of the sun, that of the five other planets, and that of the fixed stars. See Part IIe of this work at the end of Chap. IX, and Chap. X, p. 82 ff. The prophet attributes to the 'hayyôth a human face, a lion's face, an ox's face, and an eagle's face, making them the representatives of what is most noble among the different species of animals. According to our author, the three faces of irrational animals are also human faces; but he does not tell us why he insists on this, and he leaves us to guess what he means by the symbol of the four faces. We believe that the author is alluding to the four causes of the movement of the spheres, indicated according to him by the four wings (v. 6), and of which he spoke in Chaps. IV and X of Part IIe; these are: the shape of the sphere, i.e., its sphericity, its soul, its intellect by which it conceives, and the separate Intelligence, the object of its desire (see Vol. II, p. 88). In the sublunary world, man is the only being in whom these four causes of movement are reflected; man alone possesses a soul endowed with conception and an intellect, which are set in motion by the desire to unite with the separate intelligence, i.e., with the universal active intellect; and from this point of view, man's movement has nothing in common with that of irrational animals and can only be compared to the circular movement of the spheres. Cf. Vol. II, Chap. IV, p. 52. The explanation we have just given is indicated by Samuel ibn Tibbon in his treatise Yikkawou ha-maïm, Chap. XI, p. 47: וענין הנפש והשכל רמז אליו בשרמז שכלם יש להם פני אדם וכל הפנים פני אדם.
fn.2473.sub_1: We omit other explanations given by Moses of Narbonne and Ephodi, which relate to what the author said about the four forces emanating from the four spheres and acting on the four elements (Vol. II, Chap. X, p. 89); these explanations offer no interest for science or its history, and we shall limit ourselves to what is strictly necessary for the understanding of Maimonides' obscure words. — Furthermore, the entire interpretation that Maimonides gives here, in veiled terms, of Ezekiel's vision, is based, as we have said, on Peripatetic cosmology; but if the prophet, as is probable, used astronomical symbols, he could only have borrowed them from the astronomy of his time, and one would have to look to Chaldean science for an explanation. Isaac Abravanel completely overturned Maimonides' interpretation by rightly observing that, if this were the meaning of Ezekiel's vision, there would be no reason to make such a mystery of it, since it would only concern a science taught in all schools of philosophy and familiar to scholars of all faiths. See Abravanel's second Preface to the book of Ezekiel and his commentary on Chap. I of the same book; cf. also Abravanel's commentary on various parts of the Moreh Nevukhim, Book IIe, fol. 48 ff.
fn.2474: It is thus, as Abravanel observes (loc. cit., fol. 53 b), that Judah is called a young lion cub (Genesis 49:9), and Joseph a bull (Deuteronomy 33:17; Genesis 49:6).
fn.2475: The Arabic verb אבהמת is inaccurately rendered in Ibn Tibbon's version as שלא נזכרו, which had not been mentioned. Ibn Falaquera rightly observes that it should have been: דברים שנעלמו. See Append. to Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 156.
fn.2476: That is: each of the cherubim, for the beings called 'hayyôth (animals) in the first vision are called cherubim in the second. However, Maimonides evidently erroneously refers verse 14 of Chap. X to the cherubim, or, what is the same thing, to the 'hayyôth; for it appears from the discourse as a whole that in the verse in question the four faces are attributed to the wheels (ophannim), and not to the cherubim. See Abravanel's commentary on Ezekiel, Chap. I, v. 5, and Chap. X, v. 14.
fn.2477: The author seems to allude to a passage from the Talmud, tractate Hagigah, fol. 13 b: מאי כרוב אמר ר׳ אבהו כרביא שכן בבבל קורין לינוקא רביא. 'What does Kerub mean? Rabbi Abbahu says: like a child (KE-RABYA), for in Babylonia a child is called RABYA.'
fn.2478: That is: since the first two are human faces, the last two are as well.
fn.2479: All manuscripts read: ואנמא חדׄף פני שור; the author speaks of the omission, in the second vision, of the ox's face and its replacement by the cherub's face. Instead of חדׄף, Ibn Tibbon appears to have read חרף, for he translates (mss. and editio princeps): ואמנס מלת פני שור; the editors, finding this version somewhat obscure, added before מלת the verb אמר. However, the Arabic word חרף is used only in the sense of letter or particle, and could not have been used here to designate the expression פני שור. Al-Harizi translates more accurately: ואולם עזב לזכור פני שור.
fn.2480: See Vol. II, Chap. XLIII, p. 327, where the author states that the prophets, when naming an object that appeared to them in a vision, sometimes allude to another object bearing an analogous name. The author does not state which etymology he intends to speak of here. Perhaps he means that the word שור (ox) was replaced by cherub, designating a young man, to indicate the idea of contemplation contained in the Hebrew root שור and which can only apply to a human being. Cf. Ephodi's commentary.
fn.2481: Literally: that with which we began the explanation; that is, what we deemed necessary to explain previously before entering into the details of Ezekiel's vision. Ibn Tibbon's version, מה שהחלונו לבארן, is not accurate; it should be translated: מה שהחלונו בביאורו.
fn.2482: The four 'hayyôth represent, according to Maimonides, the four spheres, as we have stated above, p. 7, note 1. We have seen the meaning of their human figure; the symbol of the four wings has been explained elsewhere, and we have seen that, according to our author, they represent the four causes of the movement of the spheres. See Vol. I, p. 179, and ibid., note 2; Vol. II, p. 88, and ibid., note 1.
fn.2483: The two hands represent the double action of the forces emanating from the celestial spheres, of which the author spoke in Chap. X of Part II (Vol. II, p. 89); this double action consists in giving birth to all things and in preserving what is born. In the place just indicated, the author also compares this action to that of art or the artistic faculty of man (أغنية).
fn.2484: According to the author, feet or legs without joints indicate the perpetual motion of the spheres, for whoever wishes to sit down to rest from walking requires joints.
fn.2485: See Bereshit Rabbah, sect. 65 (fol. 58, col. 3): אמר ר' שמואל אין ישיבה למעלה שנאמר ורגליהם רגל ישרה אין להם קפיציי.
fn.2486: The author sees in these words an allusion to the circular motion of the spheres; the word עגל, calf, recalls the word עגול, round. Cf. Vol. II, at the end of Chaps. XXIX and XLIII.
fn.2487: Most MSS read בינהמא, in the dual, which signifies: between the ’hayyot, taken in pairs.
fn.2488: One must recall what the author states elsewhere regarding the celestial spheres, which are closely nested within one another without leaving any void. See Vol. I, Chap. <small>LXXII</small>, p. 357.
fn.2489: All the MSS read מע כונהם מתלאזקין, which is incorrect, as grammatical rules would require מע כונהא מתלאזקה̈. I believe it should be pronounced מחלאוקין, in the masculine dual, and that the author, forgetting the ’hayyot, was thinking of the spheres they represent, for the word فلك, sphere, is of the masculine gender; he here considers the spheres two by two, attached to one another. I therefore felt that, to obtain a fully correct reading, I should write כונהמא, with the dual suffix, instead of כונהם found in the MSS.
fn.2490: We have already seen that the faces and wings represent, according to the author, the causes of the movement of the spheres. Among these causes, three are inherent to each sphere: namely, its sphericity, its soul, and its intellect; the fourth is the superior Intelligence, the object of desire for each sphere. This fourth cause is an Intelligence separate from the sphere, and the various separate Intelligences are also distinct from one another, in that they are the causes and effects of each other. (See Vol. II, Introduction, sixteenth proposition, and ibid., p. 31, note 2.) This is why the prophet says that the faces and wings were separated from above, which means that the superior causes of movement are separate from their respective spheres and distinct from one another. Such appears to be the sense of Maimonides' obscure words; however, he provides no indication of how he understands the remainder of verse 11: לאיש שתים חוברות איש ושתים מכסות את גויתיהנה. Perhaps, following Maimonides, these words should be translated as: two (wings) were attached to each (of the ’hayyot) and two covered their bodies; that is to say, two of the motive causes—namely sphericity and the soul—are inherent to each sphere, while the other two hover, as it were, above it; for the separate Intelligence, the object of the sphere’s desire, is located outside of it, and the intellect that conceives this desired object is in an intimate relationship with it.
fn.2491: This last sentence, which is found in several Arabic MSS, was removed from the two Hebrew versions as a redundant repetition.
fn.2492: The author alludes on the one hand to the spheres themselves, and on the other hand to the celestial bodies they contain; the former possess a pure and transparent matter that does not emit light, while the latter, conversely, are luminous without being transparent. See Vol. II, Chap. <small>XIX</small>, pp. 159-160.
fn.2493: Instead of וגוֺהרהא, Ibn Tibbon seems to have read ווגוֺההא, for his version reads ופניהם, of their faces; Al-Harizi has ועצמם, of their substance.
fn.2494: See Vol. I, Chap. <small>LXXII</small>, p. 357, where the author states, when speaking of the spheres: 'They all have an equal circular motion, and in none of them is there any acceleration or deceleration; I mean that none of these spheres moves sometimes rapidly and sometimes slowly, but that each, regarding its speed and manner of movement, remains subject to its natural law.'
fn.2495: The author alludes to the desire of each sphere to approach its proximate cause, or the separate Intelligence that presides over it and determines its motion.
fn.2496: The author intends to indicate, it seems to me, that some doubt may remain regarding the meaning he attributes to the word face, and that it is not proven indubitably that it refers to the desire drawing each sphere toward its separate Intelligence. Indeed, the word face is equivocal, since the prophet attributes four faces to each ’hayyah. According to Shem-Tov, the author is here alluding to the objection he raised against the philosophers in Part II, Chap. XIX (p. 162), stating that one cannot attribute a spatial position to separate Intelligences and that they cannot be said to be in the east or the west.
fn.2497: In any case, says the author, it is certain that the motion of the spheres is intended here, which occurs in various directions, for some move from west to east and others from east to west. See Vol. I, p. 357, and Vol. II, pp. 151 and 158. The author cannot have intended to allude here to the superior sphere called the diurnal sphere, which moves from east to west; for, according to him, the diurnal sphere is without stars and is not among the four spheres represented by the four ’hayyot. These latter, as has already been seen (p. 7, note 1), are: the sphere of the moon, that of the sun, that which encompasses the spheres of the five planets, and finally that of the fixed stars. The proper motion of all these spheres is from west to east; if, therefore, the author alludes here to an opposite motion from east to west, he could only have had in view the spheres of the nodes of the planets, as we observed in Part II, Chap. XIX, p. 158, note 2.
fn.2498: I believe that the author again intends to speak here of the two opposite motions of the spheres, namely their periodic motion from west to east and the diurnal motion from east to west imparted to them by the superior sphere, or diurnal sphere. See Vol. II, p. 151, note 3. — Moses of Narbonne and Shem-Tov, misled by Ibn Tibbon's translation, which reads: והן חוזרות חלילה, and they turned circularly, thought that circular motion was intended, by which the spheres always return to their point of departure; but if such were the meaning, the comparison with the movement of lightning would be poorly chosen. The Arabic words והי ראג׳עה̈ עלי אעקאבהא mean: and they returned upon their tracks, and it is in this sense that Al-Harizi translates: והם חוזרות על עקבותיהם במרוצה.
fn.2499: Instead of בריא חדא, our editions of the Targum read: בְּרִיָּתָא כחדא, so that it should be translated: and the creatures (the ’hayyot) returned together, etc. Some Targum MSS read בְּרִיְתָא חדא, and others ברית חדא; in Abravanel's commentary on this verse, the citation of the Targum conforms to that of Maimonides. The Targum editions further add after ומקפן the word ומכסן, which is not found in the MSS.
fn.2500: Instead of ליסת חרכה̈, the Leiden MS, no. 18, reads ליסת תחרכהא (that is: تحرّكها), and it is perhaps this reading that Ibn Tibbon had, for he translates אין תנועתה מעצמה. Other MSS read ליסת תחרכה, which is even less correct. Al-Harizi’s version, איננה תנועה מעצמה, is consistent with the reading we have adopted.
fn.2501: Literally: that the side toward which it was the divine intention for the ’hayyâ to move, toward that same side it accomplished etc.. The words אל תלך אלגׄהה̈, toward that same side, are not rendered in Ibn Tibbon's version. That of Al-Harizi contains: אל הפאה ההיא התנועע בתנועה קלה שהיא רצוא ושוב. Instead of התנועע which our editions of Ibn Tibbon's and Al-Harizi's versions have here, one should write תתנועע, as is indeed found in the manuscripts of Ibn Tibbon and the princeps edition.
fn.2503: Literally: He says, then: the side toward which it was the divine intention for the ’hayyâ to walk, toward that very side the ’hayyâ ran. The author would have expressed himself in a manner both simpler and more correct if, instead of פפי תלך אלגׄהה̈ תגׄרי אלחיה אליהא, he had said פאלי תלך אלגׄהה̈ תגׄרי אלחיה. Ibn Tibbon reproduced this kind of pleonasm by saying: בצד ההוא תרוץ החיה אליו. Al-Harizi has: כי הפיאה אשר ירצה החפץ האלוהי ללכת החיה אליה שם הוא חפץ החיה ללכת. — According to the commentators, the author means to speak here of desire, which attracts each sphere toward its respective Intelligence, the proximate cause of its movement. It is also in this sense that Abravanel understands Maimonides' words, and he objects that the separate Intelligence has no determined place such that one could say it causes the spheres to move toward it. See Abravanel, commentary on Ezekiel, chap. I, v. 12: וגם אמרו אל אשר יהיה שמה הרוח ללכת ילכו שהרב מפרש אותו על הגלגל שיתנועע לצד מניעו יקשה לו מאד שהנבדל אין לו מקום מיוחד ויחסו לכל המקומות הוא אחד ולמה אם כן התחלפו תנועות הגלגלים. But this is precisely the objection that Maimonides himself made to the hypothesis of the philosophers, in order to show that the various movements of the celestial spheres are determined only by the free will of the Creator acting with intention. See Vol. II, chap. XIX, p. 162. Evidently, it is this same divine intention that, according to Maimonides, Ezekiel would have designated here by the word רוח, spirit, intention.
fn.2504: More literally: But as the words etc. could have this literal sense that sometimes God will will in the future that it walk toward a certain side, and the ’hayyâ will go toward that side, and sometimes he will will that it walk toward another side, opposite to that one, and it will walk... At the beginning of this sentence, Ibn Tibbon slightly modified the construction. Al-Harizi translates literally: ומפני שהיה מה שאמר אל אשר יהיה שמה הרוח ללכת ילכו שילכו לפאה אחת (read בעתיד) יורה פשט זה המאמר כי פעם ירצה בעת ותלך החיה לפאה ההיא וגו׳.
fn.2505: The author means to speak of the sublunar prime matter or the elementary body that forms the four elements, each of which has a particular specific form. Cf. Vol. I, chap. LXXII, pp. 358-359; Vol. II, chap. XIX, p. 148, and ibid., notes 1 and 2.
fn.2506: For the elements are inert bodies that have no movement of themselves, as animals do, and which are moved by the celestial sphere. See below, p. 21, note 4.
fn.2507: See Ezekiel, chap. I, v. 18; the author will shortly state what he understands by the eyes.
fn.2508: Name of a precious stone by which, according to the author, Ezekiel indicates prime matter. See further, chap. IV, toward the end.
fn.2509: That is to say, that the four faces attributed to the sublunar prime matter represent the four elements. If he calls them OPHANNIM, or wheels, one must remember that the elements also form spheres placed within one another. See Vol. I, chap. XXXVI, p. 134, note 2, and below, chap. III, where the author explains this verse: the OPHANNIM, I heard them called GALGAL (Ezekiel, X, 13).
fn.2510: That is to say, the corporeal form common to the four elements.
fn.2511: The author alludes to the mixture of the elements, which, as he says elsewhere, act upon each other and receive impressions from each other. See Vol. I, chap. <small>LXXII</small>, p. 360.
fn.2512: See above, p. 12, note 1. — The editions of Ibn Tibbon's version have here the word מורכב and shortly after שקצתם מחובר בקצתם, which results in a misinterpretation. One must put in the first place מחובר and in the second מורכב, as indeed the manuscripts do.
fn.2513: In the Arabic sentence, the suffix of אנהא can only refer to the ophannim, and Ibn Tibbon's version שהוא מלא עינים is inaccurate. That of Al-Harizi contains: כי הם מלאות עינים. As for the meaning, the commentators believe that Maimonides is alluding to the many living creatures composed of the elements, all of which have eyes. Indeed, it would be difficult to find another meaning in Maimonides' words, and Abravanel rightly objects to such an improbable interpretation of the prophet's words (commentary on Ezekiel, I, 18):
fn.2514: That is to say, that the elements contain a multitude of images of all sorts of creatures. The commentators, misled by the word דמיונות used here in Ibn Tibbon's version, explained it in the sense of imagination, "for (says Shem-Tob) from the elements are born animals that have imagination" כי מהיסודות יתחדשו בעלי חיים שיש להם דמיון. This explanation is not only too strained, but it can in no way apply to the Arabic word אמתׄלה̈ (plural of מתׄאל), which never has the meaning of imagination; and besides, it also does not fit with the example that Maimonides is about to cite from the Talmud.
fn.2515: Literally: as we find the ancients of the language expressing themselves. Ibn Tibbon has simply: קדמונינו; Al-Harizi translates more accurately: כמו שיאמרו זקני הלשון. — The expressions cited here by Maimonides are found in the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Baba Kamma, fol. 65 and 66, where it concerns the restitution of stolen goods, the principal of which must be restored similar to what was stolen, that is, according to the value it had at the time of the theft; however, the fine—that is, the double (Exodus, 22, 3, 6), the quadruple or the quintuple (Ibid., XXI, 37)—is paid according to the value the stolen goods have at the time of judgment.
fn.2516: That is to say, the word eyes has here the sense of circumstance or quality, for the elements contain many things of different qualities.
fn.2517: This passage is taken from the second book of Samuel, chap. XVI, verse 12, where the kethib has בעוני (for בְּעָנְיִי), my affliction, and the keri בעיני, my eye, which Maimonides explains as my state. Cf. David Kimhi’s commentary on this verse:
fn.2518: The author alludes to the movements that the elements make to return to their natural place, when some cause has made them leave it; this movement occurs in a straight line. See Vol. I, chap. <small>LXXII</small>, pp. 358-359.
fn.2519: That is to say, the ophannim or the four elements directed themselves each toward its natural place: the earth toward the center of the world, the fire toward the circumference, and the water and air toward intermediate places between the center and the circumference.
fn.2520: The particle בל, but, on the contrary, was not rendered by Ibn Tibbon, who has simply: ואין תנועה להם וגו׳.

Likewise, the circular movement of the spheres of the elements, which produces the mixture of the elements, is caused by the movement of the celestial sphere. Cf. Vol. II, chap. XIX, p. 148.

It is true that in chap. LXX of Part I, the author represents the Divinity himself as enthroned upon the heaven ’Arabôth. However, this contradiction is only apparent, as we have already observed elsewhere. He finds this same allusion in the words כעין אבן תרשיש, like the color of a Tarshish stone, which, according to him, likewise designate the sublunary matter or that of the elements, and it seems evident to him that the ophannîm designate the elements. One easily perceives how flawed this reasoning is, since, according to Maimonides, Jonathan sees the celestial spheres in the ophannîm, and consequently, he could not have intended to designate sublunary matter by the words precious stone. fn.2557: The following appears to be, according to Maimonides, the general sense of this passage: According to Rabbi Meir, it is permitted to explain the entire first chapter of Ezekiel up to the word וארא of verse 27, that is to say, up to verse 26 inclusive; according to Rabbi Isaac, one may also explain the first words of verse 27, that is to say, the meaning of the word ’haschmal. According to others, the prohibition against giving a clear explanation extends to the entire first chapter, even to verses 4 to 26, of which only the first elements may be taught. As for verses 27 and 28, only a sage of superior intelligence may study them. It is evidently this opinion that Maimonides attributes to Rabbi Judah the Saint, probably because the words of the Mishnah are reproduced in this passage: אלא א״כ היה חכם ומבין מדעתו, 'unless he be a sage, understanding by his own knowledge.'
fn.2558: As seen above, p. 23, note 2, the human figure represents, according to the commentators, the first of the separate Intelligences or that of the ninth sphere; this Intelligence, although emanated from the absolutely simple being, is nonetheless composite in that it perceives at once the first cause, or God, and itself. It would therefore be this double perception that the prophet indicated by the divided human figure. The theory to which, according to the commentators, Maimonides alludes, belongs to Ibn Sina. fn.2559: That is to say, because the ’hayyôth are the cause of the movement of the ophannîm, and, as such, are prior to them. Cf. above, p. 21, and ibid., notes 4 and 5.

XXXIV, p. 123: “It is therefore necessary that he who wishes to attain human perception should be instructed in logic, then gradually in mathematics, then in the physical sciences, and after that in metaphysics.” Cf. ibidem, p. 13, note 2, and Mélanges de philosophie juive et arabe, p. 357. — Abravanel correctly observes that by accepting the explanation Maimonides gives for the whole of Ezekiel’s vision, it would have been much more rational to begin with the ophannîm or elements, and to ascend from there to the ’hayyôth or celestial spheres in order then to reach the Intelligences of the spheres, or else to follow the reverse order. See Abravanel's second preface to the Book of Ezekiel, second method, fourth objection.
fn.2561: That is to say, that of the ’hayyôth and the ophannîm, or the studies of astronomy and physics.

According to one, the two prophets were equally perfect; but Ezekiel’s contemporaries, living in the Babylonian exile, were less capable of understanding divine matters than Isaiah’s contemporaries. According to the second interpretation, the difference was in the prophets themselves; Isaiah, more cultivated and more perfect, was not at all troubled by everything he saw and recounted it briefly and with simplicity, while Ezekiel’s words reveal all the astonishment and trouble caused him by his vision.
fn.2568: See Ezekiel, chap. I, verses 1 to 3, where the date and place of the vision are fixed with the greatest precision. The verb קייד (قيد) means to bind closely, to chain, to fix the reading of a word by vowels, to specify. Ibn-Tibbon seems to have taken the word תקייד in the sense of to attach; the words וקשרה במקום mean and let it be attached to a place, while the Arabic words ותקייד אלמוצ׳ע mean: and the determination or precision of the place. The suffixes in קשרו and וקשרה were added by Ibn-Tibbon and are not found in the Arabic. Al-Harizi translates: טעם כתיבת עניין המרכבה בשנה אשר נראתה בה ובחדש וביום ובמקום.
fn.2569: Ibn-Tibbon’s editions have אין עניין לו, which has no meaning; the mss. have, in accordance with the Arabic: אין עניין בו, in which there is no idea. — Maimonides leaves us to guess what the idea is that, according to him, this fixation of date and place contains. The commentators, giving free rein to their imagination, have supplemented the author’s silence as best they could, and Abravanel (Commentary on Ezekiel, I, 1-3) rightly sees in their interpretations only vain futilities (כולם הבל המה מעשה תעתועים). We content ourselves with indicating the explanation of Moses of Narbonne, who, if he did not guess Maimonides’ thought, at least gave a fairly plausible reason. According to him, the prophet intended to indicate that his narrative does not concern certain phenomena that would have been actually visible in the sky, but rather things that took place in his soul, that is to say, a prophetic vision, the fruit of an exalted imagination. The precision of the day and place was intended to show everyone that the whole narrative is only imaginary, since no one other than Ezekiel had seen these celestial phenomena on the day and at the place indicated by him. In short, we cannot say what mystery Maimonides sought in the prophet's precise indications, which probably had no other purpose than to record the place and time when he felt called to his divine mission.

fn.2571: Cf. Vol. II, at the beginning of chap. <small>XLI</small>.

Al-Harizi has איך באר האופנים לעמתם. The reading we have adopted, based on two of the best manuscripts, better highlights the word לעמתם, upon which the author particularly insists.

See above, p. 21, and ibid., notes 4 and 5.
fn.2582: Literally: its reality and its quiddity. Al-Harizi’s version bears מהות הקשת ואמתתה ידועה; here, the word quiddity is expressed, but not the word matter.
fn.2583: This obscure passage was explained by Moses of Narbonne, and after him by Ephodi and Shem-Tov, in a manner far too elaborate, and I do not believe these commentators have grasped Maimonides' thought. According to them, the author intended to say that Ezekiel here compares the disposition of the prophet's soul to receive inspiration emanating from the glory of the Eternal, or from the separate Intelligence, to the disposition of a cloud laden with rain to receive the impression of the sun's rays, which produce the rainbow. This is what the author supposedly intended to indicate by speaking of an extraordinary or highly remarkable allegory and adding the words: והוא בלא ספק בכח נבואה, as the version of Ibn-Tibbon expresses it. But evidently, the author means by these words that the comparison in question could only have come from the imagination of a prophet, strengthened by inspiration. Furthermore, as Abravanel observes (Commentary on Ezekiel, I, 28), Ezekiel’s purpose is only to recount the vision he had, and this allegory concerning prophetic inspiration would be an entirely misplaced digression here. Moreover, the glory of the Eternal here indicates something objective that the prophet believed he saw, and could not be an image to designate prophetic inspiration. Finally, one would not see, according to this explanation, what the author intended to say by these words: the matter of the rainbow, its reality, and its quiddity are known; these words, certainly, must have their significance. —We do not claim to have grasped the true sense of this passage; but we propose the following explanation, which seems at least simpler than that of the commentators. According to Maimonides, the splendor surrounding the human figure (see above, p. 23, note 2) appeared to the prophet like the rainbow, in which we see only the reverberation of light, refracted and disturbed by humidity. We know the matter or substratum of the rainbow, which is the rain cloud. We also know its quiddity or form, which is light. But we do not understand the rainbow as it appears to us, that is, the colors of which it is composed; for, according to Ibn-Sinâ, we do not know its causes (see my Mélanges de philosophie juive et arabe, p. 317, and Shahrastânî, p. 413). Similarly, we can only perceive a pale reflection of the splendor surrounding the first of the Intelligences, represented by the human figure, and it is this reflection that the prophet represents as the likeness of the glory of the Eternal (that is, according to the explanation the author gave earlier for the word likeness, as something vague and doubtful). This comparison seems to Maimonides so extraordinary that he can only see in it the product of prophetic inspiration.
fn.2584: The word שעול (for אשר על) is found in all the manuscripts of the Arabic original. The author, reproducing the textual words of Ezekiel before and after the relative pronoun ש, allowed the Hebrew pronoun ש to slip into his discourse instead of the Arabic pronoun אלדֿי.

Potentiality contains opposites at the same time, for one and the same thing can potentially possess health and disease, rest and motion; but opposite actualities cannot exist at the same time, for one cannot simultaneously possess health and be ill, and consequently, one of the two is the good. Regarding evils, the end (τελος) and actuality are necessarily worse than potentiality, since the latter contains the opposite or the good at the same time. "From which it follows," says Aristotle, "that evil does not exist apart from things, for evil is by its nature posterior to potentiality. Thus, in primitive and eternal things, there is neither evil, nor defect, nor anything corrupt, for corruption also belongs to evils." Ibn Tibbon correctly rendered this word by בטול האבריס; Al-Harizi translates it more vaguely as החלייס.
fn.2675: The editions of Ibn Tibbon’s version read: מגמילות חסדי י״י למציאותו וטובתו המבוארת; however, several manuscripts that we consulted do not have the word וטובתו. It is evident that Ibn Tibbon was initially mistaken about the meaning of the word וגודה, which he pronounced وُجُودَةٌ. Having subsequently realized that the initial ו of this word was copulative and that it should be pronounced وُجُودِهِ, he replaced the word למציאותו with וטובתו. The copyists, as we have already seen in many other passages, reproduced both the error and the correction. Al-Harizi translates: …כי הבורא טוב ומטיב וטובתו ידועה על בני אדם
fn.2676: That is to say, in relation to the Intelligences, the celestial spheres, the elements, and the species of animals, which things alone are immutable and are not exposed to what the common people call evil.
fn.2677: The words וכל מא ג̇א ··· קדרה (literally: and everything that is found in the texts of the prophetic books on this important subject, of great utility, etc.) relate to the preceding biblical citations. In Ibn Tibbon’s version, the words גדול התועלת can be considered as the predicate of the subject וכל מה שבא, such that one could translate: “is of great utility,” although in this case it would have been better to say: הוא גדול התועלת; but in the Arabic text, which reads אלעט̇ים אלפאידה̈, with the article, these words are recognizable as a simple appositive. Al-Harizi avoided all ambiguity by translating: אשר תועלתו גדולה. The words ולא יגלט begin a new sentence, and Ibn Tibbon incorrectly attached them to what precedes by translating: ושלא יטעה; it should have been ולא יטעה.
fn.2678: That is to say: the Intelligences of the spheres, or the angels, are of an essence so different from that of man that no proportion can be established between these two species of beings. — Instead of the words איך יהיה ערך על דרך האמת, found in the editions of Ibn Tibbon’s version, the manuscripts read: אין ערך על האמת.

fn.2680: We have translated this difficult verse in the sense that Maimonides appears to attribute to it, and which corresponds to the idea he has just expressed regarding the evils that strike human individuals.

fn.2682: The editions of Ibn Tibbon’s version have מאויר הנפמד; it should be written, according to the manuscripts, כהפמד האויר, as found also in Al-Harizi’s version.
fn.2683: On the meaning of the word בדו אעמק, plural of צאעקה, see Vol. II, p. 331, note 3.
fn.2684: On the meaning of the word כסוף, plural of כסף, see Vol. I, p. 369, note 1. — Al-Harizi, confusing כ̇מוף (written with a punctuated כ̇) with כמוף (كسوف), awkwardly translated: לקות המאורות, the eclipses.
fn.2685: That is to say, that particular forms succeed one another in matter, such that the latter, in order to take on one form, divests itself of another; for it is in this that the birth and corruption of things consist. See Vol. I, chap. XVII, p. 60, and passim, and above at the beginning of chap. VIII, and at the end of chap. x.
fn.2686: In the editions of Ibn Tibbon’s version, the word הווה, which precedes נמשכת and is not found in the manuscripts, must be deleted.
fn.2687: This rather obscure passage has not, I believe, been fully understood by Ephodi, the only commentator to address it, nor by Buxtorf, who reproduced his explanation. Mr. Scheyer’s translation is also lacking. Here is what seems to me to be the simplest meaning of this passage: He who, while being of flesh and bone—that is to say, a simple mortal—nevertheless wishes to be shielded from external impressions that produce evils, that person, I say, wishes to unite within himself two opposite things; for he wishes to be simultaneously a mortal, subject to impressions, and a non-impressionable being, like the celestial bodies. Obviously, if he were, like the latter, shielded from all external impression, he would not be a being subject to contingence; on the contrary, he would be like those celestial bodies, which are neither born nor perishable, and like them, he would be unique in his species and not simply one of the individuals of the same species.
fn.2688: The author is referring to Galen's work, which in the Arabic version bears the title كتاب منافع الاعضاء, Book on the Utilities of the Parts. This is the treatise entitled in the Greek original: Πεpὶ χρείας τῶν ἐν ἀνθρώπου σώματι μορίων (De usu partium humani corporis). In Book III, chap. 10 (Kühn ed., Vol. III, p. 238), the following passage is found: Σϰόπει γάρ μοι τὴν ὕλην, ἐξ ἧς ἕϰαστον ἐγένετο, ϰαὶ μὴ μάτην ἐλπίσῃς, ἐϰ ϰαταμηνίου ϰαὶ σπέρματος ἀθάνατον δύνασθαι συστῆναι ζῶον, ἢ ἀπαθὲς, ἢ ἀειϰίνητον, ἢ λαμπρὸν οὕτω ϰαὶ ϰαλὸν ὡς ἥλιον.
fn.2689: That is to say, the evil of mortality. Ibn Tibbon, I believe, did not fully grasp the meaning of this passage. He translates: ואי אפשר לזה המין מבלתי רע שימצא לו, “it is therefore impossible that this species (that is, the human species) should not be subject to evil.” The Arabic text does not allow for this meaning, as it would have required: פלא בד להד̇א אלנוע מן שר יוג̇ד לה. Al-Harizi appears to have understood the sense better; he translates: אם כן אי אפשר שלא ימצא זה המין ממיני ההזק.
fn.2690: The author refers to the evils that strike man as a mortal being and which prevent him from reaching the natural term of his existence; and he observes that the causes of accidental death are relatively very rare.
fn.2691: Word for word: none is born infirm except by anomaly. In Ibn Tibbon’s version, the words על דרך פלא ועל צד זרות appear to be a double translation of the Arabic adverb שאד̇א.
fn.2692: All Arabic manuscripts read ללמט̇לום, the one who is oppressed; it is evident that the word לעשות, in Ibn Tibbon’s version, is an old copyist’s error, and that one should write לעשׂוק. Al-Harizi translates: אבל אין לאיש העשוק יכולת לדחותם.
fn.2693: On the meaning of the word אחרי, see Vol. I, p. 300, note 2. Ibn Tibbon renders it here by the adverb מאד, which is not exact; perhaps one should read מאדי, an adjective formed by Ibn Tibbon to render the word אכת̇רי. See, for example, Part II, at the beginning of chap. XX: אינם תמידיים ולא מאודיים.
fn.2694: Ibn Tibbon, who translates וזהו הרוב, may have read אלאכת֗ר, as several manuscripts indeed indicate; however, most contain אלאכת֗רי, a form we discussed in the previous note.
fn.2695: Instead of ילאם אלמצאב עליה באלחקיקה̈, a manuscript from the Imperial Library, supplement no. 63, contains ילאם אלמצאב עלי מא יג֗תניה; according to this reading, one should translate: those who are afflicted by it deserve to be blamed for the sin they have committed. fn.2696: We have translated the final words of the verse according to the meaning attributed to them by Maimonides, which he conveys by using the word אלאפכאר, thoughts.
fn.2697: Maimonides diverges from the true meaning of these words, understanding them in the sense that man is, by his nature, the creator of his own suffering.
fn.2698: Word for word: of all diseases and bodily and psychic lesions.
fn.2699: It must be remembered that not only the vital soul, but also the rational faculty and the hylic intellect, are considered by our author as forms inherent to the body and perishable. See Volume I, p. 146, and p. 328, note 1.
fn.2700: See Volume II, chap. XXXVI, pp. 281–282, and p. 284; Eight Chapters, at the beginning of chap. VIII. Cf. Aristotle, On the Soul, Book I, chap. Ist (§ 11): ἔοικε δὲ καὶ τὰ τῆς ψυχῆς πάθη πάντα εἶναι μετὰ σώματος, κ. τ. λ.
fn.2701: The word مكة, which corresponds to Aristotle's term ἕξις, designates, as we have stated elsewhere, a disposition that has become lasting and firm, and may be translated sometimes as capacity and sometimes as habit. Al-Harizi's version contains: ותשיג קניה בתשוקתה למה שאין לו צורך בן, a translation that can scarcely be understood without knowledge of the Arabic text.
fn.2702: According to Ibn Tibbon's version, one should translate: or of everything that it is possible to find; however, the words או מכל found in the editions are obviously erroneous. The suffix in וג֗ודה refers to each of the two words אלזמרד ואליאקות; it would have been more regular to write וג֗ודהמא.
fn.2703: Allusion to the words of Jacob, Genesis, chap. XXVIII, verse 20.
fn.2704: The word حَوَاصِلُ, plural of حاصل, means that which has been obtained or gained, that which one possesses (Ibn Tibbon: הקניניס). It is evident from what follows that the word אלוג֗וד is not used here in its philosophical sense of being or universe, but in its primitive sense of finding; it is undoubtedly in this same sense that the word מציאות must be understood here in Ibn Tibbon's version, where one should read ענינינו instead of ענינו, although the latter reading is also found in the manuscripts. Saadia ibn Danan's manuscript (Hebrew Suppl., no. 63) has a variant here that deserves to be noted, as it was reproduced by Al-Harizi; it reads: פי אלוג֗וד (read האן) וינבגי אן יעדבר אעדבא ר ת֗אני; Al-Harizi's version contains: וצדיך שנתבונן התבוננות שניה במציאות.
fn.2706: These same reflections are found, in almost the same terms, in a passage from Bahya, Duties of the Hearts, Book II, at the end of chap. 5, which Maimonides appears to have had before him.
fn.2707: All the manuscripts contain: אמא אלמא פקד יבקי אליום ואליומן, as for water, he (man) can remain a day or two. It is necessary to understand without it, or without drinking it, and Ibn Tibbon has supplied this ellipsis by adding the word בלעדיו; likewise Al-Harizi: יתכן לעמוד בלתו.
fn.2708: We had to omit, in the translation, the words ולא יגתד֗י, to avoid the pleonasm: דון גד֗א.
fn.2709: Our manuscripts generally contain ללתטבב or ללטבב, and this reading is confirmed by Ibn Tibbon's version, which has לרפואה. Ibn Falaquera read ליטיב, which he translates as להתבשם, to perfume oneself. See the Appendix to Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 157. Al-Harizi seems to have had the same reading; however, he takes the verb طالب here in the sense of to enjoy, to amuse oneself, and translates it as: להנאה ולתענוג, for pleasure and enjoyment. But the reading in our manuscripts, confirmed by Ibn Tibbon, presents no difficulty; for the four substances in question were indeed used as remedies, whether real or imaginary, against certain diseases. See, in the Dictionary of Simple Medicines by Ibn al-Baitar, translated into German by Mr. Jos. de Sontheimer (Stuttgart, 1840, 2 vols. large 8vo), the articles Moschus, volume II, p. 515; Ambra, volume II, p. 210; Smaragdus, volume I, p. 537, and Hyacinthus, volume II, pp. 591–592. Maimonides himself, in a treatise composed by order of Qadi al-Fadil on the treatment of venomous bites and those who have taken poison (Book I, chap. 3), mentions emerald powder as one of the most effective antidotes. See manuscript no. 411 of the old collection of the Imperial Library, fol. 130 b. This manuscript contains the Arabic original in Hebrew characters.
fn.2710: Ibn Tibbon translates: זהו פרסום גמילות חסדי הש״י למציאותו. We see that the word וג֗ודה, which we believe should be pronounced وَجُودِهِ, was pronounced by Ibn Tibbon as وُجُودَهُ; however, if the author had intended to speak of God's goodness toward the universe, he would have said עֲלֵי וְגָ֨דָה; for the verb أفضل requires the preposition علي. Cf. above, p. 68, note 1. — We should also note that the word תבייו or הבו, which Ibn Tibbon translates as פרסום, is missing in several manuscripts, where it is replaced by the preposition מן; likewise Al-Harizi: וזהו מחסדי הבורא וטובתו.
fn.2711: All the Arabic manuscripts contain בינהם, as do the versions of Ibn Tibbon and Al-Harizi, ביניהם, between them; the plural suffix refers irregularly to the preceding word חיואן, which is often used as a collective, although here it is obviously a singular.
fn.2712: Literally: natural generation and corruption; that is to say, the natural laws governing beings subject to generation and corruption.
fn.2713: The editions of Ibn Tibbon's version read: מכל שאר; the manuscripts more correctly have: משאר. The word שאר, as well as the Arabic word סאיר, here has the meaning of כל. See volume II of this work, p. 318, note 5, and p. 334, note 5.
fn.2714: The author alludes to the three types of faculties recognized by the ancient physicians. See volume I, p. 355, note 1.
fn.2715: For the understanding of this passage, see vol. I, chap. LXXII, pp. 364-365. Regarding the meaning of the word תפאצ̇ל, see ibid., p. 365, note 3.
fn.2716: That is to say: What causes there to be no essential difference between individuals is the nature inherent in the general matter of the species, in which all individuals of the same species participate equally. For the first שכ̇ץ, most manuscripts have שכ̇צא, in the accusative; but קצד is evidently a passive verb (قَصَدَ) of which שכ̇ץ is the subject. As for the word מא, Ibn Tibbon rightly takes it in the negative sense, translating: ל א כוון בו איש מבלתי איש. Al-Harizi, neglecting the word דון, translates: מממה שהיתה הכוונה בו לאיש ואיש.
fn.2717: The word نافجة (plur. فواج), derived from the Persian נאפה, designates the type of bladder or pouch that the musk animal carries near the navel and in which the musk liquor is filtered.
fn.2718: That is to say, his person loses nothing in value. Ibn Tibbon translates inaccurately: ולא זה ··· חסר דבר מחויב, 'and he who etc. is not lacking in a necessary thing.'
fn.2719: Literally: according to its gradation, that is to say, by making things more or less accessible for each person, according as they are more or less necessary.
fn.2720: This is how the author sometimes designates Moses when the latter proclaims not a fact revealed to him, but a high philosophical truth. Cf. vol. I, at the beginning of chapter LIV, p. 216, note 2. The editions of Ibn Tibbon's version have here אדון הנביאים; but the manuscripts have אדון החכמים.
fn.2722: Ibn Tibbon neglected the word אד̇האן, the minds, and translates: הרבה נבוכו השלמים; the editors, taking הרבה, often, in the sense of many, felt they should add the preposition מן, which is not found in the manuscripts. Al-Harizi's version has, in accordance with the Arabic text: דעות השלמים; likewise Ibn Falaquera (Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 119): הרבה נבוכו שכלי השלמים. — In this chapter, the author addresses the question of the final purpose of the universe, to show how serious is the error of those who consider man as the goal of creation and attribute to him an importance he is far from having.
fn.2723: Word for word: this question falls; that is to say, the question of the final purpose of the universe is insoluble for the philosophers, proponents of the eternity of the world, as well as for the believers who admit creation ex nihilo. As the author will state later, the true final cause is in God; according to the philosophers, it is the divine wisdom, and according to the believers, it is the divine will.
fn.2724: Cf. volume II, chap. XX, p. 167: 'The idea of design and that of determination apply only to a thing that does not yet exist, and which may or may not exist as it was projected or determined.'
fn.2725: See the Introduction to Part II, XX<sup>th</sup> proposition.
fn.2726: This third proposition follows necessarily from the first two, which serve as its premises. The final cause presupposes an agent acting with intention; what is done with intention did not exist beforehand. Consequently, what has always existed is not a thing done with intention and has no final cause. Thus, as the author is about to explain, one cannot ask what the final cause of God's existence is, and according to the Peripatetics, who admit the eternity of the world, no other final cause can be indicated for the latter than the divine wisdom. As has been explained elsewhere (Part I, chap. LXIX), God is simultaneously the efficient cause, the formal cause, and the final cause of the universe.
fn.2727: The Arabic text reads, in most manuscripts (read ד̇י) בקצד ד̇ו עקל. But the version of Ibn Tibbon and the Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 119, read: בכוונת התחלת שכל, by the intention of an intelligent principle. Al-Harizi has nearly the same terms, which we find in only one Arabic manuscript (Suppl. hébr. no. 63), which reads: בקצד מבדא עקלי.
fn.2728: According to Aristotle's opinion, says the author, everything emanates ultimately from eternal and immutable laws, established by divine wisdom. God, as is stated elsewhere, is the ultimate end, the end of ends, and consequently one cannot seek another ultimate end of the universe. See vol. I, chap. <small>LXIX</small>, pp. 321-322. It is this ultimate end that is being discussed here, and not the particular final purpose that we seek in various beings, as will be discussed.
fn.2729: See, for example, Phys., book II, ch. VIII, where Aristotle demonstrates, through the regularity of natural phenomena, that everything in nature has a certain end, and that nature, obeying eternal laws, is not the result of chance: Ἔστιν ἄρα τὸ ἕνεϰά του ἐν τοῖς φύσει γινομένοις ϰαὶ οὖσιν, ϰ. τ. λ. End of the chapter: ὅτι μὲν οὖν αἰτία, ἡ φύσις, ϰαὶ οὕτως ως ἕνεϰά του, φανερόν.
fn.2730: The 'wherefore,' or the final cause, is the good, and must be regarded as what is best in things: Τὸ γὰρ οὗ ἕνεϰα βέλτιστον ϰαὶ τέλος τῶν ἄλλων ἐθέλει εἶναι. Physics, book II, chap. III. Cf. Metaphysics, book V, chap. II. — It follows from the way this sentence is phrased in our text that, according to Maimonides, Aristotle himself would have said that the final cause is unknown in most species. However, we do not see that Aristotle expressed himself in this sense anywhere, and moreover, the author himself states further on that, according to Aristotle, the end of the species lies in generation and corruption. This difficulty disappears if, instead of ואן הד̇א, one reads והד̇א, as several manuscripts indeed have; this variant was also adopted by Ibn Tibbon, who translates: וזאת המבה התכליתית … תעלם ברוב המינים. Accordingly, it would be necessary to remove the conjunction that from our translation and translate: 'but this final cause etc.', so that Maimonides would be expressing his own opinion here, or that of Ibn Sina, and not that of Aristotle.
fn.2731: See vol. II of this work, p. 119, note 4.
fn.2732: See Politics, book I, chap. VIII: Ὡστε ὁμοίως δῆλον ὅτι ϰαὶ γενομένοις οἰητέον τά τε φυτὰ τῶν ζῴων ἕνεϰεν εἶναι, ϰαὶ τὰ ἄλλα ζῷα τῶν ἀνθρώπων χάριν. Treatise on Plants, book I, chap. II: Καὶ τὸ φὺτον οὐϰ ἐδημιουργήθη εἰ μὴ διὰ τὸ ζῷον.
fn.2733: See On the Parts of Animals, Book I, Chap. 5: ἐπεὶ δὲ τὸ μὲν ὄργανον πᾶν ἕνεκά του, τῶν δὲ τοῦ σώματος μορίων ἕϰαστον ἕνεκά του, ϰ. τ. λ. In general, the treatise *On the Parts of Animals* contains details regarding the purpose and destination of each of the organs of the animal body.
fn.2734: The philosophers, recognizing a final cause in every physical thing, necessarily had to trace back the series of causes and thus arrive at a ultimate end which is the intelligent or divine principle, the absolute cause of all these intermediate causes, each of which exists for the sake of another. See Metaphys., Book II, Chap. 2, and Book XII, Chap. 7.
fn.2735: That is to say, for there to be design, it must involve something called into existence after not having existed. Cf. Volume II, at the beginning of Chap. XIX, p. 145.
fn.2736: See Physics, Book II, Chap. VII: ἔρχεται δὲ τὰ τρία εἰς τὸ ἓν πολλάϰις • τὸ μὲν γὰρ τί ἐστι ϰαὶ τὸ οὗ ἕνεϰα ἕν ἐστι, τὸ δ’ ὅθεν ἡ ϰίνησις πρῶτον τῷ εἴδει ταὐτὸ τούτοις • ἄνθρωπος γὰρ ἄνθρωπον γεννᾷ. “Often three of these causes are reduced to one. Saint-Hilaire.)
fn.2737: That is to say: in what has just been said, only the proximate final cause is concerned.
fn.2738: All the MSS of the Arabic text read: אלדֿי לא בד מנה. The pronoun אלדֿי and the suffix in מנה necessarily refer to the word דואם, permanence. According to Ibn-Tibbon's version, which reads: אשר אי אפשר מבלעדיהם, it should be translated: which are indispensable, that is to say: birth and corruption. Ibn-Falaquera (Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 120) reproduces Ibn-Tibbon's version, which does not conform to the Arabic text.
fn.2739: The text of this passage is somewhat obscure. The author means that, according to Aristotle, the final goal of each species of being is to achieve the production of what is most perfect within the species; and this final goal is reached by means of birth and corruption which perpetuate themselves, with individual forms succeeding one another continually, until matter is clothed in the most perfect form. It will be seen that the author's reasoning aims to prove this: since the final goal of species is to arrive through a series of births and corruptions at what is most perfect in each species, and subsequently at the most perfect species, which is the human species, there is no longer any reason, once this species is reached, to seek another final goal in the world, and consequently one cannot seek the final goal of the universe as a whole. This latter final goal can only be sought in a principle that is outside the universe; this principle is God (ὅ τε γὰρ θεὸς δοϰεῖ τῶν αἰτίוιν πᾶσιν εἶναι ϰαὶ ἀρχή τις.’ Metaph., I, 2). According to the philosopher, it is divine wisdom; according to the believer, it is the divine will.
fn.2740: The words יטלב בה, literally: by which one seeks, were rendered in Ibn-Tibbon's version by שיקוה להמצא בה; Al-Harizi translates more accurately: אשר יבוקש בה מה שיתכן מן השלימות.
fn.2741: The author alludes to the influence that the stars are said to have on all parts of the sublunary world, of which man, according to this opinion, is the most perfect being and the final cause. Cf. Part II of this work, Chap. <small>X</small>.
fn.2742: That is to say: I created heaven and earth, with the laws that govern them, only for the sake of my covenant with Israel and the law I gave to this people. fn.2834: Word for word: neither partial nor universal.

fn.2842: Word for word: they charged themselves (with the burden) of absurdity by saying etc.
fn.2843: Certain Mutazilites maintained indeed that animals, and even the lowest insects, if they have suffered, are entitled to compensation; and God, who is absolute justice, will grant them this compensation by bringing them back to life and making them enjoy these benefits. See volume I, p. 394.
fn.2845: In Ibn Tibbon's version, the words ובאנשי תורתינו are an addition by the translator, who in turn has suppressed the words בחמד אללה, thank God, which are found in all the Arabic manuscripts.
fn.2846: Shahrastani expresses the opinion of the Ash'arites in roughly the same terms: "God is the absolute master in His creation, where He does what He wills and where He rules according to His pleasure; if He were to bring all creatures into paradise, it would be no injustice, and if He were to bring them into the fire of hell, there would be no iniquity; for injustice consists in arbitrarily disposing of that which one has no right to dispose of, or in placing a thing where it ought not to be. But God is the absolute master, and one cannot imagine any injustice on His part, nor attribute any iniquity to Him." See Shahrastani, p. 73 (German trans., volume I, p. 110), and cf. Pococke, Specimen hist. arab., p. 252.
fn.2847: That is, the being who, without having deserved it, has suffered in this world; some manuscripts have here the words פי אלדניא, in this world, which are necessarily implied; likewise Al-Harizi: וכי זה אשר נענש בזה העולם.
fn.2848: Literally: that all these human circumstances are according to merit.
fn.2849: See Babylonian Talmud, tractate Shabbat, fol. 55a, where biblical passages are also cited in support, and cf. below at the beginning of ch. XXIV.—The commentator Shem-Tov rightly observes that this opinion is refuted in the same place by the Talmud itself, and that this is a popular doctrine taught to the common people, which the Talmudists did not intend to present as an incontestable truth. Indeed, neither Holy Scripture nor the doctors pronounce on this matter in an absolute way. Many biblical passages tend to establish that, while it is true that God's absolute justice cannot be doubted in any way, it often presents insoluble problems for our intelligence. We must be convinced of this truth, even when the facts seem to contradict it; we should not see in a man's happiness proof of his piety, nor in his misfortune proof of his impiety. This is especially what the Book of Job tends to establish.
fn.2850: See Mishnah, Part III, tractate Sotah, ch. I, § 5.
fn.2851: Ibn Tibbon's version carries וממעשה הכבוד והיושר, a reading also found in the manuscripts of this version; this is likely merely a copyist's error, and it is probable that Ibn Tibbon rendered the Arabic word אלבר by the analogous Hebrew word בֹּר, which has the same meaning (e.g., כבר ידי, Ps. 18, 21 and 25), and that he wrote ממעשה הבֹּר. Al-Harizi omitted this word and has only ממעשה היושר.

Ibn Tibbon incorrectly rendered it as שכל, intelligence; Al-Harizi translates more accurately: כי הוא מוזהר בבריאתו וטבעו.
fn.2853: See Babylonian Talmud, tractate Bava Kamma, fol. 38b; tractate Pesachim, fol. 118a. Cf. Yalkut, volume I, no. 187. — All Arabic and Hebrew manuscripts of the Guide carry: זכות כל בריה; the editions of Ibn Tibbon's version carry, like the editions of the Talmud, שכר כל בריה.
fn.2854: See Genesis Rabbah, sect. 67 (fol. 59, col. 3), and cf. Talmud, tractate Bava Kamma, fol. 50a.
fn.2855: That is, the Israelite who practices the moral duties prescribed to him by the Law is not comparable to the gentile who practices these same duties without their being prescribed to him. The terms in which Maimonides quotes this Talmudic sentence would seem to indicate that the gentile who performs a moral duty is above the Israelite to whom this duty is prescribed by the Law. However, the text of the Talmud says: גדול מצווה ועושה ממי שאינו מצווה ועושה "He who performs a duty that is prescribed to him is greater than he who performs it without its being prescribed to him"; that is, the Israelite, who by practicing virtue thereby performs a religious duty, receives a greater reward than one who performs only a simple moral duty.
fn.2856: See Babylonian Talmud, tractate Berakhot, fol. 5a, where Rashi explains the words יסורין של אהבה, chastisements of love, in the sense that God sometimes chastises man in this world without his having committed any sin, in order to grant him a reward in the future world beyond his merits.
fn.2857: The Talmud however (loc. cit.) connects it to this verse from Proverbs (3:12): "The Lord chastens him whom He loves."
fn.2858: See below, ch. XXIV, where the author will explain in what sense one must understand the passages that seem to say that God tests man. fn.2859: Among the few Geonim whose writings have reached us, we know of none who professed this strange doctrine; in the writings of Saadia, we find no trace of it. However, it was quite widespread, it appears, among the doctors of the Karaite sect, who followed the doctrines of the Mu'tazilites in all respects. Joseph ha-Roeh, called in Arabic Abu Ya'qub al-Basir, expounded the doctrine of compensation in his dogmatic treatise titled ספר נעימות (cf. on this work, Mélanges de philosophie juive et arabe, pp. 476–477). Chapter XXIII of this work is titled: בתמור ואשר ידבק בו; the word תמור is the established term by which the Karaite translators rendered the term عوض, compensation. We cite the beginning of this chapter: דע כי בארנו כי הקדמון ית׳ לא יבחר הרע וכי הוא לא ימנע החוב ואם יכאיב החוב והבהמות והטפים והם ԍינם מחוייבים כאשר נבאר בלא ספק מלתת להם תמור שיוציא עמו הכאב מלהיותו חמס. ‘It must be known, as we have explained (chap. 22), that God does not take pleasure in evil and that He does not refuse what is due. If He causes suffering to wild beasts, domestic animals, and children, without their being guilty, as we shall explain, He must undoubtedly grant them a compensation, by which He ensures that the suffering is not an injustice.’ The same subject is treated in chap. XXVII of the מחכימת פתי, an extract from the preceding work. These two works are now found in the Imperial Library, Hebrew supplement ms., no. 127. Aaron ben Elijah (עץ חיים, p. 127) also states that great doctors in Israel adopted this doctrine which reason rejects: ואלו דברים לא ישוערו בשכל וגדולי חכמי ישראל נטו בזה. Here, as elsewhere, some Rabbinite doctors among the Geonim followed the example of the Karaites. Cf. Vol. I, chap. LXXI, pp. 336–337.
fn.2860: That is to say, divine Providence exists only for beings who are most directly under the influence of the divine breath. On what is understood by the word overflow, see Volume II, chap. XII, pp. 101–102.
fn.2861: Most of our manuscripts read ואמא אן גרק, so that the word גרק should be considered a preterite and pronounced إِنَّ غَرَقَ, and it is indeed in this sense that Ibn Tibbon translated: אמנם אם טבעה הספינה, if the ship was submerged. However, the verbal noun وأحرار, which follows immediately after, proves that غرق must also be pronounced as a verbal noun. We therefore believe we should adopt the reading אן גרק (without ואמא) found in some manuscripts, and consider אן as an adverb in the sense of indeed: إِنَّ غَرَقَ السَّفِينَةِ. Al-Harizi translates accurately: אד טביעות הספינה וכל מה שיש בה ונפילה הקד על אנשי הבית.
fn.2862: As can be seen, Maimonides recognizes particular Providence only with regard to individuals of the human species, and even then he applies a restriction, saying further on 'that only he to whom something of the overflow (of divine intelligence) adheres shall participate in Providence according to the measure by which he participates in intelligence.' See also further on, chap. LI, and cf. Levi ben Gershom, Guerres du Seigneur, book IV, chap. 7. This doctrine was bound to displease the orthodox rabbis; Christian theologians were also moved by it, and Saint Thomas felt it necessary to refute it in his Summa Theologica, Part I, quest. XXII, art. 2: ‘Quidam vero posuerunt incorruptibilia tantum providentiæ subjacere, corruptibilia vero non secundum individua, sed secundum species; sic enim incorruptibilia sunt.... A corruptibilium autem generalitate excepit Rabbi Moyses homines, propter splendorem intellectus quem participant. In aliis autem individuis corruptibilibus aliorum opinionem est secutus; sed necesse est omnia divinæ providentiæ subjacere, non in universali tantum, sed etiam in singulari. Quod sic patet, etc.’ However, St. Jerome had already expressed an opinion on Providence similar to that of Maimonides. See his commentary on Habakkuk, 1:14 (S. Hieronymi opera, ed. Martianay, Vol. III, col. 1600): ‘Cæterum absurdum est ad hoc Dei deducere majestatem ut sciat per momenta singula quot nascantur culices, quotve moriantur, quæ cimicium et pulicum et muscarum sit in terra multitudo, quanti pisces in aqua natent, et qui de minoribus majorum prædæ cedere debeant. Non simus tam fatui adulatores Dei, ut dum potentiam ejus etiam ad ima detrahimus, in nos ipsos injuriosi simus, eamdem rationabilium quam irrationabilium providentiam esse dicentes.’
fn.2863: Most of the Arabic and Hebrew manuscripts cite this last verse inaccurately; the author himself, through a lapse of memory, appears to have conflated several verses from Leviticus (chap. XX, verses 3, 5, 6). The editions of Ibn Tibbon's version have ונתתי פני באיש ההוא. Al-Harizi: ונתתי את פני באיש ההוא. The citation, as we have written it, conforms to verse 6 and is found in one of the Leiden manuscripts (no. 18).

IX: ὁ δὲ κατὰ νοῦν ἐνεργῶν καὶ τουτον θεραπεύων καὶ διαπείμενος ἄριστα καὶ θεοφιλέστατος ἔοικεν εἶναι, κ. τ. λ.

fn.2898: To suppose that God could now know what He was previously ignorant of would be to attribute to Him not absolute perfection, but perfectibility, and to believe that He could pass from potentiality to actuality; therefore, it must be admitted that God's knowledge is absolutely perfect and that no change could occur within it. fn.2899: God's knowledge, being identical with His essence, must be one like the latter and cannot be multiple; this is something that even those who admit various other essential attributes in God, besides knowledge, could not contest. See Volume I, chaps. L and LIII.
fn.2900: That is, we believers who seem to contradict these two propositions by admitting that God knows individual things, which are both multiple and accidental.
fn.2901: The author here raises the following objection to believers: from what we have just said, two theses rejected by the philosophers would follow: 1. that divine knowledge has non-being as its object, since it knows what does not yet exist; 2. that it encompasses the infinite, since the individuals who do not yet exist, but who will exist in the future, are infinite. — All Arabic manuscripts have אלאעדאם, in the plural, non-beings, non-existent things. Ibn Tibbon has ההעדר, in the singular, which is inaccurate.
fn.2902: In other words: what divine knowledge cannot have as its object is the absolute non-being that never exists, just as our human knowledge cannot have as its object what does not presently have existence.
fn.2903: That is, certain thinkers, to escape the difficulty just pointed out, have claimed that divine knowledge actually has as its direct object only species, which are finite, but that by knowing the species, it thereby indirectly knows all the individuals—past, present, and future—contained within each species. — The words במעני מא, in a certain sense, refer, in my opinion, to the whole of the sentence, and not only, as one might think, to the verb ויסתרסל; I believe the author is alluding to those of the Mutakallimun who, in a certain sense, recognized for the species, as for all universals, a real existence outside the intellect. See Volume I, p. 185, and ibid., note 2.
fn.2904: The word מתשרע, which we translate as theologians, designates, like אהל אלשריעה̈, the doctors of the three monotheistic religions. Cf. Volume I, p. 68, note 3.
fn.2905: That is, he knows only what relates to the upper world, and in the sublunary world, his knowledge embraces genera and species, but not individuals. Cf. Mélanges de philosophie juive et arabe, p. 319.
fn.2906: The author shows how one has arrived successively at summarizing all knowledge of God in the knowledge He has of His essence. In short, the author distinguishes three opinions regarding divine knowledge: 1st, that which admits that God encompasses by a single knowledge diverse things and things that occur every day, so that there is in His knowledge neither multiplicity nor change; but according to this opinion, which is that of the believers, God's knowledge would encompass the infinite and non-being. To avoid this difficulty, it has been maintained 2nd, that divine knowledge extends directly only to stable things, that is to say, to individuals of the upper world and to the genera and species of the sublunary world. But others have rightly objected that this opinion would not exclude the multiplicity of divine knowledge, and they were forced to maintain 3rd, that God knows only His own essence, and that it is in the contemplation of Himself that He contemplates the things of which He is the first cause. Further details on these different opinions can be found in Averroes' Destruction of the Destruction, disputat. XIII.
fn.2907: In the editions of Ibn Tibbon's version, there is a serious error here; instead of מיוחד, one must write מחויב, as found in the MSS of this version.
fn.2908: Literally: On the contrary, this same inability of our intellects to understand His essence is also the inability to understand the knowledge of things as they are. — All our Arabic MSS read כיף הי, and the pronoun הי can only refer to אלאשיא, things; so that one should say in Hebrew איך הם. It is probably the Arabic pronoun הי that caused the translator to make an inadvertent error. It is through a similar inadvertence that a little further on Ibn Tibbon put in the feminine all the pronouns and verbs referring to the masculine word עצם, a translation of the feminine word ذات, essence.

fn.2910: That is to say, as it was imagined that God's knowledge and ours, having the same name, also have the same character, the result was that it was impossible to reconcile the multiplicity and variability of the objects of knowledge with the absolute unity and immutability of God.
fn.2911: Thus, for example, man having free will can choose the good path or the bad; God knows in advance which of the two paths he will choose, but this in no way prevents him from retaining his freedom of choice.

There is thus once again a difference between God's knowledge and ours.

The balls that descended by pulling the threads to which they were attached probably sounded the hours by falling onto a metal plate. We are at least assured that a similar mechanism existed in the clepsydra that the Caliph Harun al-Rashid sent to Charlemagne along with other precious objects: '… and also a clock made of brass, marvelously constructed with mechanical skill, in which the course of the 12 hours was directed toward a clepsydra, with as many small bronze balls, which fell at the completion of the hours and by their fall caused a cymbal placed beneath them to ring.' fn.2924: Literally: therefore, for God there is neither multiplicity of knowledge, nor renewal or change of knowledge.

Maimonides wisely stops before this insoluble problem, and limits himself to establishing that we are incapable of forming an idea of divine knowledge, which is identical with the very essence of God, and is inaccessible to our intellects.

Only accidentally and indirectly can evil be attributed to divine action; matter itself, created by God, is not an evil, but it becomes the source of evil through the privation inherent in it, which is the cause of corruption (φθορά). In the prologue to the book of Job, the sons of God should be understood as the good that God directly intended in creation, that is, the Intelligences and the spheres, as well as the forms emanating from them, which are the causes of generation (γένεσις) and the preservation of beings. Satan, on the contrary, represents privation, the accidental source of evil.

Job at least left the question intact, whereas his friends claimed to resolve it through erroneous arguments.

The author thus seeks to explain differently than the doctors the meaning of these words: "for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has."

Samuel ibn Tibbon, treatise Yikkawou ha-maïm, ch. 25, p. 101.

XVII, p. 129 ff., where the author establishes that only man, who participates more or less in the emanation of the divine intellect, participates in divine Providence to the same extent.
fn.3023: That is to say, his opinion concerning divine Providence, which, according to the author, follows from the passages he has just cited.
fn.3024: The connection between these final passages and what precedes is not clearly seen, and, in general, the author expresses the opinion he attributes to Elihu in a very obscure manner. XII) on the various evils that strike men, which would seem to contradict what was said about Providence watching over human individuals; he shows that Elihu thinks, as he does himself, that these evils, inherent in matter or human nature, happen to the individual only exceptionally and are a good for humanity as a whole. Through the examples of plague and war, the author alludes, I believe, to the first and second types of evils mentioned in Chap. XII. As a final solution to the problem, as will be seen, the author establishes that we cannot form a correct idea of divine Providence, of the divine governance, or of divine science; for we judge them by human governance, whereas it is only by mere homonymy that governance, science, and many other things are said simultaneously of God and of us, even though the two things are totally and essentially different.
fn.3025: That is to say, in the theophany that concludes the book of Job (Chaps. XXXVIII to XLI).

fn.3043: That is to say: the gentiles, seeing the unwavering faith of the Hebrews, will take it as a model and will possess solid convictions against which all the alleged miracles produced by false prophets will fail. — The words לִמְתְחַתֵר בְּמַעְגָּל, which we have translated as to the miracle-maker, literally mean: to him who struggles by means of the miracle, that is to say, who endeavors to convince by means of the miracle. מתחד (مُتَّحِد) is the participle of the Vth form of the verb خَدِيَ, which Dictionaries explain as pugnavit, certavit in aliqua re peragenda. Ibn Tibbon translates: ל עשיית מופת, and Al-Ḥarizi: למפתה במעשה נס; Ibn Falaquéra (Append. to Moré ha-Moré, p. 157) rightly criticizes these two translations and proposes translating: ל מתגבר במופת, to him who seeks to overcome by means of the miracle.

See the preceding note.
fn.3046: Literally: and that your feet might not slip.
