fn.3123.sub_0: As I have already noted in my Réflexions sur le culte des anciens Hébreux, p. 2 (published in Vol. IV of Mr. Cahen's Bible), Maimonides, like many other Arabic authors of his time, understands the word צאבה̈ or Sabians to refer to all pagan peoples in general. The books from which he drew his knowledge of pagan cults, and which he will discuss further on, led him to believe that these cults were generally based on astrolatry. Consequently, in Maimonides' language, religion of the Sabians signifies the same thing as paganism. In the Quran (II, 59; v, 73; XXII, 17), the Sabians (الصابيون) are mentioned alongside Jews and Christians as a religious community possessing revealed books and having a share in the afterlife. It is generally agreed that the Sabians of the Quran are the Mandaeans or Christians of Saint John, who, because of their frequent ablutions, are called in Syriac צביעיין (or צביין, according to the pronunciation of the Mandaeans, who omit the ע), that is to say, the Baptists. See E. Castelli Lexicon-syriacum seorsim typis describi curavit atque sua adnotata adjecit, J. D. Michaëlis, p. 749. Arabic authors, starting from the time of Caliph Al-Ma'mun, also give the name Sabians to the pagans of Harran and some other cities of Mesopotamia, who are completely different from the Sabians of the Quran, which has given rise to great confusion. Vain efforts have been made to find the etymology of the name Sabians applied to pagans. The most successful conjecture is that of Pococke (Specimen hist. ar., p. 139), who derives this name from the Hebrew word צבא, army, and who sees in it an allusion to the worship of the stars called צבא השמים, host of heaven; but this etymology is no more plausible than any of the others.
fn.3123.sub_1: We now know that in reality there is only one kind of Sabians, namely the Mandaeans, but that the pagans of Harran, threatened with extermination by Caliph Al-Ma'mun, usurped around the year 830 of the Christian era, on the advice of a Muslim doctor, the name of Sabians, and claimed to be the sect mentioned under this name in the Quran and recommended by the prophet to the protection of Muslims. This fact is reported in the Kitab Al-Fihrist by Muhammad ibn Ishaq al-Nadim (see the extract from this book given by Mr. de Hammer in the Journal Asiatique, September-October 1841, p. 254 et seq.). It had already been published by Hottinger, Historia Orientalis, p. 169, and, following him, by Spencer, De legibus Hebræorum ritualibus, Bk. II, ch. I, sect. 2 (p. 241 of the Cambridge edition, 1685, folio). It is especially in the work published on the Sabians by Mr. Chwolson that the fact in question was brought to light and supported by numerous proofs. The author shows how the name Sabians, applied in the Quran only to the Mandaeans and used in this sense by Arabic authors until the time of Al-Ma'mun, later served to designate the Harranians as well and ended, in the 6th century of the Hijra, by being used in the general sense of Pagans. See Die Ssabier und der Ssabismus (2 vols. large 8vo, St. Petersburg, 1856), Vol. I, ch. VI, p. 139 et seq., and the entire ch. VIII. This excellent work contains numerous details on the religion of the Harranians, which can clarify several facts reported by Maimonides in this chapter and in those following, where our author aims to explain a large part of the ceremonial practices prescribed by Moses by means of the superstitious customs of the Sabians or pagans that the Mosaic laws tended to abolish.
fn.3124: This way of considering paganism in general is based on Holy Scripture, which speaks only of the pagans of Western Asia, whom it generally presents as devoted to the worship of the stars, symbolically represented by idols. Cf. what our author says in his commentary on the Mishnah, treatise Avodah Zarah, ch. IV, § 7, and passim, and in his Mishneh Torah, Part I, treatise on Idolatry, ch. I. It is in the same sense that the Christian Arabic historian Abu al-Faraj, in several passages of his History of the Dynasties, speaks on the worship of the Sabians, a name by which, like Maimonides, he designates all pagan peoples. See Chwolson, loc. cit., pp. 254-55.
fn.3125: The author no doubt refers to the allegedly historical accounts found in the Nabatean Agriculture, which he discusses below, p. 231.
fn.3126: The word מנהא (by them, i.e., by these documents) is missing in several mss., and the two Hebrew versions do not reproduce it.

fn.3130: Kutha is, according to Arabic geographers, a city located in Babylonian Iraq, south of Baghdad and near the Nahr-Malca canal, between the Euphrates and the Tigris. The land of the sun would therefore be, according to Mr. Chwolson, the Deccan. It is true that the word إقليم, clima, is often used by the Arabs in the sense of region or country; but no ancient or modern geographer knows the designation "land of the sun." I believe, therefore, that the word אקלים has here its ordinary sense of clima, and that the 2nd clima is meant, which contains a large part of India. It is known that Ptolemy and the Arabic geographers divide the inhabited part of the earth, from South to North, into seven zones called climata. According to the Sabians, as will be seen below, each clima is under the influence and direction of one of the seven planets. Cf. the Hebrew work Shevile Emunah by R. Meir al-Dabi, II, 2 (Amsterdam edition, fol.
fn.3146.sub_1: 19 a): כשהבורא ברא העולם נתן כח בכוכבים למשול בארץ ולהנהיגה וחלק הארצות לשבעה כוכבי לכת וגו׳ "When the Creator created the world, he placed in the stars a force by which they were to dominate the earth and govern it, and he distributed the countries among the seven planets, etc." Yaqut, in the Introduction to his great geographical Dictionary entitled معجم البلدان, speaking of the seven climata, indicates the respective planet that dominates each clima, according to the opinion of the Persians and the Greeks, and he says that the 2nd clima is, according to the Persians, under the influence of Jupiter (المشترى), and according to the Greeks (الروم), under that of the sun (الشمس); the 4th clima, on the contrary, is, according to the Persians, under the influence of the sun, and according to the Greeks, under that of Jupiter (Arabic MSS of the Imperial Library, supplement, No. 886, at the beginning). I believe, therefore, that the words of our passage למא כׄרגׄ מן אקלים אלשמס אלמגׄאור ללהנד must be understood thus: "when he emerged from the region of the clima of the sun (that is, the 2nd clima) which is near India." One cannot think here of the 4th clima, no region of which is near India. We should recall that India is also, according to Muslim tradition, the place of Adam's first residence after his fall. Driven from paradise, according to this tradition, he fell upon the mountain of Serandib, which is the island of Ceylon. See d’Herbelot, Bibliothèque orientale, p. 55 b.

fn.3191: I have not found the slightest information on this book anywhere, and I am even uncertain about the pronunciation of the word الـمسرب; however, the reading אלסרב is guaranteed by seven Arabic manuscripts and as many manuscripts of Ibn Tibbon's version, which have ספר הסרב. In a citation by Sa'ad ben Mansur (in Steinschneider, loc. cit., p. 83, note 4), one likewise reads אלסרב. A single manuscript of Ibn Tibbon's version (Oratoire collection, no. 46) bears השרב, like the editions of this version; this variant is of no importance. In two Arabic manuscripts (Suppl. hébr., no. 63, and Leiden ms., no. 18), one reads לאסרג׳, a word that must be pronounced الشرج (pl. of السراج), for Al-Harizi, who had the same reading, renders it by ספר הנרות, Book of Lamps. We also find traces of this reading in two manuscripts of Ibn Tibbon's version, one of which (Suppl. hébr., no. 26) bears ספר הסרגי, and the other (Orat., no. 47) has ספר הנר. This latter reading is the only one that corresponds to כתאב אלסראג׳, the title of a work on alchemy and magic by Yahya al-Barmaki, cited by Hajji Khalifa (vol. III, p. 588, no. 7074), and in which M. Chwolson believes he recognizes the work designated here by Maimonides (see Die Ssabier, vol. I, pp. 713-14); but this isolated reading cannot prevail against that of most manuscripts, which we have thought necessary to adopt. Finally, the reading אלסרס, which is found only in an inaccurate manuscript from the Leiden Library (no. 221), is obviously corrupt.
fn.3193: The Arabs speak of three ancient sages named Hermes, of whom the first, called Hermes al-Harâmisa (the Hermes of the Hermes), is identified with the Enoch of the Bible, whom the Arabs call ldrîs. This is the Hermes Trismegistus of the Greeks, in whose name were forged, in the first centuries of the Christian era, several works of astrology, magic, and alchemy. The pseudo-Hermetic writings were translated into Arabic. The work indicated here by Maimonides is perhaps that which Hadji-Khalfa (vol. V, p. 247, no. 10877) cites under the title of كنز الاسرار, the Treasure of Secrets. Concerning the Arabic fables relating to Hermes and the books attributed to him, see D’Herbelot, Bibliothèque orientale, art. Hermes, and Casiri, Biblioth. arab. hisp. [Lat.: Arab-Hispanic Library], vol. I, pp. 372, 374-76.
fn.3194: We lack precise information concerning Isaac the Sabian and his works; this author was undoubtedly from Harrân. fn.3268: This sentence is somewhat obscure; here is what appears to be its sense: The Law being a divine thing, it might appear that it ought to have provided for the absolute good, as much of humanity in general as of each individual in particular. But, if one considers nature, which likewise proceeds from God, one will find that it also contains all the general advantages which the Law had in view, and that nevertheless there sometimes result therefrom injuries to individuals. Shem-Tob cites the following examples: In the legal order, the condemnation of the guilty is a good for society, and yet it may sometimes happen that innocent persons are condemned in consequence of false testimony. In the natural order, rain, necessary for vegetation, is a benefit for humanity, and yet, when too abundant, it may cause grave disasters. We see consequently that, as much in the legal order as in the natural order, God has provided for the general good of society, without regard for the individuals who, by exception, are sometimes the victims of the legal order or of the natural order. This is an incontestable fact which we are not to explain and which must be attributed to the impenetrable will of the Divinity. — The grammatical construction of this sentence further increases its obscurity; thus the suffix of פיהא evidently refers to the word אלשריעה̈ which is found at the beginning of the sentence, while the suffix in צ̇מנהא refers to the plural: אלאמור אלטביעיה̈; the natural construction would therefore be this: אלתי פי צ̇מנהא תלך (i.e. פי אלשריעה̈) אלמנאפע אלעאמה̈ אלמוג̇ודה̈ פיהא, and in Hebrew: אשר יש בכללם התועלות ההם הכוללות הנמצאות בה. Ibn-Tibbon has rendered the word פיהא by בהם, whereas it ought to have been rendered by בה, that is to say בתורה. Al-’Harîzi has suppressed the word פיהא, which he probably believed to be superfluous; he translates: כי התורה היא ענין אלהי כי יבחנו אותה בדברים הטבעיים אשר התועלות ההם הכוללות המצואות בכללם יתחייב בהם היזק אנשים.
fn.3269: That is to say, by establishing a comparison between the Law revealed by God and the laws of nature which likewise proceed from God.

fn.464: This proposition pertaineth unto the atomistic Motécallemîn, whose doctrine shall be expounded hereafter (chap. LXXIII). By מכאן (سكان), they seem to understand space in relation to its extension or its dimensions; by חיז (حيّز), space circumscribed within limits. Albeit the atom, they say, hath no extension, it is nevertheless circumscribed and separated, by limits, from that which is adjacent to it; it is, as it were, the body without dimensions, the point considered as the first element of extension, yet which possesseth none itself. Lo, thus doth Al-Djordjâni, in his Kitâb al-Ta’rifât or Book of Definitions, explain the words مكان and حيز, as they are employed by the Motécallemîn: المكان عند المتكلمين هو الفراغ المتوهم الذي يشغله الجسم وينفذ فيه ابعاده «Macân, among the Motécallemîn, is the ideal void which the body occupieth and into which it causeth its dimensions to penetrate.» الحيز عند المتكلمين هو الفراغ المتوهم الذي يشغله شيء ممتد كالجسم أو غير ممتد كالجوهر الفرد «’Hayyiz, among the Motécallemîn, is the ideal void which is occupied by a thing whether extended like the body, or non-extended like the simple substance (or the atome).» It is perceived that macân is attributed only to the body having dimensions, whilst ’hayyiz is attributed simultaneously to the extended body and to the atom. The words الجوهر الفرد signify, according to M. Silv. de Sacy, substance isolated from form (see Notices et extraits des mss., vol. X, p. 65); but this explanation is incorrect. These words, which, in truth, signify literally isolated substance, were employed by the Motécallemîn to designate the atome which they also call الجزء الذي لا يتجزأ or simply الجزء, as might have been seen somewhat further back. Thus expresseth himself Ibn-Roschd, in his Epitome of the Metaphysics, Book I, when speaking of the substance الجوهر; we cite the Hebrew version: וכן מי שראה כי העצמות הרמוז אליו יתחבר מחלקים אשד לא יתחלקו קרא אותם עצמים כמו שנשמע המדברים מאנשי זמננו יקראו החלק אשר לא יתחלק העצם הפדדי «In like manner, those who think that the indicated substance is composed of atoms give to these latter the name of substances, even as we hear the Motécallemîn of our day call the atom the isolated or simple substance (الجوهر الفرد).» The term الجوهر الفرد resembleth that of the monad, used by Leibnitz, albeit it doth not designate exactly the same thing; the proposition of the Motécallemîn, quoted here by Maïmonides, offereth a striking analogy with what Leibnitz saith, when speaking of monads: Substantia nempe simplex, etsi non habeat in se extensionem, habet tamen positionem, quæ est fundamentum extensionis. See the Works of Leibnitz, Dutens edition, vol. II, part I (Epistolæ ad P. des Bosses), p. 280.
fn.481: The word אלתלאזם (التلازم) betokeneth the close and necessary connection between two things. In the Kitâb al-Ta’rifât, at the word ملازمة, we read: that this word expresseth the impossibility of separating two things from one another, and that the words لزوم and تلازم are employed in the same sense. Cf. Freytag's Dictionary, at the root لزوم. The enunciation of this connection or inherence formeth a necessary proposition or judgment, such as, for example, the proposition cited here by our author: every man is rational. — The author appeareth to have in view that which Aristotle saith regarding demonstration, in explaining the three terms whereby he designeth the different degrees of the necessary. See Posterior Analytics, book I, chap. 4. He seemeth to allude especially to the terms ϰατά παντός and ϰαθ’ αὑτό. The ϰατά παντός designeth an attribution which pertaineth unto every individual, and not merely to such or such an one, and which is at all times and not merely at such or such a time. Thus, animal being predicated of every man (ϰατά παντός άνθρώπου), it will suffice that it be true that such an individual be a man for it to be true to say of him that he is an animal. The term ϰαθ’ αὑτό, in itself (which hath four principal senses), designeth first the attribution which expresseth that a thing is essential or inherent unto another, and wherein the attribute entereth into the essential definition of its subject; e.g., the line in the triangle, the point in the line. Secondly, the ϰαθ’ αὑτό designeth the attribution wherein the subject entereth into the essential definition of the attribute, or, in other words, wherein the attribute is so essential to the subject that the latter containeth the definition thereof (ὅσοις τῶν ἐνυπαρχόντων αὐτοῖς αὐτὰ ἐν τῷ λόγῳ ένυπάρχουσι τῷ, τί ἐστι, δηλοῦντι). Thus, e.g., the line necessarily entereth into the definition of the straight and of the curved, and number into that of the even and of the odd. Ibn Rushd observeth that, in the first case, that is to say, when the attribute entereth into the definition of the subject, it concerneth either the complete definition or a part of the definition, as, per- adventure, when one defineth the triangle by saying that it is a figure bounded by three straight lines; in the second case, that is to say, when the subject entereth into the definition of the attribute, it concerneth the partial definition, as, for example, when one taketh the line as the definition of the straight and of the curved, which exist in the line, or else number as the definition of the even and of the odd, which exist in number. That which, saith he, entereth especially into the propositions subserving demonstration, are these first two kinds of ϰαθ’ αὑτό (אשר בעצם), wherein there is a necessary and essential attribution; for, he addeth, the partial definition findeth itself in a necessary relation with the thing defined (כי יחם חלק הגדר אל הנגדר יהיה הכרחי). See the Middle Commentary on the Posterior Analytics, Hebrew version, at the passage in question. One will now understand what our author had in view in saying that there is here the idea of inherence etc.
fn.594: From the manner in which the author here expresseth himself, one might believe that it concerneth a well-known proposition belonging to Aristotle; but, as several commentators observe, this subtle distinction between the quiddity of a thing and its existence belongeth to Ibn-Sînâ, and it hath been impugned by other Arabian philosophers, and notably by Ibn-Roschd, who informeth us that those who have seen in existence an accident have based their view, among other things, upon the fact that the Arabic word موجود, which the philosophers employ in the sense of existent or that which is (τὸ ὄν), is primarily a passive participle signifying found, and indicateth, by its etymology, something accidental. At the commencement of the 1st book of his Epitome of Metaphysics, Ibn-Roschd, after having set forth the divers meanings of the philosophical term درو جود (that which is, τὸ ὄν), thus summarizeth (Hebr. vers.): ולכן היה שם הנמצא שב אל שני אלו הענינים לבד ר״ל אל הצודק ואל מה שהוא נמצא חוץ לשכל, that is to say, that in summary, the said term is used either for that which the mind judgeth to be true (ἔτι τὸ εἶναι σημαίνει ϰαί τὸ ἔστιν ὅτι ἀληθές, ϰ. τ. λ. Arist., Metaph., book V, chap. 7), or of being in itself, of that which hath an objective reality outside the mind, and, in this sense, it applieth to all the categories (ϰαθ’ αὑτὸ δέ εἶναι λέγεται ὅσαπερ σημαίνει τὰ σχήματα τῆς ϰατη-γορίας, ϰ. τ. λ. Ibidem). Accidental existence, addeth Ibn-Roschd, cannot be conceived in the isolated being or in being in itself (ϰαθ’ αὑτό), for the substance of the thing and its quiddity cannot be accidental; it can only be conceived in the mutual relation of beings, that is to say, when the ὄν expresseth an accidental relation of one thing to another, or when it is said, as Aristotle expresseth it, ϰατὰ συαβεβηϰός: אולם הנמצא במקרה הוא לא יצויר במציאות הנפרד כי עצמות הדבר ומהותו אי אפשר ש׳היה במקרה ואמנם יצויר מיחם הנמצאות קצתם لا קצת. He then refuteth the opinion of Ibn-Sînâ, according to whom existence is an accident supervening upon the essence or the quiddity of the thing which existeth, and, after having shown all that is false in this way of viewing the matter, he addeth: אבל זה דרך האיש הזה ברוב מה שיביאהו מצד עצמו «But such is the manner of this man in almost all that he allegeth of his own accord.» Ibn-Roschd looked with disfavour upon a proposition which appeared to him to be in opposition to the Aristotelian doctrines. In truth, this ideal separation between what the thing is (τὸ τί ἦν εἶνο ι) and its existence is contrary to the spirit of Aristotle’s doctrine; it would be at most in artificial objects that one might separate the what from the existence, the idea of the thing being in the mind of the artist before existing (cf. Aristotle, Metaph., book VII, chap. 7: ἀπὸ τέχνης δὲ γίγνεται ὅσων τὸ εἶδος ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ, εἶδος δὲ λέγω τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι ἑϰάסטου ϰαί τὴν πρώτην οὐσίαν’). According to the partisans of Ibn-Sînâ, the same would hold true of all that is produced by nature; for, say they, all things being in the first cause, or in God, who knoweth them beforehand, the quiddity of things is prior to their existence, which, consequently, is an accident of the quiddity (vide the commentary of Shem-Tob, on our passage). But this reasoning leadeth to the admission, with Plato, of pre-existing ideas or forms, and is little in accordance with the Peripatetic doctrines. —Vide also note 1 of the following page.
fn.597: As the commentator Shem-Tob observeth, that which the author saith here is nowhere to be found in the Metaphysics of Aristotle, but rather the contrary. Indeed, the one (τὸ ὄν) per se, unto which Aristotle assigneth four principal significations, which are: the continuous, the whole, the individual, and the universal (according as one considereth therein the indivisibility of motion or that of the idea), is inseparable from the very nature and quiddity of the thing which is one, and cannot be considered as an accident of the quiddity. The one is not in itself an essence, and it can exist only in a subject. Its proper character is to be indivisible and the first measure in every genus, and notably the measure of quantity; but, even as being (τὸ ὄν), with which it is confounded and identified, it applyeth to all the categories, and is not found particularly in one alone. The manifold is opposed to the one, as the divisible to the indivisible, and not as non-being to being; for the manifold is in being, as well as the one, and is attributed, like the latter, to all the categories. The one and the manifold in number, designating quantity alone, are abstractions and entirely distinct from being. See the details in the Metaphysics of Aristotle, book V, chap. 6, and book X, chap. 1 et seq. — Maimonides, who seeth in the one and the manifold naught but accidents distinct from being, hath further followed the opinion of Ibn-Sīnā, who, as Ibn-Roschd observeth, hath confounded the one of number with the absolute one: “A difficulty which may be found here,” saith Ibn-Roschd (loc. cit., book III), “is this: how, whilst admitting that the one of number belongeth to the category of quantity, can we subsequently admit that it is found in all the categories, and moreover that it is in the categories themselves, and not something which is accessory thereto? Wherefore Ibn-Sīnā hath thought that its substratum must be an accident which is found in all the categories.” “But it is not so; for the one in number is of another nature than other unities. Indeed, the numerical one is individuality, abstracted from that which is quantity and quality—I mean from that whereby the individual is an individual; for it is an individual only in the sense of the indivisible, and the mind abstracteth it from material things, limiteth it, and taketh it for something separate. The one in number, the numerical unity, is but a thing which the soul effecteth in individual beings, and without the soul there would be neither numerical unity nor number in general, contrary to that which obtaineth for the line and the surface, and, in general, for continuous quantity; wherefore number is, more than any other thing, pure from matter. Ibn-Sīnā hath confounded the nature of the one, the principle of number, with the absolute one, which embraceth all the categories, and since the one, the principle of number, is an accident, he hath admitted that the absolute one, which is the same thing as being, is also an accident.” Cf. R. Levi ben-Gerson, Mil’hamôth, book V, 3, chap. 12.
fn.607: Literally: know that to describe (or designate) God — may He be glorified and exalted! — by means of negations, is the true description (or manner of assigning attributes unto Him), which is affected by no improper expression (on تسامح , vide supra, page 235, note 1), and in which there is in no wise, nor in any manner whatsoever, a defect in respect of God; that is to say: the attributes expressed by negations are alone true, containing, within their terms, nothing which one need regard as an improper expression, and saying naught, in respect of God, which implieth an imperfection. — Already before Maimonides, the Jewish theologians, and notably those of Spain, had insisted upon this point and had established that one cannot express what God is, but only what He is not, and that the attributes which are commonly ascribed unto Him, far from having an affirmative sense, indicate nothing else than the exclusion of their contrary; by one, it is meant only that God is not manifold; by eternal, that He is not created, and so forth. Vide Bahya, Duties of the Hearts, bk. I, chap. 10; Judah ha-Levi, Khozari, bk. II, § 2; Abraham ben David, Emunah Ramah (The Sublime Faith), bk. II, 3rd foundation (p. 51 of the text, and p. 65 of the German translation by M. Simon Weil, Frankfort, 1852). The Arabian philosophers pronounce themselves in the same sense, and certain Muslim sects had made of negative attributes an essential point of their doctrine, as, e.g., the Dhirâriyya (vide Shahrastâni, Germ. transl., vol. I, p. 94). The Karaite Ahron ben Elijah, in his עץ חיים or Tree of Life (chap. LXXI), refutes the partisans of negative attributes. These latter believed they could support themselves by the opinion of Aristotle, whom Bahya cites expressly in this regard. Here follow the terms of the Arabic original of the treatise on the Duties of the Hearts: ולהדֹא קאל ארמטוטאלים אלמואלב מן צפאת אלכֹאלק תעאלי אצדק מן אלמוגֹכאת לאן כל מא יוגֹב לה מן אלצפאת לא תכֹלו פן צפאת אלגֹוהר או אלערץֹ וכֹאלק אלגֹוהר ואלערץֹ לא ילחקה פי דֹאתה וצף מן אוצאפהמא וכל מא ינפי ענה מן אלצפאת פהי צאדקה̈ לא מהאלה̈ “Wherefore Aristotle saith: The negative attributes of the Creator are more true than the affirmative; for all the attributes that one might assign Him affirmatively could only be attributes of substance or of accident, and the Creator of substance and of accident cannot have in His essence any of their attributes. But the attributes which are removed from Him (that is to say, the attributes expressed negatively) are indubitably true.” — This passage, which is cited also by Ibn-Falaquera (Moreh ha-Moreh, p. 29), is evidently apocryphal. It is true that Aristotle, in speaking of the first mover, very often expresseth himself by negative terms, such as: being immutable, separate from all that is sensible, which can have no extension, which is indivisible, etc. (Metaph., XII, 7 and passim); but he in no wise excludeth affirmative terms, and that which the doctrine of the Arabian philosophers possesseth of the absolute in this regard appeareth to be drawn from the Neoplatonic commentators and to be connected with the doctrines of Plotinus (cf. Ritter, Geschichte der Philosophie, vol. IV, p. 573 et seq.). St. Thomas in his turn, in saying that we cannot express ourselves concerning God save by the negative way, followed the Arabian philosophers, from whom he doubtless borrowed the term via remotionis (طريق النفي) . Vide Summa C. Gent., bk. I, chap. 14.
fn.637: This somewhat obscure passage hath been diversely interpreted, and the commentators appear greatly perplexed to indicate its precise meaning, as may be recognized in the varied explanations given by Shem-Tob and by Profiat Duran or Ephodi. The simplest sense, it seemeth to me, is this: One could not attribute to God that which, from our point of view, would be a perfection; for perfections, being ever certain capacities (ἕξεις), belong to one of the genera of the category of quality, and could not, consequently, be attributed to God, as resulteth from what the author hath said in chap. LII (p. 195), touching qualities. For a more ample explanation, the author addeth: and every capacity existeth not in everything (being) endowed with capacity; that is to say, that in created beings, capacities are somewhat accidental, being found not equally in all, and not being always in act where they are found. Capacities (ἕξεις), albeit more durable and more solid than dispositions (διαθέσεις), are nevertheless naught else than consolidated dispositions, and designate somewhat which hath been acquired and which hath not always existed in the being endowed therewith (cf. p. 195, note 2). As Aristotle himself saith, capacities are also dispositions; for those who are endowed with capacities are in some wise only disposed for these selfsame capacities (οί μὲν γὰρ ἕξεις ἔχοντες ϰαί διάϰεινταί γέ πως ϰατ’ αὐτά. Categ., chap. 8). Let us add thereto that capacities are often opposed the one to the other, and cannot exist together in the same subject. It resulteth from all this that, if one attributed to God all that which, in relation to us, is a perfection, one would attribute unto Him acquired capacities and even opposing capacities, two things equally inadmissible. — Moses of Narbonne, the most profound commentator of Maimonides, confessing the embarrassment which he had long experienced in explaining the words of the author, supposeth that this entire passage, beginning from these words: Thus it is clear unto thee, etc., relateth to a passage of the Metaphysics (book XII, chap. 9), where Aristotle saith that the intelligence perceiveth naught else than itself, being unable to be affected by anything outside of itself. Maimonides, in speaking here of all that must be denied of the supreme intelligence, or of God, would allude to this absolute negation, in God, of every perception which should not have for its object the divine intelligence itself. The latter hath its perfection in itself, and cannot be affected by anything. In denying that it perceiveth aught else than itself, one doth not attribute unto it any imperfection; for all perfections are capacities, but these capacities do not constitute perfection for every being endowed therewith. There be many privations which are preferable to capacities; for, as Aristotle saith in the passage indicated, to not see certain things is better than to see them (ϰαί γὰρ μὴ ὁρᾶν ἔνια ϰρεῖττον ἢ ὁρᾶν). Such is, in substance, the interpretation given to our passage by Moses of Narbonne; but we greatly doubt whether it be the true one and whether there be a real relation between the words of Maimonides and the said passage of Aristotle.
fn.743: The visible manifestation of the Divinity consisteth, according to the theologians, in a light which God causeth to appear in a place and which is a miraculous creation; it is this light which is called Schekhînâ (שכינה, majesty) or cabôd (כבוד, glory), and which appeareth in the place that God chooseth particularly to make His presence known. Saadia likewise speaketh of this created light which God caused to appear in the sanctuary to glorify that place (להגדיל המקום ההוא); vide Beliefs and Opinions, bk. II, chap. 8 (Berlin edit., fol. 33 a). Cf. Ahron ben-Eli, Tree of Life, ch. LXIII (Leipzig edit., p. 72). Speculations of this kind go back in general to the ancient Karaites, who took for guides the Muslim theologians of the sect of the Motazalites, and it was through the impulse of the Karaites that Saadia and other Rabbanites approached this manner of questions (vide infra, ch. LXXI). The Karaite Abu-’Ali (Jepheth), in his Arabic commentary upon Exodus (chap. 19, v. 20), speaketh at length of the manner in which the manifestation of God upon Sinai must be understood; one readeth there the following passage relative to the cabôd or the created light: וד׳לף אנה אמתחאל אן יבון אלכ׳אלק ג׳ל ועלא אלר׳י לא יוצף ולא חי ולא תחויה אלאמבנה̈ בל לא יג׳וז אן יקאל פיה אנה פי אלעאלם ולא כ׳ארג׳א ענה אד׳ הד׳א מן אוצאף אלמכ׳לוקין אלד׳ין תחתוי עליהם אלאמכגה̈ ותלזמגם אלאעראצ׳ ואד׳א כאן הד׳א הכד׳א פלא שך פי אן וירד יי ישיר בה אלי מכ׳לוק מחדוד וחצ׳רה̈ מוצ׳ע פי ראשׁ ההר “In truth, it is impossible to admit that it is here a question of the Creator, who can be neither qualified nor defined, and who could not be enclosed within space. Nay, more, one could not say of Him that He is in the world, nor that He is outside the world; for such qualifications would suit created things, which are enclosed in space and subject to accidents. This being so, there is no doubt that, by the words: And the Lord came down, etc., there is indicated a thing created and limited, and its local presence upon the summit of the mountain.” Cf. infra, p. 290, note 2. According to the opinion which Maimonides setteth forth elsewhere concerning miracles in general, one must see in the said created light, as well as in all that occurreth in a miraculous manner, the effect of the primitive will of God, who, from the moment of Creation, hath disposed things in such wise that, under certain given circumstances, there might be produced extraordinary phenomena which seem to us to depart from the general laws of nature. Thus, therefore, miracles are the results of certain physical dispositions established by God at the epoch of Creation, and not the effect of a momentary will; for there can arise no change in the divine will, which is eternal and immutable. Vide what the author saith in this regard in the last of the Eight Chapters serving as an introduction to the treatise Aboth (Porta Mosis of Pococke, p. 240), and cf. the IInd part of this work, towards the end of chap. XXIX. Vide also infra, chap. LXVI, p. 296, note 1.
fn.793: The author here addresses a subject which, as he himself states at the end of this chapter, can only be well understood by those familiar with Peripatetic philosophy, and particularly the part relating to the soul and its faculties. Without entering here into developments that would exceed the limits of a note, it will be necessary, for a better understanding of the author's reasoning, to briefly recall the Aristotelian theory of intelligence and the developments this theory received among the Arab philosophers whom our author took as guides. — In considering the various faculties of the soul enumerated by Aristotle, we notice a successive progression from the less perfect to the more perfect, such that each higher faculty supposes the lower faculty, whose action it renders more complete, and that one is to the other what energy or act is to potency, or what form is to matter. One can distinguish three main faculties of the soul: nutrition (τὸ θρεπτιϰόν sc. μόριον), to which the life of plants is limited; sensation (τὸ αἰσθητιϰόν), which belongs to all animals, and reason (τὸ διανοητιϰόν), which belongs to man alone (Treatise on the Soul, book II, chap. 2); the third faculty cannot exist without the second, nor the latter without the first. Nutrition has material things as its object; through this faculty, the animal assimilates external things themselves, whereas through sensation it receives only the forms of things, just as wax receives only the form of the seal, and not its matter. Reason, or thought, is to intelligible things what sensation is to sensible things; but through the senses we know only individuals or individual forms; we know that things are, but we do not know why they are; it is reason that recognizes general forms and causes. The soul, says Aristotle, that is to say, the intelligent part of the soul, is the place of forms (τόπος εἰδῶν). Required to dominate everything, reason has no particular bodily organ; it must be impassible, that is to say, not affected by external things, but capable of receiving the form of objects. These forms it does not possess at first in act, that is, in full reality, but only in potency (Ibid., book 3, chap. 4). Just as in all beings one distinguishes on the one hand matter, or what is in potency, and on the other hand form, or the cause that makes what is in potency pass into act, so it is necessary that these differences be found in the rational part of the soul or in the intelligence. Aristotle thus distinguishes two intellects, one passive (νοῦς παθητιϰός), the other active (νοῦς ποιητιϰός). The passive intellect holds the middle ground between sensation and imagination, on one hand, and the active intellect, on the other; it is the latter especially that is separate (from the lower faculties of the soul), impassible, unmixed with anything whatsoever, being in act by its very essence (ϰαὶ οὗτος ὁ νοῦς χωριστὸς ϰαὶ ἀπαθὴς ϰαὶ ἀμιγής, τῇ οὐσίᾳ ὢν ἐνεργείᾳ. Ibid., chap. 5). Aristotle does not tell us clearly where this active intellect comes from, nor how it is perceived by the passive intellect; but he seems to see in it something divine, which comes from without through the first mover. See the treatise on the Generation of Animals, book II, chap. 3: λείπεται δὲ τὸν νοῦν μόνον θύραθεν ἐπεισιέναι ϰαὶ θεῖον εἶναι ϰ. τ. λ.; cf. Trendelenburg, Arist. de Anima, page 496. It is by the aid of this active intellect that every individual intelligence accomplishes the work of thought, and, passing from potency to act, it appropriates the forms of things and identifies itself with them. These intelligible forms, the object of thought, are themselves thought; for the intellect in act cannot be affected by something outside of itself, and it must draw from within itself what it has as its object. The intellect, therefore, in its entelechy or in its full reality, thinks itself. See Aristotle, Metaphysics, book XII, chap. 7: αὑτὸν δὲ νοεῖ ὁ νοῦς ϰατὰ μετάληψιν τοῦ νοητοῦ νοητὸς γὰρ γίγνεται θιγγάνων ϰαὶ νοῶν ὥστε ταὐτὸν νοῦς ϰαὶ νοητόν. Cf. Treatise on the Soul, book III, at the end of chap. 4. Such is, in substance, Aristotle's theory; the obscurity that prevails in this theory, notably regarding the nature of the active intellect and its union with the passive intellect, has given rise, among commentators, to long discussions and the most diverse opinions, and the Arab philosophers, confounding here as elsewhere the theories of Aristotle with those of his Neoplatonic commentators, have elaborated, on the subject that concerns us, a new doctrine which subsequently spread among the scholastics. Here, in summary, is the theory of the Arab philosophers, who differ among themselves on several essential points. The speculative faculty or theoretical reason, the highest among the faculties of the rational soul (see above, page 210, note 1), receives the impression of forms isolated from matter, whether they be general forms that it abstracts from material and individual things, or immaterial and imperishable beings, which are in themselves abstract forms (as, for example, the separate intelligences). This faculty, called intellect (عقل) par excellence, develops gradually, passing through various degrees where the lower is to the higher what matter is to form, or what potency is to act. The Arab philosophers generally distinguish three degrees of development, or three intellects: 1st The hylic intellect or material intellect (العقل الهيولانى), which is the simple disposition that the intellect has to abstract forms; it is a simple potency that has not yet begun to pass into act, and which is called hylic because it can be compared to matter (ὕλη) disposed to receive form. This hylic intellect is the νοῦς παθητιϰός of Aristotle (العقل المنفعل) in all its abstraction. The opinions of the Arab philosophers are divided on the nature of the hylic intellect: some, invoking the authority of Alexander of Aphrodisias, see in it only a pure disposition (استعداد) attached to the other faculties of the soul, and which is perishable like them, and this opinion is adopted by Maimonides (see below, chap. LXX); others, taking Themistius as their guide, maintain that, since the passive or hylic intellect must, according to Aristotle, be unmixed (ἀμιγής) with the other faculties of the soul, it must be a disposition having for its substratum a substance separate from the other faculties; for, they say, if the intellect in potency were only a simple disposition attached to the other faculties of the soul, it would have for its substratum something belonging to another genus than itself; but what is disposed to perceive intelligible things can itself only be an intellect. Ibn-Roschd, recognizing on the one hand what is inadmissible in Alexander's opinion, also sees difficulties in admitting the other opinion, according to which there would be a separate and eternal substance whose being would consist only in a disposition and a simple potency (δύναμις); he therefore chooses a middle term, by combining the two opinions, as we have explained elsewhere (see the article Ibn-Roschd in the Dictionnaire des sciences philosophiques, Vol. III, pages 166 and 167). 2nd The intellect in act (العقل بالفعل); this is the intellect that has succeeded in abstracting form from matter, that is to say, which has succeeded in distinguishing, in individual things, that which constitutes their general form, or that by which a thing is what it is. 3rd The acquired intellect (العقل المستفاد); this is nothing other than the intellect in act having become in a sense the property of man, when intelligible forms are always present in his intelligence, and he can identify himself with them at any moment without making new efforts. Having arrived at this level, human intelligence always has as its object pure intelligible forms; its object is the knowledge of its own being and that of the immaterial beings outside of it, and it rises to the knowledge of the separate intelligences and of God. In this state, it becomes in a sense a substance entirely separate from the body (see below, at the end of chap. LXXII). Between the intellect in act and the acquired intellect, some Arab philosophers also place the intellect in capacity (العقل بالملكة); they seem to mean by this the intellect in act having become a capacity (ἕξις, cf. above, page 195, notes 1 and 2), and before it has actually reached the level of the acquired intellect (cf. the book Ta’rifât cited in Freytag's Dictionary, under the word عقل, and the Analysis of the philosophy of Ibn-Sînâ, in Shahrastânî, p. 418 of the Arabic text, and Vol. II, page 317, of the German translation). This is a subtle distinction, whose scope is not well understood, and which, it appears, has not been generally admitted; Ibn Falaquera, in enumerating the different intellects (see the Appendix to the Moreh ha-Moreh, at the beginning of chap. I, page 141), does not speak of the intellect in capacity (השכל בקנין). — Studies and philosophical speculation, although they are necessary for the development of the hylic intellect, would not be sufficient on their own to bring it to the levels of the intellect in act and the acquired intellect; like everything that is only in potency, the intellect needs, in order to pass into act or entelechy, a cause that is outside of itself, and this cause is the universal active intellect (العقل الفعال), the last among the intelligences of the spheres (see Part II of this work, chap. IV, and cf. Ibn-Sînâ, in Shahrastânî's work, page 426; German trans., Vol. II, p. 328). It is through the influence of this active intellect that the acquired intellect is formed, considered as its emanation (hence, in the Hebrew versions, השכל הנאצל, the emanated intellect), and which succeeds, in certain chosen men, in identifying itself completely with the universal active intellect (cf. above, page 277, note 3, and my article Ibn-Roschd, loc. cit., pages 167 and 169). — Various details of this theory, of which we thought it necessary to present the whole here, will be discussed in other places. It is understandable that its obscurity has given rise to numerous divergences of opinion; the hypotheses, sought as far as regions inaccessible to the human mind, left a free career for the imagination, and the most enlightened Arab philosophers could not fail to abandon here the true ground of philosophical speculation, to lose themselves in reveries. 'Not a single one,' says Ibn Falaquera, 'has a well-fixed opinion on this subject, and we often see the same author change his opinion and say in one work something entirely different from what he said in another.' See Moreh ha-Moreh, book II, chap. 25 (page 111).
fn.864: The Arabic text of this passage is quite obscure; here is an approximate word-for-word translation: And likewise they have proved, for these (other) things they have enumerated, that, being (in) a relation with God, they are with Him. The word ענדה (at his place or with him) does not refer to God, but to the heaven ’Arabôth, and it would have been more regular to construct the Arabic sentence thus: וכדֹלך אמתדלוא עלי אנ תלכ אלתי עדוהא הי ענדה ללה תעאלי (i.e., באנהא נסבֹה (בכונהא מנסובֹה. Instead of נסבֹה (نسبة) which most manuscripts contain, some have נסבת (נُסִבَتْ), and one of the Leiden manuscripts has מנסובֹה (منسوبة); these last two readings appear to have been substituted for the word נסבֹה to facilitate the understanding of the passage. The meaning is: that the doctors, to prove that the other things they have enumerated also exist in ’Arabôth, limit themselves to citing biblical passages where these things are directly attributed to God; for nothing emanates from God except through the mediation of ’Arabôth, which, as has been seen, is the instrument by which God governs the universe. Thus, for example, to prove that ’Arabôth contains treasures of life, these words of the Psalmist are cited: For with you is the source of life (Ps. 36:10); for the treasures of peace, this passage is cited: And he called it (the altar) The Eternal God of peace (Judges 6:24); for the treasures of blessing: He shall receive the blessing from the Lord (Ps. 24:5), and so on.
