Most of the manuscripts and the editio princeps have only this second translation, which Ibn Tibbon had placed in the margin, adding the following note found in some manuscripts: אמר שמואל בן חבון הלשון המוגה מחוץ אינו יוצא מלשון הערכי אך הוא יוצא מגוף הענין מלשון חגיגה והוא האמת בעצמו והוא שהעיר עליו באמרו והבן זה “Samuel Ibn Tibbon says: The rectified wording found on the outside does not correspond to the Arabic text, but arises from the subject itself contained in the text of ’Haghîghâ; it is the true meaning, and it is what the author indicated by saying: Understand this well.”
fn.880: The word kalam (كلام), which means word, discourse, also designates a science that formed among the Muslims as early as the 2nd century of the Hegira, and whose goal was to combat the doctrines of heterodox sects and later those of the philosophers, by using against its adversaries the weapons of dialectic and reasoning borrowed from philosophical schools. This science can be called dogmatics, or rational theology, and it has much analogy with Christian scholasticism. Kalam developed especially since the introduction of Peripatetic philosophy among the Arabs, and it will be seen further on (ch. LXXIII et seq.) what doctrines were established by this science and how they proceeded to demonstrate the truth of the principal religious dogmas, particularly those establishing the unity and immateriality of God and Creation. As for the name kalam, the Arabs themselves do not agree on its origin; according to some, this science was so named because it primarily discussed what was meant by the divine word or by the word (kalam) attributed to God (cf. below, p. 343, note 3); according to others, the word kalam is merely an imitation of the word mantiq (منطق), which also means speech, or discourse, and by which philosophers designated one of the principal branches of their doctrine, namely, logic. See Shahrastani, History of Religious and Philosophical Sects, Arabic text, p. 18 (German trans., vol. I, p. 26); cf. Pococke, Specimen hist. ar., p. 195. From the word kalam comes the verb takallam (تكلم), having the sense of professing kalam, and whose participle mutakallim, in the plural mutakallimun, designates the partisans of kalam. Having regard for the meaning of word that the word kalam possesses, the Hebrew translators called this science חכמת הדבר and designated the Mutakallimun under the name Medabberim (מדברים), which the Latin translators, in turn, rendered as loquentes. One may also see what I have said on kalam in the Dictionnaire des sciences philosophiques, vol. I, art. Arabes (pp. 169 and 174), and in my Notice on R. Saadia Gaon, p. 16 et seq. (Bible by M. Cahen, vol. IX, p. 88 et seq.). — The two Hebrew translators did not fully grasp the meaning that the word אלכלאם has in our passage, and they took it in its primitive sense of word or discourse; Ibn Tibbon translates: מדברי ענין היחוד, and Al-Harizi: מדבריהם בענין היחוד. Following the words we have just cited, one should read in Ibn Tibbon's version: ומה שנתלה בזה הענין, as found in the manuscripts and the editio princeps; in the other editions, it was erroneously put as: ומה שנתגלה מזה הענין.
fn.924: On the humors, see below, p. 366, note 4. — The spirits are subtle fluids which, according to the hypotheses of ancient naturalists, have their seat in various organs of the animal body and contribute to the manifestations of the soul's different faculties. The three types of spirit correspond to the three faculties of the soul admitted by the ancient physicians, which are the natural faculty, the vital faculty, and the psychic (or animal) faculty. See the Canon of Ibn Sina, book I, fen. 1, ch. 6 (Arabic text, p. 38; Latin version, vol. I, p. 76); cf. Maimonides, Eight Chapters, at the beginning of chapter I, and the IIIrd part of this work, toward the end of chapters XII and XLVI, where the author alludes to these three faculties. Here is how Maimonides himself, in one of his medical treatises, explains the theory of the spirits and their different types, according to the ancient physicians: הד׳ה אלתי תסמיהא אלאטבא ארואחא הי אבכ׳רה̈ לטיפה̈ מוז׳ודה פי ז׳סם אלחיואן מבדאהא ומעט׳ם מאדתהא מן אלהוא אלמסתנשק מן כ׳ארז׳ פבכ׳אר אלדם אלמוז׳וד פי אלכבד ופי אלאורדה̈ لا נאבתה̈ מנהא יסמי אלוח אלטביעיה̈ ובכ׳אר אלדם لا מוז׳וד פי אלקלב ואלשריאן יסמי אלוח אלחיואניה̈ ואלבכ׳אר אלמוז׳וד פי בטון لا דטאג ומא ינבעת׳ מנה פי מסאם لا אעצאב יסמי רוחא נפסאניה̈ ומבדא אלז׳מיע ואכת׳ר מאדתה מן אלהוא אלמסתנשק מן כ׳ארז׳ פאד׳א כאן הד׳א لا הוא עפנא או מנתנא או כדרא תגירת תלך لا ארואח כלהא וז׳רי אמרהא עלי כ׳לאף מא ינבגי ֗֗֗֗ וכלמא כאנת אלוח אלטף כאן תגירהא בתגיר אלהוא אכת׳ר פאלוח لا טביעי אגלט׳ מן אלוח لا חיואני ואלחיואני אגלט׳ מן אלנפסאני פענד תגיר אלהוא איסר תגיר יתגיר חאל אלנפסאני תגירא ישער בה ולד׳לך תז׳ד כת׳ירא מן אלנאס קד ישערו בנקץ אפעאלהם אלנפסאניה̈ ענד פסאד אלהוא אעני אן יחדת׳ להם בלאדה̈ פהם וקצור אדראך ונקצאן חפט׳ ואן כאנת אפעאלהם אלחיואניה̈ ואלטביעיה̈ לא ישער פיהא בתגיר 'What physicians call spirits are subtle vapors that exist in the body of the animal and which derive their origin and their principal matter from the air drawn from outside by respiration. The vapor of the blood existing in the liver and in the veins that originate from it is called the natural spirit or physical (φυσικὸν πνεῦμα); the vapor of the blood existing in the heart and in the arteries is called the vital spirit (ζωτικὸν πν.); finally, the vapor found in the cavities of the brain and that which spreads from it into the channels of the nerves is called animal spirit (ψυχικὸν πν.). The origin of all (these spirits) and their principal matter come (as we have said) from the air drawn in by respiration; if, therefore, this air is corrupted, or foul-smelling, or murky, all these spirits are altered and are no longer what they ought to be... The more subtle the spirit is, the more it is altered by the alteration of the air. Now, as the natural spirit is thicker than the vital spirit, and the latter thicker than the animal spirit, it follows that at the slightest alteration of the air, the animal spirit will undergo a perceptible alteration. This is why you will find many men in whom a weakening of the animal or psychic functions (that is, the functions depending on the animal spirits) is observed when the air is corrupted; I mean that it happens to them to have dull intelligence, difficult understanding, and a weakened memory, although no alteration is noticed in their vital and natural functions.' Cf. Galen, De Hippocr. et Plat. placitis, book VII, chapter 3, and above, p. 111, note 2. — The passage we have just cited is found at the beginning of book IV of the treatise titled في تدبير الصحة (On the Regimen of Health), which Maimonides composed at the request of Al-Malik al-Afdhal, son of Saladin, and whose Arabic original, copied in Hebrew characters, is in the Imperial Library (see Hebrew mss. of the old collection no. 412, fol. 107 a.b, and no. 411, fol. 57 b and 46 a). The Hebrew version of this treatise, by R. Moses Ibn Tibbon, was published in the collection titled כרם חמד, vol. III (Prague, 1838, in-8vo), p. 9 et seq. There also exists a Latin version of it which has been printed several times.
fn.1061: The verb جوّز signifies to allow to pass, and, figuratively, to judge admissible or permitted, and the word تجهيز, which is its verbal noun, is used by the Mutakallimun as a technical term to designate the famous proposition stating that everything the imagination can picture is also admissible (جائز) to the reason, that everything in the universe could be other than it is, and that nothing is impossible, provided that an idea of it can be formed. Cf. Maimonides, Eight Chapters, or Introduction to the treatise Aboth, ch. Ist (Porta Mosis of Pococke, p. 188).—One must truly be surprised to see an author of our day assert with confidence that not only are there very essential errors in the alleged enumeration that Maimonides provides here of the principles of the Mutakallimun, but that even what he calls their primary foundation—namely, that there is no certain knowledge of things, since the contrary can always exist and be thought in our understanding—is entirely erroneous and diametrically opposed to dogmatic doctrine (Schmölders, Essays, p. 135). The same author insinuates that Maimonides only knew the doctrines of the Mutakallimun through the false reports of their adversaries; but it follows from Maimonides' own declaration that he perfectly knew the doctrines in question, and here, as everywhere else, his assertions are based on a serious and thorough study of the most authentic sources; see the beginning of chapter LXXIV. It is sufficient, moreover, to read the Destruction of the Destruction of Ibn Rushd, which contains numerous details on the Mutakallimun, and where one finds all the propositions enumerated by Maimonides. These two illustrious men must have been at least as well informed as the more recent authors that Mr. Schmölders may have consulted. As for this Xth proposition, which Maimonides calls the basis of the science of Kalam, it is so essential to the system of the Mutakallimun that it is impossible to separate it from it. Ibn Rushd also returns to it on several occasions. We content ourselves with citing here a single passage, where Ibn Rushd (speaking of the principle of causality denied by the Mutakallimun, and notably by the Ash'arites, who see in all phenomena and in all actions that occur in the world the immediate intervention of the Creator) expresses himself thus: והניחו עם זה כל הנמצאות פעולות עוברות ולא יראו שיש בם סדר ולא ערך ולא חכמה גזר אותם טבע הנמצאות אבל האמינו שכל נמצא אפשר שיהיה בחלוף מה שהוא "They have, with this, posited as a principle that all existing things are admissible facts (and not necessary), and they do not admit that there is in them either order, or proportion, or wisdom, resulting from the nature of things. They believe, on the contrary, that everything that exists could be other than it is." See Destr. of the Destruction, IIIrd question (Hebrew trans., MS of the Oratory collection, no. 93, fol. 243 a). Cf. Moses of Narbonne, Commentary on the Moreh Nevukhim, Ist part, at the end of ch. LIII; Ibn Falaquera, Moreh ha-Moreh, I, chs. LXXIII and LXXIV (pp. 58 and 63); Ritter, Geschichte der Philosophie, vol. VII, p. 737.
fn.1269: On infinity in general, see Aristotle, Physics, book III, ch. 4-8; Metaph., book II, ch. 2; book XI, ch. 10. Aristotle shows in these various passages that, in nature, the infinitely great in actuality, that is to say infinite extension, is inadmissible, and he admits as infinite only the infinitely small or the infinite divisibility of space, which he designates (as well as the infinity of abstract number) as potential infinity. Consequently, the universe itself, which is the most extended body, is limited in space (see the treatise On the Heavens, book I, ch. 7, where Aristotle says in conclusion: ὅτι μὲν τοίνυν οὐκ ἐστὶ τὸ σῶμα τὸ τοῦ παντὸς ἄπειρον ἐκ τούτων φανερόν). The most general demonstration of this first proposition is given in the very definition of body; Aristotle observes that from a logical point of view (λογικῶς), the existence of an infinite body is inadmissible: for, if the idea one has of a body is to be limited by surfaces, there can be no unlimited body, whether intelligible or sensible (εἰ γάρ ἐστι σώματος λόγος τὸ ἐπιπέδῳ ὡρισμένον, οὐκ ἂν εἴη σῶμα ἄπειρον, οὔτε νοητὸν οὔτε αἰσθητόν. Physics, III, 5, Metaph., XI, 10). From a physical point of view, Aristotle shows that an infinite body could be neither composite nor simple: 1. If it were composite, the parts of the composition would be either infinite or finite; now it is evident that they could not be infinite, for the infinity of each necessarily excludes that of the others; but neither could they be finite, for they would be consumed by the infinite and would disappear completely before it. 2. Neither could an infinite body be simple; for none of the elements, each of which has its determined region, is infinite, and there exists no sensible body outside the elements that unites them all, as several physicists have believed.— Another physical proof (which is linked in a way to the logical proof) is this: "Every sensible body is in space. The species and differences of space are: up and down, front and back, right and left. These distinctions do not exist solely in relation to us and by position, but are grounded in the whole itself." However, they could not exist in the infinite." (See Physics, loc. cit. at the end of ch. 5). Ibn Sina and other authors, Arabic and Jewish, multiplied the demonstrations of the propositions enumerated by Maimonides. Abu Bakr Muhammad al-Tabrizi, who wrote a commentary on the twenty-five propositions, went into great detail to demonstrate their truth. This 1st proposition was demonstrated by the Arabs in several different ways. We shall cite here a demonstration borrowed from Ibn Sina: Let the magnitude supposed to be infinite be a line AB أ ج ب; we may suppose that this line extends to infinity on both sides or only on one side B. In the latter case, let us imagine that from the finite side a part AC is cut; we will then have two lines, AB and CB, each of which will be infinite on side B and finite on the other side. Now, if we apply point C to point A, one of two things will happen: either line CB will extend to infinity like line AB, and then we will have AB—AC=AB, which is impossible, for the part cannot be equal to the whole; or line CB will extend less than line AB, and then it will be finite on side B, which is contrary to the hypothesis. If line AB is supposed to be infinite on both sides, it can be cut at any point so as to make two lines, each of which will be infinite on one side and finite on the other, and the demonstration will be the same as the one just given. Cf. Shahrastani, p. 403 (German trans., vol. II, pp. 295 and 296). — We cannot reproduce the proofs alleged for each of the propositions enumerated here by Maimonides, and we must limit ourselves to indicating the places from which our author drew these various propositions. As will be seen, they are not all borrowed from Aristotle, and several are taken from the works of Ibn Sina, which, as we have already stated elsewhere, are the principal source from which Maimonides drew his knowledge of Peripatetic doctrines. On this first proposition and the following two, see also the 1st part of this work, ch. LXXIII, 11th proposition, and the notes we have appended there (vol. I, pp. 413 and 414).
fn.1281: This proposition, stated in too concise a manner, has been found obscure, and when taken in an absolute sense, has met with objections (see the commentary of Moses of Narbonne). This is how it should be understood: Anything that does not have within itself the principle of its motion, but to which an accidental motion is imparted by an external cause that can cease to exist, will necessarily be at rest when that cause ceases, as, for example, a passenger on a ship, who is moved only because he is accidentally in a moving thing that can stop moving (cf. Aristotle, On the Soul, Book I, chap. 3, § 2). What proves that Maimonides understands this proposition in this way is that further on, at the beginning of chap. I, in demonstrating that the first mover cannot be considered the soul of the celestial sphere, he applies this VIIIth proposition to the human soul, which is moved accidentally with the body by an external cause, either by seeking what is suitable for it or by fleeing what is contrary to it. Therefore, the Arab commentator Al-Tabrizi is wrong to object to this proposition of Maimonides that there are certain motions which, although accidental, are nonetheless perpetual, such as, for example, the diurnal motion from east to west imparted by the ninth sphere to the eight lower spheres, which is contrary to their own essential motion from west to east; or as the circular motion of the sphere of fire and the other elements, whose essential motion is in a straight line (cf. Vol. I of this work, pp. 357-359). It is evident that these accidental motions, having as their cause an essential and perpetual motion, must themselves be perpetual. The proposition in question here appears to relate to a passage from the treatise On the Heavens (Book I, end of chap. 2), where Aristotle establishes that above the four elements which, by their nature, have a straight-line motion, there is a simple substance of another nature that has circular motion. Now, he observes, this motion must be inherent to the nature of this substance; for it would be astonishing and entirely unreasonable if this motion, which alone is continuous and eternal, could be contrary to nature, since generally what is contrary to nature is quickly destroyed: Eἰ δὲ παρὰ φύσιν φέρεται τά φερόμενα ϰύϰλῳ τὴν περὶξ φοράν, θαυμαστὸν ϰαὶ παντελῶς ἀλογον τὸ μόνέν εἶναι συνεχῆ τάυτην τὴν ϰὶνησιν ϰαι ἀίδιον, οὖσαν παρὰ, φύσιν · φαίνεται γὰρ ἔν γε τοῖς ἀλλοις τάχιστα φθειρόμενα τὰ παρὰ φύσιν. The Arabic version, which rendered the words contrary to nature (παρὰ φύσιν) as accidental, better explains the terms of Maimonides' proposition. Here is how the passage we have just cited was paraphrased in Ibn Rushd's Middle Commentary on De Caelo et Mundo, Book I, Summa IV, Demonstration 5 (Hebrew version): והוא שזאת התנועה הסבובית שהיא סביב האמצע לא המלט משתהיה לזה הגשם טבעית או מקרית ושקר הוא שתהיה מקרית בי התנועה המקרית אי אפשר שתמצא תמידית אין תכלית לה ושהצעת זה יוצאה מכל הקש כי אԃנחנו רואים הדברים המקריים כלים אובדים.
fn.1293: In this proposition, the author establishes that local motion (certainly that which, in the preceding proposition, was designated as the only one that is continuous) is prior according to nature to all other motions and changes; and by prior according to nature one must understand, in accordance with Aristotle's definition (Metaph., book V, chap. 11), that which can be without other things being, but without which other things cannot be. The terms of this proposition are drawn from Aristotle's Physics, book VIII, chap. 7 (Cf. book VII, chap. 2), although the author, it seems to me, does not strictly follow the reasoning of the Stagirite. It was seen above, p. 6, note 2, that according to Aristotle, the idea of motion applies to the categories of quantity, quality, and place. Now, he says, of these three kinds of motion, that of place is necessarily the first: for it is impossible for there to be growth without there having first been transformation. Transformation is change into what is opposite; but when there is transformation, there must be something that transforms and which causes, for example, that which is hot in potentiality to become hot in act. Now it is evident that the mobile [agent] of this transformation is sometimes closer and sometimes further from the thing to be transformed, and that the transformation cannot take place without local motion; the latter, consequently, is the first among the motions. Further on, Aristotle establishes by other proofs that local motion, although it is the last to develop in the individual beings of this world, is the first in the universe and even precedes the birth (γένεσις) of all things, which is followed by transformation and growth (μετὰ γὰρ τὸ γενέσθαι πρῶτον ἀλλοίωσις ϰαὶ αὔξησɩς; Phys., VIII, 7, page 260 b, line 32). One might initially find it surprising that Maimonides places transformation before generation and corruption; however, it appears that our author considers transformation from a more general perspective—that is, not only in relation to the category of quality, as in the IVth proposition, but also in relation to generation, which is itself in some sense a transformation of matter by form, a transformation effected by an agent more or less remote, which needs to draw closer to the matter to be transformed. It is also in this sense that Averroes explains the passage in the Physics. See the Works of Aristotle with the Commentaries of Averroes, folio ed., vol. IV, fol. 180 c: «Deinde dicit: Et manifestum est quod dispositio motoris tunc non currit eodem modo, sed forte quandoque erit propinquior alterato et quandoque remotior, etc. Id est, et quia primum alterans, quod non alteratur, non alterat semper, sed quandoque, necesse est ut non habeat se cum alterato in eadem dispositione, sed quandoque appropinquetur ei, et alteret, et quandoque removeatur, et non alteret: et propinquitas, et distantia non est, nisi per translationem: ergo translatio præcedit naturaliter alterationem, scilicet quod, cum utraque fuerit in actu: deinde alterans alteravit, postquam non alterabat: necesse est ut alterum moveatur in loco aut alterans, aut alteratum, aut utrumque. Si autem alterum fuerit generatum, aut utrumque, et posuerimus hoc esse causam ejus, quod quandoque alterat, et quandoque non, manifestabitur quod translatio debet prœcedere eodem modo, cum alteratio etiam prœcedat generationem; generatio enim aut est alteratio aut sequitur alterationem.»
fn.1374: This demonstration appears to be based on a passage from Aristotle's Physics, which may be summarized as follows: Three things may be considered in motion: the thing moved, the mover, and that by which the latter moves. That which is moved does not necessarily communicate motion; that which serves as an instrument or intermediary communicates motion at the same time as it receives it; finally, that which moves without being an instrument or intermediary is itself immobile. Now, since we see (in the universe), on the one hand, that which is moved without having within itself the principle of motion—that is, without moving anything else—and on the other hand, that which is simultaneously moved by another and the mover of another, it is reasonable, if not necessary, to admit a third thing which moves without being moved. See Phys., Book VIII, ch. 5 (Bekker ed., p. 256 b): τρία γὰρ ἀνάγκη εἶναι, τό τε κινουμένον, καὶ τὸ κινοῦν, καὶ τὸ ᾧ κινεῖ. κ. τ. λ. In the Metaphysics, Book XII, chap. VII, Aristotle summarizes himself in these terms: ἔστι τοίνυν τι καὶ ὃ κινεῖ, ἐπεὶ δὲ τὸ κινούμενον καὶ κινοῦν, καὶ μέσοντοίνυν ἐστί τι ὃ οὐ κινούμενον κινεῖ, ἀΐδιον καὶ οὐσία καὶ ἐνέργεια οὖσα. Alexander of Aphrodisias explained this passage in nearly the same terms used by Maimonides in this second demonstration; and it is evidently from Alexander that our author borrowed his argumentation, as well as the proposition he places at the head as having been stated by Aristotle himself. Alexander's explanation was cited by Averroes in his large commentary on the Metaphysics. We reproduce it from the Latin version of this commentary (folio ed., f. 149 verso): "Alexander said: This is the reason why [there is] some mover [which] is not moved, and it is stated briefly and as a reminder of what was said in the last [book] of the Physics. And it is founded upon two propositions, one of which is that every composite of two things, of which one can exist by itself, the other will also possibly exist by itself, unless the composition be of substance and accident; for example, because hydromel is composed of water and honey, and honey is found by itself, it is therefore necessary that water be found by itself. And, because we find something moved and moving as if composed of a mover and a moved, and we find something moved by itself and not moving, it is manifest that it is necessary for there to be some mover and not moved." "This mover, therefore, is immune from potentiality, and exists in no matter." As for the proposition attributed by Maimonides to Aristotle, some commentators have objected that, in what is composed of substance and accident, one cannot imagine the existence of the accident alone, although evidently the substance can exist alone. This objection fails due to the express condition set by Alexander: nisi compositio sit substantiæ et accidentis. Maimonides, in copying Alexander, perhaps omitted this condition through inadvertence.
fn.1429: As we have said, the author, in this enumeration of the Intelligences, followed Ibn Sina, who, besides the supreme Intelligence, or God, admits ten Intelligences, the first of which, emanating directly from God (cf. below, ch. XXII), is that of the sphere of diurnal motion, which surrounds the entire universe, and the last of which, emanating from the Intelligence of the lunar sphere, is the active intellect. See Avicennæ opera, Metaph., IX, loc. cit.: «Si autem circuli planetarum fuerint sic quod principium motus circulorum uniuscujus-que planetarum sit virtus fluens a planeta, tunc non erit longe quin separata sint secundum numerum planetarum, non secundum numerum circulorum; et tune eorum numerus est decem post primum (that is to say, God). Primum autem eorum est Intelligentia quæ non movetur, cujus est movere sphæram corporis ultimi (that is to say, the diurnal sphere). Deinde id quod sequitur est quod movet sphæram fixarum. Deinde sequitur quod movet sphæram Saturni. Simililer est quousque pervenitur ad Intelligentiam a qua fluit super nostras animas; et hæc est Intelligentia mundi terreni, et vocamus eam Intelligentiam agentem.» Ibn Rushd, identifying the sphere of diurnal motion with that of the fixed stars, admits only eight spheres. See Epitome in libros metaph., tract. IV (fol. 182, col. a): «Tandem apud me est remotum quod inveniatur orbis nonus sine stellis; nam orbis est stellarum gratia, quæ sunt nobilior pars ejus…. Orbis autem qui movet motum magnum est nobilior cæteris or-bibus; quapropter non videtur nobis quod sit sine stellis, immo apud me est impossibile.» According to this, there would be in total only nine separate Intelligences, the last of which, as in Ibn Sina's theory, is the active intellect. This, therefore, according to the theory of the Arabs, is in a close relationship with the Intelligence of the lunar sphere, from which it emanates directly, but with which it must not be identified. — [In my Mélanges de philosophie juive et arabe, at the beginning of page 332 (cf. also pp. 165 and 448, and Vol. I of this work, p. 277, and note 3), I expressed myself on this matter in an inaccurate manner, and I should have said: «From the last of these separate Intelligences, which presides over the movement of the sphere closest to us (that of the moon), the active intellect emanates, etc.»] — The passage from Ibn Rushd (loc. cit., fol. 184, col. d), which has often been cited to show that, according to this author, the active intellect is itself the mover of the lunar sphere (see Ritter, Geschichte der philosophie, Vol. VIII, p. 148), is thus phrased in the Hebrew version: והשכל הפועל הוא יםודר מםוף אלו המניעים במדרגה ונניחו מניע גלגל הירח. The word מםוף seems to me to be an inaccurate translation of the Arabic words من آخر , and it should be translated as follows: «The active intellect emanates from the last of these movers in rank (i.e., from that one of these movers which by its rank is the last), which we assume to be the mover of the sphere of the moon.» To leave no doubt in this regard, I shall cite here a passage from Moses of Narbonne's commentary on Al-Ghazali's Maqāṣid, towards the end of the IInd part, or of the Metaph., where the theory of the spheres and their intelligences is set forth (according to Ibn Sina) (see Hebrew MS. of the Oratory collection, no. 93, fol. 179 a): ואמנם בן רשד ובל הפילוםופים מודים שהשבל הפועל בלתי מניע לגלגל רק שהוא עשירי לשבלים הנפרדים לפי בן רשד והשבל הראשון בבלל והוא עשירי לשבלים העלולים מבלתי מנוה במחוייב המציאות לפי אבוחמד. «Ibn Rushd and all the philosophers agree that the active intellect is not the mover of any celestial sphere. But, according to Ibn Rushd, it is the tenth of the separate Intelligences, if the first Intelligence (or God) is also included; whereas, according to Abu Hamid (al-Ghazali), it is the tenth of the caused Intelligences, without counting the Necessary Being (i.e., the first absolute cause, or God).»—Cf. Albert the Great, De Causis et processu universitatis, bk. I, tract IV, ch. 8 (Opp. Vol. V, p. 562 a): “Moreover, after the Intelligence of the lunar sphere and the lunar sphere itself, which (as Aristotle says) is in some way terrestrial, there is an Intelligence that illuminates above the sphere of the active and passive [elements], whose light it diffuses in the active and passive, which illuminates above the souls of men, and whose power is conceived in the seeds of generated and passive things.”
fn.1527: The four astronomical terms used here by the author are borrowed from Ptolemy's theories on the motion of the planets. By اختلاف, one designates the anomaly or the inequality of a celestial body; the word رجوع designates the apparent retrogradation (προνήγησις) of the five planets, as opposed to their direct motion (ὑπόλειψις) designated in Arabic by the word استقامة, rectitude; finally, by إقامة, is meant what Ptolemy calls the station (στηριγμός) of these same planets, that is, the position where the motion of the celestial body appears to stop. Cf. Almagest, book XII, chap. I. In the Arabic version of the Almagest (Hebrew ms. of the Imperial Library, old collection, no. 441), the terms προνήγησις and ὑπόλειψις are rendered more accurately, the first by تقدّم, moving forward, the second by تأخر, remaining behind. Later, the Arabs substituted the first of these two terms with رجوع, retrogradation, and the second with استقامة, rectitude. Indeed, since the periodic motion of the planets occurs from west to east, the planet, when it appears to retrograde, i.e., when it appears less advanced in longitude, is forward in relation to the diurnal motion from east to west; the more advanced it is in longitude in relation to the periodic motion, the further behind it is in relation to the diurnal motion. Delambre, to explain the two terms used by Ptolemy, expresses himself thus (Notes on the Almagest, following the edition by Abbé Halma, vol. II, p. 16): "One says of a star that precedes another at the meridian, which passes it before him, which moves at its head, that it is προηγούμενος; of a star that passes after him, that it is ἑπόμενος." "But the one that passes first at the meridian is less advanced in longitude; the one following it, ἑπόμενος, which remains behind, ὑπολειπόμενος, is on the contrary more advanced in longitude; thus a star is προηγούμενος when its longitude decreases and it retrogrades; προνήγησις in the language of the Greeks, therefore, corresponds to retrogradation; it is the same motion considered in relation to two different points, just as, in the theory of curves, one may at will place negative abscissas either to the right or left of the center indifferently." — The terms retrogradation and rectitude introduced by the Arabs are also found in the Epitome of the Almagest by Ibn Aflah, book VIII, where the Hebrew version, which alone we can consult, uses for the former the word חזרה, and for the latter the word יושר. It is probably in the work of Ibn Aflah that Maimonides took these terms (cf. above, p. 81).
fn.1598: It can be seen that, according to Maimonides, the difference between Plato and Aristotle is this: that the latter admits not only the eternity of prime matter, but also that of motion and time; whereas Plato, while admitting the eternity of matter and chaos, nevertheless believes that the world, as it is, had a beginning, that the heavens were, like sublunary things, produced from chaos, and that consequently motion and time had a beginning. It is in this sense that Plato's opinion was generally interpreted by the Arabs and the Scholastics, and it is in this sense also that one of the most learned adherents of the new Platonic school of Italy expresses himself. This is how Leone Ebreo speaks on this question (Dialoghi di amore, III, Venice edition, 1572, fol. 145 et seq.): «Concedendo tutti gli huomini che’l sommo Dio genitore et opifice del mondo sia eterno, senza alcun principio temporale, son divisi nella produttion del mondo, se è ab eterno, o da qualche tempo in quà. Molti dei filosofi tengono essere prodotto ab eterno da Dio, e non havere mai havuto principio temporale, così come esso Dio non l’ha mai havuto, et di questa opinione è il grande Aristolile, et tutti i peripatetici… Ma gli fideli, et tutti quelli che credono la sacra legge di Moise, tengono che’l mondo fusse non ab eterno produtto, anzi di nulla creato in principio temporale, et ancora alcuni dei filosofi par que sentino questo; per quali è il divino Platone, che nel Timeo pone il mondo essere fatto et genito da Dio, produtto del chaos, che è la materia confusa, del quale le cose sono generate… È ben vero che lui fa il chaos, di che le cose sono fatte, eterno, cioè eternalmente produtto da Dio, laquai cosa non tengono gli fideli; perche loro tengono che fino all’ hora della creatione solo Dio fusse in essere senza mondo, et senza chaos, et che l’omnipotentia di Dio di nulla tutte le cose in principio di tempo habbia produtto, che in effetto non par già chiaramente in Moise, che’l ponga materia coeterna a Dio.— Sono adunque tre opinioni nella produttione del mondo da Dio: la prima d’Aristotile, che tutto il mondo fue produtto ab eterno; la seconda di Platone, che solamente la materia, o chaos, fue produtto ab eterno, ma il mondo in principio di tempo; et la terza delli fideli, che tutto sia produtto di nulla in principio di tempo.» — But one recognizes from our passage that in the time of Maimonides, as in all eras, opinions were divided on the true sense of Plato's doctrine; and, indeed, Plato's poetic language and the mythical veil under which he often presents his doctrines only too well justify this divergence of opinions. While several of the oldest Platonists, and later the Neoplatonists, claimed that Plato had admitted, like Aristotle, the eternity of the world, others on the contrary (notably some Christians, such as Clement of Alexandria) went so far as to maintain that Plato had professed the doctrine of creation ex nihilo, considering God to be the author not only of the order of the world, but of matter itself. The same divergence is still observed among the scholars of our day. On this subject, see Zeller, Die Philosophie der Griechen, vol. II, p. 508 et seq. (2nd ed. Tübingen, 1859), and Henri Martin, Études sur le Timée de Platon, vol. II, p. 179 et seq. This latter scholar, after a thorough examination of the texts, arrives at conclusions that agree with the opinion of Maimonides and Leone Ebreo, namely that, according to the Timaeus, 1. God did not create the prime matter of bodies, that is, the indeterminate substance; 2. he did not even create secondary matter, that is, eternal chaos; 3. he produced the order of the world, but not from all eternity. — The distinction between incorporeal prime matter and corporeal chaos is of no interest to us here, any more than the question of how Plato understood prime matter and in what way his doctrine, in this regard, differs from that of Aristotle. Suffice it to say that Plato admits an eternal principle opposed to the idea, as blind necessity is to reason, non-being to being, the variable and the multiple to the permanent and the absolute one. But this is not the ὕλη of Aristotle, that being in potentiality which necessarily calls for form to become being in actuality; for, according to Plato, it is with consciousness and freedom, and not by necessity, that the idea realizes itself in the indeterminate substratum, which it causes to pass from confusion to order. The term ὕλη is itself unknown to Plato, although Aristotle uses this term when speaking of his master's doctrine. This confused and indeterminate substance that the idea orders and in which it manifests itself is called by Plato: that which receives the imprint (τὸ ἐϰμαγεῖον), that in which things are born, the place, space, etc.; it is also presented as the mother or the receptacle and the nurse of all generation; and Plato himself says (Timaeus, p. 49 a) that it is a species quite obscure and very difficult to understand. Cf. Ritter, Geschichte der Philosophie, vol. II, p. 347 et seq.; Brandis, Handbuch der Geschichte der griechisch-römischen Philosophie, vol. II, A, p. 297 et seq.; Zeller, l. c., p. 457 et seq.; Henri Martin, l. c., vol. I, p. 16 et seq.
fn.2473: Maimonides, in approaching his oblique explanation of Ezekiel's vision, in which he seems to find the principal cosmological doctrines of the Arab Peripatetics, deems it necessary to indicate first what is to be understood by the four faces attributed to each of the four 'hayyôth, or animal figures (Ezekiel 1:10), in which he sees the celestial spheres, reduced to four: that of the moon, that of the sun, that of the five other planets, and that of the fixed stars. See Part IIe of this work at the end of Chap. IX, and Chap. X, p. 82 ff. The prophet attributes to the 'hayyôth a human face, a lion's face, an ox's face, and an eagle's face, making them the representatives of what is most noble among the different species of animals. According to our author, the three faces of irrational animals are also human faces; but he does not tell us why he insists on this, and he leaves us to guess what he means by the symbol of the four faces. We believe that the author is alluding to the four causes of the movement of the spheres, indicated according to him by the four wings (v. 6), and of which he spoke in Chaps. IV and X of Part IIe; these are: the shape of the sphere, i.e., its sphericity, its soul, its intellect by which it conceives, and the separate Intelligence, the object of its desire (see Vol. II, p. 88). In the sublunary world, man is the only being in whom these four causes of movement are reflected; man alone possesses a soul endowed with conception and an intellect, which are set in motion by the desire to unite with the separate intelligence, i.e., with the universal active intellect; and from this point of view, man's movement has nothing in common with that of irrational animals and can only be compared to the circular movement of the spheres. Cf. Vol. II, Chap. IV, p. 52. The explanation we have just given is indicated by Samuel ibn Tibbon in his treatise Yikkawou ha-maïm, Chap. XI, p. 47: וענין הנפש והשכל רמז אליו בשרמז שכלם יש להם פני אדם וכל הפנים פני אדם. We omit other explanations given by Moses of Narbonne and Ephodi, which relate to what the author said about the four forces emanating from the four spheres and acting on the four elements (Vol. II, Chap. X, p. 89); these explanations offer no interest for science or its history, and we shall limit ourselves to what is strictly necessary for the understanding of Maimonides' obscure words. — Furthermore, the entire interpretation that Maimonides gives here, in veiled terms, of Ezekiel's vision, is based, as we have said, on Peripatetic cosmology; but if the prophet, as is probable, used astronomical symbols, he could only have borrowed them from the astronomy of his time, and one would have to look to Chaldean science for an explanation. Isaac Abravanel completely overturned Maimonides' interpretation by rightly observing that, if this were the meaning of Ezekiel's vision, there would be no reason to make such a mystery of it, since it would only concern a science taught in all schools of philosophy and familiar to scholars of all faiths. See Abravanel's second Preface to the book of Ezekiel and his commentary on Chap. I of the same book; cf. also Abravanel's commentary on various parts of the Moreh Nevukhim, Book IIe, fol. 48 ff.
fn.3123: As I have already noted in my Réflexions sur le culte des anciens Hébreux, p. 2 (published in Vol. IV of Mr. Cahen's Bible), Maimonides, like many other Arabic authors of his time, understands the word צאבה̈ or Sabians to refer to all pagan peoples in general. The books from which he drew his knowledge of pagan cults, and which he will discuss further on, led him to believe that these cults were generally based on astrolatry. Consequently, in Maimonides' language, religion of the Sabians signifies the same thing as paganism. In the Quran (II, 59; v, 73; XXII, 17), the Sabians (الصابيون) are mentioned alongside Jews and Christians as a religious community possessing revealed books and having a share in the afterlife. It is generally agreed that the Sabians of the Quran are the Mandaeans or Christians of Saint John, who, because of their frequent ablutions, are called in Syriac צביעיין (or צביין, according to the pronunciation of the Mandaeans, who omit the ע), that is to say, the Baptists. See E. Castelli Lexicon-syriacum seorsim typis describi curavit atque sua adnotata adjecit, J. D. Michaëlis, p. 749. Arabic authors, starting from the time of Caliph Al-Ma'mun, also give the name Sabians to the pagans of Harran and some other cities of Mesopotamia, who are completely different from the Sabians of the Quran, which has given rise to great confusion. Vain efforts have been made to find the etymology of the name Sabians applied to pagans. The most successful conjecture is that of Pococke (Specimen hist. ar., p. 139), who derives this name from the Hebrew word צבא, army, and who sees in it an allusion to the worship of the stars called צבא השמים, host of heaven; but this etymology is no more plausible than any of the others. We now know that in reality there is only one kind of Sabians, namely the Mandaeans, but that the pagans of Harran, threatened with extermination by Caliph Al-Ma'mun, usurped around the year 830 of the Christian era, on the advice of a Muslim doctor, the name of Sabians, and claimed to be the sect mentioned under this name in the Quran and recommended by the prophet to the protection of Muslims. This fact is reported in the Kitab Al-Fihrist by Muhammad ibn Ishaq al-Nadim (see the extract from this book given by Mr. de Hammer in the Journal Asiatique, September-October 1841, p. 254 et seq.). It had already been published by Hottinger, Historia Orientalis, p. 169, and, following him, by Spencer, De legibus Hebræorum ritualibus, Bk. II, ch. I, sect. 2 (p. 241 of the Cambridge edition, 1685, folio). It is especially in the work published on the Sabians by Mr. Chwolson that the fact in question was brought to light and supported by numerous proofs. The author shows how the name Sabians, applied in the Quran only to the Mandaeans and used in this sense by Arabic authors until the time of Al-Ma'mun, later served to designate the Harranians as well and ended, in the 6th century of the Hijra, by being used in the general sense of Pagans. See Die Ssabier und der Ssabismus (2 vols. large 8vo, St. Petersburg, 1856), Vol. I, ch. VI, p. 139 et seq., and the entire ch. VIII. This excellent work contains numerous details on the religion of the Harranians, which can clarify several facts reported by Maimonides in this chapter and in those following, where our author aims to explain a large part of the ceremonial practices prescribed by Moses by means of the superstitious customs of the Sabians or pagans that the Mosaic laws tended to abolish.
fn.3146: Instead of אלשמס, one of the two Leiden MSS, No. 18, reads אלשאם; similarly, the version of Ibn Tibbon has השאם (in the editions תשאם), which, as is known, is the name of Syria, including Palestine. Al-Harizi had the same reading, for he translates the word in question as ארץ הצבי, land of beauty, an expression which among the rabbis designates Palestine. However, it would be absurd to think here of Palestine or Syria, since it is stated immediately thereafter that the country in question is near India. The reading אקלים אלשמם, found in nearly all the Arabic MSS, is moreover confirmed by other passages of the Nabatean Agriculture, where there is also mention of plants brought by Adam from southern regions to Babylon. See, for example, the passage cited by Mr. Chwolson in his Memoir on Tammuz: Ueber Tammuz und die Menschenverehrung bei den alten Babyloniern, in the Russian collection entitled "Acts of the Imperial University of St. Petersburg" for the year 1859 (St. Petersburg, 8vo, 1860), p. 167. Mr. Chwolson translates the words אקלים אלשמם as Sonnenland or "land of the sun" (ibid., p. 175), and he says in note 2 that this country, according to other passages, was situated to the south of India proper (that is, the Punjab), from which it was separated by a desert. The land of the sun would therefore be, according to Mr. Chwolson, the Deccan. It is true that the word إقليم, clima, is often used by the Arabs in the sense of region or country; but no ancient or modern geographer knows the designation "land of the sun." I believe, therefore, that the word אקלים has here its ordinary sense of clima, and that the 2nd clima is meant, which contains a large part of India. It is known that Ptolemy and the Arabic geographers divide the inhabited part of the earth, from South to North, into seven zones called climata. According to the Sabians, as will be seen below, each clima is under the influence and direction of one of the seven planets. Cf. the Hebrew work Shevile Emunah by R. Meir al-Dabi, II, 2 (Amsterdam edition, fol. 19 a): כשהבורא ברא העולם נתן כח בכוכבים למשול בארץ ולהנהיגה וחלק הארצות לשבעה כוכבי לכת וגו׳ "When the Creator created the world, he placed in the stars a force by which they were to dominate the earth and govern it, and he distributed the countries among the seven planets, etc." Yaqut, in the Introduction to his great geographical Dictionary entitled معجم البلدان, speaking of the seven climata, indicates the respective planet that dominates each clima, according to the opinion of the Persians and the Greeks, and he says that the 2nd clima is, according to the Persians, under the influence of Jupiter (المشترى), and according to the Greeks (الروم), under that of the sun (الشمس); the 4th clima, on the contrary, is, according to the Persians, under the influence of the sun, and according to the Greeks, under that of Jupiter (Arabic MSS of the Imperial Library, supplement, No. 886, at the beginning). I believe, therefore, that the words of our passage למא כׄרגׄ מן אקלים אלשמס אלמגׄאור ללהנד must be understood thus: "when he emerged from the region of the clima of the sun (that is, the 2nd clima) which is near India." One cannot think here of the 4th clima, no region of which is near India. We should recall that India is also, according to Muslim tradition, the place of Adam's first residence after his fall. Driven from paradise, according to this tradition, he fell upon the mountain of Serandib, which is the island of Ceylon. See d’Herbelot, Bibliothèque orientale, p. 55 b.
